P.name: William Thompson Jr.
P.place: Six years old at Jeter in 1940. Born at Jeter, Choctaw County; died in Hugo.
kv: Age 6, at home with parents, four siblings, and the Pisachubbe grandparents, Jeter
Age 16, living with his parents, brothers and sisters and his Pisachubbe grandmother at Jeter, Choctaw Co., Okla.; his father was a farmer working his own land
Hugo schools in 1947; still enrolled in 1950, age 16
5 Dec 1956: William Thompson Jr., Speer, and Mary Ellen Hulsey, Hugo
body: William “Junior” Thompson Jr. grew up on his parents’ farm at Jeter in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1940 he was six, sharing the household with Simon and Frances Thompson, his brothers and sisters, and his Pisachubbe grandparents.

At sixteen, in 1950, he was still at home in Jeter and still in school, as he had been at Hugo a few years before. His father worked his own farm, and his Pisachubbe grandmother still lived with them; Junior grew up in a house where children and elders lived side by side.
By December 1956 Junior was living out at Speer, and that month he and Mary Ellen Hulsey of Hugo took out their marriage license, joining the Thompson and Hulsey branches of the family.

He stayed close to Hugo all his life. He was living there when his father Simon died in 1990 and when his sister Ethel Hamill died in 2002, the same year he lost Mary Ellen. He died on 17 February 2007.

He and Mary Ellen share one granite marker at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County, under a scroll lettered THOMPSON: "Mary E. / Aug. 22, 1938 / Nov. 4, 2002" on one side and "William, Jr. / Mar. 14, 1934 / Feb. 17, 2007" on the other.
He died on Saturday, 17 February 2007, at 72, and Miller & Miller of Hugo held his funeral three days later.

P.title: The baby of the 1899 enrollment
P.hook: Enrolled as a Choctaw at seven and a half months, a 19-year-old farmer in 1918, and in 1940 the head of a house with three generations under its roof.
body: Simon was born on 4 May 1899, and by autumn he was the youngest person in the family's Choctaw enrollment, only 7½ months old. His mother Betsy and his grandmother Emeline Tims, who had been the midwife at his birth, both swore statements so that he could be enrolled, and he received his own land allotment near his parents'.
When he registered for the World War I draft on 12 September 1918 he was 19, a farmer working for his father at Corinne, of medium height and build, with black hair and brown eyes.

By 1940 he and Frances owned a $400 farm at Jeter, in a county where nearly three of every four farmers were tenants, and were raising five children: Ethel 13, Leonard 10, Junior 6, Bernice 3 and a baby daughter. Frances's parents Robert and Lizzie Pisachubbe lived with them, with Robert and Lizzie's orphaned niece and nephews, Frances's double first cousins. Simon had three years of schooling and had worked all 52 weeks of 1939. When he died in 1990 he was remembered as a retired farmer and a Methodist who had lived in the Hugo area for 64 years, and he left 17 grandchildren and 20 great-grandchildren. He and Frances, who married in 1925, are buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, also called Choctaw Cemetery.

The timing was close. His mother's family applied for enrollment on 1 May 1899, three days before the 4 May birth date given in the sworn statements, so his own statement was added afterward. His enrollment was recorded on 19 December 1899; the statement was returned for correction and the corrected one filed on 20 February 1900. A later account gives 14 May 1899 as his birthday, but the statements, made much closer to the event, say 4 May. At four he received a 160-acre homestead, the northeast quarter of Section 11, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, and on 6 December 1907 he was issued a citizenship certificate at Hugo.

His wife's parents had been enrolled that same year: her mother Lizzie, a 7-year-old daughter of Legion and Molsey Austin of Fowlerville, and her father Robert Pisachubbe, who was 11 and lived at Goodland. The two families lived forty miles apart in 1899 and joined in 1925 when Simon married their daughter Frances.

P.src: U.S. Censuses (Ancestry); Dawes Cards 1363 and 1580; Newborn Card 1203; Act of Congress approved 26 April 1906 (birth affidavit forms); 1930 and 1940 U.S. censuses; 1950 U.S. census, Jeter, Choctaw Co., Okla. (dwelling 421); Act of April 26, 1906, ch. 1876, section 2, 34 Stat. 137, https://govtrackus.s3.amazonaws.com/legislink/pdf/stat/34/STATUTE-34-Pg136a.pdf; National Archives, Enrollment Cards for the Five Civilized Tribes, M1186, https://www.archives.gov/files/research/microfilm/m1186.pdf; 1930, 1940, 1950 U.S. censuses as previously cited for Frances and Simon Thompson.
body: Frances Pisachubbe was born in 1907 to Robert Pisachubbe and Lizzie Austin. Her parents came from Choctaw families who had been enrolled together in 1899: Robert with his mother Eunice, and Lizzie with her parents Legion and Molsey.

Enrollment in the Choctaw Nation was bound by dates set in law. An act approved on 26 April 1906 allowed a limited application period for children who were minors living on 4 March 1906. Frances was born the following year, which helps explain why she was never enrolled herself.

Frances married Simon Thompson in 1925. In 1930 the couple shared a household at Jeter, Oklahoma, with her parents. Ten years later Simon and Frances were on a farm they owned, valued at $400, with five children in the household.

In 1950 the family was still at Jeter. Frances, then about 42, lived with Simon, five children and her mother Lizzie Pisachubbe, so that the household still held the older generation of the Austin and Pisachubbe families. Frances died in 1979 and is buried at Long Creek Cemetery.
P.title: Frances Thompson and the family at Jeter
P.hook: Frances and Simon built a household at Jeter that included three generations of the family.
P.note: The 1906 enrollment cutoff concerns eligibility under the act; it should not be described as determining modern tribal citizenship. Census details and family relationships follow the existing sourced profiles. The family tree gives her birth as about 1909 (from the 1940 census age) and her death as April 1978; the dates here follow her grave marker, which reads 1907 and 1979.

P.title: Judge and Choctaw senator
P.hook: Spencer Academy, Mount Hermon and Roanoke College, then county clerk, legislator and judge in Cedar County.
body: Joseph was a full-blood Choctaw, born in Cedar County in December 1861, two miles west of High Hill church. His parents were John and Betsy Thompson, both dead by 1899; his son Joel said John died when Joseph was nine.

In 1891, while he was still a young man, it was written of Joseph that he was educated at Spencer Academy and at 'Mount Harmon Institute, Northfield' (D. L. Moody's Mount Hermon School for boys in Massachusetts), and finished at Roanoke College in Salem, Virginia, where he stayed until 1886. Joel remembered it in a different order: three years at Roanoke, then three years at a college in Massachusetts studying law.

In 1885, at 24, he was farming 20 acres of his own in Cedar County, with a horse, six cattle and 30 hogs. He began as a schoolteacher, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889, and the next year was elected to the lower house of the Choctaw Council, 'one of the youngest members of the legislature.' Joel said he later served as County Judge of Cedar County, holding court at Sulphur Springs near present-day Rattan, and about six years as a Senator.

He married Betsy Tims in 1889. They started in a one-room log house. In 1901 he built a big white house with two front rooms, a wide hall, an L-shaped kitchen and dining room, and lots of porches, 300 yards from High Hill Methodist Church. He sat on the school board, raised an orphan boy named Wister Davis, and had a son named Peter Pitchlyn Thompson.

By 1910 Joseph, 48, was farming his own allotment free of mortgage in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. He named Mississippi as the birthplace of both his parents, which fits a family that came west on the Removal. Living with them was 19-year-old "David Wister," the orphan the family raised, whom Joel remembered as Wister Davis. Their nearest neighbors included Henry W. Thompson and two Tims households, one headed by James Tims, very likely Betsy's brother Jimmie. Henry, despite the shared surname, was the son of Simon and Lucy Thompson, while Joseph's parents were John and Betsy.

Joel said his father was 'second of nine children' and that the 1901 house stood on a farm that raised 'plenty of hogs' and 'lots to eat.' He added that his father 'was always interested in the government of his people.' The county officers Joel named were Robert S. Frazier, High Sheriff, and Noah Frazier, Clerk, with James Brown Tims as a representative in the Council.

After statehood Joseph still had business with Washington over his land. He filed a petition on 27 August 1908 from Fort Towson, and again on 10 September 1915 from Corinne; the Secretary of the Interior approved removal of restrictions on his land on 28 March 1916. In 1903 he had gone to Atoka to pick out the allotments for his wife and children.

The Mount Hermon part of the story fits the school's own history: by 16 October 1883, as the boys moved into the new brick cottages, "four Indians had arrived as pupils from the Indian Territory." They were not named, so no one can say for certain that Joseph was among them.

quotes.t: He could have sentenced criminals to be shot, but I don't know whether he did or not. I do know that he had lots of them whipped at the old whipping post on the Sulphur Springs Court ground.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: Dad could go out early any morning and kill a deer within a quarter of a mile of the house… We boys would listen for his gun to fire, then we would run to get the deer and bring it in.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: He was always interested in the government of his people.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

P.note: The 1891 sketch heads him 'Joseph B. Thompson,' probably a printer's error; everything else in it fits. It also calls his father 'Rev. John Thompson,' a Presbyterian minister in Cedar County for twenty years, which does not fit Joel's memory that John died about 1870. Roanoke College had about 35 Choctaw students between 1876 and 1896, but Joseph does not appear in the 1881-82 catalog; that fits the sketch, which has him at Mount Hermon first, but the 1882-86 catalogs have not been seen. Joseph's terms as judge and senator have not yet been found in Choctaw Nation records. A Find a Grave memorial gives his birth as 1862 and has him at High Hill, but his burial there is unverified; his death in 1927 comes from family files. The orphan he raised is 'Wister Davis' in Joel's interview.

P.title: Betsy Tims and the Pine Ridge school
P.hook: A Choctaw woman of Towson County, and the girl from the Pine Ridge school.
body: Betsy and her family applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899, and the Secretary of the Interior approved it on 12 December 1902. She was enrolled as Choctaw by Blood and received a land allotment that included a 160-acre homestead north of Doaksville.

She went to school at the old Pine Ridge mission near Doaksville, founded by the missionary Cyrus Kingsbury in the 1830s, where the Choctaw Nation's Chuwahla Female Seminary opened in 1844. Her son Joel said her family was "quite prominent in public affairs." Her brother James Brown "Jimmie" Tims served in the Choctaw Council as a Representative.

She was 'Miss Betsey Ann Tims' before her marriage, and her first child, Alexander, was born in March 1890. Her parents were Vinson and Emeline Tims; her brothers and sisters included James, Mitchell, John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie and Calvin.

Her son Joel added a correction to the family story about her schooling: he believed it 'was after the Mission school had been suspended and that it was very likely neighborhood schools which she attended, schools held at the old Academy site.' Whatever the building, she remembered it. Her father, whose name was written 'Vincent Tims,' was dead by 1899, and her mother, 'Emiline Tims,' was still living in Towson County.

Joel named seven children who lived to be grown: Alex B., Joel J., Peter Pitchlyn, Simon W., Joseph W., Jincy and Marietta. A daughter, Ella, died in May 1899, and another child, born later, was enrolled under the Act of 3 March 1905. In March 1920 her own petition from Corinne to lift restrictions on her land was approved.

quotes.t: She always told us, as we passed that old Pine Ridge school site, "There is where I went to school."
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: Mother attended Pine Ridge Academy, a school for girls.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

P.title: The Pisachubbes of Speer and Jeter
P.hook: A full-blood Choctaw farmer who registered for both world wars and lived with his daughter's family in 1940.
body: Robert was a full-blood Choctaw, enrolled at age 11 along with his widowed mother Eunice. In 1917 he was 28, married with one child, farming for himself at Speer; the registrar wrote "Indian" for race, black eyes and black hair, medium height, slender. In 1942, at 53, he registered again for the WWII draft of older men, still at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.
In 1940 he and Lizzie were living with their daughter Frances and son-in-law Simon Thompson at Jeter, with their niece Alice and nephews Eli and Edward: twelve people in the house.

The three young relatives were orphans. Robert's older brother, William Harrison Pisachubbe, had married Lizzie's younger sister Adline Austin, so two Pisachubbe brothers had married two Austin sisters, and their children were double first cousins of Frances. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and William Harrison in 1937.

When William Harrison died in 1937, his relative Judge T. W. Hunter gave the Hugo Daily News a family history: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi with the first group of Choctaw exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. His funeral was held at the family home near the Long Creek school house, with Choctaw Presbyterian minister Rev. Logan Harlin officiating.
The name Pisachubbe ends the way many Choctaw war-names do; its exact meaning is not recorded.

His land stayed in the family. In 1979 a court decree of heirship for his daughter Frances Pisachubbe Thompson covered Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section as his allotment, and an order in his own estate followed in 1982.

His father was the late Joseph Pisachubbe, and Robert was 11 when the family was enrolled in 1899; he was approved as Choctaw by Blood on 12 December 1902. His wife Lizzie came from the Austin family of Fowlerville; her brother James, who died in 1899 before enrollment, was struck from the rolls by the Department on 16 September 1904.

P.name: Lizzie (Austin) Pisachubbe

imgs.cap: Dawes Card 1363: Legion and Molsey Austin's family, Towson County, 1899

P.place: Full-blood Choctaw of Fowlerville (now Valliant). The records disagree on exactly when her baby brother James died in 1899. Her younger sister Adline married Robert's brother William Harrison Pisachubbe. Age 42 in 1940, living with her daughter Frances at Jeter; buried at Long Creek Cemetery.
body: Lizzie Austin was enrolled as a Choctaw on 21 May 1899, when her father Legion applied for the family at Fowlerville in Towson County. She was written down as 7 years old, full-blood, the daughter of Legion and Molsey; by the time the enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902 she was put at 10. Her age moved around in later years too: 42 in 1940, 58 in 1950. The earlier ages point to a birth about 1892, and the 1950 age agrees.

Her small family was already losing members. Her brother James, born 15 November 1898, was enrolled with a note that he died in April 1899, and a younger sister arrived the next year: Adline, born 5 August 1900 and enrolled in June 1901. The two girls grew up to marry brothers. Adline married William Harrison Pisachubbe, and Lizzie married his younger brother Robert, the son of the widow Eunice Pisachubbe of Goodland. The children of the two marriages were double first cousins.

In the summer of 1915 Lizzie, listed as "Lizzie Pisachubbee, nee Austin," applied to have federal restrictions lifted from her land. By 1917 Robert was 28, married with a child, and farming for himself at Speer. In 1920 Lizzie and Robert owned their farm in Jeter Township with their daughter Frances, Robert's widowed mother Eunice, and a young cousin.

The house grew crowded as the old generation died. Her mother Molsey died in 1924 and Eunice in 1927. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and her husband William Harrison in 1937, leaving their children, and by 1940 Lizzie and Robert shared one household at Jeter with Frances, her husband Simon Thompson and their five children, and Alice, Eli and Edward, the orphaned niece and nephews: twelve people. Frances had married Simon in 1925, and so the Austin and Pisachubbe families were joined with Joseph and Betsy Thompson's line. Lizzie was still in that household in 1950 and died in 1964. She is buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, the cemetery where Simon and Frances lie.

P.name: Vinson Tims

imgs.cap: Vinson W. Tims marker, High Hill
1896 Choctaw census, Towson County: Vinson, Emeline and family, with brother Edward's household below

P.place: Lived north of Doaksville in the High Hill neighborhood, where he and Emeline farmed. Brother of Judge Edward Ward Tims. His marker at High Hill is a cenotaph bearing only his name; a memorial there gives 1891 as the year of his death, though he seems still to have been living in 1896. His grandson said he was buried at the old home place.
P.title: The old place north of Doaksville
P.hook: Vinson Tims farmed north of Doaksville, where his daughter Betsy married Joseph Thompson in 1889 and where he is said to be buried.
body: Vinson W. Tims was born in 1838, the elder son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims. He and Emeline farmed in the High Hill neighborhood of Towson County, 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' on land later called the Charley Blankenship place. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie (Mrs. James Wilson) and Calvin.

Betsy married Joseph Thompson at that house in 1889. Joel remembered his grandparents as 'buried there at the old place,' which fits the marker at High Hill, a cenotaph that carries only his name and no dates.

The memorial at High Hill Cemetery gives his years as 1838 to 25 October 1891, but a Choctaw census of 1896 seems to show Vinson still living with Emeline and their family in Towson County, and in 1899 Betsy's father, written 'Vincent Tims,' was said to be dead. So when he died is unsettled: 1891 on the memorial, or after 1896 if the 1896 entry is his.

A memoir of his son Robert, printed in 1944 in the minutes of the Methodist Indian Mission, calls Robert "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." So the family's own church used "Vincent" for him where the High Hill marker says "Vinson."

Vinson never enrolled, because he was gone by 1899, but his name survives in his children's enrollments. In 1899 clerks wrote it as "Vinson W. Tims" for James B., "Vincent Tims" for Betsy, Robert and Willie, and "Benson Tims" for Mitchell. In every case he was marked dead and placed in Towson County, where the family lived.
kv: Towson Co., about 4 miles north and a little west of Doaksville
James, Mitchell, Betsy, John, Robert, Willie, Rosie, Calvin
P.note: The date of Vinson's death is in conflict: 25 October 1891 on a Find a Grave memorial and in a local history, against a listing in the 1896 census. The marker is a cenotaph, and his grandson said he was buried at the old home place.

P.name: Emeline (Steadman) Tims
P.title: The midwife of Doaksville
P.hook: Daughter of John Steadman and O-we-na, she was the midwife at the birth of her grandson Simon.
body: Emeline was born on 26 January 1842. She was enrolled as Choctaw by Blood, one-quarter blood, along with her sons Johnny and Calvin. Her father, John Steadman, was not a Choctaw citizen, and her mother, O-we-na, had died in Towson County; nothing states John's race or O-we-na's ancestry.

She and Vinson farmed in the High Hill neighborhood north of Doaksville. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie and Calvin, and several of them later lived around Spencerville.

When her grandson Simon was born on 4 May 1899, Emeline attended as the midwife. On 17 October 1899 she swore before a notary at Doaksville that "there was born to her on said date a male child… said to have been named Simon Thompson," the affidavit that put Simon on the rolls. She died on 16 March 1918 and is buried at High Hill Cemetery.

Her grandson Joel did not remember her maiden name ('Grandmother Tims first name was Emmaline'), so the name Steadman comes from her enrollment, not from family memory. Joel placed her home 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' in Towson County, 'known as the Charley Blankenship place now.' A local history says six or seven miles. Betsy and Joseph were married there in 1889.

Emeline and Vinson are 'buried there at the old place,' Joel said. Her memorial at High Hill Cemetery gives her dates, while a Tims headstone photographed in a local history is captioned Hampton Chapel Cemetery and may belong to a child. Her husband's marker at High Hill is a cenotaph.

Her son, the Rev. Robert James Tims, was remembered in a 1944 Methodist memoir as born six miles north of Fort Towson, "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." Another son, James Brown Tims, was born on 25 June 1864 at Doaksville.

Her name appears in the enrollment of nearly all her children: her sons James B., Robert, Mitchell and Willie and her daughters Rosanna and Betsy each named "Emiline Tims" as mother. The men's father is written variously as "Vinson W. Tims," "Vincent Tims" and "Benson Tims," always dead by 1899. In the 1900s she kept being asked to vouch for births.

Her daughter Rosanna was first enrolled with her mother on 24 April 1899 and in October 1900 was moved to the enrollment of her husband James Wilson; the notary who sorted out the name wrote that Rosanna's "mother name is Emaline Times." Emeline swore as midwife to the birth of Rosanna's son (23 March 1903) and, signing as "midwife" on 29 April 1905, of Betsy's son Joseph W. (5 March 1903), swore with Rosanna to the birth of Rosanna's daughter Candace (16 June 1905), and swore with Mildred to the birth of Mitchell's son Vincenta (1904; the Commission acknowledged the affidavits in April 1905).

P.name: Eunice (Gardner) Pisachubbe

imgs.cap: Dawes Card 1580, Eunice is line 1
Choctaw County court petition in the estate of Eunice Pisachubbe, Roll No. 4465: her sons Robert and William, her only heirs, ask approval of a full-blood deed. It records her death on 19 May 1927.

P.place: Full-blood Choctaw of Goodland, Kiamitia County, the Presbyterian mission settlement whose school survives as Goodland Academy. A widow in 1899 raising her sons William Harrison and Robert and a ward, Edward Pisachubbe, son of Simpson and Sallie. Daughter of Jackson and Viney Gardner of Blue County.
body: After Eunice died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. Pisachubbe, "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," petitioned the Choctaw County court to approve the sale of her allotment of about 159 acres for $1,200. As full-blood Choctaw land, it could not be sold without a judge's approval. Joseph, their father, had died long before her, and she never remarried.

When Eunice was enrolled at Goodland in Kiamitia County on 10 May 1899, she was 49, full-blood, the daughter of Jackson and Viney Gardner, both dead, of Blue County. Her sons William H., 16 (on the 1896 roll as "William Harrison"), and Robert, 11, were enrolled with her, their father, "Joseph Pisachubbe," dead. Also with them was not a son but Edward Pisachubbe, 17, her ward, whose own dead parents were Simpson and Sallie Pisachubbe of Jackson County, and who was already the husband of Frances Byington.

In 1896 Eunice, Robert and Edward had been counted together as one household in Kiamitia County. William was not with them; he had been listed separately as a student at Armstrong Academy, and a finding in 1911 held that he had been enrolled twice. All four were approved by the Secretary of the Interior on 12 December 1902.

William's son Colbert was enrolled as a newborn in 1906. To settle the question of William's double enrollment, testimony was taken in 1911 from four witnesses, and the Commissioner's letter of 1 August 1911 lists them: William H. Pisachubbe, Eunice Pisachubbe, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter.

Eunice’s land lay in Section 29 of Township 5 South, Range 17 East, less two strips for the St. Louis and San Francisco Railway’s right of way: 10.80 acres from one tract and .01 acre from another, leaving 159.19 acres. Robert and William asked the court to approve a $1,200 deed to L. C. Hudgens; whether the court approved it is not known.

P.name: Joseph Pisachubbe
P.place: Kiamitia County, Choctaw Nation. Dead by May 1899, when his sons William Harrison and Robert were enrolled. A family remembrance places their ancestors’ arrival from Mississippi in 1832 and settlement near Fort Coffee, established in 1834.
P.note: His parents are given in trees as Pisachubbe, also called Wilson, and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, but the link is not proven. The Nancy on Dawes Card 1278 was listed as 69 in 1899; her age alone neither proves nor rules out the proposed relationship.
body: Joseph Pisachubbe is hard to find. When his widow Eunice enrolled the family at Goodland in Kiamitia County on 10 May 1899, the clerk entered his name as the father of her sons William H., 16, and Robert, 11, with the single word "Dead" beside it. He left no enrollment of his own. His sons were born about 1883 and 1888, so he was alive into the late 1880s. Eunice, Robert and their ward Edward Pisachubbe were counted together in 1896, and he was not with them; that alone does not say when he died.

Eunice's widowhood is nearly all that remains of him. When she died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. petitioned the Choctaw County court as "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," and said that he died long before her and that she never remarried. The 159-acre allotment she asked to sell lay in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section where Robert's own allotment lies.

The only account of where the family came from was given at William Harrison's death in 1937 by his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi in 1832 with the first group of Choctaw exiles and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. The date has to be read with care. Fort Coffee was established on the Arkansas River only in June 1834, so the family's "in 1832" and "at Fort Coffee" describe the neighborhood by the later landmark; by 1899 they were in Kiamitia County, where a Presbyterian mission had worked at Goodland since 1848. No one says whether Joseph himself was born in Mississippi or among the first children born in the new Nation.

His own parents are unknown. Some family trees give them as a man called Pisachubbe or Wilson and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, but the Nancy of that name enrolled in 1899 was 69, born about 1830, and her age alone neither establishes nor rules out a mother-and-son relationship; nothing links her to Joseph. A "Case Pisachubbi" and a Sarah Pisachubbi also appear among the Choctaw enrolled, but nothing connects either to Joseph. What his descendants can be certain of is the name, which they carry through Robert and Lizzie to Frances Thompson, and which the clerks spelled Pisachubbe, Pisachubbee and Pisachubbi from one document to the next.

P.hook: Dead by 1899, he left two sons, William Harrison and Robert, and a name his descendants still carry.

P.name: John & Betsy Thompson
P.place: Full-blood Choctaw of Cedar County, both dead by 1899. Joel said John died when Joseph was nine and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy, and that his grandmother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and had not taken an English one.
P.src: Dawes Card 1283; WPA interview #7392 (Joel J. Thompson, 1937); Dawes Card 1283. Dawes Card 1283; 1910 U.S. Census, Wilson Twp, Choctaw Co.; H. F. O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891), p. 162; Spencer Academy NRHP nomination (NRIS 75001562).
body: When Joseph P. Thompson was enrolled at Doaksville in Cedar County on 1 May 1899, he gave his parents as "John Thompson" and "Betsy Thompson," both dead, both of Cedar County. Joseph's wife shared his mother's first name, and both women were Betsy. Joseph was born in December 1861, the year the Choctaw Nation sided with the Confederacy, and in 1910 he named Mississippi as the birthplace of both his parents.

His son Joel, interviewed in Hugo in 1937, remembered the rest. Joseph was the second of nine children. John died when Joseph was nine, about 1870, and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy. Spencer, which had closed in 1861, reopened in 1871, and Joseph, who had lost his father the year before, was of school age during its reopened years; he was educated at Spencer, and from there he went east to Roanoke College in Virginia.

Betsy's side was a harder subject. Joel said his father's mother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and never took a white man's name, which fits a pattern seen elsewhere in this family: surnames such as Thompson, Austin and Gardner came into use among the Choctaw after the 1830s, often borrowed from the given name of a respected white man, while others, like Pisachubbe and Ata-sa-ha-bi, kept their Choctaw names to the end.

The neighborhood that marked their lives was High Hill, where the Methodist church stood two miles east of their son's birthplace; Joseph later built his white house 300 yards from it, and Emeline Tims, his mother-in-law, is buried in its cemetery. Henry W. Thompson, who was enrolled the same day, was not their son: his parents were Simon and Lucy. The names of Joseph's eight brothers and sisters are unknown.
kv: Dawes Card 1283, line 1: "John Thompson" (dead, Cedar) and "Betsy Thompson" (dead, Cedar)
P.title: John and Betsy Thompson, Joseph's parents
P.hook: Two names, and a grandson's memory of a burial, are all that survive of the parents of Judge Joseph Thompson.

P.name: Legion Austin

imgs.cap: Dawes Card 1363: Legion Austin on line 1, Molsey Austin, their children and their parents’ names
Legion Austin's affidavit for his son James, born 15 November 1898, sworn at Fowlerville in May 1899 with Leonidas Willis as neighbor-witness

P.place: Full blood, once written down as "Legend Austin." Son of Ata-sa-ha-bi and Lotima of Towson County. In 1899 he gave his age as 33, but in November 1902 he testified he was "about fifty," and he had a grown daughter, Viny, born about 1879 to an earlier wife, Betsy. He also raised his nephew Nicholas Greenwood.
body: Legion Austin, 33, a full-blood Choctaw of Towson County, lived near Fowlerville. His father was Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County. His wife Molsey's parents, Brazil and Siney of Red River, were also dead.
Fowlerville's post office was established on 7 July 1894 and renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902.

Legion applied for enrollment on 21 May 1899 for his household at Fowlerville. In the end it counted five people: Legion, Molsey, their daughter Lizzie, a son James, whose date of death is told two ways, and a baby daughter Adline, born on 5 August 1900. Legion himself wrote to the Commission from Garvin in October 1900 asking for a blank application for an infant child; the Commission sent it on 9 October. The baby was enrolled on 4 June 1901, as a Commission letter of 5 June 1901 to William Swink at Fowlerville records: "Adline Austin, the infant daughter of Leageon and Muley Austin, born August 5, 1900," the clerk's spellings of Legion and Molsey.

James was recorded as having died in April 1899, with proof of death filed, and his enrollment was canceled in 1904. Yet the birth statement signed by Legion and his neighbor Leonidas Willis on 2 May 1899 still carries the printed words that the child was then living. Which date is right, no one can say.

In 1896 the family had been counted in Towson County, where the clerk wrote his name as "Legend Austin." The Commission approved Legion, Molsey, Lizzie and Adline on 12 December 1902. By then Legion's age was put at 36, three years more than the 33 given in 1899, and neither agrees with his own testimony in November 1902 that he was "about fifty."

He signed by mark. For the statement about his infant son James, sworn at Fowlerville in early May 1899, the clerk crossed out the form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" and wrote "Father" above it, and Legion, "33 years of age and a citizen by blood," swore as the husband of Molsey that the boy was born 15 November 1898. The man who vouched for the birth was a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who also signed with a mark and is written in as "a Neighbor," not a physician. Nobody named a doctor or midwife for that birth.

P.name: Molsey Austin
P.place: Full blood. Daughter of Brazil and Siney of Red River County.
body: On 19 April 1901, Molsey Austin gave a sworn statement about the birth of her daughter Adline, who was born on 5 August 1900 to Molsey and her husband Legion Austin. The family's post office was Fowlerville, Indian Territory, and both parents were citizens of the Choctaw Nation.

Below Molsey's statement stands a second one, made by Sinie Hall, the midwife who attended the birth. Both women signed by mark. J. R. Moore and Sallie Johnson witnessed the marks, and William Swink signed as notary. Together they preserve a mother's account and the name of the woman who helped at the birth.

Molsey's parents were Brazil and Siney of Red River County, and her children were Lizzie, James, who died in April 1899, and Adline. The name Siney belonged both to Molsey's mother and, in a similar form, to the midwife, but no one can say whether the two women were related.

The clerks spelled the family's names in several ways, including “Mulcy” for Molsey and “Leageon” for Legion. A later land list gives her as “Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin,” which suggests she later carried the name Pisachubbi.

P.name: Vincent B. Tims
P.title: Witness to the Treaty of Doaksville
P.hook: His name is on the 1837 treaty, and his trading firm fed Chickasaw families arriving from Mississippi.
body: On 17 January 1837, "at Doaksville, near Fort Towson, in the Choctaw country," the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations signed the treaty that let the Chickasaws settle inside the Choctaw Nation. The witness list reads: Wm. Armstrong, Henry R. Carter, Josiah S. Doak, Vincent B. Tims, Daniel McCurtain (U.S. Interpreter)… followed by the marks of the three Choctaw district chiefs.

Born in South Carolina (family accounts say Chester County), Vincent was a trader and the partner of Josiah Doak, whose trading post gave Doaksville its name; a missionary later remembered the town's founders as "Josiah Doak and Vinson Brown Tims, an Irishman." Doak & Tims held the army contracts of 1838 and 1839 to feed Chickasaw emigrants arriving at Doaksville, at 13 cents a ration, and handled the annuity payments that drew crowds to Doaksville. The partnership was dissolved by public notice in 1844.

On 29 May 1847 he bought the Dancing Rabbit Creek treaty allotment of Henry Graves, "son of Chief Netachachie," one of the three district chiefs whose marks appear on the 1837 treaty. That December "Jos. R. Berthelet and Vincent B. Tims of the Choctaw Nation" were invited within the bar at the Red River Raft Convention, which pressed Congress to clear the great logjam that blocked steamboats on the Red River.

He and his full-blood Choctaw wife stayed at Doaksville the rest of their lives. Family accounts say Vincent died at Doaksville in June 1864, while Confederate troops held Fort Towson a mile away, but he was still signing letters as the Confederate postmaster there on 9 September and 1 November 1864.

The trader's origins, in the one local history that traces him, are modest: 'Born in South Carolina, V.B. Tims is said to be of Irish descent.' He came to the Doaksville area with Josiah Doak in the early 1830s. In March 1843 he ran an office there for letters to the Agent for Claims, and in February 1844 the partnership with Doak was dissolved 'by mutual agreement,' after which he kept the business on his own. One of the firm’s unpaid store accounts, for 1840 to 1844, was still being pursued in 1848 and reached the Supreme Court of Texas in 1849.

Three of his children are known by name: Vinson W. (born 1838), Edward Ward (born 1842) and a daughter, Phoebe, who died before final enrollment. His great-grandson Joel Thompson said that 'Venson Brown Tims' was the first postmaster at Doaksville and that Edward succeeded him on his death. Edward was appointed postmaster on 24 October 1887, and a 'V. B. Tims' had been appointed on 17 May 1871, seven years after the family date of Vincent's death. Local history says that in 1861 he was 'designated' to be Indian Agent for the Choctaws had the Confederacy won, but only one local history says so.

William Gardner, a Choctaw merchant born in 1830, was said in 1891 to have opened his own store at Hamilton, in Blue County, "after he had been to work for E. B. Tims, the sutler at Doaksville." The initials are printed "E. B." rather than "V. B.," but the trade and the town point to the Doaksville trader, so this was probably Vincent.

Two more glimpses show him as a man of business. In December 1845 a New Orleans commission house named "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation" among its references in a newspaper advertisement, next to Maj. William Armstrong of the Choctaw Agency. And by June 1854 "V. B. Tims, Choctaw Nation" held 10 shares at $25 each in the Cairo & Fulton Railroad Company of Arkansas, among other Choctaw Nation stockholders; the road was chartered to link Cairo, on the Mississippi, with Fulton on the Red River.
The army contracts behind the thirteen-cents-a-ration figure were signed on 1 January 1838 and 1 January 1839, each naming "Doak & Tims."
In April 1841 a clerk in the Doaksville trading house wrote home that "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with is now in New York purchasing a stock of goods."

The post office he is remembered for was still in the government's list in 1877: "Doaksville," "Choctaw," "V. B. Tims," with a year's compensation of $37.77. An 1871 list likewise carries a "V. B. Tims" among the postmasters. The initials are the trader's, though whether the postmaster of the 1870s was Vincent himself or his son Vinson, who would have used the same initials, is not known.

His wife was Betsy Tims, a Choctaw of Towson County who, like Vincent, was dead by 1899; their son Edward W. Tims named them as his parents when he enrolled, calling Vincent a non-citizen. Betsy Thompson, born in 1870, was a granddaughter of that Betsy Tims and shared her name.
P.note: Vincent was white, so the family's Choctaw citizenship came through his wife, known only as "Betsy Tims" on their son Edward's Dawes card. His date of death is given as 14 June 1864 in a descendants' account and 17 June 1864 in family files, but he signed letters as Doaksville's Confederate postmaster on 9 September and 1 November 1864, so both dates look wrong. The postmaster rolls name a 'V. B. Tims' on 17 May 1871, which may be Vincent himself. The 'first postmaster' detail rests on Joel's memory, and the Confederate office had an earlier postmaster, J. P. Kingsbury, in 1862-63.

P.name: John Steadman
P.place: Emeline's father, dead by 1899 and marked as a noncitizen of the Choctaw Nation. Family says he was Irish; nothing has confirmed it.
body: When Emeline was enrolled in 1899, the clerk wrote her father as "John Steadman," dead and "Non Citz."; she herself was enrolled as a Choctaw citizen by blood, and her mother was O-we-na. The noncitizen label does not say John's race or birthplace. Emeline was put down as one-quarter Choctaw, but no fraction was written for either parent, so O-we-na's ancestry cannot be worked out from it.

Emeline was born on 26 January 1842, while Fort Towson was still an army post and Doaksville a trading town. Her grandson Joel Thompson could not recall her maiden name when he was interviewed in 1937, so the name Steadman comes from her enrollment and not from family memory. In 1896 she was counted in Towson County as Emeline Tims, aged 57; by the time the final roll was made she was put at 60.

He may have been Irish; family says so. Nothing gives his birthplace, residence or death year, only that he was dead by 1899. But his line traveled far from him. His daughter married Vinson W. Tims, a son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims, and bore eight children, among them Betsy, who married Judge Joseph P. Thompson in 1889. Emeline herself lived to see her grandson Simon born on 4 May 1899, attended his birth as midwife and swore the statement that put him on the roll.

The law John Steadman married under was strict on paper. An act of October 1840 barred any white man from marrying in the Choctaw Nation until he had been a citizen for two years and required a license from a judge or the district clerk and a ceremony by a minister "before he shall be entitled and admitted to the privilege of citizenship." It forbade a white husband to dispose of his Choctaw wife's property without her consent. Emeline was born in January 1842, so her parents' marriage falls close to the passing of that act. No license or marriage for John and O-we-na has been found, and the "Non Citz." of 1899 records only how the Commission classed him, not whether he ever held Choctaw citizenship.

P.name: O-we-na
P.place: Emeline’s mother, dead by 1899 and of Towson County. Her name is written O-we-na; its meaning is not established.
body: O-we-na is the only parent of Emeline whom the clerks placed in a Choctaw county. In 1899 she was written down as dead and of Towson County, the same county in which her daughter Emeline Tims was counted in 1896 and lived near Doaksville in 1899. Emeline's father, John Steadman, was marked as no citizen. O-we-na herself never had an enrollment of her own.

The hyphens are the clerk's. Clerks wrote Choctaw names by ear and broke them into syllables, and O-we-na may have been spelled differently by the person who said it. Its meaning is not recorded, and neither is any year of birth or death for her. Emeline's birth on 26 January 1842 is the one date that frames her.

Emeline was recorded as one-quarter Choctaw and her father John Steadman as a noncitizen, but nothing was written of O-we-na's ancestry, so it cannot be known from that. Through Emeline, O-we-na is an ancestor of the Tims and Thompson families of High Hill.

P.name: Jackson & Viney Gardner
P.place: Blue County, Choctaw Nation. Both dead by May 1899, when their daughter Eunice was enrolled.
body: When their daughter Eunice was enrolled at Goodland in Kiamitia County on 10 May 1899, she gave her parents as "Jackson Gardner" and "Viney Gardner," both dead, both of Blue County. Eunice was 49, which puts her birth about 1850. She was counted in Kiamitia, her husband's county, not her parents'.

Blue County in the Choctaw Nation lay in the Pushmataha District, and Armstrong Academy, the Choctaw boys' school where Eunice's son William Harrison's name turned up on a student list in August 1899, stood in it. By 1894 Blue sent one senator, like Kiamichi, Atoka and Jack's Fork. In 1886 the Council cut a new Jackson County from Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka. Samuel G. Gardner of Blue County was a probate judge, but nothing connects Jackson and Viney to him.

Family trees suggest that Jackson was born in Mississippi around 1820, but nothing establishes his birthplace or birth year. A Carney maiden name and other given names for Viney also appear in trees without support. Their daughter Eunice married Joseph Pisachubbe and lived at Goodland, where she raised two sons and a ward. After her death on 19 May 1927, her sons petitioned to sell her 159-acre allotment in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East.

The Choctaw Nation counted its own people decades before the federal commission made its rolls. A surviving 1860 census of Towson County, for example, lists households, ages, occupations and places of birth, and counts like it may one day carry Jackson and Viney back a generation. A matching name alone would not prove that a person was this Jackson or this Viney, and for now they remain two names beside the word "dead."

P.name: Brazil & Siney
P.place: Red River County, Choctaw Nation. Molsey's parents, both dead by 1899; her mother's name was written "Siney" in quotation marks.
body: When their daughter Molsey Austin was enrolled in 1899, the clerk wrote her parents down as "Brazil," dead, of Red River, and "Siney," dead, of Red River, setting the mother's name in quotation marks. The quotation marks may mean the clerk was unsure of the spelling or that it was a nickname. Brazil was given no surname.

Red River County was one of the Choctaw Nation's counties along the Red River on the Texas border. Molsey was counted in Towson County in 1896 , after her husband Legion Austin, so she had moved from Red River County to Towson. Molsey was 22 in 1899 and swore she was 25 in April 1901, which puts her birth about 1876 or 1877.

A midwife named Sinie Hall attended the birth of Molsey's daughter Adline on 5 August 1900, and signed her statement with her mark at Fowlerville. The two spellings may be the same name; nothing says the two women were kin. What Brazil and Siney left is Molsey, who signed with her mark as "Mulcy Austin" and was later listed as "Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin," and the children of her household: Lizzie, James and Adline.

P.name: Ata-sa-ha-bi & Lotima
P.place: Towson County, Choctaw Nation. Known only by their Choctaw names as Legion Austin's parents, both dead by 1899. Ata-sa-ha-bi ends in -abi, like many Choctaw war-names.
P.src: Dawes Card 1363 (NARA); Dawes Card 1363. Dawes Card 1363 and jacket 7-1363; Ovid Vickers, 'Mississippi Choctaw Names and Naming' (Names).
body: Legion Austin's parents were written down in 1899 as "Ata-sa-ha-bi," dead, of Towson County, and "Lotima," dead, of Towson County, with "Ded" beside both and no year of death. Because Legion had already been counted in 1896 as "Legend Austin," the clerk had the parents' names from that earlier count and not from fresh testimony in 1899.

The first name ends in abi, which the Choctaw linguist Ovid Vickers calls a war-name element; "a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination abi signifying killer." The Choctaw Nation's language staff cautions against reading the ending simply as "killer," and the meaning of Ata-sa-ha-bi is not recorded.

Legion himself bore an English surname, Austin, and signed by mark. In 1899 he gave his age as 33, but in November 1902 he testified he was "about fifty," so his birth falls somewhere between about 1852 and 1866. He had a grown daughter, Viny, born about 1879 to an earlier wife named Betsy, and he raised his nephew Nicholas Greenwood, so the household was wider than the enrollment shows. His daughters Lizzie and Adline married the Pisachubbe brothers Robert and William Harrison, and the line runs through Frances Pisachubbe Thompson.

P.name: Mary Ellen Hulsey
P.place: Born 22 August 1938 at Broken Bow; died 4 November 2002 in Hugo. At two, living at South Fork, Arkansas. Buried in Woodlawn Cemetery beside William Thompson Jr.
body: Mary Ellen Hulsey was born on 22 August 1938 at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, the fifth child of Oscar and Katie Hulsey. Broken Bow had grown up around the Dierks lumber company and was incorporated in 1911, a mill town in the pine hills of McCurtain County. In the spring of 1940, at two, she was living with her parents and four older brothers and sisters at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas.

The family kept pictures of her from those years. At three, at Fort Towson in Choctaw County, she is a smiling little girl with a straight fringe cut across her forehead. In 1942, at four, she sits beside her little brother Charlie, who is two and has his arm around her shoulders; that picture was mounted next to one of the two eldest, Delphia and Leon, with Leon holding a guitar.

Her parents' marriage came apart in her childhood. An Arkansas divorce was entered in Montgomery County on 26 September 1941, when she was 3, and Katie filed again in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in 1945; that divorce was granted in January 1946, when she was 7. In July 1947 her brother Bennie George, 13, was killed on his bicycle west of Hugo; she was 8. By April 1950 she was 12, living at Jeter in Choctaw County with her mother, who now ran the household on her own, and three of her brothers, Glen, Charley and Willis.

She went to school in Hugo from the age of seven until she was nearly eighteen. Her school picture for 1955–56, printed “School Days,” shows her at seventeen with her dark hair set in soft curls, a high-necked sweater and a level, steady look.

The day after her grandmother Jane died, in January 1956, seventeen-year-old Mary was riding through Hugo with her mother and her aunt from Grand Prairie when their car was struck at Second and Kirk streets. She and her aunt bumped heads, shaken but not badly hurt.

In the first days of December 1956, at eighteen, she and William “Junior” Thompson Jr., four years older and living out at Speer, took out their marriage license at Hugo, and The Hugo Daily News printed their names among the week’s licenses on 5 December. The marriage joined the Hulsey line, from Arkansas and Georgia, to the Thompson family of Choctaw County.

A photograph from her later years shows her in a red top, her hair still dark and cut short, smiling down at something beside her. She died at Hugo on 4 November 2002, aged 64, and is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County beside her husband. Her mother Katie outlived her by more than six years, and when Katie died in 2009, Mary was among the children she had already buried.

For a time around 1990 she went by Mary Christian, and in December 1991, with that name, she stood on a porch with her mother and her brothers Charlie, Leon and Willis for a family picture. After she died at Hugo on 4 November 2002, her funeral was held two days later through Prater-Lampton-Mills & Coffey.

P.name: Oscar Franklin Hulsey
P.title: A WPA laborer in the Ouachitas
P.hook: Out of work 48 weeks of 1939, on a government job, with five children in a rented house.
body: Oscar Hulsey was born at Hot Springs, Arkansas, on 27 October 1910. In April 1940, at 29, he and Katie, also 29, were renting a house valued at $2 at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas, with Leon 11, Delis 9, Benney 6, Glen 4 and Mary 2. Oscar was a laborer in "Government work" (the Depression-era WPA), had been unemployed 48 weeks, had worked 16 weeks in 1939 and earned $140. He had five years of schooling.

He had married Katie Stevenson on 27 October 1927, his 17th birthday; she had turned 17 twelve days earlier. He registered for the WWII draft at Mount Ida on 16 October 1940. The family later moved to the lumber towns of McCurtain County, Oklahoma. Oscar died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71, and was buried at Wheelock Cemetery near Millerton, the old Choctaw mission ground.

Oscar and Katie had seven children: Franklin Leon (1929-2015), Delphia (1931-2005), Bennie George (1933-1947), Glen (1935-2001), Mary Ellen (1938-2002), Charlie (1940-2010) and Willis Delane (1943-2004). Mary Ellen was born at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, and the family was back in Montgomery County by 1940.

At his death in 1982 Oscar was remembered as a Hot Springs native who had 'lived in the area for many years.' He died at his home at Holly Creek, between Broken Bow and Wright City in the old sawmill country. His funeral was held at 2 p.m. on Sunday at Wheelock Cemetery, with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was survived by four sons, two daughters, two sisters, four brothers, ten grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.

Wheelock was the Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws; its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, whose 1853 gravestone stands in the same graveyard. Oscar was buried among the missionaries' graves in 1982.

A McCurtain County marriage license for "Oscar F. Hulsey" and Katie "Steveson," as the clerk spelled it, was filed on 27 February 1943. It probably belongs to this couple, though it gives no ages or residences. The family's own account puts the marriage on 27 October 1927 and their children began in 1929, so the 1943 license may be a later or second legal marriage, or a re-licensing; the paper license is held by the clerk in Idabel.

Four events mark the middle of his life. In January 1938 he was arrested after a two-day search and charged with assault with intent to kill in the stabbing of Eddie Stevenson, his brother-in-law. He was divorced from Katie in Arkansas on 26 September 1941 and married Hester May Whittington at Mount Ida on 3 November 1941. In 1945 Katie sued for divorce in McCurtain County, and the district court granted it in January 1946; and when his son Bennie was killed on a bicycle near Hugo in 1947, Oscar was living at Wright City.

P.hook: Born at Danville, Arkansas, in 1910 and married at 17, Katie Stevenson Hulsey raised her children alone at Jeter and Hugo and outlived five of her seven children.
body: Katie Cornelia Stevenson, born 15 October 1910, was the youngest of Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' and Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson. When the family was counted in Frank's rented house at Danville, Arkansas, in April 1910, the last of the seven children was "Katie, a baby," so one of the two dates is off by months; at nine, in 1920, she was still 'Kate.' Danville was a Yell County seat laid out in 1841 and named for a steamboat on the Petit Jean River; her father was a Methodist clergyman there and had children born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma before her.

By 1920 the family was farming a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, near Valliant, a railroad town founded in 1902 in the Choctaw Nation. On 27 October 1927, twelve days after her seventeenth birthday, Katie married Oscar Hulsey, the son of the Rev. George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves. Two preachers' families, one from Tennessee and Indiana, the other from Georgia and Arkansas, were joined, and their children grew up in the Ouachita hills at places like South Fork, Montgomery County, where they were living in 1940.

The 1930s were hard on the marriage. Oscar was charged after a stabbing in January 1938 that involved Katie's brother Eddie Stevenson ("A family quarrel ends in a stabbing"). An Arkansas divorce was entered on 26 September 1941, and Katie filed in McCurtain County in 1945; the district court granted her divorce from Oscar in January 1946. In July 1947 her 13-year-old son Bennie George died after turning his bicycle in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo, and she moved to Hugo that year. In April 1950 "Kattie," 40, "Separated," was head of a household at Jeter, Choctaw County, with Glen, 14, Mary, 12, Charley, 9, and Willis, 6.

She died at Hugo on 30 January 2009, aged 98, with services on 2 February and burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery, where her parents lie in Block 2. She left 16 grandchildren, 32 great-grandchildren and 26 great-great-grandchildren, and had outlived her daughters Delphia and Mary and her sons Willis, Bennie and Glen. Her daughter Mary Ellen's marriage into the Thompson family connects this line to the Choctaw County side of the tree.

P.title: Working at Camp Pike
P.hook: In 1918, George Hulsey registered for the draft while working at Camp Pike near Little Rock.
body: George Washington Hulsey was forty-two when he registered for the draft on 12 September 1918. He gave his birth date as 24 December 1875 and his permanent address as Story, in Montgomery County, Arkansas. For work he was away at Camp Pike, the Army’s large training camp near Little Rock, employed as a laborer by the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company. His nearest relative was Sarah Rebecca Hulsey at Story. He was short and slender, with blue eyes and black hair.

He married Sarah Rebecca Graves on 22 December 1901, when she was seventeen. They had ten children, among them Oscar, born in 1910. George died in 1935 and is buried in Breashears Cemetery near Story. Family accounts also place a Benjamin F. Hulsey there, but the shared cemetery does not by itself establish their relationship.

Rebecca and George Washington Hulsey had ten children: William Roy (1904), John Wesley (1906), Noah (1908), Oscar Franklin (1910), Fred (1913), Ruby Ellen (Stipe, 1915), Grady (1918), Louis Daniel (1920), Grace Irene (Dunagan, 1923) and George Paul (1925). Oscar was the fourth. Rebecca was 17 at the wedding and 41 when the last child was born.
Accounts differ on George’s exact death date, 5 August or 21 August, but the year 1935 is sure. A death date of 22 December in one family tree seems to repeat his wedding anniversary.
At Oscar’s death in 1982, two sisters and four brothers survived him. Of his nine siblings, three had therefore died before him.
When he died in 1935, the oldest child, William Roy, was about 30 and the youngest, George Paul, about 9 or 10; his widow, Sarah Rebecca, was 51. She died at Bandon, Oregon in 1972.

Camp Pike was under heavy strain when he signed. Eleven days after the draft card, on 23 September 1918, the camp base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a single day, and by the end of October 12,393 men had reported sick with the disease.

In June 1880, B. F. Hulsey, a thirty-two-year-old Georgia-born miner, lived in Center Township with his wife Sarah G., thirty, and children Margaret M., six, George W., four, and infant Charles F. George’s later December 1875 birth date fits the child’s age. These point toward this household as his childhood family, though that is only probable.

His flat granite marker in Breashears Cemetery reads "George / Hulsey / Dec. 24, 1876 / Aug. 5, 1935." The stone settles the day of death as 5 August. Its birth year, though, is a year later than the December 1875 that George himself gave in 1918 and that appears in 1900; the marker was cut after his death, and George's own word carries more weight.

P.title: Benjamin Hulsey: from Georgia to Arkansas
P.hook: A Georgia-born Benjamin turns up in a blacksmith’s household, on an Arkansas cavalry roster and in later family accounts, but nobody can yet join them into one life.
body: Hulsey family accounts trace Benjamin Franklin Hulsey to the mountains of Union County, Georgia, and a household headed by the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey and Elizabeth. In November 1850 that household held a Benjamin, three years old, with a six-year-old girl just above him. Three fits the family birth date of 2 February 1847, but nothing gives an exact birthday or shows that this child grew into the later Arkansas man.

A private Benjamin F. Hulsey served in Company D of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment recruited during the winter of 1863–64, while a grave account instead gives Benjamin Confederate cavalry service. Similar unit names blur the line between the two armies, and without a service or pension file no one can say which, if either, was his.

Family accounts name Sylvania Susane Partin as a wife, while a 1977 family account names Margaret Partain. The 1880 Montgomery County household that probably includes young George Washington Hulsey names the wife as Sarah G. None of those women has been securely identified with another, and Sylvania has not been established as George’s mother.

In September 1893 in Garland County, Benjamin F. Hulsley and Lucy Morgan, fifteen, took out a marriage license dated 25 September, though no one can read when the ceremony itself took place, so the license date should not automatically become their wedding date. Whether this couple belongs with the 1880 household is unresolved.

Two later households in Garland County carry the same name and may be this man, though that is not proved. In June 1900, in Mountain Valley and Union townships, "Benjaman F Hulsey," fifty-nine, headed a household with a wife, Lucy L., and six children: Charles F., Martin S., Mary J. B., Francis M., Lillian and Thomas M. The first four were probably children of an earlier wife, since Lucy, who was fifteen in 1893, was too young to be their mother, and only Lillian and Thomas hers. In 1910, in west Hot Springs township, a Benjamin of sixty-eight lived with Lucy and the children Lillie, Thomas, Ada and Sadie. The ages given for Benjamin (59 and 68) and for Lucy do not agree with each other or with 1847, which is one more reason the identification stays open.

In February 1910 a $175 land transfer was reported from B. F. Hulsey and wife to C. Floyd Huff: the west half of the northwest quarter of section 10, township 2 south, range 19 west. With neither his full name nor his home address given, it is only a possible match.

A family account places Benjamin’s death at Story on 16 December 1924 and his burial at Breashears Cemetery; a 1977 family account instead gives 1921. These accounts hold clues worth following, but they do not yet make one continuous life or prove that he was George Washington Hulsey’s father.
P.note: This profile preserves a family-account lead separately from the B. F. Hulsey household recorded in 1880. Their identity, Benjamin’s parents, his military service and the identity of George Washington’s mother remain unconfirmed. The original 1850 census resolves the copied age discrepancy in favor of three; the competing wife names and death years remain unresolved.

P.name: Sarah Rebecca Graves
P.place: Born 5 May 1884 (her grave memorial says St. Francis County, its biography Little Rock). Married G. W. Hulsey in 1901 at 17. Died at Bandon, Oregon, on 23 December 1972, at 88.
P.hook: Sarah Rebecca Graves arrived on 5 May 1884, married a Hulsey at 17, bore ten children, and ended her life on the Oregon coast.
body: Sarah Rebecca Graves was born on 5 May 1884. A family genealogy names Margaret Crumpton as her mother and says Margaret died the same day, but this is unconfirmed. A 1977 family account names Jesse Graves as Sarah's father and lists Margaret as one of his wives, without saying which wife was her mother. A Jesse Graves and a Margaret Crumpton married in Garland County in 1884, though the groom's age differs from other accounts of Jesse, so it is not certain they are the same people.

On 22 December 1901, at 17, she married George Washington Hulsey in Arkansas. They farmed in Sulphur Township and between 1904 and 1925 had ten children, from Roy, the eldest, to George Paul, the youngest, with Oscar, the fourth, among them. By 1920 the family was in McCurtain County, Oklahoma. In September 1918 George Washington was a laborer at Camp Pike near Little Rock while she was at Story, Montgomery County; he died in 1935 and she was a widow at 51.

When Abe N. Graves died in 1943, the Arkansas Gazette listed Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey as his sister, which fits the family's account of her Graves relatives. A Graves family genealogy says Jesse was the son of Gilliam Graves, who came from North Carolina by way of Georgia and Alabama to Cedar Glades in Arkansas and volunteered for the Union army in January 1864.

She died on 23 December 1972 at Bandon, on the Oregon coast, at 88, and is buried at Hawthorne Memorial Gardens, Grants Pass. Her grandson Glen, Oscar and Katie's son, died at Veneta, Oregon, in 2001, so more than one branch of the Hulsey family ended up in Oregon.

Her bronze marker at Hawthorne Memorial Gardens in Grants Pass, Oregon, reads "In Loving Memory / S. Rebecca Hulsey / Mother / May 5, 1884 Dec. 23, 1972." She went by her middle name, as in the 1943 notice of her brother Abe's death: Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey.
kv: Not yet established; Margaret Crumpton is a family-history lead
Hawthorne Memorial Gardens, Grants Pass, Josephine County, Oregon
The 1977 family query names Nancy Wilborn Sutton; an 1889 record names Nancy Cutter
P.note: Her birthplace is given as St. Francis County on one memorial and Little Rock on another. The 1948 death certificate of her son Louis Daniel, for which she was the informant, gives her birthplace as Garland County, Arkansas. The Graves Family Association names Margaret Crumpton as her mother, but the 1977 family query does not identify which of Jesse's wives bore Sarah; a record naming Sarah's mother is still needed. The 1884 groom's age conflicts with that recorded for the Jesse of the 1871 marriage, so the two records may not concern the same man. Sarah's identification with the daughter of the Jesse in this tree remains probable, not proven.

P.hook: Born in 1861 at Pulaski, Tennessee, Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a Methodist preacher and went on to preach and farm in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.
body: In April 1910 Frank Stevenson was a "Clergyman" at Danville, Arkansas. He was 51, renting, married for 25 years, and his seven children had been born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas. He had begun life in a Tennessee circuit preacher's household: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born on 17 November 1861 near Pulaski, Giles County, one of fifteen children of Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson and Martha Still Watson, and the twin of George Washington Stevenson.

He was five months old when Federal troops first reached Pulaski in April 1862. Giles County was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers," and in 1863 the Federals relieved the county of "horses, cattle and grain." His first cousins Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. Giles County itself had been formed only in 1809, from Maury County, four years before his grandfather Elam came. In 1870 he and George, both 8, were in their father's household with younger children; in 1880 he was 18 and a farmer. In January 1881 his father "abandoned the idea of going to Texas," and that May "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." Texas was in the family's talk before Frank himself lived there.

He went north to Gibson County, Indiana, where the family of his wife, Parsis Jane O’Neal, lived; her grandparents Archibald and Parses O’Neal had come to the county from Tennessee in 1839. Their children Delphia and George were born in Indiana. Other family trees give them three older children, Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886) and Nellie Vashti (1889), whose link to this family is not documented. Exactly when the Texas and Oklahoma births fell between 1889 and 1902 is not known.

He married Parsis Jane O'Neal of Gibson County, Indiana, whose father Daniel had served in the 42nd Indiana. Their older children were probably born in Indiana; later ones were born in Texas (Willie, Frank and Elisha) and Oklahoma (Eddie), and the youngest, Katie, at Danville in 1910. By January 1919 his wife was "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 he farmed a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Yell County, where he was preaching in 1910, had been organized on 5 December 1840, and had two county seats, Danville and Dardanelle. Katie Cornelia’s birth is given as 15 October 1910 at Danville, which does not fit the baby Katie counted there that April; the two dates have not been reconciled.

He died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, aged 88, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery next to Parsis. A cemetery listing made in 2000 reads 'Stevenson, Frank N., 1860-1950,' a year off the family record, and his ages over the years range from 1859 to 1862. His youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey, a Hot Springs native, in 1927, and she outlived her father by almost sixty years; their daughter Mary Ellen (1938-2002) is buried in Choctaw County beside William Thompson Jr. A photograph of the grave shows a stone reading 'Gilbert Franklin Stevenson, November 17, 1861 – May 9, 1950', which agrees with the family record; the 2000 listing may come from an older marker or a misreading.

In his last years Frank Stevenson was a retired Nazarene minister, living at 506 East Lowery Street in Hugo, where he and Jane had moved from McCurtain County about 1942. He died at home just after midnight on 9 May 1950, at 89, and was buried at Mount Olivet after rites at the Coffey Chapel. His children had scattered from Tacoma to Edinburg; his daughter Katie was the one still in Hugo.

P.title: The preacher's son who followed the road west

P.name: Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson
P.place: Born 16 March 1816 in Giles County, Tennessee, son of Rev. Elam Stevenson. A Methodist preacher for 54 years who also farmed; in 1880 he called himself a "Farming Preacher," living with his son Gilbert F., 18. Buried at Bee Spring Cemetery, Pulaski.

P.hook: For 54 years Rev. Abner Stevenson rode the Giles County circuits, and in 1880 he gave the census taker his trade as "Farming Preacher."
body: In 1880, at 63, Abner Arrington Stevenson of District 10, Giles County, Tennessee, called himself a "Farming Preacher." He had been born on 16 March 1816, the fourth of eleven children of the Rev. Elam Stevenson and Lydia Payne, in a family that produced five Methodist-preaching brothers; Elam had organized the Bee Spring church in 1815 and moved to Tennessee in 1813. A grandnephew wrote in 1932 that the family counted its years in the pulpit, and set down "Uncle Abner 54 years." A Methodist history of middle Tennessee calls him "a Godly man" who "lived to be very old."

On 8 December 1838 he married Martha Still Watson, born 19 February 1823, and between 1840 and 1866 they had fifteen children. The twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington were the twelfth and thirteenth; one son, James Willis, became a minister and lived to 1943. A son-in-law, John Newton Andrew, married three Stevenson women in turn. The household was a farm first and a pulpit second: In November 1878 he was down to preach at "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m." on the Mt. Pisgah circuit, and in May 1884 two sermons were preached at Rocky Point, "one by Abner Stevenson."

The war came to his farm. His twins were infants when Federal troops reached Pulaski in April 1862, and the county was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers." His nephews Coleman L. and Wilbur M., sons of his brother William P., served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. His own sympathies are not recorded. In January 1881 he had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living," and that May his son "Judge Geo. Stevenson" had "returned from Texas last week." Another son, Frank, lived in Texas himself in the 1890s.

Martha died on 12 July 1887, and her stone at Bee Spring gives her name and dates and an epitaph. Abner died on 30 July 1896 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his father founded. The church was destroyed by a tornado on 29 April 1909 and the congregation rebuilt at Bryson; a Methodist history says "All that remains of this today is the cemetery." His son Frank carried the preaching and the road west to Arkansas and Oklahoma, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married a Hulsey.

P.name: Salathiel & Elizabeth Hulsey
P.place: A blacksmith in Hall County, Georgia, in 1840 and Union County in 1850. His 1850 household included Elizabeth, 35, and Benjamin, 3; their relationships to Salathiel are inferred. Elizabeth’s proposed maiden name Estel and the connection to G. W. Hulsey remain unconfirmed.
P.src: 1840 U.S. Census, Hall Co., Ga.; 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga. (as cited on Find a Grave and WikiTree); 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga., as transcribed in San Diego Genealogical Society, Families: Hulsey (archive.org sdgsfamilies64); San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000). Independently read and downloaded image 12 of 30: https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/7667/images/4211301_00318?pId=13097887 ; index and citation https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/records/13097887 . Original names Robert without a middle initial; infant indexed as Selatha G., handwriting uncertain.
body: In November 1850 Salathiel, 43, a Georgia-born blacksmith with $50 in real estate, lived in Union County, Georgia. His household held Elizabeth, 35; Maryan, 19; Robert, 17; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl read as Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. Arminda Burnett and J. C. Bell were living there too. Nothing states the relationships, so who was wife and who were children is inferred. In 1840 Salathiel was counted in Hall County, and in 1830 he was one of seventeen men named Hulsey in Hall County, living among the Hulseys of Charles and Adler.

Benjamin was three, and the girl just above him six; a published extract once reversed those ages. Three is consistent with the family’s 1847 birth year for Benjamin, although no exact birthday is given. A compiler of that extract suggested that Robert in this household was the Robert Hulsey found in Hempstead County, Arkansas, in 1860.

Union County, in the northern mountains, was formed in 1832 from the country the Cherokee had held until their removal in 1836-39, once a gold-rush district; settlers there were hardscrabble farmers, mostly from Virginia and North Carolina, and few kept slaves. A blacksmith in such a place shod horses and mended plows. Salathiel was born about 1807 and Elizabeth about 1815, but how Elizabeth and Maryan were related is not known. He is gone by the early 1850s.

In 1860 a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, lived in Hempstead County, Arkansas, with Sarah A., 20, and an infant son. His age and birthplace fit a possible continuation of Robert in the Georgia household, but neither record gives him a middle initial. The infant’s name, read as Selatha G., is uncertain in the handwriting; the published reading Salathel G. cannot securely link him to Salathiel. Family accounts also place Benjamin in Story, Arkansas, with a son named Martin Salatheil. The age of three in 1850 removes the apparent conflict with Benjamin’s reported 1847 birth, but neither his identity with the Arkansas man nor his relationship to George Washington Hulsey is established.

Salathiel's father may be Jesse Hulsey, the wounded Revolutionary pensioner of Hall County; some family trees say so, but they also name Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and Mary Tharp, and nothing supports either.
P.note: The original census gives Salathiel’s age as 43, Elizabeth’s as 35, the girl transcribed Lillean as 6, and Benjamin as 3. The published San Diego extract reversed the last two ages. The census does not state relationships or Elizabeth’s maiden name. Jesse Hulsey and Mary Tharp remain unsupported as Salathiel’s parents, and the connection from this household to George Washington Hulsey remains a lead.

P.name: Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson
P.place: Born at Princeton, Indiana; died in Hugo. Daughter of Union soldier Daniel W. O'Neal.
body: In 1880, in Columbia Township, Gibson County, Indiana, Parsis J. O'Neal, 11, "Works At Home" in her father's house. She was the fourth of the ten children of Daniel Waters O'Neal, a veteran of Company F, 42nd Indiana, and Vashti Pearson. Her grandmother Parses (Shaw) Watt, widow of Archibald O'Neal, was on the old home farm near Oakland City, and her brothers in the household were William (16), John (13), George J. (4, born in Missouri) and Daniel G. (2). She was born on 26 March 1868, three years after her father came home from the war.

At 16 she may already have left. A "Parsis J O Neal" is said to have married Otho Louderback, 40, on 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Arkansas, and the memorial for her grave at Hugo carries the name Louderback, though the link is unproven. Her sister Mary was in Arkansas by February 1884. By 1910 she and Frank Stevenson had been married 25 years, which puts the Stevenson household in 1885, and the oldest children, Delphia and George, were born in Indiana.

The Stevensons then followed the work. Willie, Frank and Elisha were born in Texas between about 1894 and 1904, Eddie in Oklahoma about 1907, and Katie at Danville, Arkansas, on 15 October 1910, when Parsis was 42. When her mother died in January 1919, Parsis was "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 the family farmed a rented place in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Her son George Sherman died at Kilgore, Texas, in 1978, and his death record names her as his mother.

She died at Hugo on 26 January 1956, aged 87, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery beside Frank. A cemetery listing made in 2000 reads 1887-1956, but everything from her own lifetime, from 1880 to her children's births, puts her birth in 1868, and a photograph of the stone shows 1868, so the 1887 is a misreading or comes from another marker. Her brothers stayed in Gibson County and her sister Mary lived to 100 at Tuttle, Oklahoma.

Jane outlived Frank by six years. She was living at 204 East Duke Street when she died at noon on Thursday, 26 January 1956, at 88, and the Rev. Wesley Meek of the Church of the Nazarene preached her funeral. She had come from Somerville in Gibson County, Indiana, where her brother George still lived; her sister Louisa Skomp was in Gary. Thirty-eight grandchildren survived her.
