P.name: Daniel Waters O'Neal
P.title: Union soldier, 42nd Indiana
P.hook: Enlisted in 1861 and marched through a Kentucky winter of mud and measles. How long he served is a family puzzle.
body: Daniel Waters O'Neal was born on 25 October 1838 in Tennessee, the year before his parents settled in Gibson County, Indiana. He married Vashti Pearson on 5 January 1860. On 21 October 1861, at 22, he was mustered in as a private in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, the company raised at Oakland City.

The regiment's first winter was its hardest. At Calhoun, Kentucky, the men camped on ground "fully ankle-deep in mud in its best parts," and within twenty days a third of them were in the hospital, many with measles. At Sacramento, Kentucky, they raided the hen-roosts and were arrested until the chaplain talked them free. When they marched into Nashville on 25 February 1862 they found an unlocked pork-house, and by the time headquarters sent a search party "not an ounce of the meat could be found."

A family biography says Daniel was discharged for disability, blindness, at Nashville on 15 March 1862, but the regiment's roll lists him with no remark, which usually meant a man served out his three years. Company F went on to Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge and the Atlanta campaign.

Daniel farmed in Gibson County, and he and Vashti had ten children, two of whom died as infants, among them Parsis Jane, born in 1868. He is buried in Somerville Cemetery under a family stone, with a side stone reading "DANIEL with Co. F. 42 Reg. Ind. Vol." His father, Archibald O'Neal, died in 1841; his widowed mother, Parses Shaw, later married Hugh Watt.

Daniel's funeral was held by Rev. Wright at the United Presbyterian Church of Somerville. He and Vashti lie in the same plot. A twenty-five-foot limestone monument to Company F was raised in 1893 at Oakland City, and it is said to carry the name 'D. O'Neal,' though that has not been confirmed.

A published roll of Company F reads beside his name: "O'Neal, Daniel W., vet. mustered out July 21, '65." "Vet." marks a man who reenlisted as a veteran when the 42nd did in January 1864, and 21 July 1865 is the day the regiment mustered out. If the roll is right, Daniel stayed in Company F to the end of the war rather than leaving in March 1862, and the regiment's later campaigns at Chickamauga, Atlanta and Bentonville would have included him. His application for an invalid pension in December 1865, five months after the muster-out, fits a man who came home with the regiment.

The Company F monument at Oakland City, dedicated in September 1893, carries, in the words of a 1913 booklet, "the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number," and beneath a scroll "Starved to death at Andersonville" the names of eleven company men who died as prisoners after Chickamauga.

Calhoun left a story the regiment told on itself. Col. James G. Jones kept a canteen of whisky in his quarters against "the bad weather and poisonous miasma" of the Calhoun camp, and one morning found it empty: "That d——d Lieutenant-Colonel Denby has been at my canteen, drank it all." The sentinel before headquarters, "being also a little afraid of malaria," had emptied it himself. The same camp sent a third of the men to the hospital within twenty days, and of the measles cases a few "transferred to Evansville died." In Company F's war its captain, William M. Cockrum, was wounded at Stones River and captured at Chickamauga.

Eight of his ten children lived to adulthood: Mary Elizabeth (1860-1960), William Allen (1863-1933), John Sherman (1866-1940), Parsis Jane (1868-1956), George Johnson (1875-1965), Daniel Clinton (1878-1954), David Commodore (1881-1955) and the youngest daughter, Charity Louisa (1887-1979). William was born in Tennessee, probably in 1863 while Daniel was in the army, though an 1880 listing says Indiana; for George the same listing says Missouri. Three of the five sons died at Somerville, one at Evansville and one in Pike County, all within about thirty miles of the farm. Mary and Parsis went west.

P.name: Vashti Pearson
P.place: Born 18 May 1844, daughter of John and Elizabeth Pearson. Married Daniel O'Neal on 5 January 1860. A member of the United Brethren Church of Somerville, Gibson County, Indiana; died there on 16 January 1919.
body: Vashti Elizabeth Pearson was born on 18 May 1844 and married Daniel Waters O'Neal on 5 January 1860, when she was 15 and he 21. Daniel's father Archibald had come to Gibson County, Indiana, from Tennessee in 1839 and died in 1841, leaving his widow Parses on the farm. In October 1861, with Vashti 17 and their first child, Mary Elizabeth, a year old, Daniel enlisted in Company F of the 42nd Indiana, the company raised at Oakland City, and the war carried much of the regiment from Perryville to Atlanta. A family biography has him discharged for disability at Nashville in March 1862.

Between 1860 and 1887 she bore ten children: Mary Elizabeth (1860, who lived to 100), William Allen (1863), John Sherman (1866, born the year after the war), Parsis Jane (1868), J. A. (1871, an infant death), George Johnson (1875), Daniel Clinton (1878), David Commodore (1881), Nora (1884, an infant death) and Charity Louisa (1887). In 1880 the family was in Columbia Township, and George, the child born in 1875, was listed as born in Missouri. Her five surviving sons lived into their fifties or later, and three of them died at Somerville.

She died at Somerville on 16 January 1919, of "apoplexy, 6 hrs." She professed faith early in life and was a faithful member of Somerville's United Brethren Church. She left her husband, her five sons William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, two daughters, "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville, and a brother, James Pearson of Elberfeld. Her eldest daughter Mary Elizabeth was in Oklahoma in 1919 but went unnamed in the notice of her death, and Parsis's marriage to Frank Stevenson tied the O'Neals to the Stevenson family of Arkansas and McCurtain County.

A Pearson family had been in Columbia Township long before she was born: in 1827 "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." Nothing ties that William to her father John. Her restored family stone stands with Daniel's at Somerville, and her own marker reads "Vashti, 1844-1919."

body: On 8 December 1838 Abner Stevenson "married Martha S. Watson," born 19 February 1823 in Tennessee, "the daughter of Mary Watson." She was 15. Between 1840 and 1866 she had fifteen children, the last of them about the time she turned 43, among them the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington in November 1861, five months before Federal troops reached Pulaski.

For a Methodist circuit preacher's wife that meant a farm and a houseful of children during the years her husband was riding to Blooming Grove, Rocky Point and the Mt. Pisgah circuit. She died on 12 July 1887, and the Nashville Christian Advocate noted her death in August 1887.

Her mother is given only as Mary Watson. Some trees name William Watson and Mary Brown as her parents, but without support, and the middle name Still is unexplained, so her ancestry stops at Mary. Her son Frank carried the line to Arkansas, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey.

Her stone in the Bee Spring churchyard is a plain round-topped tablet. It reads "Martha S. Stevenson / Born / Feb. 19, 1823 / Died / July 12, 1887," and below a carved rule: "She started in early life for a better world & has stopped at this Inn until the Resurrection morn, where we will meet again." The cutter's letters read "stated" and "sopped," with the r and t evidently left out. Her stone gives 1887, in agreement with the family dates, though a published notice had 1886.

In June 1880, in the 10th Civil District of Giles County, Martha S., 56, was keeping house for her husband A. A. Stevenson, a farmer and preacher, with Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16, and Jane M., 12, at home. She had been born in Tennessee, and both her father and her mother were Virginians.

One online family tree makes her a daughter of David Milton Watson (1791-1843) and Mary Ann Gary of Mountain Creek, Anderson County, South Carolina, and lists her among their eight children, but cites nothing for it. That couple were born, lived and died in South Carolina, whereas Martha was born in Tennessee to parents who, by her own household's 1880 account, were Virginians. The link does not fit. Her mother remains the "Mary Watson" of the Stevenson family history.
P.note: Her parents are not proven. The Casey family history names her mother as Mary Watson; WikiTree's William Watson and Mary Brown rest on no cited record. The Isham Brown of Giles County lead noted elsewhere remains unchecked. The published abstract of her notice in the Nashville Christian Advocate of 20 August 1887 gives her death as 12 July 1886 and her marriage as 6 December 1837. Family compilations and the existing grave-memorial dates instead give death in 1887 and marriage on 8 December 1838. The original newspaper notice and marriage entry have not been examined, so these conflicts remain unresolved; the tree’s existing dates are retained pending verification. Her parents remain unproved.
P.title: Martha Still Watson, fifteen children and a preacher's stone
P.hook: Married at 15 in 1838, Martha Watson Stevenson bore fifteen children in Giles County; her stone at Bee Spring speaks of a better world and the Resurrection morn.

P.place: Vashti's parents, both dead by 1919. Her only surviving brother was James Pearson of Elberfeld, Indiana. The maiden name Carman comes from a grave memorial.

P.title: The Pearsons behind Vashti
P.hook: John and Elizabeth Pearson are known only through their daughter Vashti and a son in Elberfeld.
body: John and Elizabeth Pearson were the parents of Vashti Elizabeth, born 18 May 1844, who married Daniel Waters O'Neal in Gibson County, Indiana, on 5 January 1860. Both were dead by January 1919, when Vashti died. The only brother named at her death was James Pearson of Elberfeld, Indiana, a Warrick County town a few miles from Gibson County. Elizabeth's maiden name, Carman, comes from a memorial for her grave.

A Pearson family had been in Columbia Township since at least 1827, when "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." Nothing names that William as John's father or brother. Decades later several Pearsons, among them a Charles, a Samuel and an L. S., worked as carpenters in Oakland City, though nothing ties them to this family.

Vashti's husband, Daniel Waters O'Neal, served in Company F of the 42nd Indiana. The regiment was organized at Evansville on 9 October 1861, fought at Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga and Lookout Mountain, took part in the Atlanta campaign and the march through Georgia and the Carolinas, and was mustered out at Louisville on 21 July 1865. Vashti and Daniel had ten children.
P.note: The family tree carries dates for them (John 1803-1850; Elizabeth 1807 to 1 October 1879) that no record seen for this story confirms.

P.title: A family of Methodist preachers
P.hook: Elam Stevenson broke with his Presbyterian parents, carried a preacher’s books to Tennessee in his wagon, founded Bee Spring church and preached for more than sixty years.
body: Elam Stevenson was born on 24 September 1787 in what is now Alexander County, North Carolina, the son of James and Jane Stevenson, who were Presbyterians. About 1805 he married Lydia Catherine Payne in Burke County, a daughter of William Payne, who had served six months in the Revolutionary militia, and Catherine Arnold, as her son Rev. John Baxter Stevenson remembered them. In 1806, against his parents’ wishes, Elam joined the Methodists, the first of his family to do so.

In 1813 he was licensed to preach and moved his family to Giles County, Tennessee. Family tradition says they went by pack horse because there were no wagon roads, but Elam remembered it differently: the preacher Philip Bruce asked him to bring a part of his books “in my wagon,” and he did.

Bee Spring Methodist Episcopal Church near Pulaski was his doing. Elam himself dated it to 1814; others put it in 1815, when, as its chief founder, he bought 15 acres for $20 and organized the church with the help of Stephen Loyd, Meshack Boice and James McCowan. He preached for more than sixty years and was ordained an elder in 1859. The frame church built in 1855 was destroyed by the tornado of 29 April 1909, and of the old site only the cemetery remained, ‘sadly neglected.’

Elam and Lydia had eleven children, eight of them sons: Catherine A. (1808–1888), who married William Hamilton and lived in Limestone County, Alabama; William Payne (1810–1892); James Calvin (1813–1899); Abner Arrington (1816–1896); Willis McKendree (1818–1900); Minerva J., born in 1820, an infant who died that December; John Baxter (1821); Thomas Coleman (1825–1906); Lydia Amanda (1827–1901); Elam Augustus (1829–1886), who moved to Arkansas; and Gilbert Worth (b. 1830), a schoolteacher and minister who married Martha J. Tharp. In 1886 a grandson, Coleman L. Stevenson of Giles County, gave the same roll in the family’s own words: “Rev. Elam and Lydia Stevenson, natives of North Carolina, who were married about 1805, and located in Giles County, Tenn., about 1813. To them were born these children: Katherine, William P., James C., Abner A., Willis M., Minerva J., John B., Thomas C., Amanda, Elam A. and Gilbert. The grandfather died in 1875 and the grandmother in 1872.”

How many of the eight sons followed him into the pulpit depends on who is counting, and the answers run from three to five. His grandson Rev. J. B. Stevenson named five in a family letter of 1932: James, Abner, John, Elam Augustus and Gilbert. In 1871 the church historian McFerrin wrote that “four of his sons are preachers of the gospel”; in 1886 Coleman’s father, William P., was said to have “four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister”; and a neighbor in 1884 remembered “James and John and one other.” The family reckoned 292 years of preaching among Elam and his sons.

That neighbor was F. T. M’Laurine, whose family farmed the next place on Little Bradshaw Creek. In an 1884 piece, “Old Times in Giles,” he remembered: “Elam Stevenson and family settled 1½ miles south of us near Bee Spring church in 1815 or 1816; he soon after obtained license to preach and was a Methodist preacher all his life; died a few years since a very old man. He had one daughter, Catharine, who married a Mr. Hamilton. His sons were William, James, Coleman, John and others; James and John and one other were Methodist preachers, all good, industrious citizens. William married a Miss Malinda Rowe, a daughter of Joseph Rowe who lived near by. She was a beautiful young lady. James married a daughter of Mr. Duncan Brown, sister of ex-Gov. N. S. and J. C. Brown. John is a noted Methodist preacher.”

The Browns were the family of Neill S. Brown, governor of Tennessee from 1847 to 1849, and John C. Brown, governor from 1871 to 1875, both Giles County men, so James married into the family of two governors. The unnamed “one other” preacher fits Abner, and the neighbor’s Coleman was the son also known as Thomas C. Seventy years on, M’Laurine’s dates had drifted a little: Elam himself put Bee Spring’s founding in 1814, and the family was in Giles County by about 1813, a little earlier than the 1815 or 1816 he remembered.

Our line runs through Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson (1816–1896). In 1880 Abner, 63, gave his occupation as “Farming Preacher,” and his household in Giles County included his wife, Martha, and their son Gilbert F., 18: the Frank Stevenson who later brought his family to Hugo. Frank was apparently named for his uncle Gilbert.

Lydia died on 6 March 1872. Elam lived three more years. “Died, at the residence of W. M. Stevenson, near Bethany, on the 13th inst., Rev. Elam Stevenson, in his 88th year,” ran the notice of 18 March 1875, which called him “this venerable minister of God” and said he “had been greatly afflicted, but never complained.” Family tradition says he was buried under the pulpit. The stone over Elam and Lydia at Bee Spring reads, on his side, “Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life,” and on hers, “Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church.” In May 1878 another writer, describing the Bee Spring graveyard, wrote of “old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort” as among “the founders and upholders of Methodism at Bee Spring.”

Elam is remembered today in an encyclopedia article of his own, which follows his life from his marriage and his turn to the Methodists to his license in 1813, the move to Giles County that year and the founding of Old Bee Spring Methodist Church. It calls his father a captain in the Revolution, but James Stevenson served as a private.

P.name: Archibald O'Neal
P.place: A Tennessean by birth and a farmer, he came to Gibson County, Indiana, in 1839 and died there on 25 April 1841.
body: An 1884 county history sets him down in one plain paragraph: "Archibald O'Neal was an early settler. He came here in 1839. He was a Tennesseean by birth. He died April 25, 1841." He farmed in Columbia Township with his wife Parses, whom the book calls "a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio." Their son Daniel Waters had been born in Tennessee in October 1838, the year before the move.

His death date appears twice, and the two differ: 25 April 1841 in one place and "Died Ap'l 22,'41," "First Husband of Mrs. P. W." in another. The year is certain, the day is not. His widow Parses then married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down, who died in September 1871. In 1884 she was still on the old home farm, and she died in 1901.

Some family trees give Archibald a birth in Virginia in 1796 and parents named Charles and Martha, without support; the county history says Tennessee. His son Daniel enlisted in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, in October 1861, married Vashti Pearson, and had ten children, among them Parsis Jane, who married Frank Stevenson.
P.note: The 1884 history says he was born in Tennessee, while online trees say Virginia. His parents in trees (Charles and Martha O'Neal) rest on an uncited memorial and are doubtful.
P.src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), Columbia Township; History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), pp. 212 and 239; WikiTree O'Neal-2667 (parents field: ONeal-3586).

P.name: Parses (Shaw) O'Neal Watt
P.place: A native of "Lawrenceburg, Ohio." Widowed in 1841; later married Hugh Watt and was still living on the old home farm in 1884. Died in 1901.
body: In 1884 “Mrs. Parsis Watt” was a farmer in Section 32 near Oakland City, Indiana, a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio, who had come to the county in 1839. Listed beneath her name were two others: Archibald O’Neal, her first husband, and Hugh Watt, her second. Lawrenceburg is a town on the Ohio River in Dearborn County, Indiana, so the book's "Ohio" may be a slip.

Archibald O’Neal, a Tennessean, came to Gibson County in 1839 and farmed there. Parses was about twenty-eight, and their son Daniel Waters, born in Tennessee in October 1838, was an infant. Archibald died in April 1841, leaving Parses a widow with their son, then two. She later married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down. Decades after Archibald’s death, she was still living on the old home farm.

Hugh died in September 1871. Thirteen years later Parses was farming in her own name, a widow twice over, and the household had changed over more than forty years. Her son Daniel enlisted in Company F of the 42nd Indiana in October 1861 and he and his wife Vashti Pearson had ten children. Their daughter Parsis Jane, who carried her grandmother's name in a different spelling, married Frank Stevenson, and Parsis Jane's daughter Katie married into the Hulsey family, so Parses is Katie's great-grandmother and stands behind the Hulsey line of Arkansas and Oklahoma.

Archibald’s death is given as April 25, 1841 in one place and April 22 in another; both agree on the year. A family-tree entry gives 12 December 1901 for her death in Gibson County. Her parents are not known. Some trees link her to Noble and Sicily (Nordyke) Shaw of Guilford County, North Carolina, but the Quaker register at Dover shows only a Parris who died in infancy, so that link remains a lead.

P.name: James & Jane Stevenson
P.place: Presbyterians of Rowan, later Iredell County, North Carolina, married in 1781. James's will of June 1828 names his son Elam among his heirs. He served in the Rowan County militia in 1781.
P.src: Will of James Stevenson, Iredell Co., NC (1828); State Records of North Carolina, vol. 17; Christian Advocate obituary of Elam Stevenson (1875). SAR Patriot Research System, James Stevenson, P-297560: https://sarpatriots.sar.org/patriot/display/297560.
body: James Stevenson was born, it is said, in Bladen County, North Carolina, on 27 May 1746, or perhaps in 1747. His father took up 640 acres at Vashti, in what is now Alexander County, and James made his life in Rowan, later Iredell, County. He and his wife, Jane, were Presbyterians. They were married in 1781, or perhaps as early as about 1765, and their children included James, William, Elam and Phineas. Phineas, Elam’s brother, is otherwise unknown to the family story.

In 1781 James served in the Rowan County militia as a private, under Captain Joseph Sharpe and Colonel Francis Locke, and the Sons of the American Revolution count him among their patriots. Later family accounts made more of his service: a compiler called him a soldier of the Revolution, and a descendant credited him with Ramsour’s Mill and later battles, though nothing confirms it. He should not be confused with Captain James Stevenson of Rowan and Cabarrus counties, an elder at Poplar Tent, who died in 1832.

Jane died in 1814, and James outlived her by fourteen years. In June 1828 he made his will in Iredell County, naming his son Elam among his heirs, and he died on 3 September 1828. He is said to lie in the Stevenson, or Lackey-Stevenson, Cemetery at Vashti, on the land his father had taken up.

Their son Elam was born on 24 September 1787 in what is now Alexander County. He was the first of the family to join the Methodists. He married Lydia Payne in Burke County, was licensed to preach in 1813, and that year moved his family to Giles County, Tennessee, by pack horse in family tradition, though in his own account he mentions a wagon. He told the story of those years himself in 1869, and the Christian Advocate marked his death in April 1875. Three to five of his sons, depending on who was counting, became preachers; Abner, whose farm and pulpit were near Pulaski, carries this line on.

Who James’s own parents were is uncertain. A family book of 1955 names his father as another James, an Irish immigrant who died in 1820, and his mother as Sally Kelly of Maryland, and gives Jane’s parents as John Stevenson (d. 1794) and a Thompson. The dates are strained: a father who died in 1820 and a mother who died in 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old.
P.title: The Iredell Presbyterians who raised a Methodist preacher
P.hook: James and Jane Stevenson lived out their lives in Rowan and Iredell counties, North Carolina, and their son Elam took the family into Methodism and Tennessee.

P.name: Noble Shaw and Sicily (Nordyke) Shaw
P.place: Guilford County, North Carolina.
body: In March 1857 J. H. Leak and Sicily Shaw, having qualified as administrators of the estate of Noble Shaw, with a will annexed, gave notice that on 16 April they would sell "a tract of land, consisting of 268 acres, well timbered and well watered, convenient to the Oak Ridge Institute, and on the direct road from Danville, Va., to Salisbury," on credit. They signed at Oak Ridge on 24 March 1857, and the notice ran in a Greensboro paper that week.

The sale was to be held “at the dwelling of said deceased,” and the notice ran again on 2 April 1857. “With a will annexed” is the old legal phrase for administrators who carry out a written will when the executor it names cannot or does not act. So Noble left a will, and Sicily, then 66, was one of the two people the court trusted to settle his estate and sell his land.

The farm lay near the Oak Ridge Institute, the academy in northwestern Guilford County, on the road that runs from Danville, Virginia, down to Salisbury. Sicily was born on 2 August 1790, the first of the children of Aden and Martha Nordyke in the Quaker records. Her father Aden had been born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, was shot in the arm in an attack in Georgia, and married Martha Johnson in 1787 at Deep River Meeting in Guilford County; he later went on to Indiana, while Sicily lived out her years in Guilford County. She died on 16 May 1861, four years after the sale.

Noble was born on 22 April 1787 and was a member of Dover Monthly Meeting, whose register lists his wife Sicily and children Aaron (16 December 1809), Parris (7 July 1817, died 30 May 1818) and Mary (17 November 1820). He died on 25 December 1855. It was a time when Friends were leaving for Ohio and Indiana: seventy-one took certificates from Dover between 1816 and 1860, nearly all of them to Indiana. The Shaws stayed.

Parses Watt of Gibson County, Indiana, who was born about 1811 and died in 1901, is thought to be the Shaws' daughter, but the Quaker register shows only a Parris who lived a year, so she would have to be an earlier child missing from it. If she is theirs, her son Daniel O'Neal's Union service and her great-granddaughter Katie Stevenson's marriage to a Hulsey tie the Guilford County Quakers to the Ouachita hills of Arkansas and Oklahoma.

His small stone stands among the leaves in the Dover Friends Meeting burying ground near Colfax, Guilford County. Lichen covers most of the face; "Noble Shaw," "Died," "25 Dec. 1855" and an age beginning "68" can still be read, matching a birth date of 22 April 1787.

P.name: Sicily (Nordyke) Shaw
P.place: From a Quaker family.
body: Sicily was born on 2 August 1790, the first among the children of Aden and Martha Nordyke. Her father Aden had been born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, shot in the arm in a Georgia attack, and married Martha Johnson in 1787 at Deep River Meeting in Guilford County. Sicily married Noble Shaw of Dover Monthly Meeting and lived out her years in Guilford County while her father went to Indiana.

Her husband Noble Shaw was born on 22 April 1787 and belonged to Dover Monthly Meeting. Their first child, Aaron, was born on 16 December 1809, when she was nineteen. A daughter, Parris, was born on 7 July 1817 and died on 30 May 1818, and Mary was born on 17 November 1820. Between 1816 and 1860 seventy-one Friends took certificates from Dover, nearly all of them to Indiana, and Sicily's father was among those who went. She stayed in Guilford County.

Noble died on Christmas Day 1855. In the spring of 1857, aged 66, she and J. H. Leak signed, as administrators, the notice offering Noble Shaw's 268-acre farm at Oak Ridge at public sale on 16 April. The court trusted her, with Leak, to carry out her husband's will. The notice sold the land as convenient to the Oak Ridge Institute, a school that had opened only a few years earlier, in the 1852-53 year, on the road from Danville, Virginia, to Salisbury.

She died on 16 May 1861, four years after the sale. Whether Parses Watt of Gibson County, Indiana, who was born about 1811, was an elder daughter of Noble and Sicily is not proven: the Dover register shows only the Parris who lived a year, and Parses would have to be an earlier child missing from it. That is why Sicily stands on this tree as a proposed ancestor.

P.name: Aden Nordyke

imgs.cap: The Marmon "Wasp," winner of the first Indianapolis 500 in 1911
Marriage license of Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, New Jersey, 1731

P.title: Quakers and the first Indy 500
P.hook: A New Jersey Quaker family that moved west, a grandson who fought for the Union, and a cousin whose firm won the first Indianapolis 500.
body: The Nordykes were Quakers from Burlington County, New Jersey. Henry Nordyke married Rebecca Perkins there in 1731. Their descendants moved to Guilford County, North Carolina, then on to Ohio and Indiana with the Quaker migration away from slavery.

Aden was the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers, born in Burlington County in 1762. An Ohio county history says that while the family lived in Georgia he was shot in the arm during an Indian attack. He married Martha Johnson at Deep River, Guilford County, in 1787, and later moved on to Indiana, where he died in 1842.

An 1899 biography of Captain Adin Nordyke of the 63rd Indiana calls his father Robert Nordyke "son of Adin and Sarah Nordyke," and his mother Elizabeth Shaw. If this is our Aden, the captain was his grandson. Raised a Quaker, he "still holds to that doctrine," yet he fought at Resaca, Atlanta, Allatoona, Franklin and Nashville. Since our Sicily Nordyke married Noble Shaw, the two Guilford County families were probably linked twice.

Aden's brother Micajah moved to Clinton County, Ohio, in 1806 and gave the land for the East Fork Friends burying ground at New Vienna. Micajah's son Ellis, born in 1807, was a Quaker millwright who founded a flour-mill machinery works at Richmond, Indiana, with his son Addison. Daniel W. Marmon joined in 1866, and the firm moved to Indianapolis in 1876 as Nordyke & Marmon. On 30 May 1911 Ray Harroun drove its yellow No. 32 Marmon "Wasp" to victory in the first Indianapolis 500, averaging 74.6 miles per hour.

A Quaker entry dated 12 December 1787 reads: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." If this is Aden's wife, her parents were Robert and Cecilia of Surry County. The name would also fit Aden's daughter Sicily, a form of Cecilia. The entry gives no surname for Martha, so the link to Martha Johnson is unproved. The same records list Aden's children with Martha beginning "Sicily b. 8-2-1790. Mary 2-15-1792."

The Deep River Quaker meeting recorded the marriage intention of Adin Nordyke and Martha Johnson on 12 December 1787, naming his parents as Abraham and Mary Nordyke, which ties Aden to the Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers household that had come south from Burlington, New Jersey.
P.note: The 1899 biography names Adin's wife as Sarah, not Martha Johnson, so either Aden married twice or the captain descends from another Adin. Ellis being Micajah's son rests on cemetery records and a family account; it is very likely but not proven by a single document. Sources disagree on whether the Richmond works began in 1851 or 1859.

P.name: Martha Johnson

P.title: The Quaker bride at Deep River, 1787
P.hook: Martha Johnson was born at Deep River in the Quaker country of Guilford County and married Aden Nordyke there in December 1787.
body: A Quaker marriage entry of 12 December 1787 reads: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." She was Martha Johnson, born in 1766 and living with her family in the Quaker settlements of the North Carolina piedmont. One genealogy gives her parents as Robert Johnson and Virginia C. Elmore, daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson; Cedar Creek Meeting in Virginia recorded the couple as moving to North Carolina on a certificate dated 29 March 1766. The marriage entry gives her mother as Cecilia, while the Cedar Creek minutes name Robert's wife as Virginia and do not name Martha at all, so her parentage is unsettled.

Her husband Aden was born in 1762 in Burlington County, New Jersey, the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers. Their daughter Sicily, born 2 August 1790, married Noble Shaw. Martha died in 1844, two years after Aden, who is said to have died in Indiana in 1842.

P.name: Abraham Nordyke & Mary Rogers

imgs.cap: Abraham Nordyke's headstone
Marble tablet said to mark the grave of Mary (Rogers) Nordyke, wife of Abraham Nordyke; the inscription is illegible in the photograph (identification lead).

P.place: Burlington County, New Jersey Quakers, married 1 June 1761. They moved through Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee before settling in Clinton County, Ohio, in 1806. Their children included Aden, Israel, Benajah, Beulah, Micajah, Daniel, Phebe and Hiram.
body: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers were married on 1 June 1761 in Burlington County, New Jersey, and were members of Chesterfield Monthly Meeting. Mary was the granddaughter named in her grandfather Thomas Staples's will of 1758, where he left bequests to "Mehetable and Mary Rogers", the daughters of his daughter Ann and her husband Thomas Rogers. Abraham was probably the son of Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, who married at Willingboro in 1731.

Their moves can be followed in order. In 1771 they transferred to Hopewell Monthly Meeting near Winchester, Virginia. They then lived for eight years in Georgia, where their son Aden was shot in the arm in an Indian attack, and where their son Micajah, born in 1771 in Stafford County, Virginia, hid through a night in the woods at the age of four when an invasion was feared. In 1788 they joined Deep River Meeting in North Carolina, where their son Aden had married Martha Johnson the December before. In 1798 they moved to Lost Creek Meeting near Knoxville, a settlement whose Friends had been refused leave to meet in 1787 because the land title was still disputed with the Indians, and in 1805 to a farm near New Vienna in Clinton County, Ohio, where they helped start East Fork Meeting.

Lost Creek, near New Market a few miles north of Knoxville, was already a settlement with a history of trouble. In 1787 Friends there, near the Holston River, asked New Garden Monthly Meeting for the right to hold meetings and were refused, because they had “settled on lands the title to which was still in dispute with the Indians,” and were told to move off. The Western Quarterly Meeting added in 1792 that no Friend should “remove and settle out of the limits of a Monthly Meeting without first applying to and having consent.” A meetinghouse went up at Lost Creek in 1796. The Nordykes reached it two years later, and it was from there that, as a Quaker historian wrote, many Tennessee Friends “drifted on, like Charles Osborn and William Williams, to the Northwest.”

The last move put Micajah, then 34, his wife Charity, 26, with an infant in her arms and children of three, five and seven, and the “aging grandparents” on the road north. They bought land near what became New Vienna and “helped start a Friends Meeting which was called East Fork,” on a lot that was part of the Nordyke farm. “Micajah had to go to Chillicothe, forty miles distant, to get flour and sugar,” and Charity kept wolves off with brimstone on the fire. One account dates this move to 1805, another to 1806.

Their children included Aden, Israel, Benajah, Beulah, Micajah, Daniel, Phebe and Hiram, and the Quaker habit of recording the hour of birth survives: "Aden was born at 7:00 P.M.; Israel at 3:00 P.M.; Benajah at 9:00 P.M." Mary died in 1814 and Abraham’s burial at East Fork was recorded in 1825, at 89, though another account gives 1822, so the year of his death is unsettled. Aden's daughter Sicily, born in 1790, married Noble Shaw in Guilford County, North Carolina; if Parses Shaw of Gibson County, Indiana, was their daughter, the line runs on to the O'Neals, the Stevensons and the Hulseys of Arkansas.

P.title: Six homes in forty-four years
P.hook: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers married in a New Jersey Quaker meeting in 1761 and kept moving, through Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee, until they reached Ohio in 1805.

P.name: Henry Nordyke & Rebecca Perkins

imgs.cap: New Jersey marriage license for Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, dated 6 January 1731/2 (1732 in modern year numbering). The image includes a later family note giving 3 January 1731 as their marriage date; the license itself does not establish a ceremony date. Copy from the New Jersey State Archives.

P.place: Married at Willingboro, New Jersey, on 6 January 1731. Rebecca's father, Jacob Perkins Jr., named her in his will that October; her brother David's will calls her "Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike."
P.note: A compiled family page gives Henry Nordyke's birth as 2 January 1710 in the Netherlands, and the name looks Dutch, but no ship, church or immigration record has been found. Trees call him 'Stephen Henry'; the marriage records say just 'Henry.' A Dutch origin is a lead, not a fact.
P.title: The man who owed Jacob Perkins money
P.hook: Henry Nordyke married Rebecca Perkins at Willingboro, New Jersey, on 6 January 1731, and the Perkins estates were settled around him that same year.
body: Henry Nordyke of Burlington County and Rebecca Perkins of Wellingborough were granted a New Jersey marriage license on 6 January 1731/2. A license gives permission to marry, not the ceremony or its date. Her father’s will of 26 October 1731 names his daughter Rebeckah without a husband; her brother David’s will, dated January 1731/2, calls her Henry’s wife. A family page places Henry’s birth on 2 January 1710 in the Netherlands, but no ship or church record has been found, so his Dutch origin is only a possibility.

Henry's name appears again in the estates of his wife's family. Her father, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his will on 26 October 1731, naming his wife Sarah and ten children, among them Rebeckah, and listing bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington. The will was proved on 7 December. Rebecca's brother David then died too; his will of January 1731/2 names "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and was witnessed by Henry himself, and it was proved on 4 March 1731/2.

Their son Abraham, who died at 89 in 1825, was born about 1736; he was a member of Chesterfield Meeting when he married Mary Rogers in 1761. From there the line goes to Guilford County, North Carolina, to Ohio and Indiana.

P.title: In the Navy in the Pacific
P.hook: Born at Frogville. Enlisted in the Navy at 18 and served on a floating drydock that came under air attack at Leyte.
body: Born 25 October 1925 at Frogville, Oklahoma, a Red River community of about 40 families, to Grady and Mary Moffitt; his older brothers were Alvin, Odis and Dois. In 1930 the family was living with his mother's parents in Martin County, Texas, and in 1940 he was "Johnnie," 14, at 411 North H Street in Hugo. In August 1941, when he was fifteen, a "John Moffitt" was among the twenty members of Hugo's Boy Scout Troop 81, sponsored by the Masonic Lodge, who left for a five-day camp at Paris, Texas, for swimming, life saving, hiking and a round of Scout tests; the name, age and town fit, but nothing else in the notice identifies him.

He enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 17 December 1943, at 18. It has been said that he trained as a corpsman (medic) at the Navy Hospital Corps School in San Diego, but nothing confirms it, and the one rating found for him, aboard USS Chief in November 1945, is F1c, fireman first class, an engineering rating. From the day it was commissioned, 22 March 1944, he served on ARD-19, a floating drydock towed across the Pacific to Manus and then to Leyte in the Philippines. In late November 1944, while ARD-19 held the mine-damaged destroyer USS Ross, a Japanese fighter crashed into the dock and started gasoline fires, and the crews shot down a second attacker. ARD-19 earned a battle star for Leyte, then moved to Subic Bay on Luzon, where it kept repairing ships until after the war. For nearly all his time aboard, its commanding officer had a name much like his: Lieutenant Commander Allan P. Moffat.

Chief had a war behind her before he joined. She was an 890-ton Auk-class minesweeper, commissioned on 9 October 1943. In June 1944 she swept mines ahead of the Saipan and Tinian landings, and she was at Okinawa from late May to late August 1945. In September 1945 she swept minefields at Wakayama, Japan, ahead of the occupation forces and helped salvage the minesweeper YMS-418. He came aboard on 7 November 1945 from Mine Squadron Four, rated F1c; where he joined her, in the Philippines or in Japan, is not known.

From November 1945 he was aboard the minesweeper USS Chief, which had swept mines off Japan and was on occupation duty at Nagoya and Sasebo until March 1946, when she sailed home to San Francisco. He was discharged on 9 May 1946 and married Faye Renee Smith in Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947. He belonged to Emanuel Baptist Church in Hugo and died at Choctaw Memorial Hospital on 19 September 1990. His funeral followed two days later at Grant Cemetery.

Chief arrived at San Francisco in April 1946. She went out of commission in reserve at San Pedro on 17 March 1947, was recommissioned for the Korean War, and was sold to Mexico in 1973 as ARM Jesus Gonzalez Ortega.
His flat bronze marker at Grant Cemetery names the service first: "John W Moffitt / US Navy / World War II / Oct 25 1925 / Sep 19 1990."
In April 1950 John and Faye were renting at 907 South J Street in Hugo, where he ran a filling station and worked sixty-hour weeks; he had finished the tenth grade before the Navy.

His rate on ARD-19 has not been seen; on Chief in November 1945 he was rated F1c (fireman first class), and no record seen shows hospital corps training. The muster index labels his second ship MCM 14, a mix-up with a later ship; AM-315 is correct. The rolls run past his 9 May 1946 discharge, probably because the index follows roll dates. P.title: Timberman at Ervin, laborer in the Depression
P.hook: Tall, stout and gray-eyed in 1917, Grady supported his family as a timberman and faced long periods without work in 1939.
body: Born 6 November 1891 at Mountain View, Arkansas, the youngest of Henry and Hannah Moffitt's children at home in 1900. In 1910, at 18, he was living with his widowed mother in Stone County and working in the timber, apparently making barrel staves.
Grady and Mary married about 1914, and their first son, Alvin, was born in September 1915.

When he registered for the WWI draft on 5 June 1917 he was 25, working as a timberman for C. D. Neese at Ervin, Oklahoma, married and supporting a wife, his mother and a child. He was tall and stout, with gray eyes and dark hair.
Ervin existed as a place only from 1904 to 1922, and which sawmill Grady worked for there is not known. The county’s biggest was the Pine Belt Lumber Company at Fort Towson, begun in 1902.

In February 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, with Mary, sons Alvin and Odis, and a nephew and niece; his brother Tom farmed next door. In April 1930 the family, now with six boys, was living with Mary’s parents, John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford, on a farm near Stanton, Martin County, Texas, the county where her father is buried, and Grady, a road-work laborer, was out of work. Martin County had been nearly empty a decade before: its population grew from 1,146 in 1920 to 5,785 in 1930 as cotton farming spread across the plains, and the lean years that followed were hard on its farmers.
Hugo was a young town. It was founded in 1901 where the Frisco’s north-south line crossed the Arkansas & Choctaw, and the Frisco depot went up in 1914.

In 1940 the family was renting at 411 North H Street in Hugo: Grady, 48, a laborer with five years of schooling, had been unemployed 50 weeks, worked 12 weeks in 1939 and earned $100. At home were Mary ("Manile"), 44, and the children Odis 21, Dais 19, Johnnie 14, the twins Alton and Eldon 11, Donald 8, and two little ones.

Their children were Alvin B. (1915-1994, U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II), Odas Eugene (1918-1995; “Odis” in 1940, “Ottis” in 1920), Dois L. (1921-1947), Jimmie Gaynell (1923-1926), John Winfred (1925-1990), the twins Alton V. (1928-1975) and Eldon Herman (1928-2014), Donald K. (1931-2014) and Henry Wayne (1934-1937).

One of the twins seems to turn up in September 1953: "Vernon Moffitt, 24, son of Mr. and Mrs. W. E. Moffitt, Box 255, Grant, Okla.," was finishing his Air Force basic airmen's course at Lackland, the "Gateway to the Air Force," near San Antonio. The age fits a twin born in 1928, probably Alton V., but the father's initials are printed as W. E. rather than W. G. and no twin is named.

Grady and Mary lost two children at three years old, Jimmie Gaynell (17 January 1923 to 26 October 1926) and Henry Wayne (13 January 1934 to 12 May 1937), dates confirmed at the cemetery, and their son Dois died in 1947, after breaking his neck in the Red River. Grady died on 21 June 1972 and is buried beside Mary at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo. His brother Tom, who farmed beside him in 1920, later lived in Paris, Texas, where he died in 1953; his stone is marked WW I and WW II. Their brother Jesse is buried at Tahoka, Texas.

When he registered in 1942 for the "old man's" draft, Grady was 50, living on North Broadway in Hugo, unemployed, with his birthplace given as Stone County, Arkansas. The person who would always know his address was "Mrs. Mannie Moffitt," Mary's nickname in 1940 too.

P.title: Mamie: from Gadsden to the Red River, with eleven children
P.hook: Born in Alabama, raised in Texas, married into the Moffitts, and called Mamie by the people who knew her.
body: Mary Tinsley Shackleford was born on 4 June 1895 in Alabama, a daughter of John Morgan and Lizzie (Newton) Shackleford. She would later be called a native of Gadsden, Etowah County. In June 1900 she was “May, 5” in her parents' household at Gilbert, Etowah County. Where the name Tinsley came from is still unknown.

The family did not stay in Alabama long. Her brother Robert was born at Gadsden in 1897, but her sister Hazel was born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family had crossed to northeast Texas by then. About 1914 Mary married Woodford Grady Moffitt, and by June 1917 Grady was working as a timberman at Ervin in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, supporting a wife, his mother and a child. Their first son, Alvin, had been born in September 1915.

She had at least eleven children, and two died as toddlers. The family moved where the work was. In 1920 they were tenant farmers in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. In April 1930, with six boys, they were living with her parents on a farm near Stanton in Martin County, West Texas, where Grady was an out-of-work road laborer. By 1940 they were renting in Hugo, and in 1950 she was “Mamie,” 54, at Grant in Choctaw County, with Grady and three of the children still at home.

“Mamie” was the name her family used too. When her brother Robert died in California in 1961, “Mamie Moffett” of Oklahoma was named among his six sisters. Mary died the next year, on 26 August 1962, at Paris, Texas, still living at Grant. She was remembered as 67, the wife of Grady and the mother of John Moffitt. She is buried beside Grady at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo, on a stone that reads “Mary Tinsley — Jun 4, 1895 – Aug 26, 1962.”

She died at St. Joseph Hospital in Paris, Texas, on 26 August 1962 after three weeks in a doctor's care, and Grady, giving the details for her death certificate, named her parents as John Shackelford and Lizzie Newton.
P.note: The origin of her middle name Tinsley remains unknown. The 1900 census, as transcribed on her brother Balis’s Find a Grave page, gives May’s birth as June 1894, a year earlier than her stone.

P.name: Henry H. Moffitt
P.place: Born in Lawrence County, Arkansas; died at Mountain View, Stone County, at 46.
P.title: Henry and Hannah in the Ozarks
P.hook: From Randolph County to the Stone County hills: a farm owned free and clear, and a widow who kept going for 22 years.
body: Henry was born in August 1855 in Lawrence County, Arkansas, the son of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt, and appears as "Henry, 4" in their 1860 household. He and Hannah Grimes married about 1876. In June 1880 they were farming in Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, with daughter Josephine, 3, and son Jesse, 1.

By 1889 they were in Stone County, where son Tom was born at St. James, the old Buck Horn settlement. In May 1864 Buck Horn had seen the county's bloodiest Civil War fight, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers. Grady was born near Mountain View in 1891, the year after the town incorporated.

In 1900, in Franklin Township, Henry was a farmer who owned his farm free of mortgage, with Hannah and five children at home: Jesse, Gimsa, Bertha, Tom and Woodford (Grady), 8. Henry died at Mountain View the next year, at 46. No grave has been found for him.

Hannah, who could not read or write, kept the family going. In 1910 she was a widow renting a house with Tom, a railroad section hand, and Grady, who worked in the timber. She had borne seven children, six still living. She died at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou settlement east of Mountain View, on 4 April 1923, and her stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."

body: In 1910 Hannah Moffitt, a widow of 53, was renting a house in Franklin Township, Stone County, Arkansas. Two sons lived with her: Thomas, who worked as a railroad section hand, and Grady, who made barrel staves. Asked how many children she had borne and how many were living, Hannah answered seven and six. She was already nine years into her widowhood: her husband Henry H. Moffitt had died at Mountain View in 1901, and she lived on without him until 1923.

Henry, a farmer who owned his land free and clear in 1900, died at Mountain View in 1901 at 46. Family accounts give the date as 9 September. No grave has been found and he has no memorial of his own; Arkansas did not register deaths in Stone County until 1914. That May, on 26 May 1901, Henry’s brother Patrick had lost his wife, Alice Ann (Cole) Moffitt, who is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery in Stone County. Hannah could not read or write, but she kept the family together for another two decades.

Henry and Hannah were the same age. Henry was born in 1855, when his father Nathan Moffitt, the wheelwright, and Rebecca Williams were farming in Lawrence County; Hannah was born in July 1855, the daughter of David H. Grimes of Wayne County, Tennessee. Their children were Josephine, Jesse Gee (1879-1957), Gimsa, Bertha, Thomas Berry (1889-1953) and Grady (1891-1972). Jesse Gee went to Texas and died in Amarillo in 1957; Tom died in Paris, Texas, in 1953. In June 1900 she gave her birth as July 1855 in Arkansas, with both of her parents born in Tennessee; her 1910 age of 53 would put it nearer 1857. Where in Arkansas is in dispute: one family tree gives Arkansas City, Desha County, and another gives Illinois instead. The Desha County name cannot be right as written. In 1855 the Mississippi River landing that became Arkansas City lay in Chicot County and had seen little growth; the town was not incorporated until 1873 and was not in Desha County until the boundary moved in 1879.

What the records do show is where she ended up. By 1910 she was among the Moffitts of Stone County, a county only 37 years old. It was created in 1873; its seat, Mountain View, had 99 residents in 1880, got its first wooden courthouse in 1888 and was incorporated on 14 August 1890. Her brother-in-law Patrick Moffitt also lived in Stone County. After Henry's death Hannah kept a household of grown sons going on rented ground, and the two sons at home worked for wages, Tom on the railroad and Grady making barrel staves.

She spent her last years at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou community about six miles east of Mountain View, with a grist mill, a cotton gin, a stave mill and a sawmill. Its post office ran from 1907 to 1957. The Herpel Missionary Baptist Church laid its cornerstone on 5 March 1923, and Hannah died on 4 April 1923, about a month later. She is buried in Herpel Cemetery. Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930), also buried at Herpel, may be her daughter Bertha, whose birth was given in 1900 as March 1886, but that is not proved. Her stone reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt," the only memorial the couple have, since Henry's own grave has not been located.

Hannah’s marriage connected the Grimes and Moffitt families. Through her husband she was the daughter-in-law of Nathan and Rebecca, whose road led from Randolph County, North Carolina, to Arkansas and Missouri; through her father David she belonged to the Grimes family of Hardin Creek in Wayne County. Her youngest son Grady carried both lines to Hugo, Oklahoma, where he raised his family.
P.note: Birth conflict: the 1900 census gives July 1855 in Arkansas, which matches the dates above; the 1910 census age of 53 would give c.1857. The Arkansas City, Desha Co., birthplace comes from a family tree, and a second WikiTree profile says Illinois. No birth record has been seen.

P.name: Nathan H. Moffitt
P.place: Born in Randolph County, North Carolina; moved west and died in Oregon County, Missouri.
P.title: A wheelwright on the move
P.hook: Four censuses follow Nathan from North Carolina to Arkansas to Missouri, and from owning land to owning almost nothing.
body: Nathan was born in 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, a son of Robert and Martha (Chamness) Moffitt, and grew up in the Center Quaker Meeting community, which hosted meetings of the North Carolina Manumission Society in those years. He married Rebecca Williams in Randolph County on 13 October 1835. In 1840 he was in the county’s South Division, and a son, Calvin, was born there on 4 December 1841.

The family's route shows in its children's birthplaces: the older children were born in North Carolina up to about 1842, the younger ones in Arkansas from about 1843. In 1850 Nathan, 36, was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, with Rebecca and eight children.

By 1860 he was working as a wheelwright near Smithville, with land worth $1,200 and personal property worth $1,000, and the family had grown to include twin girls born in 1859. Henry, our ancestor, was 4.

Lawrence County in the 1850s was a mix of small farms around the county seat at Smithville; in 1860 it counted 494 enslaved people among 8,875 white residents. Patrick was born in May 1853 (one source gives 11 May, at Sylamore) and Henry in 1855. The war brought jayhawkers and bushwhackers to the county, though no major battle.

The Civil War brought raiders on both sides to Lawrence County. By June 1870 Nathan and Rebecca had moved to Dent County, Missouri, where he was farming with no land of his own and $300 in personal property.

Oregon County, where they next lived, was largely pro-Southern and suffered raids. Its courthouse at Alton burned in October 1863; the historical marker says Union troops burned it, while a 2024 survey says Southern partisans did, and the marker adds that Lee’s surrender “did not end the Civil War in Oregon County.” Rebecca died there in 1871, and that year Nathan married a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole. Nathan died in Oregon County on 23 December 1873. That August his son Patrick had married Alice Ann Cole there. (Patrick’s own death is given as 20 December 1905 at Mountain View in one source and as November 1904, with burial at Sallisaw, in another.)

Nathan’s brothers and sisters spread widely: Sarah and Naomi to Iowa, Robert to Strawberry Township and then Howell County, Missouri, while Hannah, Lydia, Aaron and William C. stayed in Randolph County. Aaron’s son Veno Moffitt died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira.

A Calvin V. Moffitt served as a private in Company L, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union). The regiment was organized at Little Rock in December 1863, and Company L was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. Whether that soldier was Nathan’s son is uncertain, though a Calvin V. Moffitt of Lawrence County is also said to have served in two Confederate units and later claimed a few months in a Union one. Family accounts place Nathan’s son Calvin later at Duncan, Oklahoma, where he died on 13 February 1913.

P.name: Mary Rebecca Williams
P.place: Married Nathan Moffitt in Randolph County, North Carolina, on 13 October 1835. Called "Rebecca" from 1850 to 1870; still living in Dent County, Missouri, in June 1870.
body: The marriage began with a printed form from the North Carolina Governor's office, filled in by hand. "KNOW all men by these presents, that we Nathan Moffitt & David Moffitt are held and firmly bound unto David L. Swain Esquire, Governor, &c.... in the full sum of five hundred pounds current money," and it is dated the 13th of October 1835. The condition reads that Nathan "hath made application for license for marriage to be celebrated between him and Rebecca Williams of the County aforesaid." The bond would be void if no lawful impediment appeared. Both men signed with seals. David Moffitt was almost certainly Nathan's older brother, born in 1802, one of Robert and Martha's nine children.

The form names her "Rebecca," and so does every later record. She is Rebecca Moffet in Nathan's household in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850 and Rebecca Moffit in 1870. The county lists the marriage as Rebecca Williams to Nathan Moffitt, 13 October 1835. Some family trees add "Mary," but every record calls her Rebecca. Her birth is given as 1814 above and as about 1816 elsewhere, in Randolph County. Nothing names her parents. Some trees suggest James S. Williams and Polly Garner, but the Williams families of Randolph County were numerous and none can be tied to her.

Her husband's family surrounded her. Nathan's mother Martha Chamness, who was born in 1778 and lived until 1865, was in the same county when Rebecca married, and Rebecca's sister-in-law Thalitha Williams (born 1804 at Deep River) had married Nathan's brother William C. on 7 August 1827. Whether the two Williams women were sisters is not shown. A son, Calvin Vestal, was born in Randolph County on 4 December 1841. By 1850 the couple were in Arkansas, where Patrick Green was born in May 1853, and in 1860 Nathan was a wheelwright with 1,200 dollars in land. Nathan's sister Sarah went to Iowa with her husband, Rev. Beeson Barker, and his brother Robert followed him to Strawberry Township by 1860.

Her last move was to Missouri. In 1870 she and Nathan were farming in Dent County, Missouri, with no land of their own, and she was still living in June of that year. She is said to have died in Oregon County, Missouri, in 1871, and Nathan married the widow Nancy (Rowe) Cole that same year. Her sons were Calvin Vestal (1841-1913) and Patrick Green (1853-1905), among others, and one of the others, Henry, married Hannah Grimes and raised the Moffitts of Stone County.
P.note: Her death year, 1871, comes from a family-tree profile and differs from the 1870 shown in the dates above; she was still living in June 1870. Her birth is 1814 in the dates above but 'about 1816' in the text.

P.name: David H. Grimes
P.place: Born in Wayne County, Tennessee.
body: David H. Grimes was born in 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, a young county on the western edge of the Highland Rim. The legislature created Wayne County in 1817 and had to pass the act again in 1819 because the clerk never signed it; its first county court met at the home of Benjamin Hardin on Factor's Fork, where the old Natchez Trace crosses Shoal Creek. It was wooded country of ridges and hollows with iron deposits, and Clifton, on the Tennessee River, became its main commercial town and shipped cotton, livestock, lumber and cross ties downriver. David's world was the Hardin Creek farm of John Grimes and Penelope Blackshear, his probable parents, whose children were James B., Elisha S., John Anderson and William Jasper.

His father John died on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm, when David was about fifteen. His brothers stayed. John Anderson was farming on the home place in 1860 and 1900, and in 1872 William Jasper left a will naming "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor." David is not named in that will. His birth in 1829 fits an unnamed son placed in the Grimes family after William Jasper (1826), and a family tree names John Grimes as his father, but the link is unproved.

The rest of his life is known mostly through his daughter. A family tree has Hannah born in July 1855 at Arkansas City, Desha County, and David dying there in 1876. The place name is a later label: in 1855 the Mississippi landing now called Arkansas City was in Chicot County, and Desha County took in the area only in 1879. Hannah's 1910 age of 53 would put her birth nearer 1857, and a second profile gives Illinois. Whatever the town, the tree puts David in the lower Mississippi country of Arkansas by the mid-1850s, a long way from Hardin Creek, and has him dying in 1876. Hannah herself gave both of her parents' birthplace as Tennessee in 1900, which fits a father from Wayne County. His daughter's stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."

P.name: Robert Moffitt & Martha Chamness

P.place: Married 20 September 1797 at Providence meeting house, under Centre Monthly Meeting, North Carolina. Robert inherited 250 acres his father had bought of William Cox and was still living in 1820. Martha, born 6 October 1778, a daughter of Joseph Chamness, lived until 1865. Their nine children were Naomi, Sarah, David, William C., Aaron, Hannah, Lydia, Nathan and Robert.
P.src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Centre Monthly Meeting); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681–1935 (Centre Monthly Meeting marriage certificate, 20 Sep 1797); wills of William Moffitt (1796) and Mary Moffitt (1820); 1830 and 1840 U.S. censuses, Randolph Co., N.C.; Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922); NCpedia, Randolph County: https://www.ncpedia.org/geography/randolph; WikiTree Moffitt-108 and Chamness-49.
body: On 20 September 1797, Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness married at a public Quaker meeting at Providence. Their Quaker certificate names Robert as the son of William Moffitt, deceased, and Mary, of Randolph County; Martha was the daughter of Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton. The witnesses include William Moffitt, Joseph Chamness, Hannah Chamness and Mary Moffitt: the groom's mother Mary, a William Moffitt who was probably his brother, the bride's father, and Hannah, who was Joseph's second wife and Martha's stepmother. Margaret had been dead since 1784, when Martha was five.

Robert had come to the altar with an estate. His father William's will of 1796 named "my son Robart Moffitt" executor and left him 250 acres bought of William Cox, except "the new field that is cleared upon the River," which Mary kept for life. His brother William got the 225-acre plantation, and the youngest, David, land on Tibs Run, wagon iron brought from Pig River and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown. Mary got the wagon, the still and the stock. Martha, born 6 October 1778, was eighteen when she married him. Her father had served the meeting as its recorder of marriage certificates, and she was a granddaughter of Anthony Chamness.

They raised nine children in Randolph County. Randolph had been cut from Guilford in 1779, and Asheboro, its seat, was incorporated in 1796, the year William Moffitt wrote his will. The children were Naomi (1800), Sarah (1801; 21 April 1800 in her own profile), David (1802), William C. (1803; 17 April 1802 in his), Aaron (1805), Hannah, Lydia (1811), Nathan (1814) and Robert (1815). Robert was alive in 1820 when his mother dated her will "the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820," naming "my three sons," and he is in the Randolph County census of 1830 and 1840. Martha lived until 1865.

The family that Robert and Martha founded scattered with the century. Sarah and Naomi went to Iowa with their Barker husbands; Sarah died at Lorimor in 1860; Hannah and Lydia stayed in Randolph County; Nathan went to Arkansas in the early 1840s, and the youngest Robert died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Missouri, in 1872. Their grandson Veno died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira. Both of the families behind that wedding, Moffitt and Chamness, signed the same certificate in 1797.

P.note: A memorial gives 6 October 1778 for Robert’s birth and 6 October 1844 for his death, but that birth date also appears for Martha; neither date has been verified. As executor in 1796, Robert was probably born by about 1775. Martha’s death is given as 11 October or 11 November 1865. Her parents and the children’s list come from compiled Quaker abstracts. The records do not establish that Robert was the Patriot Robert Moffitt of Brush Creek or Robert son of Hugh; neither married Martha. Robert’s exact birth date is unverified; 6 October 1778 duplicates Martha Chamness’s documented birth date and has been removed from the tree.

P.title: A Regulator the Governor wouldn't pardon
P.hook: One of thirteen men left out of Governor Tryon's 1768 pardon.
body: The Regulators were backcountry farmers in North Carolina who rose up (1766–1771) against corrupt officials and illegal fees. William Moffitt of Deep River was in the movement from its start: in August 1766 the inhabitants of Deep River chose "Wm Cox and Wm Masset" (a misreading of Maffet) to attend the Regulators' first general meeting. In 1768 he signed their petitions alongside the movement's leaders, Herman Husband and James Hunter, and on 21 May 1768 he was named first on the committee to carry their grievances to the Governor.

On 3 October 1768, at Hillsborough, Royal Governor William Tryon pardoned the Regulators except thirteen named men, and "William Moffitt" is one of them. He was never outlawed, and a general pardon in 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection." His name is on the memorial trail at Alamance Battleground, and James Otis listed him among "the patriots of upper Carolina" in his 1901 boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators.

William married Mary Davies at Cane Creek Quaker Meeting on 2 April 1763, when he was 23. He and Hugh Moffitt, probably his brother, married sisters, and Hugh ran the first mill on Richland Creek, which gave the community of Moffitt, North Carolina, its name; the Moffitt's Mills post office lasted from 1823 to 1935.

His will, dated 13 March 1796, begins “I William Moffitt of Randolph County in the province of North Carolina, being weak in body.” He gave his sons Robert, William and David land, and his daughters Naomi (Neomi Macky), Catharine Cox, Hannah Cox, Mary Wilkinson and Margaret £3 each, with Margaret also getting cows, sheep and a bed.

Robert, our ancestor, received the 250 acres William had bought of William Cox, except “the new field that is cleared upon the River,” which his mother kept for life. William got the 225-acre plantation where his father lived, with a share reserved for Mary while she was a widow. David, who was clearly under age, got land on Tibs Run, wagon iron “brought from Pig River,” and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown in Cumberland County. If David died young, his brothers inherited and each sister would get £15.

“My Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt” received the wagon, the still, the plantation tools and the stock, and was named executrix with “my son Robart Moffitt” as executor. The witnesses were Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt. The Quaker records of Center Meeting show Robert, “son of William & Mary,” marrying Martha Chamness in 1797.

William and Mary had eight children: Naomi (born 11 June 1763), Catharine (1765), Hannah (22 December 1771), Mary (1773), Margaret (1774), Robert (1778), William (1781) and David (4 February 1785). All five daughters and three sons are named in Mary's will.

Family legend says the Moffitts came from Dumfriesshire, Scotland, descended from a "Robert Bruce Moffitt" born in 1716. No record names such a man. The Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance instead says William was born about 1740 in Donegal, Ireland, to Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt and came through Philadelphia, which fits Ulster Scots, but gives no source.

His name is also on the Regulators' letter, address and indictment of September 1768. Court records add two earlier items: a deed proved by "Wm. Moffitt" in May 1765 and his witnessing of William Cox's will, proved at Hillsborough in February 1767.

A Moffitt genealogy of 1928 for the descendants of Silas Moffitt of Hamilton County, Indiana, gives that family's own tradition of William's origins: sons of "Robert and Margaret Moffat" who "migrated to Donegal County, Ireland," and whose children included James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Catharine, Robert, Mary, Hugh, Patrick and John. It says that "William married Mary Davis and Hugh married Hannah Davis, both being daughters of Charles Davis," and that Mary Moffitt Wilkinson, "our own foremother," was "said to have been their fifth child," married to William Wilkinson, "an Englishman, on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795." This agrees with the "Mary Wilkinson" of William's will, and the two witnesses to that will, Hugh and Charles Moffitt, match two of the brothers in the book's list. The parents differ from the Book of Remembrance's Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt, so the Donegal family is tradition, not record.

The book also repeats a story about "the Davis millions." Hamilton County heirs, it says, raised money to send an agent to the old country to look into an inheritance, but "this supposed wealth, like the fortune at the foot of the rainbow, was always just out of reach."

The Bible record of Abijah Moffitt names William's parents: Robert Moffitt, born in Scotland and later of County Donegal, and Margaret Stuart, with eleven children, six of whom came to America. It adds that William and his brother Hugh both married Davis daughters in North Carolina, which matches William's 1763 marriage to Mary Davies. The Alamance Battleground Book gives the mother as Martha Steward. Both accounts are family-based, not contemporary records.

In an 1853 letter, Hugh's son Joseph Moffitt named his father's brothers, including William, and said their parents were Robert Moffitt and Margaret Stewart. Joseph also named his mother Hannah Davis and said her sister Mary married a Moffitt. This fits the William and Mary Davies of Randolph County, though the letter does not explicitly name Mary's husband as William. The surviving account is a 1924 printed transcription, not the original manuscript. Hugh's 1799 Chatham County will independently names his wife Hannah and son Joseph, strengthening the identification of the letter's family.

P.title: The blue-and-white coverlets in Mary's will
P.hook: Mary Moffitt divided a household among eight children: pewter, bedding, a coffee mill, her big Bible, and the work of settling her estate.
body: On 23 September 1820, Mary Moffitt made a will that records her household almost object by object. She was weak in body but declared herself sound in sense and memory. For each of her five daughters she set aside a pewter dish, six plates and two basins. Bedding received the same careful attention: white sheets, checked sheets, blankets, a blue-and-white flowered coverlet and a blue-and-white double-diamond coverlet. These were separate possessions to be passed to particular people, rather than an anonymous lot to sell.

Naomi Mackie was to have Mary's saddle and best cloak. Catharine Cox received the dresser and cupboard. Hannah Cox received the walnut chest and the big Bible. Mary Wilkinson was left the copper kettle and a five- or six-gallon pot. Margaret Moffitt received a feather bed, bedstead and pillows, the case of drawers, pewter teapot, coffee mill, square walnut table, flax and cotton, provisions and forage, and half the cattle, sheep and hogs. Mary was dividing the tools of cooking, sleeping, dressing and keeping a farm household.

Her sons Robert and William each received bedding and fifty dollars; David received the still, livestock, plantation utensils, cider vessels and 150 dollars. Leftover money was to be divided equally among all eight children, or the gifts reduced equally if the estate fell short. Mary directed the remaining household furniture and clothing to her daughters and the jack screw to her three sons. She appointed Margaret executrix alongside David as executor, and William Cox and Stephen Cox witnessed. The daughter who received the coffee mill would also share responsibility for carrying out the whole plan.

Mary had married William Moffitt at Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 2 April 1763. His 1796 will had left her the wagon, still, household goods, farming tools and livestock, with rights in the home plantation during her widowhood. More than twenty years later, her own choices show how those broad provisions had become a detailed set of gifts to Naomi, Catharine, Hannah, Mary, Margaret, Robert, William and David. She dated the will “the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820,” in the Quaker style, and her son Robert, our ancestor, was alive when she wrote it. Her death is given as February 1822 in one account, but that may only be when the will was filed.

She was a daughter of Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies. Her family had followed the Quaker road from Pennsylvania through Virginia to Cane Creek, North Carolina. Her sister Hannah married Hugh Moffitt, joining the Davies sisters to two Moffitt households. Mary's will brings that large family down to a smaller scale: one saddle, one Bible, particular coverlets and the people she wanted to have them.

P.name: Joseph Chamness & Margaret Norton
P.place: Married 17 March 1763 at Cane Creek Meeting. Joseph, born 1740 in Baltimore County, Maryland, was Anthony's eldest son and became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Margaret, a daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton, bore eleven children and died in 1784; their daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt.
P.src: Cane Creek MM marriage certificate (1763) and Centre MM births, in Hinshaw vol. 1 and Hanson (1922); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Cane Creek MM, marriage of Joseph Chamness and Margret Norton, 17 Mar 1763) Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922), the Chamness family: Joseph's children and the 1791 certificate of his son William
body: Joseph Chamness was in his twenty-third year when he married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek Meeting on 17 March 1763. All four parents signed their certificate as witnesses. The next year, in 1764, the meeting made him its Recorder of Marriage Certificates, and the certificate book in his handwriting was kept in the vault at Guilford College when the family's history was written in 1922. He was born in Baltimore County, Maryland, in 1740, and had come south with his father at the age of nine.

Eleven children were born to Joseph and Margaret between 1764 and 1784, the first three in Orange County and the rest in what became Randolph. The children were Sarah (1764), William (1766), Elizabeth (1768), Mary (1770), Joseph (1771), Anthony (1773), Margaret (1776), Martha (1778), Lydia (1780), Edward (1782) and Mourning (1784). Joseph later took a certificate of removal from Cane Creek to Providence meeting in Randolph County, where he owned a farm. Martha, the eighth child, married Robert Moffitt at Providence in 1797, joining the Chamness and Moffitt families.

On the 12th of Fourth month 1784 Margaret died, with the youngest of her eleven, Mourning, a newborn. The family history says that the eldest daughter, Sarah, then in her twentieth year, took charge of the infant and was the guiding star of the household until a stepmother appeared; some three years after her mother's death she married Obadiah Elliott in Randolph County and took the little sister into her own home. Joseph's second wife was Hannah Beeson, daughter of William and Mary Beeson, and they were married at Deep River meeting on 6 March 1786. Their daughter Susanna, born in 1788, was the twelfth child. Twelve Beesons are counted among the relatives of the bride when Joseph's son William married Isabel Beeson in Providence meeting, and records that William's stepmother signed that certificate too.

Joseph died on 17 May 1818 in Randolph County and is buried at Providence Cemetery. He lived to see all his children married and settled, the youngest, Susanna, then about thirty. His own wedding certificate ties the Chamness line to the Nortons, and his daughter's marriage to Robert Moffitt in 1797 tied both to the Moffitts.
P.note: Joseph's birth is given as 3 May 1740 in one source and 3 November 1740 in another; Margaret's is given as 3 November 1740. Martha, born 1778, is not the same Martha as Anthony's daughter born in 1747.
