P.title: An indentured boy from London
P.hook: Bound for seven years' service in Maryland at 15, he ended up a landowner and overseer of a Quaker meeting.
body: Anthony Chamness was the son of John and Ann, born about 1713 in East Smithfield, London. The church at St John’s, Wapping, recorded his baptism there in February 1713, the name written “Chamniss,” as son of John Chamness and Ann Weary, who had married at the same church on 4 January 1704. On 9 February 1724/5, giving his age as 15 and his home as Whitechapel, he bound himself to John Cooke, a London victualler, for seven years' service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)." A boy baptized in 1713 would not have been 15 in February 1724/5, and the two dates have not been reconciled. He was out of his time by 1732.
On 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole in St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County, into a Cole family that had been in the county since the 1690s.

The Chamnesses moved with the Quakers from Gunpowder Meeting in Maryland to Monocacy (1741), Carver's Creek in North Carolina (1749), and Cane Creek, where Anthony received a 490-acre grant in June 1751. When Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized that year he was named its overseer. As a Quaker historian wrote, “the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants,” and Anthony is one of them: an English servant boy who became a landowner and the officer of a meeting. His farm, a mile west of the meetinghouse, had a grist mill. He married three times and died on 20 September 1777.

His son Joseph, born in Baltimore County in 1740, married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek in 1763, became the meeting’s recorder of marriage certificates, and later farmed near Providence in Randolph County. Joseph’s daughter Martha was born on 6 October 1778 at Center, then in Guilford County (Randolph County was not cut from Guilford until 1779). She married Robert Moffitt at Providence, under Center Monthly Meeting, in 1797 and lived until 1865. Her son Nathan Moffitt, born in 1814, left Randolph County for Arkansas in the early 1840s rather than for Indiana.

The Chamness name did also leave by the Quaker road. Dover Monthly Meeting's list of Friends who took certificates to Indiana between 1830 and 1860 includes “Camness,” one more spelling of a name the Wapping clerk had written “Chamniss” a century earlier, though the match is by surname only.

Anthony married three times: Sarah Cole in 1735; then Rachel Haworth, the widow of Stephanus Haworth, who died on 19 March 1775 and is buried at Deep River; and, on 9 May 1776, Margaret Evans Williams, a widow. He made his will on 24 November 1776 in what was then Chatham County and died the next September.

A Hussey family tradition, written down in 1928, differs from the indenture. A letter of 30 April 1917 from Dr. John M. Hussey of Somerville, New Jersey, states "that Martha Chamness, who married Stephen Hussey, was the daughter of Anthony Chamness and his wife, Sarah Cole; that Anthony Chamness had been kidnapped in England as a child and brought to America where he was 'bound out' till he reached a certain age; that he was the heir of an estate in England, which he had to go to England in order to claim but his wife would not consent to his going." The 1928 writer thought the inheritance "somewhat of a myth," since immigrants often told such stories. The kidnapping tale and the indenture of February 1724/5, in which a fifteen-year-old of Whitechapel bound himself to a London victualler for service in Maryland, may be two tellings of one event. The same book dates Martha's marriage to Stephen Hussey to September 1762.
He and his wife Sarah signed as witnesses at their son Joseph's wedding at Cane Creek on 17th of the 3rd month 1763.

The London parents of Anthony's father John Chamness are unknown. One family tree proposes Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts, who married at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686, but John's baptism in November 1682 is earlier than that wedding.

A family history of 1922 describes the home Anthony and Sarah kept near Cane Creek, as remembered by a neighbor about a century earlier: "The farm lay a mile west of Cane Creek Friends church, was a good body of land and lay fine. The dwelling was large, perhaps 20x80 feet, consisted of two main rooms, made of hewn oak logs, with two shed rooms with porch the whole length on the front side." A small creek ran through the farm with a grist mill, and in the barn stood "a stationary thrashing machine propelled by horse power," to which neighbors hauled their wheat. It calls the home "one of hospitality, and a kind of social center," and says Sarah taught her daughters to spin and weave. The family register lists the children's births in Baltimore County, Maryland, then in Frederick County, Maryland (1742 to 1746), then in Orange County, North Carolina (1749 to 1761). Sarah was "the mother of thirteen children" and died probably about 1773; a tradition holds that Anthony was drafted for the army but not forced into it because of his conscience, though that is judged "barely credible" given his age.

P.name: Faye Renee (Smith) Moffitt
P.place: Married John W. Moffitt in Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947. Died in Paris, Texas.
body: Faye Smith was the youngest child of Charles Oscar and Artie Pearl Smith, born at Forney, Choctaw County, on 23 March 1929. Her father had been born at Hagansport, Texas, in 1889 and her mother in Butler County, Kentucky, in 1898; they married in 1915 and crossed the Red River into Oklahoma, so Faye's farm childhood sat at the end of two families' moves from Kentucky and Texas. She was "Fay May," 2, at Jeter in 1930, the youngest of four, and "Fay," 12, in 1940, when the family was still on a rented farm on Hugo Route 1 and her father, who had worked every week of 1939, reported an income of $105.

She married John W. Moffitt at Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947. She was eighteen. John, born at Frogville in 1925, had been discharged from the Navy on 9 May 1946 after service on a floating drydock in the Pacific and the minesweeper USS Chief, a little more than a year before.

She made her home around family life. Singing, shopping, visits with friends and trips to the Nutrition Center filled her days. Holidays were a particular pleasure, and her Christmas portrait catches her smiling beside the tree.

John died on 19 September 1990, and she outlived him by more than twenty-four years. By her death at Paris on 23 December 2014, the family had grown to 20 grandchildren, 38 great-grandchildren and two great-great-grandchildren. Her funeral was held in Hugo, with burial at Grant Cemetery beside John, in the cemetery where her parents also lie.
In the 1950 census, at 907 South J Street in Hugo, her name was taken down as “Marylyn F.”

P.title: Neighbors at Hagansport
P.hook: In 1910 Oscar Smith, 19, and Pearl Satterfield, 11, lived a few doors apart in the same Texas farm community. Four years later they married.
body: Charles Oscar Smith was born on 29 May 1889 at Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas, a farm community that grew up around a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port. In the 1880s it had about 150 people, a gin, a mill, four churches and a one-room school.

In June 1900 "Oscar," 10, was in the Franklin County household of John and Emma Smith, with Vera, Luina, Lona, Allie and baby Jimmie. John owned his farm free of mortgage. Emma died on 15 March 1905, at 37, and her stone at Hagansport reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten."

By April 1910 John B. Smith had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. On the same day, a few doors away, were the Satterfield family: John C. and Samantha, lately from Kentucky, and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in Franklin County, Texas, on 15 November 1915.

They later crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Charles died on 17 August 1971 and Artie on 21 July 1983, and they are buried together in Grant Cemetery, south of Hugo. John B. Smith died in 1918 and lies beside Emma at Hagansport, in a grave "marked with a wooden stob."

When he registered for the draft in 1942 he gave his name as Charlie Oscar Smith, 52, of Forney in Choctaw County, with mail at Hugo Route 1, working on a farm. He gave his birthplace as 'Higgensport, Texas,' the Franklin County community more often spelled Hagansport, and named Mrs. Pearl Smith as the person who would always know his address.

Charles and Pearl can be followed from Texas to the Choctaw County farms. Their first daughter, Nellie Mae, was born at Talco, Texas, on 3 April 1917, three years after their marriage; by 1920, "C O Smith," 28, and Pearl were renting a farm at Oakes Township in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1930 they were at Jeter with four children, and in 1940 "Oscar Msith," 50, was a farmer on rented land on Hugo Route 1 who had worked all 52 weeks of 1939 for an income of $105. When Nellie died in 1973 her parents were given as "Charley O. Smith" and "Pearl Satterfield."

P.title: Pearl's family across the Red River
P.hook: A Kentucky-born girl became a Texas farm neighbor, married Oscar Smith, and raised four children in southeastern Oklahoma.
body: Artie Pearl Satterfield was born in Butler County, Kentucky, in 1898, into the household of John C. and Samantha Johnson Satterfield. By 1910 the family had moved to Hagansport in Franklin County, Texas. Eleven-year-old Pearl and nineteen-year-old Oscar Smith lived a few households apart. They married in Franklin County, Texas, on 15 November 1915. Their first daughter, Nellie Mae, was born at Talco, Texas, on 3 April 1917.

The Smiths crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1920, Pearl, Oscar and little Nellie were living on a rented farm in Oakes Township. By 1930 they were at Jeter with four children: Nellie, Robert Lee, Virgil and Faye. Faye had been born at Forney on 23 March 1929. In 1940 the household was still on rented farmland along Hugo Route 1. Pearl's family had gone from Kentucky to Texas to Oklahoma in one generation; the children's birthplaces mark the different stops.

Pearl outlived Oscar and her eldest daughter. Nellie Mae Choat died in Paris, Texas, on 7 July 1973, aged 56, after breast cancer; her parents were given as Charley O. Smith and Pearl Satterfield. She was brought home to Hugo for burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery. Pearl lived until 1983 and was buried beside Oscar at Grant Cemetery. Her youngest daughter Faye lived until 2014, carrying the Smith and Satterfield connection into the Moffitt family.
She was a member of Immanuel Baptist Church in Hugo, and she died at Choctaw Memorial Hospital on 21 July 1983.
P.note: The census records support the household timeline. Nellie’s death certificate names her parents; Faye’s obituary independently names Charlie Oscar and Artie Pearl Smith.

P.name: John C. Satterfield & Samantha (Johnson)
P.place: Farmed at Horse Mill, Butler County, Kentucky, in 1900, with seven children at home.
P.title: From Butler County to the Red River
P.hook: A Kentucky farm family that moved to Texas about 1907 and ended up around Soper and Hugo.
body: John C. Satterfield was born in 1864 in Allen County, Kentucky. In 1880, at 16, he was a farm laborer at Renfrow, Butler County, in the household of his father, James H. Satterfield, with his brothers and sisters. His mother, Melissa Gibson, had died in 1877.

A widower with three children, Henry B. (born May 1883), Martha A. (August 1884) and John W. (January 1887), he married Samantha D. "Mantha" Johnson, about 20, in 1892. In 1900 they were farming at Horse Mill, Butler County, with seven children at home. Their son Wavey Lincoln was born near Morgantown on 28 December 1895 by his own draft cards; his headstone gives 9 January 1896. Artie Pearl followed in August 1898. Wavey later served as an Army private in World War I. A family account identifies an early son, Joseph, who died before 1910.

About 1907 the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. In April 1910 John, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, with Wavey, Pearl, James, Ira and little Stella. A family account says their last child was born in Texas in 1912. John died in Franklin County a few years later. On 28 July 1917 Samantha married Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens at Mount Vernon, Texas, and they moved across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Wavey died at Soper in 1952. Their daughter Artie Pearl married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914; both are buried at Grant Cemetery. Samantha died in Choctaw County in 1928 and is buried as Samantha Stephens in Soper Cemetery.
John's father was James Henry Satterfield and his mother Melissa Gibson.

Samantha's husband John C. had a larger family than the two households show. His full brothers and sisters, children of James H. and Melissa, included Sidney Rufus (1865-1949), James Doiser (1867-1929, who went to Clay County, Arkansas) and A. M. (born in Minnesota in 1870, died 1892). His nine half-siblings by Lucinda Phelps lived mostly around Texarkana. He and his brother Sidney both married women of the Clark-Johnson family of Butler County.

The farm John C. Satterfield rented at Hagansport in 1910 was in a county where, by 1908, tenants on the usual share plan gave up half the crop, and farms averaged under 80 acres. The Hagansport soil was heavy clay that stayed sticky after rain and suited cotton better than corn.
kv: Renting a farm at Hagansport, Franklin Co., Texas, with Samantha and five children
Samantha m. Bird Alexander Stephens, 28 Jul 1917
b. 28 Mar 1872, Ky.; d. 1 Oct 1928, Choctaw Co., Okla.
P.note: A family biography places John's death between 1912 and 1916; no grave or death record has been found, so the 1919 date in family trees is uncertain. Most details about Samantha come from a Find a Grave biography written by a Stephens family member; the 1892 marriage record itself has not been seen. Wavey’s draft cards and headstone differ on his birth date.

P.title: John B. Smith, who owned his Hagansport farm free and clear
P.hook: A farmer on the Sulphur River divide who buried his wife at thirty-seven and lay beside her under a wooden stob.
body: In June 1900 John B. Smith, 44, was farming land he owned free of mortgage in Justice Precinct 2 of Franklin County, Texas. With him were his wife Emma, their son Oscar, 10, daughters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie, and a baby, Jimmie. The family lived around Hagansport, a community that grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port and that by 1884 had about 150 people, four churches, a one-room school, a mill and a gin. Oscar, later Charles Oscar Smith, had been born there on 29 May 1889.

Emma Elizabeth Langley, called Emma Liza on her memorial, was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas. She was probably one of the two daughters, Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8, of George W. Langley, a Georgia-born widower of Precinct 5 in neighboring Hopkins County in 1880. She died on 15 March 1905, aged 37, and her stone in Hagansport Cemetery reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten." Six children were in the house in 1900, the youngest a baby.

John did not stay a widower. By April 1910 he had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. A few doors away lived John C. Satterfield, lately of Kentucky, with his wife Samantha and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in 1914. Owning rather than renting set John apart in the county: in 1900 only 44.1 percent of Franklin County farms were run by their owners, and the usual tenant gave up half the crop.

John B. Smith died in 1918 and was buried at Hagansport beside Emma; his grave is marked with a wooden stob. His father was very probably Noah Smith, a Kentucky-born farmer and justice of the peace whose 1880 household in the same Franklin County precinct included “John B. Smith, 20, son.” His mother is still unknown. His son Charles carried the farm tradition across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where he is buried at Grant.

Emma's marble stone at Hagansport gives her dates beneath "Emma / wife of / J. B. Smith" as "Born Dec 11 1869[?]" and "Died Mar 15 1905." The last digit of the birth year looks like a 9, two years later than the 1867 used here; her age of 12 in 1880 fits 1867 or 1868 better, so 1867 is kept.

P.name: Thomas Rogers & Ann Staples
P.title: Three wills from Quaker New Jersey
P.hook: A grandfather's will names Ann Staples, her husband Thomas Rogers, and their daughter Mary, who married into the Nordyke family.
body: Thomas Rogers married Ann Staples on 30 October 1736 at Upper Springfield Meeting in Burlington County, New Jersey. When Ann's father Thomas Staples wrote his will on 25 October 1758, he named his daughter "Ann, wife of Thomas Rogers" and his granddaughters "Mehetable and Mary Rogers." That Mary Rogers married Abraham Nordyke in 1761, which ties the Rogers family directly to the Nordykes.

John Rodgers of Burlington left his son Thomas one-third of the residue in a will dated 23 January 1764 and proved 26 March 1767. That son is probably Ann Staples's husband, but his wife is not named, so the identification is only probable. Ann's mother Mehitable was the daughter of Hananiah Gaunt of Springfield Township, whose 1720 will names "Mahitable Staples" and his son-in-law Thomas Staples.
The Staples and Gaunt wills name the relationships on Ann's side of the family. John Rodgers's will adds a probable connection on Thomas's side; though it does not by itself complete the link.

P.note: Ann is sometimes listed in online trees as "Ann Rogers (1714–1791)". Rogers was her married name; she was born Ann Staples. The probable identification of John Rodgers's son Thomas with Ann's husband is separate from the documented relationships named in the Staples and Gaunt wills.

body: Thomas Staples of Burlington, New Jersey, wrote his will on 25 October 1758, naming his daughter "Ann, wife of Thomas Rogers" and his granddaughters "Mehetable and Mary Rogers." His wife Mehitable was the daughter of Hananiah Gaunt of Springfield Township, whose 1720 will names "Mahitable Staples" and "son-in-law Thomas Staples." Ann married Thomas Rogers at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736.

An estate settled on 6 December 1748 may belong to the next generation: "Staples, Thomas, Jun'r, of Burlington Co., innholder" died without a will, and administration went to Thomas Rogers, the husband of Ann Staples, with John Deacon and John Antram of the City of Burlington as bondsmen. The inventory was only 30 pounds 7 shillings. If this Thomas Jr. was Ann's brother, it fits Thomas Rogers acting for the estate.
Granddaughter Mary Rogers married Abraham Nordyke on 1 June 1761.
P.title: Thomas Staples and Hananiah Gaunt's daughter
P.hook: Thomas Staples's will of 1758 names a daughter Ann and two granddaughters, and through one of them the line passes to the Nordykes.

P.name: John Rodgers
P.place: Burlington, New Jersey. His wife is said to have been a daughter of Martha Middleton, whose 1712 will names "son-in-law John Rogers" as executor.
kv: Dated 23 Jan 1764; proved 26 Mar 1767; son Thomas received one-third of the residue (published calendar abstract).
P.src: A. Van Doren Honeyman, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. IV, 1761–1770 (1928), pp. 360–361, John Rodgers of Burlington, will dated 23 Jan 1764, proved 26 Mar 1767; citing Lib. 13, p. 57. Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer04newj/page/360/mode/2up . Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. V, 1771–1780, p. 431, John Rogers of Windsor, will dated 6 Jan 1769, proved 10 Apr 1776; citing Lib. 17, p. 354. Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer05newj/page/431/mode/1up . Proposed earlier family: WikiTree Rogers-3993 and Rogers-3994; Martha Middleton’s 1712 will. The original manuscript wills have not been examined here.
body: John Rodgers of Burlington, New Jersey, made his will on 23 January 1764. He gave his son Thomas one-third of the residue. An inventory was made on 7 March 1767 and the will was proved on 26 March. The other thirds went to his daughter-in-law Elizabeth, then wife of William Lyndon, with her three daughters, and to the children of his daughter Martha, wife of Robert Hosier.

The son Thomas is taken in this family to be Thomas Rogers, who married Ann Staples at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736; their daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761. The will names Thomas but not his wife, and gives no name for John’s own wife or parents.

A proposed connection to Martha Middleton and to the John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary Groom is unproven. A different John Rogers of Windsor, Middlesex County, made a will on 6 January 1769 that was proved on 10 April 1776, naming sons Isaac, Abraham, Joseph, John, Robert, Amos and Mathew, and daughters Mary and Martha, but no Thomas. Those dates and beneficiaries distinguish the Windsor estate from the Burlington estate proved in 1767, though they do not show which family belongs to the 1687 birth.

One line of the will deserves more than it has had. John Rodgers left fifteen pounds each to “Martha, the wife of John Jones, and Hetteble Staples, daughters of my late daughter Mary Staples.” So a Rodgers daughter, Mary, had married into the Staples family before 1764 and died. That is the same Burlington County family Thomas Rogers married into when he took Ann Staples at Upper Springfield in 1736.

It also explains something nobody had asked about. When Thomas Staples Jr., an innkeeper, died in Burlington in December 1748 without a will, it was Thomas Rogers who took out administration, with John Deacon and John Antram as bondsmen. A brother-in-law could do that. If Thomas Jr. was Mary Rodgers’s husband, which nothing states, Thomas Rogers was his brother-in-law twice over, through Ann on one side and through his own sister Mary on the other. Either way, a Rodgers married a Staples within the same circle, which is what a Rodgers son marrying Ann Staples would look like.
P.title: John Rodgers and a third of the residue
P.hook: John Rodgers of Burlington left his son Thomas one-third of the residue in a will proved in March 1767.
P.note: Evidence stays probable. The will names Mary Staples’s daughters but not her husband, and nothing says Mary was married to Thomas Staples Jr.; that is a suggestion. What the new reading adds is a second Rodgers–Staples tie, which makes the identification of the testator’s son Thomas with Ann Staples’s husband more likely than the will alone did. Source for the sentence: Honeyman, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. IV (1928), p. 360, John Rodgers of Burlington, will dated 23 Jan 1764 (printed with the year misread in the OCR as ‘1704’; proved 26 Mar 1767, Lib. 13 p. 57); Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. II, Thomas Staples Jr. administration, Lib. 5 p. 547, 6 Dec 1748.

body: On 3 May 1678 Hananiah Gaunt posted his intention to marry Dorothy Butler, daughter of Thomas Butler of Sandwich, at the Sandwich Friends Meeting on Cape Cod. Dorothy had been born at Sandwich on 23 January 1649/50. The next day he and his brother Israel exchanged their Sandwich land for land in New Jersey. On 10 May they were married. His father Peter Gaunt, who had been fined in cattle by the Plymouth Colony court for Quaker meetings, is recorded as dying on 10 May 1678, the same day; one of the two dates is probably wrong. Dorothy's brother Daniel had been whipped for helping a Quaker in 1660.

The couple lived at Dartmouth, Massachusetts, until about 1685. On 11 May 1685 George Hutcheson of Burlington conveyed "to Hananiah Gaunt of Rhode Island, yeoman, for 500 acres in the First Tenth," and the proprietors' survey of July 1685 enters "500 a. near Honeonickon" (later Oneanickon, then Springfield Township). On 18 May 1687 "Hananiah Gaunt of near Oneanickon, yeoman," sold 100 acres to William Bustill, a carpenter of Shrewsbury, and in 1690 Hutcheson deeded him one twenty-fourth of a share of West Jersey, a proprietary right to land.

The 1685 deed calls him “of Rhode Island,” but a list of Dartmouth land owners for 1684-1694 carries his name, and a family history notes undivided Dartmouth land he deeded to William Ricketson on 13 January 1684. Both are later accounts, so this is probable.

He added to the farm. A later survey is entered for him “of 220 a. adjoining Samuel Houghton and Tho. Clark; incl. 9 a. of meadow on a brook near Mount Pisgah; 20 a. of the whole being an allowance for highways for other land.” A neighbor’s survey for Daniel Leeds of 188 acres at Oneanickon is described as lying beside “said Gaunts 9 a. lot,” the meadow ground on the brook.

The 1687 deed to Bustill describes the hundred acres as “N. grantor, E. Ralph Trenoweth, part of 500 a., bought of George Hutchinson May 11, 1685”: Hananiah’s own land lay on the north side and Ralph Trenoweth’s on the east. The West Jersey deed is dated 3 November 1690. It calls Hutcheson a distiller and Hananiah “of Burlington Co., yeoman,” and the share was one Hutcheson had bought of Godfrey Newbold of Handsworth, Yorkshire, on 22 August 1684, “excepting 200 acres.” A West Jersey share was a proprietary right to a portion of the province’s unsurveyed land, and such rights were bought and sold in England and Burlington before the land was laid out.

Surveys of his neighbors' land show him as a settled neighbor. Land "surveyed for William Biddle, at Oneanickon, 8th month, 1686, two hundred and seventy acres of land, and in 4th month, 1689, one tract of two hundred and thirty acres, and two other tracts, containing together three hundred and twenty-three acres" adjoined "lands of Hannaniah Gauntt, John Days, Peter Harvey, Charles Read, Samuel Barker, Daniel Leeds, Michael Buffin, John Browne, and John Shinn."

Dorothy died there on 26 April 1714 and is buried at Jobstown. Hananiah made his will on 17 July 1720, naming his children Daniel, Zebulon, Mahitable Staples and Mary Webb, and his son-in-law Thomas Staples; it was proved on 17 November 1721. His daughter Mehitable, born about 1685, married Thomas Staples, and her daughter Ann Staples, born in 1714, married Thomas Rogers in 1736, and Ann's daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761, so the farm at Hananicon is where this line's New Jersey roots begin.
Dorothy's birth date, her father's name and the Sandwich marriage are known only through later family accounts and not from the meeting record itself, so those points are probable.

P.name: Jacob Perkins Jr. & Sarah
P.place: Wellingborough (Willingboro), Burlington County, New Jersey. Parents of Rebecca, who married Henry Nordyke in 1731.
kv: Jacob Perkins Sr. dies intestate; inventory 91 pounds 18s 5d
Jacob Perkins Jr.'s will ("Wife, Sarah. Children ... Rebeckah ..."); proved 7 Dec; inventory 205 pounds 14s 6d
David Perkins's will ("Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike. Mother, Sarah Perkins."); proved 4 Mar 1731/2
P.src: Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Administrations, etc. (New Jersey Archives, 1st series), Perkins estates, 1731–32, Lib. 3 pp. 102 and 169 and Lib. 8 p. 184: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer01newj
body: In May 1731 administration of the estate of Jacob Perkins of "Wellenborrow," Burlington County, who died without a will, went to his son Jacob Perkins, yeoman. The inventory, made on 20 May by Robert Lucas and Joseph Fenimore, comes to 91 pounds 18 shillings 5 pence and "includes cane and sword, £1.10; debt of 14 shillings from Benja. Perkins; 8 years rent due from Benja. Perkins and Wm. Makintass, £1."

The son, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his own will on 26 October 1731. He left his wife Sarah and his children "Abraham, Rebeckah, David, Mary, Ann, Susannah, Hannah, Sarah, Bethseda and Martha." He disposed of "land in Chester, which I bought of John Ward March 15, 1728," and listed bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He also left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington, the Church of England parish, which points to Church of England ties. His son David was executor and the witnesses were Joseph Fenimore, Eliza Fenimore and Sam. Scattergood. The will was proved on 7 December 1731, and the inventory of 6 December, by Fenimore and Scattergood, was 205 pounds 14 shillings 6 pence.

Henry Nordyke had married Rebecca Perkins at Willingboro on 6 January 1731, the same year. He appears in her father's will as a man who owed him money. Then David died too. His will, made in January 1731/2 "of Wellingborrow, yeoman," leaves his brother Abraham "plantation in Wellingburrow, which came to me by will of my father, Jacob Perkins, dated Oct. 26, 1731," and names his "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and "Mother, Sarah Perkins." It was witnessed by Joseph Fenimore, Sam'l Scattergood and Henry Nordike, and was proved on 4 March 1731/2.

So within about a year the Perkins household of Willingboro lost a grandfather, a father and a son, and the new son-in-law Henry Nordyke witnessed the last of the wills. Henry and Rebecca's descendants are the Nordykes of the family tree. Abraham, to whom David left the plantation, was also his executor.
P.title: A cane and a sword
P.hook: Wills and inventories from 1731–32 trace three generations of a Perkins family and their connection to the Nordykes.

P.src: Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 3 p. 102. Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 3 p. 102; Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 3 p. 169 (will of Jacob Perkins Jr.); Willingboro Township, New Jersey (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willingboro_Township,_New_Jersey)
body: Jacob Perkins lived at "Wellenborrow," which is Wellingborough in Burlington County, New Jersey, a township first laid out as the Constabulary of Wellingborrow on 6 November 1688 and named for the English town that Thomas Olive, who led the first settlers there, had come from. Jacob died without a will, and in May 1731 administration of his estate went to his son Jacob Perkins, yeoman.

The inventory, made on 20 May by Robert Lucas and Joseph Fenimore, comes to 91 pounds 18 shillings 5 pence and includes "cane and sword, £1.10; debt of 14 shillings from Benja. Perkins; 8 years rent due from Benja. Perkins and Wm. Makintass, £1." The sword is the item that stands out in a farm inventory, and what it says about him is not known. The rent owed over eight years suggests he had let land or a house to those two men, though the entry does not say which.

The son who took on the estate lived only a few months longer. Jacob Jr. made his own will on 26 October 1731, and his son David died by January 1731/2. Jacob Sr.'s granddaughter Rebecca married Henry Nordyke in the winter of 1731/2 (a license is dated 6 January 1731/2), and their descendants are the Nordykes of this tree. Jacob Jr.'s will left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church in Burlington, the Church of England parish, so this branch seems to have belonged to the Church of England rather than to the Quaker meetings of the Nordykes and Gaunts.

Some trees make Jacob Perkins Jr. the son of a Jacob Perkins of Hampton, New Hampshire, who married Mary Philbrick in 1669, but nothing shows that Hampton man moved to New Jersey, so that line stays out of the family tree. Jacob Sr.'s own birth, wife and parents are not known.
P.title: Jacob Perkins, who died without a will
P.hook: Jacob Perkins of Wellingborough died in 1731 without a will; his inventory lists a cane and a sword.

P.name: Sarah (Cole) Chamness
P.title: A murder trial in early Maryland
P.hook: Anthony Chamness's wife came from a Baltimore County family whose patriarch was murdered.
body: Anthony Chamness, the London boy indentured to Maryland, married Sarah Cole on 24 November 1735. Her father Joseph Cole had died young: his will, written 22 January 1720/1 in Baltimore County, names his wife Susanna and his little daughter Sarah. Nearly fifty years later her uncle William Cole's 1769 will still called her "dau. and heir of testator's bro. Joseph." The Quaker meeting at Cane Creek in North Carolina named her as "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole."

Joseph was the son of John Cole and Johanna (Hannah) Garrett. Johanna's father, Dennis Garrett, was murdered. John Cole testified at the trial of a Captain John Oldton for the killing of his father-in-law.

Dennis's widow Barbara remarried, to a Broad (John in most records; Marye calls him Thomas). In August 1712, as Barbara Garrett Broad, she deeded property to "her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole, s. of John and Hannah Cole," a boy named for the grandfather he never knew.

quotes.t: Sarah, dau. and heir of testator's bro. Joseph.
quotes.c: Will of William Cole, 1769

P.note: The murder trial and the 1712 deed come from Robert Barnes's Baltimore County Families, which abstracts court and land records; the original court papers have not been seen yet.
P.src: Will of Joseph Cole, 22 Jan 1720/1; will of William Cole, 1769; Cane Creek Monthly Meeting records; Barnes, Baltimore County Families 1659–1759 (Cole and Garrett entries; deed of Aug 1712).

P.name: Charles Davies & Hannah Matson
P.place: Quakers. Married in February 1733 under a Radnor Monthly Meeting certificate, Pennsylvania, which places the wedding at the house of Charles Read, a Philadelphia justice of the peace, and settled at Cane Creek, North Carolina, about 1751. Charles died in 1801 and Hannah in 1812.
P.src: Radnor MM marriage certificate (1732/3); Davis, Davis: A Quaker Family (1985); Hinshaw vol. 1; U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Cane Creek MM minutes, 6 Dec 1766); Cane Creek Monthly Meeting minutes, 6 December 1766, manuscript page 36, U.S. Quaker Meeting Records, 1681–1935.
body: At Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 6 December 1766, Charles Davies came before Friends as a disciplinary matter. His complaint concerned the women's minutes: he had charged them with being mixed with an untruth. What passage he disputed, and his side of the argument, were not written down; only what the meeting decided to do about it was.

Friends had already made repeated efforts to change his mind. The meeting found that the labor had been to no purpose, and it disowned him. The same day, ordinary business went on around the dispute: certificates of membership, a marriage report and appointments to attend the quarterly meeting. The break with Charles was set down in the same practical way as those routine decisions.

Charles and Hannah Matson Davies had raised the family from which Mary Davies married William Moffitt in 1763. Charles owned 187 acres purchased in 1758 and was recorded as a minister in 1761. The 1766 decision was a rupture within that Quaker community, though it does not mean that he left North Carolina or ceased to believe. He lived until 1801. His daughter Mary's own will, written more than fifty years after the dispute, still used the numbered-month date familiar in Quaker records.
P.note: The original meeting page proves the complaint, unsuccessful repeated intervention and disownment. It does not explain which entry was disputed or prove that the women's minutes were false. Overall family relationships retain the prior probable evidence level.
kv: Disowned by Cane Creek Monthly Meeting, 6 Dec 1766

imgs.cap: Cane Creek Monthly Meeting minutes, 6 December 1766: the meeting disowns Charles Davies for accusing the women's minute of an untruth.

P.title: The charge against the women's minutes
P.hook: In December 1766, Cane Creek Friends expelled Charles Davies after a dispute over the truth of the women's meeting record.

P.name: Edward Norton & Elizabeth Brown
P.place: Margaret's 1763 marriage certificate names her parents as Edward and Elizabeth Norton of Rowan County. They were very likely the Edward Norton and Elizabeth Brown married at West Nottingham Meeting on 16 October 1739, who moved to Hopewell Meeting in Virginia, then Fairfax, and came to Cane Creek in 1762. Edward died in 1776 and is buried at Providence, Randolph County.
P.src: Cane Creek MM marriage certificate (1763); Nottingham MM records (Cecil Co., Md.); Hinshaw vol. 1; U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Nottingham MM, marriage of Edward Norton and Elizabeth Brown, 16 Oct 1739) Gilbert Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864), p. 8 (children of William Brown 12 and Elizabeth Cowgill); Albert Cook Myers, Immigration of the Irish Quakers into Pennsylvania (1902), p. 376
body: Their marriage on 16 October 1739 was recorded by the Nottingham Quakers in a few lines. The bridegroom was Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of the late Edward Norton of the Parish of Armagh in the Kingdom of Ireland. The bride was Elizabeth Brown, "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec." She had been born in the twelfth month of 1718, early 1719 by modern reckoning. Her mother died before her father married again in March 1721/2, and her father, William Brown Jr., died about 1727; her stepmother, Margaret Davis, then married William Kirk. Her grandfather, the emigrant William Brown, was an elder of the meeting.

Edward's own connections were tangled with hers from the start. His sister Mary Norton had married Elizabeth's uncle Richard Brown in November 1733, and both couples took certificates to Hopewell Monthly Meeting in Virginia, Edward and Elizabeth on 19 January 1739/40. Richard died before 1747, and when Fairfax meeting looked into the settlement of his will to protect his children, Mary married William Kirk, the widower of the same Margaret Davis who had been Elizabeth's stepmother.

From Hopewell the Nortons went on to Fairfax and then south. They reached Cane Creek in 1762, and the next March their daughter Margaret, born about 1740, married Joseph Chamness. The certificate calls the bride's parents "Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County," and both signed as witnesses. Edward died in 1776 and is buried at Providence, Randolph County. Their granddaughter Martha married Robert Moffitt in 1797, which is how an orphan from West Nottingham and a family from Armagh come into the Moffitt story.
kv: Born 12th month 1718 (early 1719), daughter of William Brown Jr. and Elizabeth Cowgill; orphaned by about 1727
16 Oct 1739, West Nottingham Meeting, Chester Co., Pa. (Nottingham Monthly Meeting certificate)
Took a certificate to Hopewell MM, Virginia, 19 Jan 1739/40
Of Rowan County; signed daughter Margaret's marriage certificate as witnesses

P.title: Married as an orphan at West Nottingham: Elizabeth Brown and Edward Norton
P.hook: Elizabeth Brown was about eight when her father died. At twenty she married a Quaker born in Ireland, and their road ended at Cane Creek.

P.name: John Matson of Merion
P.place: A Quaker farmer of Merion, Pennsylvania. His daughter Hannah's 1733 marriage certificate calls her "daughter of John Matson of Merion" and says she married with his consent. Buried at Radnor in 1748.
P.src: Radnor MM marriage certificate (1732/3); Haverford MM minutes. WikiTree Matson-27 and Matson-13, citing Swarthmore College Quaker Meeting Records (Radnor MM; Philadelphia YM) and the Chester County estate papers; Craig, The Mattson & Dalbo Families of West Jersey, Swedish Colonial News 2:2 (2000); Walmsley, Genealogy of the Mattson Family (1983)
P.title: John Matson of Merion, and the daughter who married at a justice's house
P.hook: John Matson gave his consent in February 1733 for his daughter Hannah to marry Charles Davis; their daughter Mary married William Moffitt at Cane Creek.
body: John Matson comes into view through his daughter's marriage. In the twelfth month of 1732, by the Friends' count, Charles Davis of Blockley (Davies in the Cane Creek records) and Hannah Matson, "daughter of John Matson of Merion in the same county and province aforesaid with consent of her father," published their intentions under a Pennsylvania law against clandestine marriages and met at the house of Charles Read, Esq., a justice of the peace for Philadelphia. The witnesses were John Matson Jr. and Daniel Matson, probably Hannah's brothers, along with Evan and Jane George, Richard and Thomas George, Ellin Jones and Mary Andrew. Hannah was born about 1715.

John was a Quaker farmer of Merion, in the Welsh settlement west of Philadelphia. By the usual reckoning he was born about 1686 at Upper Merion and married a woman named Margaret before 1709. Their children were Daniel, Hannah, Morris, Catherine, John, Peter and Joseph. Matson is a Swedish name, and Swedes had farmed along the Schuylkill and the Delaware before Penn's grant, but nothing makes him a son of the Swede Johann Mattson; his parentage is undocumented. In 1742 he and his wife took a certificate from Chester Monthly Meeting to Goshen.

John Matson was buried on 3 May 1748, and his will was proved in Chester County on 16 July 1748. By then his daughter Hannah and Charles Davis had left Pennsylvania for Virginia and then Cane Creek, North Carolina, where Charles was disowned by the meeting in 1766 and died in 1801; Hannah lived until 25 October 1812. Their daughter Mary married William Moffitt there on 2 April 1763, sixteen days after the Chamness-Norton wedding, and her son Robert married Martha Chamness in 1797. John Matson of Merion is Robert Moffitt's great-grandfather on his mother's side.

P.name: Joseph Cole & Susanna
P.place: Baltimore County, Maryland.
kv: 22 Jan 1720/1, names wife Susanna and daughter Sarah
Nov 1712: his father John conveyed him part of "Daniel's Whimsey"
Born 5-1-1718 (Friends' register); m. Anthony Chamness 24 Nov 1735, St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore Co.; thirteen children; d. about 1773
P.src: Will of Joseph Cole; Barnes, Baltimore County Families. Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922), on Sarah Cole and the Chamness farm
P.title: Joseph Cole's will, and the two-year-old who became Sarah Chamness
P.hook: Joseph Cole made his will on 22 January 1720/1, leaving a widow and a daughter, Sarah, not yet three, who later married Anthony Chamness.
body: Joseph Cole of Baltimore County, Maryland, was the son of John Cole and Johanna Garrett. In November 1712 his father conveyed him part of a tract called "Daniel's Whimsey." His mother's father was Dennis Garrett, the early settler killed in 1691.

He made his will on 22 January 1720/1, and it names his wife Susanna and his daughter Sarah. Sarah was born on the 1st day of the 5th month 1718 in the Friends' register, so when her father wrote the will she was not yet three. The Cane Creek register later wrote her down as the "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole, of Baltimore Co., Md., now married to Anthony Chainness."

On 24 November 1735 Sarah married Anthony Chamness at St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County. Anthony, a London-born servant who had finished his indenture, was about twenty-two, and she was seventeen. They went to Monocacy, then to Carver's Creek in 1749 and Cane Creek in 1751, and Sarah bore thirteen children. A family history describes their farm, a mile west of the Cane Creek meetinghouse: a hewn-oak log house with a porch the length of the front, a grist mill on a small creek and large meadows on either side. Sarah died about 1773 and is buried in the Friends' graveyard at Cane Creek. Her son Joseph Chamness married Margaret Norton, and their daughter Martha was Robert Moffitt's wife.

P.name: John Cole & Johanna Garrett
P.place: Baltimore County, Maryland. John testified at the trial for the murder of his father-in-law Dennis Garrett.
P.src: Barnes, Baltimore County Families: "COLE, JOSEPH (6), s. of John (5) and Johanna". William B. Marye, 'The Baltimore County Garrison and the Old Garrison Roads,' Maryland Historical Magazine 16:2-3 (1921), pp. 115-119, 214-242; William B. Marye, "The Baltimore County ‘Garrison’ and the Old Garrison Roads," Maryland Historical Magazine 16:2 (June 1921), pp. 118-119, and 16:3 (September 1921), pp. 214, 218, 242.
body: John Cole was a witness when his wife's father was killed. The court's 1692 indictment of John Oldton for the sword blow that killed Dennis Garrett listed these witnesses: Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, "John Cole (son-in-law of the deceased)," Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett, the widow. John had married Dennis's daughter Johanna. Oldton was condemned to hang and was pardoned; he later served as captain of the county's rangers. John Cole was then about twenty-two.

The records that follow are surveys. Surveys list "Cole's Choice," surveyed for him on 28 July 1694 and never patented; "Cole's Addition," 67 acres surveyed on 29 May 1698 "on the north side of Patapsco River in the woods"; and "Cole's Adventure," surveyed in 1706 on a run called Gwin's Run. In March 1737/8, when a land commission sat on Cole's Adventure, "John Cole, Senior, aged about 67 years," testified that the beginning tree stood about a hundred yards east of Gwinn's Run.

Cole’s Choice was later taken up again under the name “Orange,” and the same survey appears as “Cole’s Chance,” with a deed from John Cole to Robert Green dated 1702. Cole’s Addition lay beside the path called Darley Path, where Chase Street and the Bel Air Road now cross in Baltimore. The 1737/8 commission on Cole’s Adventure was held by Thomas Demmett.

In August 1750 another commission took depositions about Cole's Addition from men who had known him. John Ensor, Sr., aged 55, called him his father-in-law and said that about eighteen years earlier, around 1732, Cole had come with him to the spot and shown him where the boundary oak stood. William Green, aged 58, told the same story: “the aforesaid John Cole said there should have been a bounded tree of Coles Addition.” Ensor was born about 1695, and the Ensor family is counted among the descendants of Dennis Garrett. By then Cole had died, in 1746, at about seventy-six. His land lay in and around the site of Baltimore, which was laid out as a town in 1729.

The family is easy to follow. His son Joseph made a will in 1720/1 and left a daughter, Sarah, who married Anthony Chamness in 1735; a son named Dennis Garrett Cole received land from his grandmother Barbara Garrett Broad in 1712. Sarah's son Joseph Chamness was the father of Martha, who married Robert Moffitt in 1797.
kv: Named "John Cole (son-in-law of the deceased)" in the 1692 indictment for Dennis Garrett's death
Cole's Choice (1694), Cole's Addition (1698, 67 acres), Cole's Adventure (1706)

P.hook: John Cole was about twenty-two when he was named as a witness in the Garrett case, and about sixty-seven when he gave evidence on the bounds of his own land in 1738.

P.name: William Brown & Ann Mercer
P.place: William Brown came from England in 1682 and was one of the first settlers of the Nottingham Quaker settlement on the Pennsylvania–Maryland line. Ann was his second wife.
P.src: Maryland Quaker Records: Nottingham Monthly Meeting; WikiTree Brown-2504 and Mercer-123, citing Wellingborough MM and Northamptonshire QM registers Gilbert Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864), pp. 6-8 (children of William Brown and Ann Mercer; marriages of William and of his sons); Bi-centennial of Brick Meeting-House (1902), pp. 33-43; Wellingborough Monthly Meeting, original birth register, TNA RG6/1380, image 20 of 150, first entry: Willyam Browne, son of Richard Browne, born the 29th day of the first month 1658 (29 March, Old Style); https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/7097/images/41815_b0153703-00019?pId=524194. The entry does not name a mother.; Ringwood Quaker birth register, TNA RG6/1027, Ancestry image 18 of 206, stamped 00011, handwritten p. 6: Ann Mercer, daughter of Thomas and Ann Mercer of Ringwood, born the 24th day of the 12th month 1666; original visually reviewed, https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/7097/images/41815_b0153345-00017?pId=452488. Old Style date 24 February 1666/7 (1667 in modern year numbering); no Gregorian day conversion implied.; Catalogue of Eighty-Seven Public Friends, read at the Yearly Meeting in 1709, printed transcription of Devonshire House manuscript, London, Portfolio 8:89, reprinted in The Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine 31, no. 2 (1979), pp. 114 (editorial explanation of Public Friends), 119–120 (Chester County list); Thomas Mercer and Anne Browne appear on p. 120 (PDF p. 30), https://genpa.org/wp-content/uploads/publications/pennsylvania-genealogical-magazine/PGM-Volume-31-Number-2.pdf#page=30. Printed transcription independently examined; manuscript not examined.
body: Ann Mercer, daughter of Thomas and Ann Mercer of Ringwood, was born on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666: 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. That she was the Ann Mercer who became William Brown’s second wife in Pennsylvania is probable. Later accounts place Thomas at Andover before he and his daughter crossed to Pennsylvania about 1682–83 and settled in Aston Township, Chester County. William was born on the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658 (29 March, Old Style), the son of Richard Browne; his mother is not named. William had married Dorothy in England, and their son Joseph was born there on 12 June 1682. Dorothy died at sea on the voyage to the Delaware. William went first to his brother James, a weaver at Marcus Hook, and in 1684, when Ann was seventeen, he married her.

The Nottingham Quaker registers give the children Ann bore him: Mercer, born the 27th of the 12th month 1685; Ann, 1st of the 10th month 1687; William, 21st of the 7th month 1689; John, 3rd of the 5th month 1691; Richard, 31st of the 1st month 1693; and Thomas, 17th of the 11th month 1694. Mercer, named for her family and often written "Messer," was the first. Ann Mercer died in 1696; a 1709 Quaker list of deceased Friends names her as "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer." Her father Thomas had died on 22 November 1694, eight weeks before her youngest, Thomas Brown, was born in January 1695.

In 1709 the Yearly Meeting remembered Anne Browne among the deceased Public Friends, the people who spoke in meeting. She was named as Thomas Mercer’s daughter, had crossed with her father, received a Testimony for Truth after arriving, and was buried in 1696. This preserves a part of her life beyond the names and dates of her children.

William married Catharine Williams of Philadelphia in 1699, and in 1702 he moved to the Nottingham Lots on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line, where Lots 23 and 33 were assigned to him. A history of the Brick Meeting House says that he "was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots" and that the first meeting was held at his house in 1704. The meeting records put it a little later: Concord Monthly Meeting received the request for a meeting at his house in the 2nd month of 1705, and Concord Quarterly Meeting approved it on 9 April 1705, so meetings were held there by 1705. His fourth wife, whom he married in 1711, was Mary Matthews. A family memorandum of 1786 calls him an elder and a substantial Friend, and puts his death on the 23rd of the 6th month 1746 (23 August, Old Style) in his ninety-first year (another account gives 1 October 1746); the Wellingborough register, which gives his birth in 1658, would make him about eighty-eight.

Ann Mercer’s descendants connect several branches of the family. Her sons William and Thomas married the Cowgill sisters Elizabeth and Ellin; her son Richard married three times and ended with Mary Norton of Armagh in 1733; and William's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Mary's brother Edward Norton in 1739. Their daughter Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Ann Mercer is Martha Chamness's great-great-grandmother, and so the ancestor of every child Martha bore Robert Moffitt.

23rd of 6th month 1746 (23 Aug, O.S.), West Nottingham, by the 1786 family memorandum; 1 Oct 1746 in another account

P.title: Ann Mercer’s six children and her Quaker ministry
P.hook: Ann Mercer bore six children with William Brown and was remembered among the Friends who spoke in meeting.
P.note: The original English birth entry names Richard as father and leaves the mother unnamed. The child’s identification with the later Pennsylvania emigrant remains probable. The Old Style date is retained; no Gregorian day conversion is implied. Ann Mercer’s original Ringwood birth entry names Thomas and Ann as parents; identifying that English child with the Pennsylvania wife remains probable. The elder Ann’s maiden surname is unknown. The 1709 catalog directly names the immigrant Anne Browne as Thomas Mercer’s daughter and was independently read in a later printed transcription; its original manuscript has not been examined. This corroborates the immigrant father-daughter relationship, while the identification with the Ringwood birth family remains probable.

P.name: Dennis & Barbara Garrett
P.place: Baltimore County, Maryland. Dennis was murdered; Barbara later married John Broad of Broad's Choice on Herring Run.
kv: Bought with Thomas Stone; the tract on the site of Fell's Point (Marye, 1921)
2 Sept 1691, of a sword blow given 30/31 July (court record)
Oldton's execution stayed 11 Apr 1692 by the Governor and Council (Archives of Maryland, vol. 8, p. 314)
Aug 1712: Barbara Garrett Broad to her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole
173 acres on Herring Run, patented 10 Nov 1695 by John Broad, Barbara's second husband; he died Jan 1709, and Barbara d. 1733
P.src: William B. Marye, “The Baltimore County Garrison and the Old Garrison Roads,” Maryland Historical Magazine 16:2 (June 1921), pp. 115–116 and note 18, quoting Provincial Court Proceedings Judgments, Liber D. S. No. C, 1692–1693, folio 15; Archives of Maryland, vol. 8, p. 314 (11 Apr 1692 council stay); “The Gorsuch and Lovelace Families,” Virginia Magazine of History and Biography 24:4 (Oct. 1916), p. 438; Barnes, Baltimore County Families; will of John Broad, 1702; Herring Run Park History, "The Broad Family, 1692-1709," Herring Run Archaeology Project (herringrunarchaeology.org/park-history/the-broad-family-ownership/), citing Maryland State Archives records, read 4 Nov 2026.
body: Dennis Garrett was one of the first settlers on the site of Baltimore. With Thomas Stone he bought "Long Island Point," a tract surveyed for William Poultney on the site of what became Fell's Point, and his descendants are numerous through the Cole, Gorsuch and Ensor families. He and his wife Barbara had a daughter, Johanna, who married John Cole.

Dennis died on 2 September 1691, weeks after being struck on the forehead with a sword. John Oldton, a Baltimore County tailor, was indicted for the assault. The indictment gives the attack as 31 July, yet says Dennis languished from 30 July until his death; the two dates are inconsistent.

The witnesses included Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, John Cole, Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett. Cole was the husband of Dennis’s daughter Johanna; Barbara was his widow. Oldton was condemned to be hanged, but the Governor and Council ordered a stay on 11 April 1692 and a royal pardon followed. He became captain of the county rangers in 1694/5.
A later account describes the death as the result of an affray.

Barbara married again within the year, to John Broad, who had come to Maryland in 1670 or earlier as an indentured servant brought over by Henry Hosier. The only land he ever bought was Broad's Choice, 173 acres along both banks of Herring Run, which he patented on 10 November 1695, in what is now Herring Run Park in Baltimore. After Dennis died, Thomas Stone had given his interest in Long Island Point to Barbara; she left the point and carried her three Garrett children to the farm on the Run, where she raised two more, Thomas and Jane. John Broad was listed in the 1692 tax list with John Cole as a near neighbor. When he died in January 1709 the inventory showed a modest household: two feather beds, pewter and earthenware, a very old horse, twelve cows, five steers, a bull, some ailing pigs and about 4,000 pounds of tobacco hanging in the sheds. The family signed with marks. His will, written about 1702, left Broad's Choice to Thomas and Jane, and Barbara ran the farm for them while they were minors. In August 1712 she signed herself "Barbara Broad of Back River" and gave her property to her children and grandchildren, among them her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole. She died in 1733. The family line runs through Johanna to her son Joseph Cole and his daughter Sarah, who married Anthony Chamness.
P.title: Dennis Garrett of Long Island Point, struck with a sword in 1691
P.hook: Dennis Garrett helped buy the point that became Fell's Point, was struck on the forehead on 31 July 1691, and lingered until 2 September.

P.name: John & Ann Chamness
P.place: East Smithfield, London. Parents of Anthony Chamness.
kv: 4 Jan 1704, St John of Wapping, London (Ann Weary)
"Anthony Chamness, s. John & Ann, b. about 2 mo. 1713, Est. Smithfield, London" (Cane Creek Meeting)
From Wapping to East Smithfield by 1713
9 Feb 1724/5: bound seven years to John Cooke, London victualler, for Maryland
P.note: Ann's maiden name is often given as Jones in online trees, but no record has been found for it.
P.src: Cane Creek Monthly Meeting birth register; Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. I; WikiTree Chamness-25 and Chamness-8, citing the London Metropolitan Archives register of St John of Wapping Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness of London, England (1922); Cane Creek MM register; London Metropolitan Archives, St John of Wapping parish registers (via WikiTree Chamness-25 and Chamness-8); the Anthony Chamness indenture, as cited on this site
body: John Chamness and Ann Weary were married on 4 January 1704 at St John's Church, Wapping, the riverside parish beside the Thames, east of the Tower. The parish clerk spelled the name "Chamniss," and Ann's surname Weary or Wearey. Trees that call her Ann Jones have nothing behind them. Their children came steadily: at least eight between 1705 and 1717, baptized in the same parish. Anthony, the one who matters here, was baptized in February 1713 when he was eighteen days old. Cane Creek Meeting later wrote him down as "Anthony Chamness, s. John & Ann, b. about 2 mo. 1713, Est. Smithfield, London," so the family lived at East Smithfield, close to Wapping.

Anthony was bound as a servant on 9 February 1724/5. The indenture, which describes him as of Whitechapel, bound him for seven years to John Cooke, a London victualler, for service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)." It gives his age as fifteen; counted from his baptism he was about eleven. Either way he was out of his time by 1732 and was in Baltimore County, where on 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole, the great-granddaughter of the murdered Dennis Garrett.

John and Ann are the founders of the American Chamness line, and they leave only the parish registers: no will, no trade and no death date. Their son, the boy sent to Maryland at the age of eleven or fifteen, became overseer of the Cane Creek meeting and in 1751 took up 490 acres there.
P.title: Chamniss of Wapping: the London parents of a boy bound for Maryland
P.hook: John Chamness married Ann Weary at St John's, Wapping, in January 1704; twenty years later their son Anthony was bound as a servant for seven years in Maryland.

P.name: James Henry Satterfield & Melissa Gibson
P.title: James Satterfield's own account of his family
P.hook: James Satterfield told the story of three generations of his family, and it was printed in 1885.
body: In 1885 a history of Kentucky printed short biographies of farmers and businessmen county by county. One was of James H. Satterfield, then of Butler County, and it reads like his own account of the family.

It says his father, Henry Satterfield, was a native of Maury County, Tennessee, and died in 1861. Henry married Mary, daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County. Henry was the son of Ephraim Satterfield, "a native of Virginia, who died about 1850."

James married Melissa A. Gibson, "daughter of James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson, of Allen County." They were married in Allen County on 17 September 1859. Their children were Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C. John C., born in February 1864, is our John C. Satterfield, who later farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County. Melissa died in 1877.

After Melissa died in 1877, James married Lucinda Belle Phelps on 2 June 1878 in Butler County. They had nine children between 1879 and 1899. Several of those half-siblings of John C. married in Bowie County, Texas, or nearby Arkansas between 1909 and 1917, and James himself died in Bowie County on 24 November 1922 (the sheet also gives 1924).

His account says more than the family papers do. James "was born April 14, 1838, in Allen County, Ky., where he grew to manhood. In 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky, and located in Warren County. In 1876 he settled in Butler County, where he has since resided." James spent eight years in Minnesota; if the family went with him, John C. was three when they left and eleven when they came back.

He described his war service as brief: "In 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service." He dated his first marriage to "September 15, 1859," two days before the 17 September of the county's marriage register, named his second wife as Lucinda B., "daughter of Solomon and Sarah J. (Deweese) Phelps, of this county," and listed the three children of that marriage, Martha B., Alonzo T. and Minnie E.

He was 23 that year, a young farmer in Allen County, and his father died the same year. The 9th Kentucky Infantry was organized at Camp Boyle, Adair County, and mustered in for three years on 20 November 1861; its first winter was spent in camp at Columbia, Kentucky, until it marched for Bowling Green and Nashville on 15 February 1862. If James joined in the autumn of 1861, his three months fit that camp period. His account does not say whether he was discharged, detailed or transferred, and his service has not been matched to a roster. The regiment went on to Shiloh, Corinth, Perryville (in reserve), Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge, the Atlanta campaign and Jonesboro, and mustered out on 15 December 1864. Its dead numbered 357: 8 officers and 96 enlisted men killed or mortally wounded, and 3 officers and 250 enlisted men dead of disease. Butler County, where James settled in 1876, put up a veterans’ monument on the courthouse lawn in 1907 to the soldiers of both armies, described as one of two such Kentucky monuments.
By 1885 he was well off for a farmer: "Mr. Satterfield is a farmer, and owns 1,340 acres of land, where he now resides, and 425 acres in Tennessee."

Melissa died on 2 May 1877. James's birth is given elsewhere as 14 April 1837, and he died on 28 November 1922 at Redwater in Bowie County and was buried at Reed Cemetery. A daughter, A. M., was born in Minnesota in 1870, and a son, James Doiser, in Allen County in February 1867.

No James H. Satterfield appears on the rolls of any Kentucky Union regiment, which does not disprove his account of three months' service. His Minnesota years, on the other hand, are borne out: a James H. Satterfield was the first director of School District No. 95 in Marshan Township, Dakota County, in 1874.

P.name: Henry Satterfield & Mary Garrison
P.place: Henry was born in Maury County, Tennessee, and died in 1861. Mary (1811–1896) was a daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County, Kentucky.
P.src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885); Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County, p. 676; WikiTree Garrison-4365 and Cannon-4655; Garrison et al. v. Clark et al., 151 Ky. 565 (1913); Acts of the General Assembly of Kentucky, session of 1847-48, ch. 600, sec. 6, p. 410, approved 29 Feb 1848: https://archive.org/details/actspassedatses72kentgoog (read 3 Nov 2026). WikiTree Satterfield-568 and Garrison-5361 (death register 24 Dec 1861).; Find a Grave memorial 153803198 (Mary Cannon Garrison Satterfield, Big Springs Cemetery, Lineville, Wayne Co., Iowa), headstone photographs by BlueSkies and portrait posted by Linda Fitzgerald Alexander; linked memorials 65255165, 198808680, 16538594, 17756438, 142911548 and 156286215
body: His son James described him in one sentence: "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years." His death was entered on 24 December 1861, with his parents given as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield. He was born about 1811, two years after Ephraim Satterfield married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Maury County is where the sketch places the young couple. His son James was born in Allen County on 14 April 1838.

Henry married Mary Garrison, born 17 October 1811, the daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County and, it is said, of Martha "Patsey" Cannon. Their twelve children were Louisa J. (Roy), David E., Samuel A., James H., Ruth M. (Massey), John E., Euphema P. (Liles), Hettie C. (Jones), Martha C. (deceased), Sarah E. (Hues), Joseph W. H. and Abraham W. Of the twelve, James H., born in 1838, married Melissa Gibson in 1859 and is the line to the Smiths. In 1861, the year his father died, James enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky, and an S. A. Satterfield, perhaps their son Samuel A., was sued with A. W. Garrison in 1871 in Warren Circuit Court over a lot in Bowling Green, though the court gave only initials.

Mary's parents' marriage ended in the legislature. By an act approved on 29 February 1848 the Kentucky General Assembly dissolved the marriage of her father John M. Garrison and Patsey; Mary was then 36. She outlived Henry by thirty-five years and died on 2 March 1896.

Mary did not die in Kentucky. Her stone stands in Big Springs Cemetery at Lineville, in Wayne County, Iowa, just north of the Missouri line, and reads: "M. C. Satterfield / Died / Mar 2, 1896 / Age 84 Ys 4 Ms 16 Ds." Counting back from the age gives a birth in mid-October 1811, which matches the 17 October 1811 birth given for Mary Garrison, and the initials fit Mary Cannon. Her memorial names John Milton Garrison as her father. No one knows when or why she went to Iowa.

Her children's graves show how far the family spread. Her children lie far afield: Samuel Addison (1835-1913) at Strawn in Palo Pinto County, Texas; James Henry (1837-1922) at Reed Cemetery in Bowie County, Texas; Ruth Melissa Massey (1840-1935) at Llano Cemetery in Amarillo; Euphema Lyles (1845-1922) near Stephenville in Erath County, Texas; Hettie Caroline Jones (1847-1907) at LeGrande in Hart County, Kentucky; and Abraham W. (1860-1933), the youngest, at Eldora in Hardin County, Iowa.

A studio portrait of her, captioned "Age 78," would date to about 1889 or 1890 if the caption is right. It shows an elderly woman in a dark dress and a ruffled, lace-trimmed cap. Who identified the sitter is not known, so the identification rests on the caption.

P.name: James & Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson
P.place: Allen County, Kentucky. Parents of Melissa A. (Gibson) Satterfield.
P.src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885). Allen County, Ky., marriage register, 1859; Find a Grave (Melissa Satterfield, d. 2 May 1877).
P.title: James and Cynthia Gibson of Allen County, Melissa's parents
P.hook: Two names from a county history, and the daughter who married a Satterfield in 1859.
body: James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson are named once, in the account James H. Satterfield of Butler County gave of himself in 1885: Melissa A., his first wife, was the "daughter of James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson, of Allen County." Melissa married James Satterfield in Allen County on 17 September 1859.

Allen County, created in 1815 from Warren and Barren, was where both families lived. Melissa and James had children together; their children were Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C., among them John C., born in February 1864. In 1867 the Satterfields left for Dakota County, Minnesota, and returned in 1875 to Warren County and then, in 1876, Butler County. Melissa died on 2 May 1877, the year after the move. A fire at the Allen County courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records.

Melissa's son John C. Satterfield farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County and moved to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907. His daughter Artie Pearl Satterfield married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914, and their daughter Faye (Smith) Moffitt is the link to this family.

P.name: Ephraim Satterfield
P.place: A native of Virginia, as his grandson told it in 1885.
P.src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885); WikiTree Satterfield-568, Satterfield-20 and Knowles-2027 Warren Co., Ky., Will Book D p. 262 (John Satterfield, proved 10 Nov 1847); Joshua Knowles will, 1824; Kentucky death register, Henry Satterfield, 24 Dec 1861.
body: His grandson James mentioned Ephraim only in passing, as the father of Henry Satterfield and "a native of Virginia, who died about 1850." The Warren County, Kentucky, records say more. John Satterfield's will, proved on 10 November 1847, names Ephraim among thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John. On 12 November 1809 Ephraim married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Ruth's father Joshua Knowles named "Ruth Saterfield" among his daughters in a will of 1824.

Their son Henry was born about 1811, in Maury County, Tennessee, by his grandson's account. Henry's death in 1861 was entered with his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield, which ties Henry to this Ephraim and Ruth. The accounts disagree about Ephraim himself. One family tree has him born in South Carolina in 1787 and dead in 1848, with Henry born in Warren County, while his grandson gave Virginia and Tennessee. A birth in South Carolina fits the will of his father John, who had lived in South Carolina before Kentucky.

By 1850 Ruth was a widow in Allen County, living with her daughter Elizabeth. Ephraim's death falls between his father's will of 1847 and that census, and his grandson dated it about 1850. James H. Satterfield was twelve in 1850.

P.name: John Milton Garrison
P.place: Allen County, Kentucky.
P.src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County, p. 676; Find a Grave; Acts passed at the session of the General Assembly for the Commonwealth of Kentucky (1847–48), ch. 600, sec. 6, p. 410 and index: https://archive.org/details/actspassedatses72kentgoog; WikiTree Garrison-4365, Garrison-3085 and Cannon-4655 (biography and census transcriptions); Tennessee State Marriages 1780–2002, Garrison–Cannon, Wilson County, 1809.; Find a Grave memorial 63780211 (John Milton Garrison), marker photograph by Freddy Brown; Find a Grave memorial 153803198 (Mary Cannon Garrison Satterfield)
body: John Milton Garrison was born on 4 October 1788 at Cowans Ford in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, and came as a boy with his parents to Warren County, Kentucky. On 6 December 1809 he married Martha "Patsey" Cannon in Wilson County, Tennessee. Patsey is said to have been born about 1788 in Mecklenburg County. John’s daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield; whether Patsey was her mother is not known, since no record names Mary’s mother. In 1815 Allen County was formed from Warren and Barren counties, placing the family in a newly named county.

In 1810 he was in Warren County in a household of five that held one enslaved person, a man of about 21. Allen County households in 1820, 1830 and 1840 (7, 11 and 7 people) held no slaves. In 1850 he was 62, a farmer, with real estate valued at $2,250. Whether he held anyone after 1810 is not known.

The marriage ended in the legislature, by statute. The Kentucky legislature's act of 1847-48 read: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." The chapter was approved on 29 February 1848. It gives no reason.

One family account gives a reason, without a source. It says that during the marriage he "fathered children by Sarah Stamps who lived nearby," that he "had the KY legislature declare those children legitimate," and that after the divorce he married Sarah. In 1850 J. M. Garrison, 62, lived with an "S" aged 57 and three younger Garrisons aged 21, 19 and 6. The legitimation act has not been found, so that part is unconfirmed. He died in Allen County on 18 September 1860. Patsey is said to have died about 1850 in Allen County, an estimate not independently verified.

Mary Garrison married Henry Satterfield and bore twelve children. Her son James called her father "John M. Garrison, of Allen County, Ky." and adds "(now living at the age of seventy-five years)"; because John died in 1860, the parenthesis most likely describes Mary, who would have been 73 or 74 in 1885. His parents were probably Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison, who came to Warren County from Mecklenburg: Samuel's family record book lists John Milton, born 4 October 1788, among their nine children, though no county record names him as their son.

His grave is in the Mount Pleasant United Methodist Church Cemetery near Scottsville, in Allen County, under a modern flat granite marker: "In memory of John Milton Garrison 1788-1860." His daughter Mary is buried far from him, in Wayne County, Iowa, where she died in 1896.

P.name: Melvina (Clark) Johnson
P.place: Mother of Samantha "Mantha" Johnson, who married John C. Satterfield in 1892. Her parents were given as Newton Clark and Mary Dunn.
P.note: The original death certificate records a birth date read and indexed as 10 November 1851 and an age of 78 years, 2 months, 6 days; these do not agree. Its informant was Polly Nash. The mother is recorded as Mary Dunn; identification with the Polly Clark of 1850 or the Polly Elms of compiled profiles remains unresolved. The age-three girl in Newton’s 1850 household is indexed as Vina, not explicitly named Melvina.

Elms marriage papers, license 20 January 1839 and minister’s return recording ceremony 24 January, signed 25 January 1839 by William Anderson; FHL film 982456, DGS 007728005, images 902–903; originals examined: https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C9BG-W71Y ; https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C9BG-WW3Y
body: Melvina died, as Melvina Johnston, at Big Reedy in Edmonson County on 17 January 1929, a widow; her father was given as Newton Clark, born in Kentucky, and her mother as Mary Dunn. Polly Nash of Big Reedy supplied the information. Her husband’s name was left blank.

The certificate’s birth date is read and indexed as 10 November 1851, although the final year digits are not perfectly clear. It also records an age of 78 years, 2 months, 6 days. That age is inconsistent with the written birth and death dates. Both fields are preserved here without choosing a corrected birth year.

In 1850 Newton Clark’s Butler County household held Newton, 32; Polly, 32; Martha, 10; Granville, 9; Stanford, 8; Hester, 6; William, 5; a girl aged 3 indexed as Vina; and Mary, 11 months. The handwriting of the age-three girl’s name does not unambiguously identify her as Melvina. The former claim that this census establishes Melvina’s birth about 1847 is therefore withdrawn. The census has no relationship column, and the identification of Vina with Melvina remains open.

Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms were married in Butler County: license issued 20 January 1839, ceremony 24 January, return signed 25 January. Melvina’s death certificate instead gives her mother’s name as Mary Dunn. Nothing reconciles Dunn and Elms or proves that the same woman bore both names. The identification of the mother named in 1929 with Polly in Newton’s 1850 household and with the 1839 bride remains probable. Some family trees link Newton to William and Lavina (Willis) Clark; that parental link is a separate question.

Her married name was Johnson; her husband's first name is not recorded on the memorials. Samantha D. was born on 28 March 1872 and Charlie in 1885. Samantha married John C. Satterfield in 1892, moved with him to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907, and crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, after marrying Bird Alexander Stephens in 1917. She died on 1 October 1928 and is buried at Soper Cemetery.

She was buried at Mount Pleasant, the cemetery at Big Reedy, on 18 January 1929. Samantha had died on 1 October 1928; nothing shows that Melvina attended her Oklahoma burial. Charlie remained in Butler County and died in 1959.
