P.title: The consent folded into their marriage book
P.hook: A father’s permission survived with John and Lizzie’s Alabama marriage papers.
body: John M. Shackleford and Lizzie Newton obtained their marriage license in Etowah County, Alabama, on 30 November 1889. A small note was kept over the page: permission from her father, Balas Newton, for the couple to marry.

The consent is dated 28 November. John certified two days later that he had written and signed it at Balas’s direction. In a separate statement, sworn before the probate judge, he presented the permission and explicitly identified Lizzie as Newton’s daughter. The wedding was on 1 December 1889.

By 1900 John and Elizabeth were raising their family in Gilbert Precinct, Etowah County. Their daughter Mary Tinsley later married Woodford Grady Moffitt, carrying this Alabama branch into the Moffitt family in Oklahoma.

Etowah County had been created only 23 years before the wedding, and for two of those years, 1866 to 1868, it was called Baine County. In 1900 the household at Gilbert held John, 37, Elizabeth, 28, and five living children: “Balous” 8, Myrtle 6, May 5, Robert 3 and Eddie 8 months. Mary, born 4 June 1895, was the “May, 5.” Her brothers and sisters were Balis Anthony (1892-1982, who died in Los Angeles County), Robert Yates (1897-1961), John Newton (1906-2002), Hazel Marzee King (1908-1980), Edward Richard (1910-1988) and Helen Elizabeth Josey (1915-1997). Notices of 1961 and 1981 also name sisters Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins, who do not fit the 1900 household.

Hazel was born at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family was in northeast Texas about 1908 before reaching Martin County. By 1930 John Morgan was there with his wife and children, and Grady and Mary and their six boys were living with them. In 1930 his birth year was given as 1863; his marker says 1862.

John Morgan Shackleford's grave in Evergreen Cemetery at Stanton, Martin County, Texas, lies on the far north side, to the right of the first gate. The flat granite marker is carved with a bird and flowers and reads "John M. Shackleford / Sept. 30, 1862 / May 22, 1930." Lizzie, who outlived him by twenty-one years, is buried in Oklahoma at Apache. His own parents are unknown.

In 1933 Lizzie moved from Dawson County, Texas, to Apache, Caddo County, Oklahoma, where several of her grown children lived. She died at her son Ed’s home southwest of town on 8 November 1951 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache.

The Shackelfords of Virginia trace to an immigrant, Roger, who received a grant in Gloucester County in 1658. A Shackleford family history of 1940 says the family had no coat of arms, and Mary’s descent from Roger is not proved.

P.name: Edward Norton of Armagh
P.place: His son's 1739 marriage record calls him "Edward Norton, dec., of the County & Parish of Armagh, in the Kingdome of Ireland," which makes the Nortons Irish Quakers.
P.src: Nottingham MM records; Myers, Immigration of the Irish Quakers into Pennsylvania (1902), p. 376. Gilbert Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864), p. 8 (Richard Brown's marriages); Albert Cook Myers, Immigration of the Irish Quakers into Pennsylvania, 1682-1750 (Swarthmore, 1902), Nottingham Monthly Meeting certificate list, https://archive.org/details/immigrationofiri00myer_0; Maryland Quaker Records: Nottingham Monthly Meeting (Brown entries for William Jr., Richard and Margaret Davis)
body: At his son's wedding on 16 October 1739 the bridegroom was described as "Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased." That is all it says. His wife's name is not given, nor is his trade or the year of his death. He was dead by October 1739.

The other marriage is his daughter's. On 24 November 1733 , "Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton, 'of ye County of Armagh,' Ireland," married Richard Brown, son of William Brown of West Nottingham. Another account gives the same marriage as the 24th of the 5th month and calls her "dau. of Edward Norton of Co. Armagh, Irel'd." She was Richard's third wife. Together the two marriages put two adult children of the same Armagh Quaker in Chester County, near the Maryland line, within six years, part of the Irish Friends' emigration.

Richard, born in 1693, was the son of William Brown the emigrant and his second wife Ann Mercer; he had married Hannah Reynolds in 1717 and Rachel Beeson in 1730/1 before Mary Norton. The bridegroom of 1739, Edward Norton the younger, married Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William Brown Jr. and Elizabeth Cowgill, so he married his sister Mary’s husband’s niece. Elizabeth’s mother had died before March 1721/2 and her father about 1727, and she married at West Nottingham as an orphan; the meeting’s book calls her “dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec.”

Both Norton marriages were into the Brown family, and both couples went on to Virginia. Edward Norton the younger and Elizabeth Brown are the Moffitt ancestors; their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Mary and Richard Brown had three sons, Richard, Joseph and Mercer; Richard died before 1747, and in April 1747 Mary married William Kirk. The elder Edward, who stayed in Armagh as far as the certificates show, is the earliest Norton on this line.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton took a certificate to Hopewell Monthly Meeting in Virginia on 19 January 1739/40, and Richard and Mary Brown with their family took one to Hopewell too. Mary and Richard’s three children were Richard (born 18 September 1734, died 4 September 1738), Joseph (1 April 1736, died 19 May 1751) and Mercer (7 May 1740). Richard left a will. Fairfax Monthly Meeting appointed a committee on the 28th of the 12th month 1746/7 (28 February) to inquire into its settlement, to protect the children, and found it satisfactorily settled. On the 21st of the 1st month 1746/7 (21 March) Nottingham gave William Kirk, the widower of Margaret Davis, a certificate to Fairfax, clear to marry Mary Brown. Margaret Davis, who had died in February 1744/5, had been the second wife of Elizabeth’s father, so Mary Norton’s new husband was Elizabeth’s stepmother’s widower.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton later lived in Rowan County, North Carolina, as their daughter Margaret’s marriage in 1763 shows. That they are the couple of 1739 is probable, not proven, though the names and the Hopewell and Fairfax trail suggest it. If so, Margaret’s grandmother was Elizabeth Cowgill of Neshaminy, and the line from the Settle certificate of 1682 runs through Brown and Norton to the Chamness wedding that put the family into Robert Moffitt’s household.
P.title: The Norton from Armagh who left a son and a daughter in Pennsylvania
P.hook: Edward Norton of Armagh is known only from what his children's marriage certificates say of him, but it is enough to place his family in Ireland.

P.name: William Brown Jr. & Elizabeth Cowgill
P.place: Nottingham Quakers. William was born in 1689; Elizabeth, a daughter of John Cowgill of Duck Creek, Delaware, died before March 1721/2, leaving their daughter Elizabeth an orphan.
P.src: Maryland Quaker Records: Nottingham Monthly Meeting; WikiTree Cowgill-353 and Cowgill-28, citing Middletown MM minutes Gilbert Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864), p. 7-8 (children of William Brown 12); The Stout Family of Delaware (1915), pp. 60-70 for John Cowgill's tan-yard; Quakers in Britain, Quaker calendar guide: https://www.quaker.org.uk/documents/quaker-calendar-lib-guide-2018
body: William Brown Jr. was born on the 21st day of the 7th month 1689, the third child of the Nottingham pioneer William Brown and Ann Mercer. In 1715 he married Elizabeth Cowgill, born on the 24th of the 6th month 1694 at Middletown, Bucks County, to John Cowgill and Bridget Croasdale. Her father had come from Yorkshire in 1682; accounts differ on which ship carried the Settle families. He was a tanner who moved about 1713 or 1714 to the Delaware shore, where on 10 May 1718 he asked for another hundred acres, "having erected a tan-yard on a branch of Black Bird's Creek." The marriage was recorded in Duck Creek Monthly Meeting, on 1 December 1715 by the Quaker count, as that of Elizabeth Cowgill, "daughter of John Cowgill, of Duck Creek in New Castle," and William Brown, "son of William Brown, of Nottingham."

The couple had two children. John was born on the 27th of the 2nd month 1717 and died on the 12th of the 7th month 1723, aged six. Elizabeth was born in the twelfth month of 1718, which in modern dating is early 1719. Her mother died within about three years of that birth, before March 1721/2, when William married Margaret Davis. That marriage produced William (1722) and Jacob (1724), and William Jr. himself died about 1727. His widow married William Kirk on the 6th of the 3rd month 1730. Her stepdaughter Elizabeth was eight or nine when her father died. In 1739 the Nottingham book called her "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec."

The Cowgill sisters had already made two marriages with the Browns. Elizabeth's sister Ellin, born on the 14th of the 10th month 1700, married William's brother Thomas Brown in 1718/9; Thomas died on 19 February 1746/7, and Ellin married again on 13 November 1768, to Lewis Clothier of Kent County, Maryland, and lived to 5 January 1772, aged 71. Two immigrant families, one from Yorkshire and one from Northamptonshire and Hampshire, had become a single network of cousins at Nottingham.

The child they left carried the line. Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton at West Nottingham on 16 October 1739, her uncle Richard Brown having married Edward's sister Mary six years before, and their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763. Through Elizabeth Brown, the Cowgill and Brown families became part of the Norton and Chamness lines.
P.title: Two Cowgill sisters, two Brown brothers, and a daughter left behind
P.hook: William Brown Jr. married a Cowgill in 1715, lost her within about six years, died himself about 1727, and left a daughter who married at West Nottingham as an orphan.
kv: John, 2 mo 27 1717, d. 7 mo 12 1723; Elizabeth, b. 12th mo 1718 (early 1719); by Margaret Davis, William (1722) and Jacob (1724)
Second wife of William Jr. (m. March 1721/2); after his death she m. William Kirk, 3rd month 6th, 1730 (Cope)

P.name: Gilliam Graves
P.title: A 45-year-old farmer joins the Union army at Cedar Glades
P.hook: Born on Toms Creek, North Carolina, he served on Georgia juries, farmed in the Arkansas hills and enlisted in 1864 at 45.
body: Gilliam Graves was born about 1813 in North Carolina, on Toms Creek in Randolph County. On 18 August 1832 he married Mary Tyler there. The county had been cut from Guilford in 1779, and his neighbors on the Deep River side included Friends whose meetings were draining toward Indiana. Gilliam went south instead. He was in Cherokee County, Georgia, by December 1835, when he served on a county jury; he served again on 5 November 1838 and is on the county's 1840 census. By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, at Cedar Glades, and in 1860 he was written down as 'Galem' Graves.

On 14 January 1864 he volunteered at Cedar Glades for the Union army, in Company D, 4th Arkansas, the same company that carried Benjamin F. Hulsey. He was 45, a farmer, five feet ten inches tall, with black eyes. He deserted on 12 October 1864 and returned on 25 December 1864. His second marriage, on 18 August 1845 in Montgomery County, was to Delila Hawthorne; if that is right, he was in Arkansas well before the 1853 tax list. Both of his first two marriages are dated 18 August, thirteen years apart, which may be a copying error; neither date has been checked. The children Aaron and John, listed in 1860 as born in Alabama about 1847 and 1849, also sit awkwardly with an Arkansas marriage in 1845. His third wife was Mary 'Polly' (Gray) Washburn.

He died, supposedly killed by robbers, in January 1876 in Garland County (another account gives 22 October 1876; the two dates conflict and neither rests on a record), and is buried beside Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery. His son Jesse is the Graves who stands behind our Sarah Rebecca. Jesse is said to have been born about 1855 in Blount County, Alabama, which does not square with Gilliam’s Arkansas tax roll of 1853 and is unresolved.

Garland County was not yet three years old when he died: a history of the Ozark region says it “was established April 5, 1873,” with Hot Springs the seat, and that “the greater part is mountainous, leaving only a small area worthy of the labor of the husbandman.” Hot Springs is given as the birthplace of G. W. Hulsey, on 24 December 1876 in one account (his 1918 draft card gives 24 December 1875), and of Oscar Hulsey in 1910.
Gilliam's parents are unknown; no sourced father has been found.

His later years are recorded in some detail. He was on the Montgomery County tax lists in 1853-59, 1861, 1865, 1867-68, 1871 and 1872, and in 1860, as "Galem Graves," his household held children Sarah 15 (born Georgia), Aaron 13 and John 11 (Alabama), Julia 9 and Nancy 5 (Arkansas). No trace of his family has been found for 1850 and 1870. A history of the county he came to says it “was organized December 9, 1842,” its settlers “came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties,” “in 1845 there were twenty-one slave-owners,” and “the spinning-wheel and loom have not yet disappeared.” Its seat is Mount Ida.

In January 1854 he was made guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves, and again in April 1861 of the minor heirs. His first wife, Mary Tyler, married him in Randolph County on 18 August 1832; a Charles Tyler, 79, lived in Cherokee County, Georgia, in 1850 with a boy, William D. Graves, 10, born Georgia, who may be Gilliam's son left with his grandfather.

His third wife, Polly Gray Washburn, died about 1879; his second, Delila Hawthorne, died about 1860 at Cedar Glades. His family tradition, recorded twice in the genealogy, makes his father an American Indian , though no record supports it.

The Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Cedar Glades was a company of neighbors. A petition of 10 March 1864 from Union men of Montgomery County said "Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down" on 1 March, and the men who enlisted with Gilliam on 14 January included William Haskins, 45, John Stroud, 45, John Tidwell, 32, born in Blount County, Alabama, and others.

The regiment he joined was the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), organized at Little Rock in December 1863. Its Company L wrote from Montgomery County on 10 March 1864 that wives and children of Union men at Cedar Glades were being shot, and a battalion of the regiment fought through the county in July. His desertion on 12 October 1864 and return on 25 December 1864 fall in the period of the autumn expedition from Little Rock to Fort Smith, but no record places his company on it.

P.note: The Graves family genealogy gives his name as Gilliam, not William Gilliam, and identifies him as Jesse's father from family records. His birth is given as about 1813 or about 1819: marriage in 1832 favors the earlier year and the 1864 army age of 45 the later. No original record seen names the father-son link, so this stays probable.

P.name: Jesse King Graves
P.title: From Alabama to the Cedar Glades
P.hook: A family account traces Jesse Graves from Alabama to Arkansas, where his household grew through several marriages.
body: Jesse S. Graves is placed by the Graves family in Blount County, Alabama, about 1855, a son of Gilliam Graves. He may be the Jesse King Graves of the family tree, but that is not settled. The family traces Gilliam from North Carolina through Georgia and Alabama to Cedar Glades, Arkansas.

Jesse married Sarah Emma Fisher at Jack Phillips's home in Montgomery County on 2 April 1871, at 18 and 15. A family account of 1977 names Margaret Crumpton as his second wife, and a Jesse Graves married Margaret Crumpton in Garland County on 31 January 1884, but the groom's age differs from the age given for Jesse in 1871.

A Jesse Graves married Nancy Cutter in Garland County on 19 September 1889. One family account calls his third wife Nancy Wilborn Kyle Cuttler, another Nancy Wilborn Sutton; the names are unverified. The 1977 account names Sarah Rebecca as Jesse's daughter but not her mother.

The ages do not fit together. Jesse was 18 in 1871, yet the grooms in 1884 and 1889 are each 38, five years apart. There may be an error, or they may be different men, and whether they were Sarah Rebecca's father is unsettled.

The 1977 account lists John and Henry Crumpton, Cindy Sutton, and Issas and Prince Cuttler among Jesse's stepchildren. A list of burials made in 2002 names Jesse in McGill Cemetery, Garland County, though the family places his grave in the yard of his old home on Walnut Valley Road.
His widow Nancy, who lived to 20 November 1932, was living in 1920 with their daughter Lucinda and son-in-law Benjamin Hogue.
kv: About 1853–55 in family accounts; other records conflict
Montgomery County Book A, p. 278, cited as Jesse age 18
Garland County register: a Jesse Graves, age 38, and Margaret Crumpton, age 28; identification needs verification
The 1977 query names Sarah E., Margaret Crumpton and Nancy Wilborn Sutton; the 1889 marriage record names Nancy Cutter
The 1977 query names Sarah Rebecca among Jesse’s children

P.note: The genealogy calls him Jesse S. Graves, while the tree calls him Jesse King Graves. The 1884 and 1889 marriage registers each record their groom as 38, five years apart. The 1871 Montgomery County marriage, as quoted in the genealogy, gives Jesse's age as 18, suggesting 1852–53. These records could contain errors or concern different men. Sarah Rebecca's maternal identity has not been established by a record naming her mother. The stated Blount County birthplace also needs checking against Gilliam Graves's reported Arkansas tax records.

P.place: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County (now Person County), North Carolina, lived in South Carolina, and settled in Warren County, Kentucky. His will was proved there on 10 November 1847. His wife Mary, born about 1768, is named in it, and their thirteen children included Ephraim.

The 1885 Kentucky sketch says Ephraim was a Virginian and Henry a native of Maury Co., Tenn.; WikiTree has Ephraim born in South Carolina and Henry in Warren Co. John's own father is disputed and is not shown. The Person County tradition (sons John and William moving to Tennessee and Kentucky) is the compilers' report of Earl Satterfield's family account and has no documents behind it; it is a hypothesis for John's origin, not a finding.
P.title: John Satterfield's will, with thirteen children in a single line
P.hook: Born in Orange County, North Carolina, and dead in Warren County, Kentucky, at about eighty-one.
body: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County, North Carolina, a county formed in 1752 and since divided so that his birthplace lies in Person County. He lived in South Carolina and later settled in Warren County, Kentucky, where he made a will proved on 10 November 1847. It lists thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John.

His wife Mary, born about 1768, is named in the will. Her maiden name is not settled: one memorial gives Jones, and a 1786 marriage in Surry County, North Carolina, gives Haga. John's own father is disputed and is not shown here. Ephraim's place in the list is the link to this family. Ephraim's son Henry died on 24 December 1861, and Henry's death was entered with his father as Ephraim, which matches the Ephraim of the will.

Where John came from is the open question. A Person County family tradition holds that a John Satterfield who died there in 1802 had five sons, Isaac, Jesse, John, William and James, and that John and William "migrated to Tennessee and Kentucky as young men." No document supports the story, though its detail deserves some credit. The 1802 will itself names only a wife Sarah and sons James and Isaac. If the tradition holds, our John, born in Orange County when it still covered Person, would be one of those sons; so far it is a hypothesis and no record joins them.
The sources differ on where Ephraim was born: one family tree has South Carolina in 1787, where John had lived, while his grandson called him a Virginian.

P.title: Ruth Knowles Satterfield, who died in Missouri at eighty-one
P.hook: Born in Virginia, married in Warren County in 1809, widowed by 1850, and buried a long way from either.
body: Ruth Knowles was born about 1783 in Virginia, the daughter of Joshua Knowles, whose 1824 will names "Ruth Saterfield" among his five daughters. On 12 November 1809 she married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County, Kentucky, a county that dated only from December 1796. Her son Henry was born about 1811, in Maury County, Tennessee, by a grandson's account, and his death in 1861 was entered with his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield.

Where the couple lived in the years between is not recorded. Ephraim's father John named him among thirteen children in a will proved in November 1847, and a grandson put Ephraim's death about 1850. By 1850 Ruth was a widow in Allen County, Kentucky, a county cut from Warren and Barren in 1815, living with her daughter Elizabeth. Her father had died in 1832, and her son Henry would die in 1861.

In 1860 "Rutha Satterfield," about 77, lived in the household of Elizabeth and her husband Jesse Agee in Gasconade County, Missouri. She had been in her daughter's house in 1850 as well, so she probably went west with Elizabeth and Jesse rather than alone. Gasconade County, created in 1820, had filled with settlers from Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee and the Carolinas, and from 1837 with Germans of the Hermann colony. She died there in 1864, having outlived her husband by about fourteen years and her son Henry by three.
Why she went to Missouri is not known. That she was our Ephraim's wife rests on Henry's death entry and her father's will, and is probable.

P.title: Joshua Knowles's will: a wife named Jemima and five daughters
P.hook: A Warren County man, counted between 80 and 90 in 1830, who wrote his will in 1824 and lived about eight more years.
body: Joshua Knowles was born about 1747, and the 1830 census counted him in Warren County, Kentucky, between 80 and 90. He wrote his will on 11 November 1824, and it was proved in October 1832. It names his wife Jemima, his son Matthew as executor, his son John of Franklin County, Virginia, and five daughters: Sarah Hays, Polly Stephens, Leaner Jones, Ruth Saterfield and Elizabeth Bailey. Ruth was born in Virginia.

Warren County had been created only in December 1796, when Joshua was about forty-nine, and in 1830, at about eighty-three, he was still living there. His will hints at where he started: his son John was "of Franklin County, Virginia," and his daughter Ruth was born in Virginia, so Joshua probably came to Kentucky from Virginia, though no record of his own birthplace has been found.

Ruth is the daughter that matters here. She had married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County on 12 November 1809, and her father's will, written fifteen years later, calls her "Ruth Saterfield" in the clerk's spelling. The will does not say whether Jemima was Ruth's mother or a later wife.

By 1824 his five daughters carried five married surnames, Hays, Stephens, Jones, Saterfield and Bailey, and a son was still in Virginia, so the family was already spread across two states. Ruth's husband Ephraim came of a family that had moved from the Carolinas to Warren County, and Ruth later followed a daughter to Missouri, where she died in 1864.
He is buried in Knowles Cemetery at Motley in Warren County. The will comes from a family account and has not been read in the original.

body: Martha "Patsey" Cannon was born about 1788 in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. On 6 December 1809 she married J. M. Garrison, John Milton Garrison, in Wilson County, Tennessee. The couple settled in Warren County, Kentucky, and their daughter Mary was born on 17 October 1811. No record names Mary's mother; that it was Patsey rests on Mary's birth falling inside this marriage and on the name Cannon already in the family tree.

The act that ended the marriage reads: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." It was one section of an act of the December 1847 session that dissolved several marriages at once, and it gives no reason. Whether Patsey asked for it or accepted it is not known.
She is said to have died in Allen County about 1850. Her daughter Mary, who married Henry Satterfield, died on 2 March 1896.

P.name: Robert & Margaret (Stuart) Moffitt
P.place: Robert Moffitt, said to have been born in Scotland, moved young to County Donegal, Ireland, where he and Margaret Stuart raised eleven children. Six sons are said to have crossed to America, among them our William, who settled at Cane Creek, North Carolina.
kv: James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Mary, Catherine, Robert, Hugh, John, Patrick
Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt, quoted on WikiTree
P.title: Six brothers from Donegal and the extra T
P.hook: A descendant's Bible record says Robert Moffitt of Donegal had eleven children, and that six sons came to America and agreed to end the name in 'itt'.
body: The Bible record of Abijah Moffitt says Robert Moffitt was born in Scotland, went to Ireland when young, and there married Margaret Stuart. It names eleven children: James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Mary, Catheren, Robert, Hugh, John and Patrick.

An earlier account comes from a member of the next generation. On 4 August 1853, Joseph Moffitt wrote from Randolph County, Indiana, naming his parents Hugh Moffitt and Hannah Davis, Hugh's brothers including William, and Hugh's parents Robert Moffitt and Margaret Stewart. Joseph said Hannah's sister Mary married a Moffitt, but did not name her husband. The letter as printed in 1924 fits the William Moffitt who married Mary Davies at Cane Creek; identifying him as Hugh's brother remains an inference rather than an explicit statement in this letter.

A separate 1799 Chatham County will helps anchor Joseph's account: Hugh Moffit named his wife Hannah, his son Joseph and other sons. Joseph's letter names brothers Robert, John, Joshua, Charles, Jeremiah and Nathan, all also named in the will. The letter adds three sisters and says the children were raised in Chatham County. This is first-hand family testimony about Joseph's parents and siblings, though his statements about earlier generations and places still need corroborating records.

In the Bible record, John crossed first and went back to Ireland; liking the country, he returned with five brothers to Philadelphia. From there they went to North Carolina, to what became Chatham and Randolph counties. William, Adam and Charles died in North Carolina. It says Hugh went to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and died near Chillicothe about 1800. A will made by Hugh Moffit of Chatham County on 1 October 1799 says he had disposed of his affairs in preparation to move his family to the Northwest Territory; this fits a late-1799 move but makes the earlier departure uncertain. Robert started back for Ireland and was never heard of again, and was supposed lost at sea. Patrick never left Ireland. The record adds that 'William and Hugh married Davis daughters of North Carolina,' which matches William Moffitt's marriage to Mary Davies at Cane Creek in 1763.

Family tradition explains the spelling: the brothers agreed to end the name in 'itt' so that kin could recognize each other wherever it turned up. That part is tradition, not record. North Carolina papers of the 1760s write the name Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt.

The Carolina end is on record. At Cane Creek Meeting in 1763 William married Mary Davies and, in the family's account, his brother Hugh married her sister Hannah, which shows the brothers had joined the Quaker neighborhood of Charles Davies rather than a Presbyterian one. The counties give a sense of how little the family needed to move. Orange was formed in 1752 from Johnston, Bladen and Granville; Chatham in 1770 from Orange; Guilford in 1770 from Rowan and Orange; and Randolph in 1779 from Guilford. A household on one stretch of the upper Deep River could have been written into the Orange court records in 1765, the Chatham records in the 1770s and the Randolph records in 1796, the year William made his will, without anyone leaving home, if the family stayed put.

The Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance gives William's parents as Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt, without citations. The two accounts agree on Robert and Donegal and differ on whether his wife was Margaret or Martha. Neither names Robert's own parents; the Moffat ancestors some trees give for Robert have no sources.

A Moffitt genealogy of 1928 tells the crossing differently from the Bible Record: "William came first, alone, and went back," and then "he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time." It says Robert and Margaret migrated to Donegal after the marriage, and that all of their children but Catharine and Patrick crossed to America. Eastern Donegal was settled from Ayrshire and Galloway by the Cunninghams and Stewarts, which fits the bride's surname but names no parish.

The claim that Robert was 'Robert Bruce Moffitt,' born in 1716 at Moffat Wells in Dumfriesshire, does not hold up. The 1928 genealogy says Robert Moffat married Margaret Stuart 'at Moffat Wells, Scotland,' which it describes as 'a mineral spring' near the town of Moffat, so the 'Wells' is a spa, not a birthplace, and it gives the date of the wedding as 'supposed to be about 1750,' an impossible date since William, listed third among their children, was born about 1740. The 1928 account places the wedding in Scotland; the Bible account places it in Ireland. The book gives no birth year for Robert and no middle name. One family tree gives about 1705, not 1716, and has no 'Bruce.' No record carries either detail.

Donegal Moffitt researchers report that Robert and Adam Moffitt held the lease of the townland of Doagh Crabbin in Clondavaddog parish in 1743, when Gustavus Hamilton's estate was sold to Nathaniel Clements, and that Robert married a Margaret Stewart. Nothing ties that Robert to William of Randolph County except the family story. An unsourced tree gives Robert's father as an Alexander Moffat born in 1670, and no record supports that.

A. Hanna, The Scotch-Irish (1902): https://archive.org/details/scotchirishorsco01hann_0; D. L. Corbitt, The Formation of the North Carolina Counties 1663–1943: https://archive.org/details/formationofnorth00corb.
P.note: Joseph's 1853 family letter survives here as a 1924 transcription; Hugh's will names Hannah and Joseph. The letter supports Robert and Margaret as Hugh's parents and names his brother William, but does not explicitly identify that William as Mary's husband. The link to the Randolph County couple remains a reasoned lead. Robert and Margaret's precise dates and places, the crossing account and earlier parentage remain unverified. The Bible record and 1928 book disagree on who crossed first; the Alamance Battleground book names the wife Martha Steward. No Donegal parish record has been seen.

P.name: Richard Browne and his family
P.place: Richard Browne and his family appear in the Wellingborough Quaker registers. His sons James and William later settled in Pennsylvania.
kv: c.1620, Husbands Bosworth, Leicestershire (Northamptonshire FHS inference)
Nine reported; births of James (1656), William (1658) and Jeremiah (1660) are in the Wellingborough Quaker register
29th day, first month 1658 (29 March, Old Style); father Richard; mother not named
P.title: Stripped of their property for fines
P.hook: William Brown's memories, written into the Nottingham Quaker minutes in 1786, say his parents lost most of what they owned to fines for their faith.
body: Willyam Browne, son of Richard Browne, was born on the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658; in the Friends’ calendar then in use, the first month was March. His mother is not named at his birth. Sons James in 1656 and Jeremiah in 1660 are also reported; the mother’s name appears as Mary, Marrey or Margery in later accounts and is unresolved. Richard is described as of Boasworth, usually taken to be Husbands Bosworth in Leicestershire.

Forty years after William Brown died, a great-nephew set down William's stories in the East Nottingham Quaker minutes on the 28th day of the 1st month 1786. They say Richard had leaned toward both the Baptists and the Puritans and was reputed a teacher among both, and that about 1663 William's parents 'had suffered greatly and were much stripped of their property for fines &c.' The memorial miscalls the father 'William senior'; the birth register gives Richard.

James Brown reached Pennsylvania by 1677. William followed between 1682 and 1684, after marrying Dorothy in England, and married three more times in Pennsylvania, the second time to Ann Mercer in 1684. He died in West Nottingham in 1746, on 23 August by the 1786 family memorandum or 1 October by another account.

The East Nottingham memorandum tells how the Brownes became Friends when William Dewsbury sat at their table, how Richard's wife asked why he had brought "that madman" into the house, and how his landlord made him pay his rent twice because he would not swear that it was paid.
P.src: WikiTree Browne-440, Brown-2504, Unknown-278288, citing Wellingborough MM and Northamptonshire QM Quaker registers; Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864); Wellingborough Monthly Meeting, TNA RG6/1380, William Brown birth entry, image 20 of 150, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7097/records/524194; Northamptonshire Quarterly Meeting, RG6/502, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7097/records/246957. Wellingborough Monthly Meeting, original birth register, TNA RG6/1380, image 20 of 150, first entry: Willyam Browne, son of Richard Browne, born the 29th day of the first month 1658 (29 March, Old Style); https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/7097/images/41815_b0153703-00019?pId=524194. The entry does not name a mother.
P.note: The original RG6/1380 entry has been visually reviewed and directly names Richard as Willyam’s father. It does not name a mother. Mary, Marrey and Margery in other accounts remain unverified; no mother is attached in the tree. Identifying this English child with the Pennsylvania emigrant remains probable. The Nottingham memorial misnames the father and has a chronology conflicting with the reported 1662 burial; its stories remain later family recollections rather than a secure source for exact dates.

A 1709 Quaker list of public Friends who died in Pennsylvania names him and 'Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer', who died in 1696.

P.note: The original Ringwood entry has been visually reviewed: it names Thomas and Ann Mercer as the parents of the child Ann and gives their residence as Ringwood. Her birth is written 24th day, 12th month 1666, rendered 24 February 1666/7 (1667 in modern year numbering). No Gregorian day conversion is implied. The child’s identification with William Brown’s later wife in Pennsylvania remains probable; the birth entry alone does not establish that connection. Thomas’s own parents and the elder Ann’s maiden surname remain unknown. The independently examined printed 1709 catalog directly identifies Anne Browne as the immigrant Thomas’s daughter; its original manuscript remains unexamined. It calls Andover’s county Wiltshire, rather than the Hampshire identification used in later family accounts.
P.title: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who crossed with his daughter Ann
P.hook: A Hampshire Quaker widower brought his teenage daughter to Pennsylvania in 1682-83; she married at seventeen, and he died there in 1694.
body: Thomas Mercer and his wife Ann lived at Ringwood in Hampshire when their daughter Ann was born. The Quaker register names both parents and dates the birth to the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666. In the Friends’ calendar then in use, this means 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. The entry gives the mother’s first name but no maiden surname. Later family accounts place Thomas at Andover before crossing to Pennsylvania with his daughter about 1682–83; identification with the Ringwood family remains probable.

He took up land in Aston Township, Chester County, and his daughter was married there in 1684 to William Brown, born in Northamptonshire, who had landed a year or two earlier. Ann was seventeen. Her first child, born in February 1685/6, was named Mercer for her family. Thomas Mercer lived long enough to see five grandchildren born, and died on 22 November 1694. A 1709 Quaker list of public Friends who died in Pennsylvania names him and "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer," who died in 1696.

Thomas Mercer's own parents are unknown. Through Ann his line runs to her son William Brown Jr., his daughter Elizabeth Brown, her daughter Margaret Norton and her daughter Martha Chamness, who married Robert Moffitt.

The two Anns belong to different generations: Ann, wife of Thomas, was the mother; Ann Mercer, who married William Brown, was the daughter. The elder Ann’s maiden surname and life dates remain unknown.

The 1709 list remembers the immigrant father and daughter: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who arrived about 1682 or 1683 and died in 1694, and Anne Browne, his daughter, who came with him and was buried in 1696. It also remembers Anne’s public testimony after her arrival. It places Andover in Wiltshire rather than Hampshire, and gives no further parents for Thomas or maiden surname for his wife.

P.name: John & Bridget (Croasdale) Cowgill
P.place: John Cowgill came from Yorkshire in 1682 with his widowed mother and married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy, Bucks County, in 1693. About 1713 he moved to New Castle County, Delaware, and built a tan-yard. Their daughter Elizabeth married William Brown Jr.
kv: 30 Aug 1671, Settle Meeting transcription; other meeting dates vary
24 Aug 1694, sixth month in the Middletown register
1703/4, Rachel (Baker) Bunting, widow of Job Bunting of Darby
Warrants for tracts on Appoquinimink Creek and Black Bird’s Creek, with a tan-yard
Elizabeth Cowgill → Elizabeth Brown → Margaret Norton → Martha Chamness → the Moffitts
P.title: The Settle families’ 1682 crossing
P.hook: The 1682 Settle certificate names both families; eleven years later John Cowgill married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy.
body: In June 1682, Friends at Settle in Yorkshire prepared a certificate for families leaving for Pennsylvania. Among them were Ellen Cowgill, a widow, and her children, and Thomas Croasdale, his wife Agnes and six children. John Cowgill and Bridget Croasdale belonged to those two families. Later accounts differ over whether the party sailed on the Lamb or the Welcome; the certificate does not name a ship.

Bridget was born on the thirtieth day of the sixth month, 1671; in the Quaker calendar then in use, sixth month was August. She was about eleven when the family left England. On 19 October 1693, she married John Cowgill at Neshaminy in Bucks County, Pennsylvania.

Their daughter Elizabeth was born on 24 August 1694. Elizabeth later married William Brown Jr.; their daughter Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton, and their granddaughter Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness. That is the path from Bridget’s Yorkshire family to the Moffitts.

Bridget died on 26 April 1701. They had four children: Elizabeth (born the 24th of the 6th month, 1694), Thomas (21st of the 4th month, 1696), John (8th of the 5th month, 1698) and Ellin (14th of the 10th month, 1700); some family trees convert Elizabeth’s birth to June rather than August. In 1703/4 John married Rachel Baker, the widow of Job Bunting of Darby, and had four more children: Rachel, Mary, Ebenezer and Eleazer.

About 1713 or 1714 he moved to the lower part of New Castle County, Delaware. Land records say that on the 26th of the 3rd month 1715 (26 May) a warrant was signed to John Cowgill “for the resurvey of a tract of land in a fork of Appoquinimink Creek,” and on the 1st of the 5th month 1715/6 he “desired the grant of about 100 acres of vacant land, near his other tract in New Castle county, where he had planted a tan-yard.” On the 10th of the 3rd month 1718 (10 May), “having erected a tan-yard on a branch of ‘Black Bird’s Creek,’” he asked for another hundred acres on rent.

His sons Thomas and John followed him and married sisters, daughters of Joshua Clayton of Little Creek Hundred. Thomas had Thomas, Ezekiel and Jane; John married Lydia Clayton “of Kent county” in 1720. The daughters Elizabeth and Ellin married the Nottingham brothers William Brown Jr. and Thomas Brown. John Cowgill died on 2 July 1731. His grandson John Cowgill of Little Creek was hauled through Dover in a cart in the Revolution for refusing Continental money.
His later land records also concern land near Blackbird Creek in New Castle County.
P.src: Thomas Maxwell Potts, Our Family Ancestors (1895), pp. 25–29, reproducing the Settle certificate and family entries, https://archive.org/details/ourfamilyancesto1895pott; Middletown Monthly Meeting, Minutes 1664–1807, John and Bridget Cowgill children, image 58 of 118, https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/2189/images/31906_283855-00057; WikiTree Cowgill-28 and Cowgill-353, citing meeting and Delaware land records; Quakers in Britain, Quaker calendar guide, https://www.quaker.org.uk/documents/quaker-calendar-lib-guide-2018.; The Stout Family of Delaware, with the Story of Penelope Stout (1915), pp. 60-70, https://archive.org/details/stoutfamilyofdel00stre; Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864), generation list; Maryland Quaker Records: Nottingham Monthly Meeting, entries for William Brown Jr. and Thomas Brown
P.note: The Settle certificate and children’s list are reproduced in Potts’s 1895 book. He cautions that Settle and Middletown birth dates differ. The John-and-Bridget parentage of Elizabeth comes from a specific Middletown register transcription; its original page has not yet been independently reread. The servant detail and ship identifications depend on later accounts.

P.name: Ellen Cowgill
P.place: A widow in the 1682 Settle certificate, which reads 'Ellen Cowgill widow & her children'; her children are thought to have been Edmund, Jennet, John and Jane. Accounts differ on the ship that carried the party. She settled at Middletown, Bucks County, Pennsylvania, and is buried in the Middletown cemetery. Her husband's name is not documented: tradition says Ralph Cowgill, but some think Edmund Cowgill, baptized 1634 at Thornton in Craven. The maiden name Stackhouse of Giggleswick is traditional and disputed.
P.src: WikiTree Stackhouse-56, Stackhouse-58 and Cowgill-16; Pennsylvania Magazine of History and Biography 9 (1885), pp. 229–30: https://archive.org/details/pennsylvaniamaga09histuoft; Potts, Our Family Ancestors (1895), pp. 25–27; The Stout Family of Delaware (1915), pp. 60–62; The Friend (Philadelphia), 24 Dec. 1853, “Cuthbert Hayhurst”; Passengers and Ships Prior to 1684 (1970); A Quaker Saga (1967), ship list.
P.note: Ellen’s identity as mother is probable; the children’s father remains unconfirmed. Ralph as Ellen's son and the Lamb as the ship are both probable, not proven; John's servitude to Hayhurst rests on the 1970 study.
body: On 7 June 1682 Settle Monthly Meeting, in the Yorkshire dales, issued a certificate for a party of Friends bound for Pennsylvania. It lists Cuthbert Hayhurst "his wife & family," Thomas Wrigglesworth and Alice, Thomas Walmsley and Elizabeth, Thomas Croasdale "Agness his wife & six children," Thomas Stackhouse and his wife, Nicholas Waln "his wife & three children," William Hayhurst, and "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children." No child is named. Ellen was born near Giggleswick about 1639, so she was about forty-three. Her children appear to have been Edmund, Jennet, John, Jane and probably Ralph, though the certificate does not name them.

Her husband's name is not documented. Many trees name Ralph Cowgill, said to have been hanged in 1682 as a Quaker, but that has no documentation, and some think Edmund Cowgill, baptized in 1634 at Thornton in Craven, more likely. Her maiden name is also disputed: some books give Stackhurst, and several Stackhouse histories say she was not a Stackhouse, so a Thomas Stackhouse of Giggleswick and Anna Evans are not added as her parents.

John, probably about seventeen, came as a servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst. Hayhurst, born at Easington in Yorkshire about 1633, had been among the Friends imprisoned in the West Riding in the 11th month of 1660 for refusing the oath of allegiance. In 1668 he held a meeting at the house of Richard Betteris in Oxford and was arrested while speaking and held for a month by the vice-chancellor. His neighbor Nicholas Waln wrote that "he went through many great exercises and imprisonments." He died in the first month of 1683, only months after landing in Bucks County.

Ralph Cowgill came by a different ship, landing about 28 September 1682. Under Randolph Blackshaw of Hallingee, Cheshire, a list of Bucks County residents prints: "These servants below came in the ship the 'Friend's Adventure.' The Mr., Thomas Wall. Arrived in this river the 28th 7th M., 1682. Servants to Randulph Blackshaw, William Beasy, Ralph Nuttall, and Ralph Cowgill, each to serve 4 years, and to have 50 acres of land apiece." John and Ralph both appear to have been Ellen's children: John, "servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst" and a probable passenger on the Lamb of Liverpool, and Ralph, who came on the Friend's Adventure.

Which ship carried the Settle families has been told two ways. Older family histories say they sailed in Penn's own Welcome, and add that smallpox killed thirty on that ship. A later study says at least four of the seven Settle families sailed on the Lamb of Liverpool, and a Watson family history lists the Lamb, "John Tench, master, from Liverpool," as arriving on 22 October 1682. The party's own certificate does not name a ship.

Ellen settled at Middletown, Bucks County, and is buried in the Middletown Friends cemetery; she died in 1705. John served his time, married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy in 1693, and had four children by her before her death in 1701, among them Elizabeth, born in 1694, who married William Brown Jr. John married Rachel Bunting in 1703/4. Jennet married Bernard Lane at Burlington on 2 February 1688. Elizabeth's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton, and the line came down through the Nortons and Chamnesses to the Moffitts.
P.title: Ellen Cowgill, widow of Giggleswick, and the sons who came as servants
P.hook: The 1682 Settle certificate calls her "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children"; two of her sons landed in Pennsylvania in service.

P.name: Thomas & Agnes (Hawthornthwaite) Croasdale
P.place: From New Hay, Yorkshire, to Neshaminy Creek, Bucks County, Pennsylvania. The Settle certificate of 1682 names Thomas, Agnes and six children.

£47 9s in goods; 500 acres listed without a valuation
Daughter Bridget married John Cowgill in 1693

P.note: Thomas Maxwell Potts’s 1895 book reproduces the inventories and meeting entries; these are printed transcriptions, not images of the original manuscripts. Thomas’s inventory supports his death in 1684 rather than 1682. Agnes’s printed inventory year conflicts with the reported 1686 death and administration. Their own birth dates and parents remain unverified. The ship name is disputed in later accounts. The Swarthmore finding aid describes the 1682 and 1728 documents; their original text has not been independently examined. The 1733 debtor’s identity is not established. The Colonial Dames roll (July 2022) is a derivative biography; it conflicts with the Potts transcriptions on the marriage day (20 May against 1 May 1664), Agnes's burial (20 October 1684 against 1686) and the ship (Welcome against Lamb).
body: Thomas Croasdale of New Hay, Yorkshire, married Agnes Hawthornthwaite of Wyresdale on 1 May 1664. The marriage was recorded by Lancaster Monthly Meeting. Eighteen years later, the couple prepared to leave England with six children. The certificate issued at Settle on 7 June 1682 names the whole household, placing their move within a group of Quaker families rather than an isolated voyage.

Before leaving, Thomas arranged to buy land in Pennsylvania by deeds dated 21 and 22 April 1682. The family history describes a purchase of a thousand acres, but the estate papers later describe a 500-acre holding; in Pennsylvania 500 acres of the purchase were laid out on Neshaminy Creek near the present Langhorne. The records concern different stages of acquiring and settling land; they should not be treated as two measurements of an unchanged farm.

One of those documents survives: the 21 April 1682 indenture from William Penn to Thomas Croasdale, a vellum document with a red seal, signed by both men, at a yearly rent of one peppercorn. It was made before the family crossed the Atlantic.

Thomas died on 2 November 1684, about two years after the move. Agnes became administrator of his estate. On 8 December, James Dillworth and Thomas Constable valued his belongings: clothing, bedding, pewter and brass, cushions, wooden vessels, chests, linen, ironware and hogs. Two mares were worth £8 10s; three cows, a calf and a yearling were valued at £12. The goods totaled £47 9s. The 500 acres were listed but left unvalued.

The inventory of “Agnes Crossdale of Neshaminah Widdowe” was taken by Nicholas Waln, who signed with his mark, and Robert Heaton. It gives the household another outline: brass and pewter, pots, a bed and bedding, a chest, a saddle, hogs, three cows, two bullocks, a heifer, two mares and a colt. This time the land was valued at £50, nearly half the £106 5s total. Small things also survived into the account: a blanket, nails and the tools used around the house and farm, or in its own words, “one Blankit Some nails all the husbandrie Tooles & hustlement about the House.”

Agnes died on 20 October 1686, according to the family account, and sons William and John received administration on 1 November. An inventory is dated the 10th of the 9th month 1685 but registered on the 1st of the 9th month 1686; neither fits a death in October 1686, so one of the years is off. The children’s list names William (born 7 February 1664/5), John, Elizabeth (who died in 1683), Mary, Bridget (30 August 1671) and Alice. Alice married David Potts, and Mary, William Smith. William, who stayed in Bucks County, made his will on the 30th of the 1st month 1715 (30 March), naming his sisters Mary Smith with eight children and Alice Potts with ten. Bridget’s marriage to John Cowgill carries this branch into the Brown, Norton, Chamness and Moffitt families.

In 2022 the National Society of the Colonial Dames of America honored Agnes as an "historic founder" of Pennsylvania on the strength of the 1682 crossing that carried the family to Penn's colony, recalling that nearly a third of the ship's passengers died of smallpox on the fifty-seven days at sea. The honor names the ship as both the Welcome and the Lamb, buries Agnes on 20 October 1684, which cannot stand against her administering Thomas's estate in December of that year, and puts the marriage on 20 May 1664 rather than 1 May.

A later trace of the family’s land survives. In 1728 John Wildman and his wife Mara, the widow of Thomas and Agnes’s son John Croasdale, transferred land in Middletown to a Thomas Croasdale, John's son. He was Bridget’s nephew. A debt involving a Thomas Croasdale and a sheriff’s sale in 1733 may concern the same nephew.

Agnes’s maiden name may link her to a Friend who was jailed. A “William Hathornthwaite” was among forty-three Friends arrested at Swarthmoor in January 1660 for refusing the oath and committed to Lancaster Castle. Nothing ties him to Agnes.
P.title: Three cows, two mares and 500 acres: Thomas and Agnes Croasdale on the Neshaminy
P.hook: Two inventories preserve a family’s Pennsylvania household: livestock, bedding, tools and a 500-acre holding on Neshaminy Creek.

P.title: A Quaker wedding at Sandwich, 1678
P.hook: Hananiah Gaunt posted his marriage intention on 3 May 1678 and the next day traded his Cape Cod land for acres in New Jersey.
body: Dorothy Butler was born at Sandwich, on Cape Cod in Plymouth Colony, on 23 January 1649/50, the daughter of Thomas Butler and his wife Dorothy. She was ten in June 1660, when the colony's court had her brother Daniel publicly whipped for rescuing a Quaker from the marshal and fined her parents forty shillings for the disorder at their house the night he was searched for. That October the court fined "Dorothy Butler", almost certainly her mother, ten shillings for attending Quaker meetings. Her mother died on 9 August 1675 and her father on 12 March 1690.

Hananiah Gaunt posted his intention of marriage at the Sandwich Friends Meeting on 3 May 1678 to Dorothy Butler, daughter of Thomas Butler of Sandwich. On 4 May he and his brother Israel exchanged their Sandwich land for land in New Jersey. Hananiah and Dorothy married on 10 May, when she was twenty-eight. Hananiah's own father, Peter Gaunt, had been fined in cattle by the court for attending the same Quaker meetings.

They lived at Dartmouth, Massachusetts, until as late as 1685, when Hananiah took up 500 acres at Hananicon (Oneanickon) in Springfield Township, Burlington County, New Jersey. Dorothy died there on 26 April 1714 and is buried at Jobstown.

Their daughter Mehitable (born about 1685) married Thomas Staples, and Mehitable's daughter Ann Staples, born in 1714, married Thomas Rogers in 1736. Hananiah's will of 17 July 1720, proved 17 November 1721, names Mehitable Staples among his children, with Daniel, Zebulon and Mary Webb, who were very probably Dorothy's too, though the will does not name their mother.

Through Ann's daughter Mary Rogers, who married Abraham Nordyke in 1761, the line runs south to Guilford County and on to Indiana, so a Cape Cod girl whose brother was whipped for helping a Friend stands at the head of the New Jersey Quaker branch of this tree.
P.src: WikiTree Gaunt-14 and Butler-294, citing McLean (NGSQ 1974), Sandwich Friends records and the Calendar of New Jersey Wills; Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England, ed. Shurtleff, vol. 3 (1855), court orders of June and October 1660; Brownson, 'Thomas Butler of Sandwich', NEHGR
P.note: The Quaker marriage record names her father; the 1720 will names her daughter. Evidence: probable (the marriage record is cited only through WikiTree and McLean).

Family trees give Peter’s death as 10 May 1678, also the date of Hananiah’s wedding; both require confirmation. The 1661 Lydia Gaunt entry is unplaced and is not evidence about Peter’s wife.
body: Peter Gaunt settled at Sandwich on Cape Cod, in Plymouth Colony, with his wife Lydia, whose surname is unknown. One proposed identification links him to a Peter baptized at St Peter at Gowts, Lincoln, on 29 June 1610, son of Thomas Gaunt and Susan Bate. That identification remains unproved. Thomas and Susan married at Rotherham on 28 August 1609, and Susan's will calls Peter her only son.

The colony’s court books follow Peter Gaunt for six years. At the court of 6 March 1654/5 he was called in "to answare for neglecting to frequent the publick worship of God." Asked to speak to the charge, "Peter Gaunt affirmed hee knew noc publicke vizable worship now in the world, whereunto the said Ralph Allen assented, but Gorg Allen dissented; the case was left to further consideration." Within three years the same court was fining him for Quaker meetings.

On 2 March 1657/8 Gaunt, Daniel Wing, Ralph Allen Jr. and William Allin were summoned "for a tumultuose carriage att a meeting of the Quakers att Sandwich." The court cleared them of that charge, "notwithstanding, for theire vnreuerent carrying themselues before the Court, coming in before them with theire hatts on," it fined each of them twenty shillings. Thomas Butler, whose daughter Dorothy would marry Peter's son Hananiah in 1678, was summoned for the same disturbance and was "admonished and cleared."

The fines were collected in cattle. In June 1660 a note was entered in the court's record that Marshal George Barlow "tooke from Goodman Gaunt, for his fine of 24li, these particulares: seauen cowes & heifers, two steers, seauen bushells and an halfe of pease; and after, when one of the cowes died, hee tooke another liue one in stead therof, because Barlow had not the hide of the dead cow deliuered to him." Thomas Burgis Jr. owned in open court that he had made the report, and was himself fined thirty shillings for refusing to help the marshal. A Quaker list of goods taken from Plymouth Colony Friends about 1658 includes "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d."

The summonses kept coming. In October 1660 a long list of people "fined for being att Quakers meetings," ten shillings each, includes "Peter Gaunt, Dorithy Butler, Obadiah Butler." In February 1660/1 the Sandwich constable was ordered to bring Gaunt and nine others to Plymouth "to answare for theire tumultuouse carriages against the marshall and cunstable of Sandwich in the execution of theire offices in the cecuring of two Strang Quakers." A ten-shilling fine on Gaunt "was leuied vpon a mistake" and was given back. In 1661 a list given into the court of those who had sheltered visiting Friends reads: "Wiliam Allin entertained Christopher Holder. Wiliam Newland entertained one forraigne Quaker. Peter Gaunt entertained two forraigne Quakers."

Peter’s death is dated to 10 May 1678, the day of his son Hananiah’s marriage to Dorothy Butler, but that is unconfirmed. Lydia died in April 1692. Their sons included Israel and Hananiah, who went to New Jersey. A Lydia Gaunt named in a 1661 court case involving Thomas Burgis Jr. may or may not have been Peter’s wife.

P.name: Thomas & Dorothy Butler
P.place: Thomas Butler was at Sandwich, Plymouth Colony, soon after the town was founded in 1637. His wife Dorothy died there on 9 August 1675 and was buried the next day; Thomas died on 12 March 1690. Their daughter Dorothy married Hananiah Gaunt. Thomas's origin is not known.

body: Thomas Butler was at Sandwich, Plymouth Colony, soon after the town was founded in 1637. In March 1657/8 he was summoned with Peter Gaunt and others over a Quaker meeting and "admonished and cleared." In 1658-9 he was fined ten shillings "for refusing to assist the marshall, Barlow, in the execution of his office," and the court assigned another fine, fifty shillings for refusing to serve as constable, to Barlow himself.

In June 1660 the court passed two sentences on the family: "Daniell Butler, for rescuing a Strang Quaker, when apprehended by the marshall, Barlow, and for his breakeing away when taken p'soner, is sentanced to bee publickly whipt, which accordingly was pformed." The next reads: "Thomas Butler, and Dorithy, his wife, for turbulent cariages the same night that theire son Daniell was serched for att theire house, fined forty shillings." In October 1660 Dorothy Butler, almost certainly the mother, was fined ten shillings for being at Quaker meetings.
The court later returned twenty shillings taken from Thomas for his wife and son attending a Quaker meeting. Its October list also names Obadiah Butler among those fined.

Thomas was also a land-hunter. In 1665 the court sent Richard Bourne and William Bassett "to view and purchase some lands desired by Edmond Freeman and Thomas Butler lying towards Saconeesett," and when the Indians would not part with that parcel it gave them leave to buy other land for him. In 1667 the court granted Butler "a necke of land called Tassacausett, lying neare to Edmond Freemans land," which he had "bought ... of an Indian called Charles, alias Pampmumitt, for a yoake of oxen," provided the Indian returned three pounds to Butler.

Dorothy died on 9 August 1675 and was buried the next day. Thomas died on 12 March 1690. Their daughter Dorothy, born 23 January 1649/50, married Hananiah Gaunt at the Quaker meeting at Sandwich in 1678, and they carried the Quaker family to New Jersey. Thomas's origin and Dorothy's maiden name are not known.

P.rel: Possible ancestors in the Gaunt line
P.place: Rotherham, Norton and Lincoln, England. Their only son, Peter, baptized at Lincoln in 1610, may be the Peter Gaunt who settled at Sandwich in Plymouth Colony (unproved).

P.title: A Lincoln husband, a Sheffield-side bride and one surviving son
P.hook: A couple married at Rotherham in 1609 and had a son Peter who may have been the later Sandwich settler.
body: Thomas Gaunt was baptized at Silkstone in the West Riding on 22 July 1571, though the register does not name his parents. On 28 August 1609 he married Susan Bate at Rotherham, about thirteen miles from Silkstone and ten from her home parish of Norton, south of Sheffield. Susan had been baptized at St James, Norton, on 23 September 1571, the daughter of James Bate.

Thomas was almost certainly marrying for the second time. His will of 1621 names children George, James, Anne and 'Dynes' as well as Peter, and Susan's own will says Peter was her only son. A Peter Gaunt was baptized at Lincoln on 29 June 1610, the year after the wedding; whether he was the couple’s son and the later Sandwich settler is not proved. The family lived in Lincoln, where Thomas was buried on 14 April 1621; Susan was buried there in February 1626, leaving a will that also names her brothers and sister, Thomas, Adam and Alice Bate.

This Thomas Gaunt is not the Thomas Gaunt of Pinchbeck, Lincolnshire, who married Isabel Wheelwright in 1602, and the unsourced parents some trees give him (Thomas Gaunt and Elizabeth Wheelwright) are set aside. His own parents are not known.
P.note: The marriage, Susan's baptism and both wills are record-based. The link from Peter Gaunt of Sandwich to this Lincoln couple rests on the wills naming Peter, as summarized on WikiTree; Thomas's parents are not known.

P.title: The Bates of Jordanthorpe
P.hook: Susan Bate's father James is known only from the Norton baptisms of his children; where he came from is not recorded.
body: James Bate and Dorothy Harrison married in 1569, and their children were baptized at St James, Norton, a mile north of the hamlet of Jordanthorpe: William in 1570, Susan in September 1571, Jane in 1576. James is called 'of Jordanthorpe' at the marriage of his daughter Elizabeth and at his own death in March 1608. Dorothy outlived him by four years.

James Bate's origins are not known. A baptism for a James 'Batty', son of Robert, at Kirkburton about twenty-five miles away in January 1547/8 fits his estimated birth year, but the name is too common to claim him.
Susan carried the Bate name to Lincoln when she married Thomas Gaunt in 1609, and she remembered her brothers Thomas and Adam and her sister Alice in her will.
P.note: Parish registers name James as father of Susan; his own parents are unknown. Dorothy's parents are not given.

P.name: William & Elizabeth (Hayhurst) Croasdale
P.place: Newhey (Newah) in the Forest of Bowland, Yorkshire. Quakers of Settle Monthly Meeting; buried at Settle Meeting, Newton.

Died 18th of 4th month 1672; buried 20th beside him

P.title: Friends of Newhey, and the son who crossed the Atlantic
P.hook: William and Elizabeth Croasdale were buried side by side at Settle Meeting; a family history calls it 'highly probable' that they were the emigrant Thomas's parents.
body: William Croasdale of Newhey in the Forest of Bowland died on the 29th day of the 11th month 1666 and was buried on the 31st at the Friends' burial ground at Settle Meeting, Newton. His wife Elizabeth died in the 4th month of 1672 and was buried next to him.

A Thomas, son of William and Elizabeth, is placed at Settle by two reference works on early Pennsylvania settlers. A family genealogist calls it 'highly probable' that William and Elizabeth were the parents of the Thomas who emigrated to Pennsylvania in 1682, while noting that other parentage has been suggested. Henry Croasdale of Newhey is another proposed earlier ancestor, but the generations connecting him to the emigrant are unproven. A William, son of Henry Croasdale of Newhey, was baptized on 24 October 1621, later than the c.1618 birth year used here; whether he is this William is not known.
Elizabeth's surname Hayhurst comes from family compilations and has no original record behind it.
P.note: Burial dates come from the Settle Meeting register as abstracted by the cited authors; the parent link to Thomas is secondary-source probable, and Elizabeth's surname is unconfirmed.

P.title: Henry Croasdale of Newhey, yeoman
P.hook: A Bowland yeoman named his son William as administrator in his September 1652 will and was buried at Waddington three weeks later.
body: Henry Croasdale lived at Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, within the parish of Waddington. The register records three of his children between 1616 and 1621: Elizabeth, buried 1 June 1616; Edward, baptized 13 January 1617/8; and William, baptized 24 October 1621.

His burial reads 'Henry Croasdell buried Oct: 10' (1652). He had made his will the month before, on 21 September 1652, as 'Henrie Croasdale, yeoman; Newhay within Bolannd', with his son William as administrator; it was registered in 1654. No wife is named.

This Henry is made the grandfather of the Thomas Croasdale who emigrated in 1682, but that step is an inference: the William baptized in 1621 would have been about 23 if Thomas was born in 1644, and some published lines give a different Henry (died 1595).

No evidence in the reviewed index names Janet Harrison as his wife, and no such relationship is established here.

P.src: Ancestry Lancashire, England, Baptisms, Marriages and Burials 1538-1812; England, Select Deaths and Burials 1538-1991, as cited on WikiTree Hawthornthwaite-8 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Hawthornthwaite-8) and WikiTree Hawthornewaite-1 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Hawthornewaite-1); NSCDA, Founding Females Qualifying Ancestor Index no. 046, Croasdale, Agnes Hathornthwaite: https://nscda.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/046-Croasdale-Agnes-Hathornthwaite.-PA.-Historic-Founder-.docx.pdf; WikiTree, Croasdale-30: https://wikitree.com/wiki/Croasdale-30; Genealogical Speaking blog, Bucks County records (Settle MM removal certificate June 1682; indenture 21 Apr 1682): https://genealogicalyspeaking.blogspot.com/2008/06/bucks-county-pa-records-hayhurst.html
P.title: A father who died the year his daughter was born
P.hook: Agnes Hawthornthwaite is said to have been born in 1633, the year her father William died at 26.
body: Agnes Hawthornthwaite, later wife of Thomas Croasdale, is said to have been born on 13 July 1633 in Tatham parish. Her father William Hawthornthwaite, born in 1607, is said to have married Elizabeth in Lancashire in 1631 and to have died in 1633, aged 26.
The sources for this are indexes of Lancashire parish registers and burials, not the register entries themselves, and nothing ties Agnes to William beyond the dates, so the link is unconfirmed.

Agnes appears at the other end of her life in the Quaker records. She married Thomas Croasdale, and in June 1682 Settle Monthly Meeting issued a removal certificate to a company of Friends bound for America that included Thomas, Agnes and six children. Thomas had bought land in Pennsylvania from William Penn by an indenture of 21 April 1682, on Neshaminy Creek in Bucks County near what is now Langhorne. Agnes was buried at Neshaminy on 20 October, in 1684 by one account and 1686 by another.
One account gives a different Agnes: born about 1646, married at Lancaster in 1664, and arriving on the Welcome. If that is the right Agnes, William, who died in 1633, cannot have been her father.
P.note: Index-level sourcing only; the parent link to Agnes is not shown from a register entry. Conflict: the NSCDA Founding Females index (citing Sheppard and McCracken) gives Agnes Hathornthwaite Croasdale as born about 1646, married at Lancaster Monthly Meeting on 20 May 1664, mother of six children born at Lancaster, and sailing on the Welcome (left Deal 31 Aug 1682), buried 20 Oct 1684. That cannot be squared with a daughter born in July 1633 to a father buried in 1633, so the parentage is probably wrong; the other trees' ship (Lamb) and her death year (1686) also differ. The Settle certificate and the 1682 indenture are known only through a blog summary, and an administration of Thomas's estate in December 1684 reported there sits oddly with a burial for Agnes in October 1684.

P.name: Anthony & Ann (Pitts) Chamness of London
P.place: East Smithfield and Wapping, London. If the link holds, they are the grandparents of Anthony Chamness, who was sent to America as a boy and settled at Cane Creek.
kv: 23 Sep 1686, St James, Duke's Place, London (FamilySearch)
John Chamness, b. c.1681, bapt. 19 Nov 1682, St Saviour, Southwark; d. 1716 London (per WikiTree)
Born c.1665; said to have died 1745 at Tedburn St Mary, Devon
P.src: FamilySearch England Marriages 1538-1973 (FHL film 374448, NV29-23V), as cited on WikiTree Chamness-43 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Chamness-43); WikiTree Chamness-8 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Chamness-8); Wikipedia, 'St James Duke's Place' (consecrated 1622; parish exempt from the Bishop of London; 'marriage factory'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James_Duke%27s_Place
P.title: A 1686 marriage in Duke's Place
P.hook: A London record shows an Anthony Champneys marrying Anne Pitts in 1686, but their son John was baptized four years earlier.
body: John Chamness, who married Ann Wearey at St John's, Wapping, in 1704, is said to be the son of Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts. The only evidence for the parents is the marriage of Anthony 'Champneys' and Anne Pitts at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686. St James, Duke's Place, stood just inside the walls at Aldgate on old priory ground that had passed to the Dukes of Norfolk; it was consecrated in 1622, its parish claimed exemption from the Bishop of London, and by the later seventeenth century it had a name as a marriage factory, with several weddings a day.

That date is four years after John's baptism, in November 1682 at St Saviour's in Southwark. Though it is said there is 'no geographical or chronological reason to dispute' the link, the order of dates is a reason to be careful. The church's reputation might explain a wedding after the child, since John could have been baptized before his parents formally married, but nothing shows that was the case here. Or the baptism belongs to another family. John, whoever his parents were, is said to have died in London in 1716.

Anthony 'appears to be' the son of a John Chamness of Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex, and his wife Mary Reffell, but those Essex generations are not added here. Ann Pitts is said to have lived until 1745, in Devon.
P.note: Marriage record exists; nothing cited ties John Chamness (b. c.1681) to this couple as their son.

P.title: A Quaker family on the Kent
P.hook: A Chesterfield Meeting birth record gives a John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary; whether he is the John Rogers whose son Thomas married Ann Staples is not settled.
body: The Burlington County Quaker John Rogers, born about 1656 at Rotherham, is said to have crossed with Friends on the Kent, which loaded at London in March 1677 and landed at the Delaware in 1678. He married Mary Groom, who died on 13 February 1693, and the couple had at least five children.

This family is tied to a John Rogers born 'the 5th day of the 1st month 1687' at Nottingham, Burlington County, by the Chesterfield Quaker birth record, and that John is given a wife Martha Middleton, whose mother's 1712 will names a 'son-in-law John Rogers'.

Two estates have been attached to John Rogers in family trees. John Rodgers of Burlington made his will on 23 January 1764; it was proved on 26 March 1767 and gave his son Thomas one-third of the residue. John Rogers of Windsor made a different will on 6 January 1769, proved on 10 April 1776, naming seven sons and two daughters but no Thomas. Neither gives the testator’s parents. The identity of the John born in 1687, and his connection to our Thomas Rogers, remain unresolved.
P.note: The Chesterfield birth record is cited through online genealogy, not independently examined here. The two published probate abstracts establish distinct estates; neither proves the parentage of our Thomas Rogers’s father.

P.title: From the Isle of Man to Belfast to Iredell
P.hook: A 1720 marriage at Downpatrick is the only solid piece in the chain behind James Stevenson of Iredell County.
body: Henry Stevenson married Ann Curlett on 2 June 1720 at Saul parish, near Downpatrick, the ground where Saint Patrick is said to have founded his first church. Ann had been baptized on 27 May 1698 at Braddan, a parish on the Isle of Man that now includes part of Douglas, a daughter of William Curlett. Their children, as family trees list them, include a James born about March 1721 at Belfast.

That James is identified with the James Stevenson who died on 5 March 1820 in Iredell County, North Carolina, a native of Ireland, nearly 90 years old, married 65 years, with 208 descendants. His estate was probated in Iredell in 1820.

Henry's own birthplace and his parents (given as William Stevenson and Katherine Alison) have no cited source. Whether this James is the father of the James Stevenson (1746-1828) in the Stevenson line here is itself only a possibility. A 1955 note in the Skinner genealogy describes an immigrant James Stevenson who died in 1820 and gives his wife as Sally Kelly of Maryland, and it does not call him Henry's son, so the picture of James's origins is unsettled.

Iredell was crowded with Stevensons. William Stevenson of County Antrim, called Little Gabriel, took up land there in 1762 and grew it to nearly 3,400 acres, and he was an elder of Fourth Creek Presbyterian Church. How James Stevenson was related to him, if at all, is unknown.
P.note: Marriage indexes are solid; the children are attached from family-tree compilations, and the obituary does not name Henry or Ann. The Skinner genealogy's 1955 note names the 1820 immigrant's wife as Sally Kelly of Maryland and does not call him Henry's son; this conflict with the tree is unresolved.

P.title: Cedar Creek Friends move south
P.hook: Robert Johnson, son of Ashley, married Cisley (Virginia) Elmore at Cedar Creek Meeting in 1758 and was sent south to Deep River with her in 1766.
body: On 19 November, in a public meeting at Cedar Creek, Robert Johnson of Louisa County, son of Ashley, took Cisley Elmore, daughter of Thomas Elmore of Amelia County, as his wife. The wedding falls in 1758 as the minute is transcribed, although a 1988 Johnson genealogy prints 1759. That genealogy names her Virginia C. Elmore and records that 'Robert and Virginia Johnson rec. on cert. from Cedar Creek M.M., Va., dated 1766-3-29'. Cisley is the old form of Cecilia, her mother's name, and the family tree carries her as Cecelia. Both were buried at Springfield Meeting in North Carolina, and Robert's estate was opened in Stokes County in 1808.

Robert was born in February 1737 or 1738 in New Kent County, probably the son of Ashley Johnson and Martha Woody, whose family later farmed Chamberlain's Creek in Louisa County. Cisley, born at Black Creek in 1737, was a daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson.

Cedar Creek's Friends had been meeting in Hanover County, near the forks of the Anna rivers, since about 1719, and in about 1744 Johnsons, Moormans and Clarks set up Camp Creek Meeting in neighboring Louisa County; the families on both sides of the line intermarried constantly. The drought of 1754-56, the French and Indian War and stricter regulation of Quakers then sent many Hanover and Louisa families to Bedford County, to southwest Virginia and on into North Carolina, where the Established Church had less hold. The Cane Creek meeting, in the North Carolina Piedmont, had held its first monthly meeting on 7 October 1751 and earned the name Mother of Meetings by starting the others, and thirty Pennsylvania families had already settled around it.
An unsourced family tree lists Martha Johnson, born 28 August 1766 at Deep River, who married Aden Nordyke in 1787, among their children. The Quaker minutes support the couple but do not name Martha.

quotes.t: Robert, Louisa Co., s Ashely; m in a public mtg, Cisley ELMORE, dt Thomas, Amelia Co.
quotes.c: Cedar Creek Monthly Meeting marriage entry, 19 Nov 1758, as transcribed on the Johnson DNA project page (Olive group)

P.note: The Quaker abstracts are good evidence for the couple. The 1758 entry calls the groom 'Robert, Louisa Co., s Ashely' and the bride 'Cisley ELMORE, dt Thomas, Amelia Co.', which supports Ashley Johnson as his father and confirms the surname Elmore; her first name is Cisley (Cecilia) there and 'Virginia C.' in the 1988 abstract, and the tree keeps Cecelia. The year is 1758 in the transcription and 1759 in the 1988 abstract; the original minute has not been seen. The step to Martha Johnson (b. 1766) as their daughter comes from a compiled family history, so it stays probable. The family tree carries the couple as Robert Valentine Johnson (8 February 1737 to 24 April 1807) and Cecelia Johnson; the dates above follow the Johnson genealogy, which has Robert's estate opened in 1808. Robert's last residence is not settled: his estate was opened in Stokes County, but both were buried at Springfield Meeting. The Cedar Creek and Camp Creek founding dates come from a secondary account.

P.title: A gift of everything for 'love and affection'
P.hook: In 1794 Ashley Johnson deeded his whole estate to his son Elijah in return for keeping him and Martha for the rest of their lives.
body: Ashley Johnson was born about 1710 in St Peter's Parish, New Kent County, and married Martha Woody in Henrico or New Kent County; the sources give 12 December 1734 and 10 or 12 October 1735. They raised at least eight sons and five daughters, including Robert, born February 1738. Their son Robert is named in the Cedar Creek marriage entry of 1758 as "Robert, Louisa Co., s Ashely."

Two Louisa County deeds fill in the later years. On 9 November 1778 Ashley gave his son Elijah 241 acres on Chamberlain's Creek. On 3 February 1794 he gave Elijah all his estate, real and personal, 'for love and affection and maintenance of the said Ashley Johnson and Martha his wife during their natural lives', except 210 acres jointly to David and James, with a feather bed and furniture each for Martha, Elizabeth and David.
Martha died on 6 September 1802 and Ashley about 1803, aged about 93; both are buried at Roundabout Castle Cemetery in Louisa County.
