P.title: John Johnson’s land on Black Creek
P.hook: A 1705 patent traces 252 acres beside Black Creek and credits John Johnson with the importation of five named people.
body: John Johnson first appears in St Peter’s Parish on 22 November 1702, when a son John was baptized. A patent dated 2 November 1705 granted John Johnson 252 acres in St Peter’s Parish, New Kent County, on the north side of Black Creek. It credits him with the importation of five people into the colony, without saying they were relatives or what their terms of service were.

The five names written beside the grant appear to read Wm Davies, Saml Mitchel, Joan Hillard, Dan Gibbs and George Abraham. Their spellings are tentative readings of the handwriting. The boundary runs between marked trees and along the creek: a pine, a white oak, a maple at a small branch and Thomas Snead’s line. The tract had first been granted to Thomas Reynolds on 25 October 1695, then deserted and granted again to Johnson under a General Court order of 17 October 1705.

A second patent, dated 9 February 1727/8, granted John Johnson of Hanover County 200 acres in Henrico County on the south side of Chickahominy Swamp, for twenty shillings. Later deeds say John and his wife Elizabeth sold that land on 1 November 1736; he is reported to have died on 5 September 1737, though these details are unconfirmed.

A Quaker abstract names Ashley Johnson's mother as Lucretia Massie, but Friends' records call John's wife Elizabeth, and Lucretia and her Massie parentage rest on uncited histories. John's own parents are also disputed.
P.note: The 1705 and 1727/8 patent manuscripts have been independently examined. The five people’s names are tentative readings; the patent says persons, not servants, and gives no ship, arrival dates, kinship or service terms. These patents document land grants and do not establish Ashley Johnson’s parentage, the identity of John’s first wife, or his earlier ancestry. The 1736 sale and reported 1737 death remain based on the separately cited references. This proposed ancestral connection remains probable.

P.title: A Spotsylvania will with six sons
P.hook: John Paine's will names six sons, one of them a William, and the line to the Stevenson wife Lydia Payne runs through that name.
body: John Paine was born in Drysdale Parish, King and Queen County, in 1705, a son of Barnett Paine. He witnessed a Spotsylvania County deed in 1740 and died there between the date of his will, 25 July 1764, and the executors' bond of 20 September 1770. The will names his wife Frances and sons John (eldest), Thomas, Barnett, William, Robert and George.
Frances is thought to be a daughter of Robert and Mary (Clayton) Coleman, but there is 'considerable disagreement' over which Coleman family. A 1750 will reportedly calls her 'Francis Pain'.

The link to the Stevensons is by way of Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia Payne, whose father William Paine (1754-1807, Burke County, N.C.) is listed as one of John's sons. That William is tied to Lydia only through a memorial, and two men named William Paine have been confused, so the whole link is unproven.
P.note: The will is a real record; whether William Paine of Burke County is John's son, and Lydia his daughter, is unproven.

P.title: The stone house on Sugaw Creek
P.hook: Hezekiah Alexander, a blacksmith turned planter and revolutionary, finished his stone house on Sugaw Creek in 1774, and his daughter Esther, it seems, went west to Kentucky as Mrs. Samuel Garrison.
body: Hezekiah Alexander was born on 13 January 1728 (or 1722, as one Garrison family history has it) at New Munster in Cecil County, Maryland. He married Mary Sample, a daughter of William Sample Sr. and Esther Garrison, and they settled in the Sugaw Creek congregation in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, where they raised a large family: eleven children by the usual count, though the 1796 will and the biography dictionary account for ten, seven sons and three daughters.

He began as a blacksmith and became a planter. From 1768 he was a justice of the peace for Mecklenburg, and in the first years of the Revolution he sat on the county and Salisbury district committees of safety. In 1776 he was one of the thirteen members of the state’s Council of Safety and a delegate to the congress at Halifax, where he served on the committees that drafted North Carolina’s first bill of rights and constitution. He was also a founder and treasurer of Queens College in Charlotte. Later tradition counted him among the signers of the Mecklenburg Declaration of May 1775, which historians doubt, since no account of it can be traced earlier than 1819; his younger brother, John McKnitt Alexander, is the man tradition names as its clerk. The Daughters of the American Revolution recognize Hezekiah as a patriot.

The stone house he finished in 1774 is the oldest in Mecklenburg County. It has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1970, and the Charlotte Museum of History keeps it and the homesite.

The plantation was worked by enslaved people: at least seventeen men, women and children, whose names survive in the Alexander wills and in the inventory of Hezekiah’s estate taken in October 1801. His will left a woman named Jean, and her children Siah, Frank and Nancy, to his daughter Esther Garrison. Esther was to hold the children, and any Jean might later have, for eighteen years, after which they were to pass to Esther’s own children as they came of age. Other bequests sent Mary to his son James R. Alexander, Ann to Silas, Jack to William Sample Alexander, and Bet and an older man named Sam to his wife, Mary. He made the will on 8 August 1796, or perhaps in 1797. Whether Jean and her children went with Esther and Samuel Garrison to Kentucky about 1800 is not known.

Their daughter Esther was born on 28 September 1762. In his will Hezekiah remembered his daughter “Esther Garrison,” with her “dau. Caroline Garrison and other ch. of Esther.” That she was the Esther who married Samuel Garrison and was the mother of John Milton Garrison of Allen County, Kentucky, is probable.

Hezekiah's younger brother left the trail of paper that his own household lost. The original records of the Mecklenburg meeting of May 1775 were burned when fire destroyed John McKnitt Alexander's house in 1800, and the rough, torn notes found after his death are all the supporters of the declaration have. A collection of forty-one items gathered by Joseph McKnitt Alexander and others, with copies of witnesses' testimony and the papers behind the state's 1831 report, is held at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
P.note: Hezekiah and Mary are well documented; that Esther (Alexander) Garrison is their daughter, and mother of John Milton Garrison, rested on compiled lists until the 1796 will abstract, which names his daughter Esther Garrison; that she was John Milton Garrison's mother rests on the Garrison family record (probable).

P.name: Col. Amos Alexander
P.place: New Munster, Cecil County, Maryland; buried at Head of Christiana, Delaware
P.title: The brother who stayed: Amos Alexander of Cecil County
P.hook: While his brother Hezekiah carried the family south to Sugaw Creek, Amos Alexander stayed on the Maryland tract where they were born: cooper, mill owner, church elder, justice, legislator and wagon colonel, dead of wounds in 1780.
kv: Sarah Sharp; four sons and six daughters
Rock Church elder; Cecil Co. justice (1774, 1777, 1778); Lower House 1777–78
Colonel in Patterson's Brigade of Wagons; deputy quartermaster general for Delaware from 29 Nov 1779
Between 16 Feb and 1 May 1780, of wounds received in the war; buried at Head of Christiana
body: Amos Alexander was born in 1729 in Cecil County, Maryland, on the New Munster tract at the head of the Chesapeake, where the Scots-Irish Alexanders had farmed and worshipped for a generation. His father was James Alexander, a yeoman, and his mother Margaret McKnitt, and he grew up in a crowded house of brothers: Theophilus, Hezekiah, Josiah, Ezekiel and John McKnitt, with four sisters.

The brothers split in two. John McKnitt went to North Carolina in 1754, and Hezekiah too made his way to the Carolina backcountry, where he became a blacksmith, a planter and a member of the state's Council of Safety. Amos stayed. He worked as a cooper, owned a mill, and married Sarah Sharp, a name that belonged to the neighborhood's Presbyterian families. They raised four sons, Walter, James, Amos and Mark, and six daughters, one of them Mary, who married John Evans. Like his brother Theophilus he became an elder of the Rock Church, the congregation that families from Head of Christiana had founded in 1720 to have a church nearer home.

As the Revolution came on, the quiet cooper became a public man. He was commissioned a justice of the peace for Cecil County in 1774, and again in 1777 and 1778. Men came to him at Elkton to swear their oaths of allegiance to the new State of Maryland, among them David Barr and John Waggoner. In 1777 and 1778 he sat in the Lower House of the Maryland legislature for Cecil County. By 1779 he was called Esquire.

The war reached him through wagons. Amos held a colonel's rank in the Continental service in John Patterson's Brigade of Wagons, and from 29 November 1779 he was deputy quartermaster general for Delaware, the man responsible for moving the army's supplies through that state, and still at it in February 1780. Sometime between 16 February and 1 May of that year he died of wounds he had received in the war. His own father had died in 1779, only the year before. His eldest son Walter, a captain in the Maryland militia, died at about the same time, and the two are remembered together among the patriots of the Head of Christiana cemetery, where Amos was buried.

Amos was a man of property, and part of that property was people. His personal estate was valued at £1,735 2s., counting books, mills and five enslaved people whose names have not been found. On his brother Hezekiah's Sugaw Creek plantation at least seventeen enslaved people are known by name from the Alexander wills and the 1801 inventory, and the 1790 census counted thirteen there at one time. The two brothers both sat as justices of the peace, one in Maryland and one in North Carolina, in the years of the Revolution, and both lived on the labor of people they held in bondage.
Hezekiah outlived Amos by twenty-one years. In Maryland the widow Sarah was charged with 247 acres on the 1783 tax assessment.
P.note: Evidence: probable. The Archives of Maryland entry (a published reference) names Amos's parents, his brothers including Hezekiah, his offices, rank, estate and death; Johnston's 1881 Cecil County history and Johns's Rock Church history independently call Amos and Theophilus brothers, elders and burials at Head of Christiana. Remaining weakness: Hezekiah's own parentage rests on the same compiled tradition, so the link of this family to Hezekiah and to our line stays probable rather than proven. Not checked in a primary record: Amos's will or inventory, his commission as deputy quartermaster general, and the manner and place of his wounding (the entry says only 'of wounds received in the war'). Son Walter's death in 1780 and burial at Head of Christiana come from a cemetery volunteer list, not a gravestone seen. The story says 'five enslaved' from the entry; ages and names unknown. Hezekiah's year of leaving Maryland is not documented here (John McKnitt's 1754 date is from Johnston). The Maryland legislature entry gives his son Walter's death as by 1779; a cemetery list puts it in 1780, so the story says only that he died at about the same time.

P.title: Two wills on one day
P.hook: William and Esther Sample each signed a will on 26 January 1769, and he was dead that month.
body: William Sample Sr. was born about 1690, in either Northern Ireland or Scotland, and lived in Cecil County, Maryland, before the family moved to Mecklenburg County. He signed a will on 26 January 1769 and died that same month; his wife Esther Garrison signed her own will the same day. The loose estate papers name five children: William, John, Joseph, Mary and Agnes.

Their daughter Mary, born 31 January 1734, married Hezekiah Alexander, a fellow Cecil County man, on 12 June 1752. In January 1769 Hezekiah was a county magistrate, an office he held from 1768, and he and Mary were living on the 600 acres or so on Sugar Creek that he had bought in 1767; their stone house was still five years from completion. Mary outlived Hezekiah, who died in 1801, never remarried, and died in 1805. Her youngest sons, Joel and Oswald, divided the land between them, and Oswald received the house. Esther's parentage is not carried further here.
William and Esther lie at Hopewell Presbyterian Church, whose congregation now worships in a stone building from about 1833.

William Sample made his will in Mecklenburg County on 26 January 1769. He named his wife Esther and “Hez: Alexander my Son in law” as his executors, left ten pounds to his daughter Mary Alexander, and remembered his sons John, Joseph and William and his daughter Esther.
P.note: The wills and estate papers are the record basis; birthplace and Esther's parentage come from compiled summaries.

P.place: Manokin Hundred, Somerset County, then New Munster, Cecil County, Maryland. Buried at Head of Christiana Church, Delaware.

P.title: A Cecil County elder and two McKnitt sisters
P.hook: James Alexander of Cecil County, a magistrate and Presbyterian elder, married two McKnitt sisters in turn; the first, Margaret, was the mother of Hezekiah, the Mecklenburg patriot.
body: James Alexander was born about 1690 at Manokin in Somerset County, Maryland, into a Scots-Irish family said to descend from a tanner, Joseph Alexander, one of seven brothers who reached Somerset County before 1670. He moved north to Cecil County, where he became a magistrate and an elder of the Presbyterian church. His first wife was Margaret McKnitt, born 26 December 1693, the daughter of John McKnitt and Jane Wallace, and she bore him twelve children by a Bible list, among them Hezekiah, born in 1722 or 1728 (1728 in one standard account). Margaret died at New Munster on 31 July 1736, and James married her sister Abigail, who gave him five more.

Hezekiah grew up in the Cecil County household, learned the blacksmith's trade, and carried the family's Presbyterian faith south to the Carolina backcountry, where he became one of Mecklenburg's leading men.

Hezekiah went first to Cumberland County, Pennsylvania, and then on to the Carolina Piedmont, where he was buying land near the Catawba River by 1764. In 1752 he had married Mary Sample, whose family would follow the same road south. In 1767 he bought more than 600 acres on Sugar Creek in Mecklenburg County and by 1774 had finished a two-story stone house on it, the oldest house in Mecklenburg County and the centerpiece of the Charlotte Museum of History. A magistrate from 1768, he sat on the Mecklenburg Committee of Safety, helped write the state's first constitution as a member of the Provincial Congress, and was a trustee of Queens College.

His father outlived Margaret by forty-three years. James died in Cecil County on 31 May 1779 and was buried at the Head of Christiana Church cemetery near Newark, Delaware. Three separate compilations give his birth as 1690, and he is recognized as a patriot ancestor.

His own parents were Joseph Alexander and Abigail McKnitt, which made his first wife Margaret his cousin. Joseph died in Cecil County by March 1730, and beyond him the 'Seven Brothers' Alexanders from Donegal are a speculative family tradition. Margaret's parents, John McKnitt and Jane Wallace, are named in print but come with no dates.
P.note: Evidence: probable. The Dictionary of North Carolina Biography names James Alexander and Margaret McKnitt as Hezekiah's parents; the dates and the other children come from a family Bible list as summarized on WikiTree, and no Cecil County record has been examined. The Donegal ancestry beyond James is not accepted. A member-tree variant that gives Hezekiah's mother as 'Abigail McKnight' is not followed.

P.place: Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, then Warren (later Allen) County, Kentucky. Samuel is said to be buried at Old Scottsville Cemetery.

P.title: A Continental private and the road to Kentucky
P.hook: Samuel Garrison, a Revolutionary soldier, moved from Mecklenburg to Kentucky; his family record names John Milton among his children.
body: Samuel Garrison was born on 24 August 1762 in Halifax County, North Carolina, by one account, served in the Revolution as a private in the Continental Line, and was buried in Old Scottsville Cemetery in Kentucky. His wife Esther Alexander was born in Mecklenburg County in 1762, but her place of death is given as Coles County, Illinois, which does not fit a husband buried in Kentucky. His pension file shows North Carolina militia service rather than the Continental Line, and the family record puts Esther's death in Allen County, Kentucky.

John Milton Garrison is said to have come from Mecklenburg County to Warren, later Allen, County, Kentucky, with his parents before 1809, which matches Samuel's move. Samuel's own family record book lists John Milton, born 4 October 1788, among his nine children; no county record names him as Samuel's son. Samuel's father is given as John Garrison of Salem, New Jersey, with no source.

Samuel wrote verse. At some point in the late eighteenth century he set down a poem called "Choice" about the wife he hoped to find, one "ruled by reason not by passion led," of mild temper and good sense, ideally nearing twenty. Whether Esther met every requirement nobody can say, but they stayed married for life and settled on Bay's Fork Creek in south-central Kentucky. The original manuscript of the poem and a family genealogy are now in the Manuscripts and Folklife Archives at Western Kentucky University, and a monument praising his life and Revolutionary service was dedicated on 12 May 2001 at Old Scottsville Cemetery. A book on his descendants, covering Samuel (1762-1833) and Esther Alexander (1762-1829), draws on that collection.
P.note: Consistent with the move to Allen County. The family record copied by Stuart names John Milton among Samuel's children (probable); no county record does.

P.name: Jesse Blackshear & Hannah (Huggins)
P.place: Jesse was born in Jones (or Craven) County, North Carolina, about 1767, married there about 1788, and took his family to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810. Hannah Huggins, born in Jones County in 1771, outlived him, remarried, and died in Wayne County, Tennessee, in 1829. Their daughter Penny is the probable wife of John Grimes.
kv: c.1767, Jones or Craven Co., N.C.
1787–89, Jones Co., N.C.; fee of 10 shillings, bride not named
77-acre grant on the south side of Trent River, 1796
Estate of 'Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd' settled Oct 1814
b. 20 May 1771, Jones Co., N.C.; remarried Isaac Mairs (Marrs); d. 4 Jun 1829, Wayne Co., Tenn.
P.title: Jesse and Hannah: a license, a grant and a widow who remarried
P.hook: Jesse Blackshear bought a marriage license in Jones County about 1788, took up 77 acres in 1796, and vanishes from North Carolina; his widow Hannah is the one who shows up in Tennessee court in 1814.
body: Jesse's North Carolina paper trail is short. He was a chain-bearer on a Jones County survey in 1782 and again in 1789. Between 1787 and 1789 he paid ten shillings for a marriage license in Jones County, with no bride named. The 1790 census for Jones County counts him as one man over sixteen with two females in the house. In 1794 he entered a plea for land, and in 1796 he was granted 77 acres on the south side of the Trent River. After 1796 he is 'not found in N.C.'

The Tennessee record picks him up. In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of 'Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd.' His widow and administrator, by then 'Hannah Mairs, wife of Isaac Mairs,' showed a balance of $227.30 'subject to a division between Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees,' who are named as Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob and Jesse. So Jesse had at least nine living children in 1814, and one of them is called Penny, the name Penelope Blackshear Grimes went by.

Jesse moved to Williamson County between 1800 and 1810; two of his sons stayed in North Carolina until after 1810. Some of the sons named in the settlement can be traced. Ezekiel (born 13 July 1792) lived in Williamson County in 1820, in Haywood County in 1830, and died at Brownsville on 23 April 1837; his widow, Isabella Dobson, was “bur. in the Ozarks” in 1882. Elisha (about 1794) farmed in Marshall County in 1840. Jacob (born 26 January 1802) moved to McNairy and Obion counties. The first child in the book’s list is “A dau., m. Grimes.”

Hannah was a Huggins, born on 20 May 1771 in Jones County; she died on 4 June 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, and was buried in Brown Cemetery, with a second husband, Isaac Mairs or Marrs, and a child by him born about 1807. Her youngest Blackshear child is given as born in March 1804, so Jesse's death and her second marriage fall between 1804 and about 1807. Her father is very probably the Luke Huggins whose Jones County will of 1784 names a daughter Hannah.

The two families were tied twice. Jesse’s father, Elisha Stout Blackshear, whose wife was Susannah, named 'James Huggins' as a son-in-law and his granddaughter 'Susanna Huggins' in his will, so a Huggins had already married a Blackshear daughter; Hannah, a Huggins, married a Blackshear son. Both families lived in Jones County.

quotes.t: subject to a division between Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees
quotes.c: Williamson Co., Tenn., Probate Court, Wills vol. 2, p. 109, Oct. 1814 (as quoted on WikiTree Huggins-10)

P.src: P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (Atlanta, 1954), entry for Jesse (archive.org blackshearianage00blac); Tennessee Probate Court Books, Williamson Co., Wills 1812-1819, vol. 2, p. 109, as cited on WikiTree Huggins-10 and Blackshear-2; Jones Co., N.C. Grant Book 91; 1790 federal census, Jones Co., N.C.; P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954), entries for Ezekiel, Elisha and Jacob; WikiTree Blackshear-160
P.note: Jesse's father is stated in a printed genealogy, not in his father's will: Elisha Stout Blackshear's will names only sons Moses and Jacob, and the book says the other sons had already had their share and left. The book names no wife for Jesse; Hannah Huggins rests on WikiTree and a Texas family website. WikiTree's date of 26 July 1803 for Jesse's death sits oddly beside an estate settled in 1814, and WikiTree's 1814 death for Penelope is wrong if she was alive in 1850. Penny as the wife of John Grimes is probable, not proved; the next link down (that David H. Grimes of Wayne County was their son) is only a lead.

P.place: A planter of Jones County, North Carolina, who made his will on 8 March 1784 and died that year. He left his plantation to his son Jacob and named his youngest children, among them Hannah, who married Jesse Blackshear.

P.title: Luke Huggins and his 1784 will
P.hook: A Jones County planter's will leaves a shilling each to his older children and the rest to the youngest, and one of the youngest is Hannah.
body: Luke Huggins was born about 1715, probably in North Carolina, and was a planter in Jones County, which was cut off from Craven County in 1779. He made his will on 8 March 1784 and it was proved in December of that year.

His will provided: to his wife Nelly, the plantation where he lived 'as long as she is a widow or as long as she lives'; to daughters Phebe Shelfer, Sarah Standley and Nelly Littleton, and sons James, Luke and Isaac, one shilling each; to his son Jacob, the land where he lived 'with all the rest of my lands'; and the remainder of the estate to 'my youngest children, namely: Esther, Hannah, Thomas, Charles, and Temperance Huggins,' at his wife's death. Simon Spight and John Parry were executors, and Nathan Bryan, Waxel Parry and Adonijah Parry witnessed.

Hannah was about thirteen. She married Jesse Blackshear a few years later, and the Jones County papers show other ties between the two families: Jesse's father named a James Huggins as son-in-law. A James is also among Luke's sons, so the two families may have married in both directions.

quotes.t: my youngest children, namely: Esther, Hannah, Thomas, Charles, and Temperance Huggins
quotes.c: Will of Luke Huggins, Jones Co., N.C., 8 Mar 1784 (abstract in Gwynn, Abstracts of the Wills, vol. A)

P.name: Elisha Stout Blackshear & Susanna (Ward?)
P.place: Born at Little Creek in Kent County, Delaware, about 1736, and brought to Craven County, North Carolina, as a boy. He farmed on the Trent River in what became Jones County, served as executor of his father's will, and made his own will on 11 December 1808.
kv: c.1736, Little Creek, Kent Co., Del.
Made 11 Dec 1808; proved Nov term 1810, Jones Co., N.C. (Will Book A, p. 325)
Alexander, James, Jesse, Moses, Jacob, Rebecca, Susanna, Agnes, Nancy, Elizabeth, Temperance (eleven, per the Blacksheariana)
P.title: Elisha Stout Blackshear's will: a black horse named Pal
P.hook: Elisha's 1808 will leaves a granddaughter a black horse called Pal and a bed, and gives two grown sons nothing but their clothes because they had already had their share.
body: Elisha Stout Blackshear was born near Little Creek in Kent County, Delaware, about 1736, the son of Alexander and Agnes Blackshear, who left Delaware for Craven County, North Carolina, in the 1740s. His wife was Susanna. She was 'probably Ward': Enoch Ward of neighboring Carteret County named a daughter Susannah in his will, and Elisha's youngest son Jacob later named a son Enoch and lived beside an Enoch Ward in Georgia. No marriage bond has been found for either of them.

He was his father's executor. When Alexander's will was proved in Jones County in September 1786, 'Elisha Blackshear one of the Executors herein named qualified.' His mother's will of 1793 left him 'one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn and her pockets and silver clasps.

His own will, dated 11 December 1808 and proved in November 1810, starts: 'I lend to my wife Susanna Blackshier (during her life or widowhood) my black Horse called Jack and all my household & kitchen furniture.' His sons Moses and Jacob get 'all my wearing clothes only, they having had their proportionable part of my Estate'; the daughters Rebecca, Susanna and Agnes 'have received their proportionable' share; Nancy gets an enslaved man and a young horse called Ball, Elizabeth gets the sheep, and Temperance gets the cattle, the hogs and the rest. To granddaughter Susanna Huggins he leaves 'my black horse called Pal, and one bed & furniture,' and to a granddaughter Koonce a bed. His sons-in-law James Huggins, Samuel Westbrook and Elijah Koonce share his carpenter's and plantation tools.

Jesse, our line, is not named in the will. Jesse was among the eleven children and 'moved to Tenn., and had Ezekiel'; the sons not named in the will, Alexander, James and Jesse, were presumed to have gotten their share earlier and 'struck out to find their fortunes in other parts.' Jesse's birth about 1767 fits Elisha, who would have been about thirty-one.

quotes.t: I lend to my wife Susanna Blackshier (during her life or widowhood) my black Horse called Jack and all my household & kitchen furniture
quotes.c: Will of Elisha S. Blackshier, Jones Co., N.C., 11 Dec 1808

quotes.t: I give unto Elisha Blackshear, my son, one Stone Jug for the service he hath done
quotes.c: Will of Agnes Blackshear, Jones Co., N.C., 6 Jul 1793

P.note: Elisha as Jesse's father rests on the Blacksheariana, which does not cite a record naming Jesse as his son; the will does not name him. Susanna's maiden name Ward is the author's guess. A WikiTree profile gives Susannah Ward's birth as 16 January 1736 at Beaufort, Carteret County; no source for that date is given.

P.name: Alexander & Agnes Blackshear
P.place: Alexander was born in Kent County, Delaware, about 1708 and farmed at Little Creek Hundred. He and his wife Agnes sold their Delaware land in 1740, were in Craven County, North Carolina, by 1747, and settled on the Trent River in what became Jones County, where he died in 1786 and she in 1793.
kv: Deed of 100 acres from Robert Blackshaw to 'My Son Alexander Blacksliare'
Alexander and 'Agnis his wife' sell the land; she is examined alone about her consent (acknowledged 14 May 1741)
Petitions for 100 acres, Craven Co., N.C.; warrant 28 Mar 1748, Onslow Co.
Taxed on 517 acres and five enslaved people, Jones Co.
3 Oct 1785; proved Sept term 1786, Jones Co. Record Book A, p. 61
James, Eleanor (Bailey), Elisha Stout, Abraham, Sarah (Clifton), and a daughter who married a Fordham
P.title: Alexander and Agnes: from Delaware to the Trent
P.hook: A Delaware clerk took Agnes aside in 1741 to ask whether she really agreed to sell the family farm; her own will of 1793, made with her mark, remembers a stone jug and some silver clasps.
body: In 1735 Robert Blackshaw deeded 100 acres at Little Creek Hundred in Kent County, Delaware, to 'My Son Alexander Blacksliare,' for 'the natural love I bear him.' The land was part of a tract called Blackshier Range, and Alexander already held a proprietary grant to survey it. Robert had been born in New Jersey and had come down the Delaware.

On 12 February 1740 (old style) Alexander and 'Agnis his wife, of Little Creek Hundred,' confirmed the sale of the 100 acres to the executors of Robert Carter of Dover Hundred, who had bought it in his lifetime for fifty pounds. The deed was acknowledged in the Court of Common Pleas on 14 May 1741, when, the clerk wrote, Agnes 'being secretly examined out of the hearing of the said husband did declare that she freely & voluntarily became a party.' Alexander signed with his mark. By 1747 Alexander was witnessing a will in Craven County, North Carolina; in 1748 he petitioned the council at New Bern for a grant.

Over forty years he built up a farm on the south side of the Trent. In 1779 he was taxed in Jones County on 517 acres and five enslaved people. He also turns up in the North Carolina Revolutionary army accounts of 1777 and 1786, in small amounts. His will, dated 3 October 1785, leaves his wife all his estate for her life, 'one Large Bible and one pair of Brass-headed Hand Irons' to his son James, a small house and one acre to his daughter Eleanor Bailey, 100 acres on the south side of the Trent to his son Abraham and then to Abraham's son Alexander, and 82 acres to Elisha until 'my Grandson Jacob Blackshear son of my son Elisha' reached twenty-one. Elisha and Nathan Bryan were executors, and it was proved in September 1786.

Agnes outlived him by seven years. Her will of 6 July 1793 gives 'Elisha Blackshear, my son, one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' Abraham 'one barrel of Vinegar and my Garden,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn due from a neighbor and 'my pockits and Silver Clasps.' She signed it 'Agnes B. Blackshear, her mark.' Her maiden name is not recorded.

quotes.t: I give unto Elisha Blackshear, my son, one Stone Jug for the service he hath done
quotes.c: Will of Agnes Blackshear, Jones Co., N.C., 6 Jul 1793

quotes.t: being secretly examined out of the hearing of the said husband did declare that she freely & voluntarily became a party
quotes.c: Kent Co., Del., Deed Book M, vol. 1, p. 108 (acknowledged 14 May 1741)

P.src: Blacksheariana (1954), entry for Alexander No. 1 with printed texts of Kent Co., Del. Deed Book M vol. 1 p. 108 (certified abstract of 1953) and the Jones Co., N.C. wills (archive.org blackshearianage00blac); Craven Co. and Onslow Co. land records and Jones Co. tax list of 1779 as cited there

The book says 'probably Stout' (Elisha Stout is the son's name), and WikiTree makes her a daughter of Benjamin Stout and Agnes Truax of Delaware. Stillwell's Stout genealogy lists only sons Charles, Benjamin and Jacob for that Benjamin, a wife Agnes of unknown surname, and no daughter Agnes. That Stout daughter is not accepted here.

P.name: Robert Blackshaw of Little Creek
P.place: Born at Piscataway, New Jersey, on 24 August 1677, the son of Thomas and Ellenor Blackshaw. He moved to Lewes in Sussex County, Delaware, where he bought a town lot in 1708, and then to Little Creek in Kent County, where he took up 200 acres in 1716.
kv: Bought a town lot on Second Street, Lewes, Sussex Co., Del. (Deed Book A-1, p. 281)
Proprietary warrants for 200 acres and a further 200 acres, Kent Co., Del.
Deed of 100 acres to 'My Son Alexander Blacksliare'
P.title: Robert Blackshaw, yeoman of Little Creek
P.hook: The Blackshear name in this family began as Blackshaw and drifted to Blackshare, Blackshier and Blackshear through the spelling of clerks writing down what they heard.
body: Robert Blackshaw is the earliest of the line that can be followed through records. He was born at Piscataway, New Jersey, on 24 August 1677, 'son of Ellenor and Thomas Blackshaw.' By 1708 he had bought a lot on Second Street in Lewes, Delaware , and in 1712 that purchase came up at the Court of Quarter Sessions. In 1716 the Proprietaries' commissioners at Philadelphia issued warrants for 200 acres and 200 more in Kent County, and a survey of 207 acres near the head of Dover River.

He is listed as a yeoman and a farmer. In 1725 he deeded 200 acres, the grant of 1716, to 'Son Randall,' and in 1735 100 acres of 'Blackshares Range' to 'Son Alexander.' His surname 'began one of its many changes with this Robert, who started out with Blackshaw and ended with Blackshare; his sons went to Blackshere, Blackshier and Blackshear.'

Robert's wife is not named in any record. Robert's son Randall, who married Eve, stayed in Kent County, and Eve's will of 1762 is in the Kent County probate records; Alexander left for North Carolina after selling the land his father gave him.

quotes.t: My Son Alexander Blacksliare
quotes.c: Deed of Robert Blackshaw, Kent Co., Del., Deed Book L, vol. 1, p. 123 (1735), as printed in the Blacksheariana

P.src: Blacksheariana (1954), entry for Robert No. 1 (archive.org blackshearianage00blac); Sussex Co., Del. Deed Book A-1, p. 281; Kent Co., Del. Deed Book L, vol. 1, pp. 123-124; Pennsylvania Archives, 2nd series, vol. 19, p. 605; Monnette, Early Settlers of Woodbridge and Piscataway
P.note: His son Alexander is named in his own 1735 deed as printed in the book (the book quotes it, and says Alexander's sale of 1740 was of the same land his father had given him). Robert's New Jersey birth rests on the book's citation of the third series of the New Jersey Archives, vol. 2, p. 73. His death date is not given in the book (WikiTree says 1747, unsourced).

P.name: Thomas & Ellenor Blackshaw of Piscataway
P.place: Thomas Blackshaw appears at Piscataway, Middlesex County, New Jersey, in 1677, the year his son Robert was born, and is listed as a freeholder in 1683. Six children are recorded for him and Ellenor between 1677 and 1688; only Robert and Joseph outlived him.
kv: Promissory note to Thomas Bloomfield of Woodbridge
Robert (b. 24 Aug 1677), Thomas (1679-80), Joseph (1681), Timothy (1682), Thomas (1685), Joseph (b. 15 May 1688)
John Blackshaw and Maude Barlowe of Adlington, Cheshire (lead)
P.title: Thomas and Ellenor Blackshaw at Piscataway
P.hook: Six babies in eleven years, four of them dead by 1688: all that is left of the first Blackshaw couple in the Delaware Valley.
body: Most American Blackshears descend from 'Robert Blackshaw, first documented as son of Thomas and Ellenor of Piscataway, N.J., 1677.' Thomas appears on a 1 January 1677-78 promissory note to Thomas Bloomfield of Woodbridge, for 'Good Merchantable Tobacco,' and as a freeholder in 1683 and again in a later list. He paid quit rents on 37 acres and is listed as an early patentee. He is not in the probate records of Middlesex or Monmouth counties.

The births were: Robert on 24 August 1677; a Thomas on 5 January 1679-80, dead two days later; Joseph on 13 April 1681, dead in October 1687; Timothy on 22 December 1682, 'd. soon'; a second Thomas on 3 September 1685, dead 24 October 1687; and a second Joseph on 15 May 1688. Only Robert and the second Joseph outlived their father.

It has been guessed that Thomas was the son of John Blackshaw and Maude Barlowe of the parish of Prestbury, Cheshire, whose son Thomas was baptised on 25 September 1631 and 'could very well be the first Blackshaw to establish a family in America.' That Thomas's marriage or death in Cheshire could not be found.

quotes.t: could very well be the first Blackshaw to establish a family in America
quotes.c: Blacksheariana (1954), entry for John Blackshaw, baptised 1608, of Adlington

Records), p. 199; Monnette, Early Settlers of Woodbridge and Piscataway, vol. 1; Prestbury parish registers; Visitation of Cheshire (Harleian Society)

P.name: William Clark & Lavina (Willis) Clark
P.place: William Clark was born in Granville County, North Carolina, on 13 October 1785. He married Lavina, called Viney, Willis in Pulaski County, Kentucky, in 1808, farmed in Butler County, and died there on 6 January 1856. Lavina, born in South Carolina about 1785, died in Butler County in 1877.
kv: 1808, Pulaski Co., Ky. (Marriage Book 1, p. 28); Henry Willis a bondsman

P.title: William and Viney Clark: a bond with Henry Willis
P.hook: In 1808 a Pulaski County marriage bond was signed by the groom and by Henry Willis; a veteran named Henry Willis said in his pension application that he had lived with William Clark during the War of 1812.
body: William Clark was born on 13 October 1785 in Granville County, North Carolina, and died on 6 January 1856 in Butler County. His wife was 'Vina Clarke' in his household in 1850 and 'Luvina Clark' in 1860.

They married in 1808 in Pulaski County, Kentucky. The county marriage book has the couple's names in the wrong places: 'William Willis & Livina Clark.' Another listing files the same record under 'Viny Willis' and 'William Clark,' 1808. William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen.

Their first child, Lewis, was born in Pulaski County on 16 April 1809. The family moved to what became Butler County, where Mary (1815), Newton Jasper (6 August 1817), and Emeline (1820) were born, and then to what became Edmonson County, where Harvey was born in 1826. Lewis and Emeline died in Edmonson County and Mary and Harvey in Butler.

Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms married in Butler County on 24 January 1839, after a 20 January license; the return was signed on 25 January. Melvina’s death record names Newton Clark and Mary Dunn as her parents; that her mother was Polly Elms is probable and the surname difference is unresolved. Melvina married a Johnson, and her daughter Samantha married John C. Satterfield, who is our line.

William Clark's gravestone, in the Clark-Whobrey Cemetery at Roundhill in Edmonson County, records the hour of his death: "In memory of William Clark consort of Vina Clark born Oct. the 13 1785 And departed this life Jan. 6 1856 on sunday morning 8 oo & 55 minutes." The sixth of January 1856 was a Sunday. The stone agrees with the dates given from the Kentucky death register and names his wife as Vina, the form the 1850 census uses.

The War of 1812 service credited to him is still unchecked. A roster lists several privates named William Clark or Clarke, all in companies from other counties. Captain Samuel Tate's Pulaski County company, the one in which a Henry Willis served in 1813, includes an Elisha Clarke but no William.

The marriage, the years and the places match. WikiTree's Lavina Willis profile names Henry Willis and a Lavina Wells as her parents. The Henry Willis profile gives his wife as Mary Cochran. Both cannot be right, and no record names Lavina's parents, so none is entered beyond the bondsman Henry Willis.

P.name: Henry Willis of Pulaski County
P.place: A Henry Willis, with his wife Mary, sold land on Clifty and Fishing creeks in Pulaski County, Kentucky, in 1800. He was excused from the county levy for age and infirmity in 1807 and was dead by about 1818. He is probably the bondsman at the 1808 marriage of Lavina Willis.
kv: 14 Oct 1800, Clifty Creek and Fishing Creek, Pulaski Co., Ky., with his wife Mary
Nov 1807, excused from the county levy for age and infirmity
Henry Willis bondsman on the 1808 marriage of William Clark and Lavina Willis
1820 suit names John, George and Daniel Willis as 'heirs of Henry Willis'
P.title: Henry Willis: bondsman, levy-exempt, dead by 1818
P.hook: The documents agree that a Henry Willis stood bond for Lavina Willis in 1808; they do not say whether he was her father.
body: A Henry Willis and his wife Mary sold land on the waters of Clifty Creek and Fishing Creek in Pulaski County, Kentucky, before 14 October 1800. In November 1807 the Pulaski County court excused Henry from the county levy because of old age and infirmity. The next year he is the Henry Willis who stood bond with William Clark for the marriage of Lavina Willis. By 1818 Mary appears alone on the Pulaski County tax list, which is the basis for his death date. In the spring court of 1820 a suit named John, George and Daniel Willis as his heirs.

A Henry Willis can be traced through Washington County, Virginia, where he took title to 400 acres in Rich Valley in 1781-82 and was presented by a grand jury in 1773 for living with Mary Cochran, then to Greene County, Tennessee, and then to Kentucky. That these are one man is 'most likely', but he disappears from each place just as a man of the same name shows up in the next.

Lavina is listed among his children only as a presumption: 'Lavina (aka Viney) Willis married William Clark in 1808. William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen. The presumption is that Viney is Henry's daughter.' Another Henry Willis, born about 1793, lived later in Edmonson County, drew a War of 1812 pension, and said he lived with William Clark in Pulaski County; that suggests William Clark lived in the household of Henry and Mary, which is how he would have met Viney.

A Henry Willis served in the War of 1812, listed among the privates of Captain Samuel Tate's company, Kentucky Mounted Volunteer Militia, "commanded by Colonel Michael Taul," with service from 23 August to 14 November 1813. The regiment was raised under Governor Isaac Shelby's address of 31 July 1813 and rendezvoused at Newport, Kentucky, on 31 August. Bennett H. Young's history of the campaign names the company's county: Taul's seventh regiment was made up of companies from Wayne, Cumberland and Knox, "and Captain Samuel Tate, of Pulaski."

Shelby's volunteers crossed into Upper Canada that autumn. At the Battle of the Thames on 5 October 1813, Young places General George E. King's brigade, the fifth and seventh regiments, "four hundred and fifty feet behind Trotter," in the second line. Where each private was that day is not recorded, and some men in Tate's company are marked "left behind," one of them "with lame horse."

The soldier was probably not the Henry Willis who stood bond in 1808. That man had been excused from the Pulaski County levy in November 1807 for old age and infirmity. The private of 1813 fits the younger Henry Willis, born about 1793, who later lived in Edmonson County, drew a War of 1812 pension and said he had lived with William Clark in Pulaski County. Nothing states how he was related to Lavina.

quotes.t: The presumption is that Viney is Henry's daughter.
quotes.c: WikiTree Willis-11599, discussion section, 7 Nov 2022

P.src: WikiTree Willis-11599 (Henry Willis) and Willis-1450 (Lavina Willis), citing Pulaski Co., Ky. Marriage Book 1, p. 28, Pulaski Co. court and tax records, and the Washington Co., Va. minute books; Report of the Adjutant General of the State of Kentucky: Soldiers of the War of 1812 (Frankfort, 1891), pp. 153-157, roll of Captain Samuel Tate's company, Taul's regiment, Kentucky Mounted Volunteer Militia: https://archive.org/details/kentuckysoldier00reporich; Bennett H. Young, The Battle of the Thames (Filson Club Publications no. 18, Louisville, 1903), pp. 40, 62, 161-162: https://archive.org/details/battleofthamesin00youn
P.note: No document seen names Henry Willis as Lavina's father; the bond shows only that he stood security. Henry's birth date and place on WikiTree (1746, Augusta Co., Va.) have no source, and the Cochran marriage is not documented. Mary's maiden name is therefore a lead. The Henry Willis of Edmonson County may be a son or an unrelated man.

P.title: Lydia Payne's parents, in her son's words
P.hook: The only direct statement of who Lydia Payne's parents were comes from her preacher son: William Payne, a six-month Revolutionary militiaman, and Catherine Arnold.
body: Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia is the mother of Abner and the grandmother of Frank Stevenson, but her own people were not named in anything the family kept. The answer comes from her son, Rev. John Baxter Stevenson, who wrote a short note about his mother: "My mother was born in Burke Co., N.C., Aug. 16. Her father was William Payne. Her mother was Catherine Arnold. Her ancestry were of English extraction. Her father belonged to the militia during the Revolutionary War, and was in the service six months." He adds that she joined the Methodist church in August 1802 and that "her parents were both of the Methodist Church."

That is a son's own written statement about his mother's parents, as direct as a family record gets, though it is a recollection and not a birth or marriage record, and no will or deed names Lydia as William's daughter. The place fits the Stevenson story: Elam is said to have married Lydia Paine in North Carolina in 1805, and Burke County lies in the same western North Carolina country as Elam's birthplace in what is now Alexander County.

A William Paine household, spelled "Wm Pain" in 1790, was in Burke County in 1790 (twelve people) and 1800 (thirteen), and a widow of the name was there in 1810. William is said to have died on 15 October 1807 and to have a gravestone at Rocky Mount Cemetery, Granite Falls. His children are given as Thomas; Abner Burgess Payne (1777-1845); Sarah, who married a Boyce; and Lydia C. Sarah is placed at Bee Spring, Giles County, in 1830 and 1840, with a grave in the Bee Spring Cemetery, so Lydia seems to have had a sister in the same church neighborhood. A history of the Bee Spring society names a Rev. Meshach Boyce among its first members and says he is buried in the churchyard there; that he was Sarah's husband is a guess.

William is made a son of John Paine of Spotsylvania County, Virginia, whose 1764 will names a son William. Two different men named William Paine have been attached to Catherine Arnold's family, and more research is needed to rule one out, so the step back from William Paine of Burke County to John Paine is unproven.

quotes.t: Her father was William Payne. Her mother was Catherine Arnold. Her ancestry were of English extraction.
quotes.c: Rev. John Baxter Stevenson, son of Elam and Lydia, on his mother (Casey family history, p. 3-98)

quotes.t: Her father belonged to the militia during the Revolutionary War, and was in the service six months.
quotes.c: Rev. John Baxter Stevenson, same statement

P.note: Probable and not proven: the statement is a son's recollection, no original record naming Lydia as William's daughter has been seen, and two William Paines are confused on the WikiTree pages. The 1790 and 1800 census entries and the death date are quoted from WikiTree transcriptions and have not been checked against the census pages. A different William Paine (b. 1744, Paine-1997) is marked there as a rejected match.

P.title: A Spotsylvania will with a daughter 'Catey'
P.hook: A 1774 Spotsylvania will names a daughter Catey, and a tree makes her Catherine Arnold, wife of William Payne of Burke County.
body: Catherine Arnold is said to have been born about 1751 in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, a daughter of William Arnold (about 1714 to after 1774) and Lydia Bell. The one record behind this is the will of William Arnold, who died there on 17 September 1774 and "names a daughter Catey." Her marriage to William Payne is unsupported.

William Paine's own family is also placed in Spotsylvania, and he and his wife are said to have sold his share of his father's estate there on 20 November 1777 before the family moved to Burke County, North Carolina. A daughter named Lydia may echo Catherine's mother Lydia. None of this has been checked against the will, the deed or a record that gives Catherine's age or origin, so Catherine Arnold's parents are carried here only as a possibility.
P.note: Lead only. The will was not seen; 'Catey' is a common Virginia form of Catherine, and the Payne-Arnold marriage record, if one exists, has not been found.

P.src: The Ancestry of Carolyn Gail Skinner (archive.org id ancestryofcaroly00skin; text seen only as search excerpts), Stevenson chapter, citing 'data received May 11, 1955'.
P.title: A family note on the Stevenson immigrant
P.hook: A family compiler's 1955 notes say James Stevenson of Iredell County was the son of an Irish immigrant James, not of the William some trees give him.
body: A family book on the Skinner ancestry covers the Stevensons because Rev. Elam Stevenson's descendants married into that line. Its Stevenson chapter first follows a chart that starts with William Stevenson, born in County Antrim, Ireland, who came to Pennsylvania in 1748 and to Iredell County, North Carolina in 1762. Then it adds a correction from "data received May 11, 1955": "The father of James Stevenson was not William Stevenson, immigrant, but was James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, who died in 1820. James I married Sally Kelly of Md., who died about 1820 or 1821. James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814."

James II is the James Stevenson whose 1828 will in Iredell County names his son Elam; his wife Jane is the Jane Stevenson of the next generation. The chapter also quotes McFerrin that Elam was the son of James Stephenson of Iredell, now Alexander County, "who was a Captain in the Revolutionary War." Another passage in the same book says James Stevenson "was born in Ireland. Settled in North Carolina about 1775" and had two other sons besides Elam, which does not agree with the 1955 note (James II would then be the immigrant).

The dates do not fit well: if James II was born about 1746, an immigrant father who died in 1820 and a mother who died about 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old. The 1955 note is therefore a family compiler's statement, not a record, and the parents of James Stevenson stay uncertain until a will, deed or church record names them.

quotes.t: The father of James Stevenson was not William Stevenson, immigrant, but was James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, who died in 1820.
quotes.c: The Ancestry of Carolyn Gail Skinner, citing data received 11 May 1955

P.note: Conflict inside the same book: one passage makes William Stevenson of County Antrim (to Pennsylvania 1748, Iredell Co. 1762, d. 1809) the father, the 1955 note rejects that and names a James. Only search excerpts of the book could be read; the item is no longer downloadable, so the full chapter was not seen.

P.name: John Stevenson & a Thompson
P.place: Parents of Jane Stevenson, wife of James Stevenson of Iredell County, North Carolina
kv: "Jane was the daughter of John Stevenson (d. 1794), and a Thompson."
Died 1814 (same source); Stephenson is taken to be her maiden name
The Ancestry of Carolyn Gail Skinner, citing data received 11 May 1955
P.src: The Ancestry of Carolyn Gail Skinner (archive.org id ancestryofcaroly00skin; full text readable at https://archive.org/download/ancestryofcaroly00skin/ancestryofcaroly00skin_djvu.txt), Stevenson chapter.
P.title: Jane Stevenson's parents: John, and a Thompson
P.hook: The same 1955 notes say Elam Stevenson's mother Jane was a Stevenson by birth, daughter of John Stevenson, who died in 1794, and a woman named Thompson.
body: Elam Stevenson's mother is only ever called Jane Stevenson, and the compiler of the Skinner book's Stevenson chapter noted that the wives' maiden names show "Stephenson was Jane's maiden name, and not a variation" of her husband's. In the same note: "James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814. Jane was the daughter of John Stevenson (d. 1794), and a Thompson."

Nothing more is given: no first name or dates for Jane's mother, no place, no will. This is the only place that names Jane's parents, and it is a compiler's statement from 1955 with no source given, so it stays unproven. Another passage of the book puts the marriage of James and Jane about 1765 and calls James a soldier of the Revolution.

Jane's household was Scots-Irish and Presbyterian, and it did not welcome her son Elam's turn to the Methodists. He joined that church in 1806, the third son and the first of the family to do so, and by his own memory his parents honestly believed he was being deceived by false teachers. He was licensed to preach in 1811. In 1813, as he got ready to move to Tennessee, a neighbor named Philip Bruce asked him to carry part of his books in the wagon. Jane died the next year. Elam settled near Bunker Hill in Giles County, founded the church at Bee Spring, and died on 13 March 1875, "nearly 62 years a minister," three years after his wife Lydia.

quotes.t: Jane was the daughter of John Stevenson (d. 1794), and a Thompson.
quotes.c: The Ancestry of Carolyn Gail Skinner, citing data received 11 May 1955

P.note: Lead only. The full text of the Skinner book is readable, and the 1955 note gives no source for Jane's parentage, so it stays unproven. The book is also internally inconsistent: its 1905 table has James II volunteering at sixteen in the Revolution and settling in North Carolina about 1775, which cannot be squared with a marriage about 1765, and a 1955 note describes an immigrant James who died in 1820 and married Sally Kelly of Maryland.

P.title: Jesse Hulsey, the wounded soldier of Hall County
P.hook: A Revolutionary veteran with an Indian wound and a North Carolina pension lived in Hall County, Georgia, when Salathiel Hulsey did; whether he was Salathiel's father is open.
body: Jesse Hulsey, "a veteran of the American Revolution," was still living in Greenville District, South Carolina, in 1800, one of only two of the family left in the state, was in Hall County, Georgia, in 1820, and drew a Revolutionary land lottery lot in Troup County in 1827 (granted 12 January 1829). In 1840, at 81, he was a Revolutionary soldier in Hall County.

Then there is his North Carolina pension: on 25 November 1822 Jesse, "of Hawl Co. Ga.," named Samuel Carson his attorney to collect the pension the North Carolina legislature allowed him "in consideration of a wound which I received by the Indians in the Revolutionary War"; he appointed another agent in 1826, and a man swore in Wake County in December 1835 that he had seen him alive in September in Hall County. Family trees call him Jesse Hamilton Hulsey, born 1760 in Goochland County, Virginia, and list the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey (born about 1807, Franklin County, Georgia) among his many children by Mary Tharp.

A North Carolina resolution of the 1834–35 session directs the treasurer to pay all pension arrears to Jesse Hulsey, then living in Georgia, or his agent N. Edmonson, and to continue payments for Jesse's lifetime. The resolution says his pension had been allowed by an act passed in 1824. It names no wife, children or Georgia county, so it supports the pension account without proving that Jesse was Salathiel's father. Its 1824 date also leaves a question about the 1822 power of attorney, which has not been checked against its original.

The link to our Salathiel is a family-tree assertion. The pieces that fit are place and names: Salathiel is on the 1840 census of Hall County, and his 1850 household in Union County has a Jesse, 10, and a Jennings, 8, while the Georgia history names a Jennings Hulsey who stayed in South Carolina with Jesse in 1800. The pieces that do not fit: the same family tree says a son Jesse Jr. married Mary Tharp in "1779" in Franklin County, Alabama, which cannot be right; the Georgia history treats Jesse as possibly a brother of James Hulsey Sr. of Hall County; and no will, deed or census that lists Salathiel as Jesse's son has been found.

quotes.t: in consideration of a wound which I received by the Indians in the Revolutionary War
quotes.c: Jesse Hulsey of Hall Co., Ga., 25 Nov 1822, pension power of attorney (as printed on WikiTree)

P.note: Lead only. Trees also name Mary Tharp as Salathiel's mother; her place is not carried here because the tree's own marriage date is impossible. Benjamin Franklin Hulsey's descent from Salathiel, and G. W. Hulsey's from Benjamin, still rest on grave memorials and family tradition; see the entries for Benjamin and Salathiel.

P.place: Hopkins County, Texas, in 1880, a farmer's household next door to the county where his daughter Emma later married into the Smiths of Franklin County.

Daughters Emma J. (12, born Texas) and Eliza J. (8); brother-in-law Jacob Black (29) and sisters-in-law Sarah J. Quinton (32) and Elizabeth Black (23)
Not in the household; the Black in-laws suggest she was a Black (lead)

P.src: 1880 U.S. census, Precinct 5, Hopkins County, Texas, dwelling 88 (Ancestry collection 6742, record 6949407); Handbook of Texas, 'Hopkins County' (https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/hopkins-county)
P.title: A widower in Hopkins County
P.hook: In 1880 George W. Langley, 38, was alone with two small daughters and his wife's brother and sisters in the house.
body: In 1880, in Precinct 5 of Hopkins County, Texas, George W. Langley, 38, born in Georgia, headed a household. His daughters were Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8, both born in Texas. No wife is listed. His own parents were born in Georgia too.

Hopkins County was a young place. The Texas legislature had created it in 1846, its seat had been Sulphur Springs only since 1870, and southerners settled most of it. A rail line, the East Line and Red River Railroad, reached the county in 1876, four years before the count. Emma was born in Texas about 1867, so George had made the move from Georgia by then.

Living with him are Jacob Black, 29, called brother-in-law, and Sarah J. Quinton, 32, and Elizabeth Black, 23, called sisters-in-law. Two Black siblings under his roof and no wife make it likely that Mrs. Langley, born a Black, had died before the count. Other family trees name her Mary F. Black, but that is only a suggestion and is not entered here. What became of George after 1880 is not known.

Emma Elizabeth Langley, wife of John B. Smith, was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas, which makes her 12 in June 1880. The daughter is Emma J., so the identification rests on age, birthplace and neighborhood (Hopkins County lies beside Franklin County, where Emma died in 1905), not on anything naming Emma Elizabeth. If it holds, George stands behind Emma's son Charles Oscar Smith, born in 1889, whose youngest daughter Faye married into the Moffitts.

quotes.t: Brother-in-law
quotes.c: Jacob Black's relation to the head, 1880 census, Hopkins County, Texas

P.note: Emma is entered as Emma J. rather than Emma Elizabeth or Emma Liza (the form on John B. Smith's Find a Grave page). The mother's name Mary F. Black is only an Ancestry suggestion from other trees and is not in the tree here.

EXTRA.name: Judge Edward Ward Tims

imgs.cap: 1896 Choctaw census: brothers Vinson and Edward Tims's households, Towson County
Dawes Card 1238: Columbus Tims, son of E. W. and Polly Tims

The Choctaw Nation capitol at Tuskahoma, Oklahoma, now a museum (photographed 2009). Wikimedia Commons, Public domain, Urbanative at English Wikipedia. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Choctaw_capitol_museum.jpg

EXTRA.title: Postmaster and judge of Doaksville
EXTRA.hook: Vinson's brother was a Towson County judge and Doaksville's postmaster, and he was considered for Principal Chief.
body: Doaksville was the capital of the Choctaw Nation from 1858 to 1863. By 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, and in 1860 a convention there adopted the constitution that governed the Choctaw Nation until 1906. At the end of the Civil War there were two surrenders at Doaksville: Principal Chief Peter Pitchlynn surrendered the Choctaw forces on 19 June 1865, and General Stand Watie surrendered his Cherokee, Creek, Seminole and Osage troops on 23 June, the last Confederate general to lay down arms.

Edward Ward Tims, Choctaw by Blood, served as District Trustee of Apukshunnubbee District in the early 1880s and for many years as County Judge of Towson County. On 24 October 1887 he was appointed postmaster at Doaksville, succeeding James T. Fleming; the office closed in 1903, when the name changed to Fort Towson.

On 29 April 1888 in Towson County he married Willie Jane Maxwell of Arkansas. After statehood he retired to his allotment southeast of Hugo. He died on 7 February 1923 and is buried in Springs Chapel Cemetery near Hugo.

His second wife, Willie Jane, was born on 27 July 1870 and died on 8 October 1922, four months before him. Their children were Lucy Ann (1889-1970), Minnie (1891-1930), Edmond (1893-1918), Benjamin (1897-1969), Myrtle (1899-1988), Abel (1901-1966) and Nora (1906-1977). By his first wife Polly, a full-blood Choctaw, he had a son, Columbus, born on Christmas Day 1860, who died on 21 October 1918 and is also buried at Springs Chapel.

In January 1940 it was proposed that his old log house, a quarter mile northeast of Fort Towson, become a museum, and Tims was remembered as 'once county judge of Towson County' and 'once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation.' The house was said to have been the setting for talk of the 1860 Council and the 1837 treaty. That detail is local lore, not a record. Joel Thompson remembered him simply as the man 'who was post master and Judge at Doaksville for so many years.'

A newspaper dispatch of the time shows how far that went. Dated Little Rock, Ark., 5 August 1886, and headed “Choctaws Hold an Election,” it read: “The election for principal chief of the Choctaw Nation was held yesterday.” It names four men: Ben Smallwood, Thompson McKinney, J. P. Folsom (printed Fulsom) and Edward Tims, and adds that a large vote was cast and that unofficial returns pointed to the election of McKinney. The dispatch gives no vote totals. Thompson McKinney went on to serve as Principal Chief, so Edward Tims, then in his mid-forties and a county judge, was a losing candidate in a four-man race for the highest office in the Nation.

When Edward applied for enrollment at Doaksville on 8 May 1899, he was "Tims, Edward W.," age 58, one-half blood, with parents "Vincent B. Tims," dead, a non-citizen, and "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. His son Columbus, born in 1860, was enrolled as "Tims, Columbus," 40, three-quarter blood, with parents "E. W. Tims" and "Polly Tims," the latter dead.

His second marriage is documented: the Commission's decision gives the wedding as 29 April 1888, and a copy of the marriage certificate, signed by R. S. Frazier, reads the same; family accounts that give 19 April are a few days off. Their youngest child enrolled, Abel E., was born on 14 December 1901. The enrollment also includes a ward, Adam Nanomantubbe, whom O. W. Seay of Oscar called Edward's orphan grandson in a letter of 1903.

quotes.t: My grandfather, Vinson Tims, was a brother to Judge Edward Ward Tims, who was post master and Judge at Doaksville for so many years.
quotes.c: Joel J. Thompson, 1937

quotes.t: Tims, a prominent Choctaw citizen, was once county judge of Towson County, I. T. and was once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation.

EXTRA.name: Pvt. Edmond Tims

imgs.cap: 142nd Infantry report, January 1919: "In the first action of the 142nd Infantry at St Etienne…" describing the Choctaw code
Soldiers of the Great War, vol. 3 (1920), Oklahoma, killed in action: "TIMS, Edmond, Hugo." (public domain)

EXTRA.title: Killed in France, 1918
EXTRA.hook: A runner in the Choctaw Code Talkers' regiment, awarded the Croix de Guerre.
body: Judge Tims's son by Willie Jane Maxwell, enrolled Choctaw by Blood, and "Edmund, 3" in 1896. He served first in Co. L, 1st Oklahoma Infantry, then as a company runner in Co. D, 142nd Infantry, 36th Division. On 9 October 1918, near St. Étienne, France, a fellow runner spoke with him at 8 a.m. and an hour later found him killed by shrapnel.

He was posthumously awarded the French Croix de Guerre with Palm and lies in the Meuse-Argonne American Cemetery. The 142nd was the regiment of the Choctaw Code Talkers. The regiment's commander wrote how Choctaw speakers were first used to send messages in this same St. Étienne fighting. Edmond is not listed as a code talker, but he served alongside them.

Two books printed in 1920 carry his name. The division's history closes with an honor roll of its dead, and under "142d Infantry" it lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date October 8, 1918. The War Department's casualty lists, printed that year, include among the Oklahoma privates killed in action "TIMS, Edmond, Hugo."

The honor roll gives 8 October 1918 where the company runner's account puts his death on the morning of the 9th. Both dates fall within the same two days of the 142d Infantry's fighting at St. Étienne.

The morning of 8 October gave Edmond's battalion a hard start. The First Battalion lost its commander, Capt. Charles Kuhlman, and "half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners," to a single shell before the jump-off, and Company D "wandered into the French sector to the left" and stayed there.

EXTRA.name: The Mississippi-born ancestors

imgs.cap: Their grandchildren on the Dawes rolls seventy years later

EXTRA.title: The Choctaw removal
EXTRA.hook: Several ancestors were born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi before the Trail of Tears.
body: Family trees say Pisachubbe "Wilson" (born 1807), Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi (born 1825) and Jackson Gardner (born about 1820) were born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi, though nothing states where any of them was born, and O-we-na is placed only in Towson County. The Choctaw were the first nation removed under the Indian Removal Act, walking and riding west in 1831–1833.
These families settled in the Kiamitia, Blue and Towson counties of the new Choctaw Nation, where their grandchildren were enrolled by the Dawes Commission seventy years later.

A 1937 account of the Pisachubbe family says they came from Mississippi with the first group of exiles in 1832 and settled first at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. At Doaksville, the trading firm of Doak & Tims, Vincent Tims's partnership, held army contracts in 1838 and 1839 to feed arriving Chickasaw emigrants at 13 cents a ration.

Two cautions on the Mississippi-born names. None of them has been found on a removal-era list. The proposed mother-and-son link between Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi and Joseph Pisachubbe is unproved; her age alone does not resolve it.

A full-blood Nancy Pisachubbi, 69, enrolled in 1899, gave her father as Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, dead, and her mother, Malindy, dead and of Mississippi. She appears to be the tree's Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, though nothing says whose mother she was.

The best-documented part of the removal's first winter is the stretch from the Mississippi to the Red River. About 18,880 Choctaws were counted in Major Francis Armstrong's census of 1831; by the first week of November four thousand were on the road, and between 26 November and 8 December about 2,500 were landed at Arkansas Post in a blizzard. A Choctaw letter of February 1833 shows Doaksville already a place where annuities were issued and 'a small town' of white traders stood below the Kiamichi.
EXTRA.note: These individuals have not yet been found on a removal-era roll such as the 1831 Armstrong Roll.

EXTRA.name: Three households in 1940
EXTRA.title: The Depression, house by house
EXTRA.hook: The 1940 census caught both of Dad's and Mom's families at the bottom of the hard years.
body: In April 1940 each man was asked how many weeks he had worked the year before. Grady Moffitt in Hugo: 12 weeks, $100, unemployed 50 weeks, eight children at home in a rented house. Oscar Hulsey at South Fork, Arkansas: 16 weeks on a government relief job, $140, unemployed 48 weeks, five children in a house worth $2. Simon Thompson at Jeter: 52 weeks on his own farm, worth $400, feeding twelve people, including his in-laws and their nieces and nephews.
Within a few years John Moffitt was in the Navy, the Hulseys had moved to the Oklahoma lumber towns, and the three families' children would meet and marry in Hugo.
EXTRA.src: 1940 U.S. Census: Hugo and Jeter, Choctaw County, Okla.; South Fork, Montgomery County, Ark.

EXTRA.name: Spencer Academy
EXTRA.title: The school where 'Swing Low' was written down
EXTRA.hook: Joseph Thompson's boarding school north of Doaksville gave the world a famous spiritual.
body: Spencer Academy was the first school created under the Choctaw Council's school law of 1842. It opened on 1 February 1844, a quarter mile north of present-day Spencerville on the old Fort Smith–Fort Towson military road, and was named for Secretary of War John C. Spencer, who gave it a 250-pound bell. Presbyterian missionaries ran it from 1846. Its three two-story halls had long porches, and the dining room served tanfula, a Choctaw crushed-corn dish.

The school closed in 1861. During the Civil War its buildings served as a Confederate hospital and sheltered homeless Choctaw families. It reopened in 1871 and ran until 1881, when a new Spencer Academy opened at Nelson, near Antlers. Joseph Thompson, born in 1861, was of school age during the reopened years. Among Spencer's earlier students was Allen Wright, later Principal Chief, who gave Oklahoma its name.

Before the war, Wallace and Minerva Willis, enslaved people hired out to the academy, sang their songs at their cabin door. Superintendent Alexander Reid wrote them down, and in 1871 he spent a day in Brooklyn teaching them to the Fisk Jubilee Singers: 'Steal Away to Jesus,' 'I'm a Rolling,' and 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot.' Whether Wallace Willis composed the songs himself is debated.
EXTRA.src: National Register of Historic Places nomination, Spencer Academy (NRIS 75001562); Robert E. Flickinger, The Choctaw Freedmen and the Story of Oak Hill Industrial Academy (1914); O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891).

EXTRA.name: Court day at Sulphur Springs
EXTRA.title: Court day at Sulphur Springs
EXTRA.hook: A log courthouse, a whipping post, and a justice system built on keeping your word.

imgs.cap: Joel Thompson's 1937 interview about his father

body: Cedar County was created by the Choctaw Nation's Doaksville Constitution of 1860 and lasted until statehood in 1907. Each county elected a judge for a two-year term to oversee county business, a sheriff, who collected taxes and took the census, and a ranger, who sold stray livestock. When an arrest or a sentence had to be carried out, the sheriff called on the district Lighthorsemen.

The Cedar County court met at Sulphur Springs, near present-day Rattan, on the first Monday of each month, in "a large log house, constructed of long, straight logs" that also served as a Choctaw Methodist church. Families camped at the springs on court days. A stump from the tree used as the whipping post is kept by the Pushmataha County Historical Society in Antlers.

Choctaw law punished crimes such as theft with lashes, fifty for a first offense and one hundred for a second. H. B. Cushman, who knew the Nation, described what came after: the whole crowd shook hands with the man who had been whipped, and the matter was never spoken of again.

From 1866 the Nation's death penalty was carried out by rifle. By custom a condemned man went home to plant and harvest his crop and came back on the appointed day, often choosing a friend or relative to fire the shot so no one would seek revenge. Capital cases went to the district court, not the county judge, so when Joel said his father "could have sentenced criminals to be shot," the whippings are the part that fits a county judge.

The court came to Sulphur Springs by an act of council. On 3 December 1891 the General Council removed the Cedar County court ground "from Pine Hill court ground to Sulphur Spring," to be known as Sulphur Spring court ground, and set its first session for the first Monday of January 1892. Joseph Thompson had been elected to the council's lower house the year before, though the printed act does not say who proposed it.

quotes.t: ...the whole assembly came out and shook hands with the 'Fummah' (whipped), thus reinstating him to his former position in society, and the subject was then and there dropped, never to be mentioned again.
quotes.c: H. B. Cushman, 1899

quotes.t: Never was a full-blood Choctaw known to evade the death penalty ... by flight.

EXTRA.name: Dois L. Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Home from the Navy, lost in the Red River
EXTRA.hook: John's older brother cooked for the Navy through the war, then died two summers after coming home.
body: Dois, "Dais, 19" in 1940, was born 16 February 1921, the third of Grady and Mary's sons. He joined the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942 and served as a Ship's Cook until 27 January 1946, the same years his younger brother John spent in the Navy in the Pacific.

On Thursday afternoon, 21 August 1947, he dove into shallow water in the Red River at Arthur City and broke his neck. A companion, Mac Davidson, pulled him out, and an ambulance took him to the Sanitarium of Paris. He died days later, at 26.
His funeral was at Grant Baptist Church, and he is buried at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo. In October 1947 his father Grady signed the application for his military headstone.

His Texas death record lists him as single, 26 years, 6 months, 9 days old, a discharged U.S. Navy man, born in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, and living at Grant. It gives the cause as a fracture of the fifth cervical vertebra with a severed spinal cord, from an accident on 21 August at the Red River bridge north of Paris, and he lived four days. His father Grady Moffitt signed as informant and gives his mother's maiden name as Mary Shackelford, born in Alabama.
His rating was SC1C, Ship's Cook First Class, U.S. Naval Reserve, and the date 25 August 1947 appears on his death record.
EXTRA.note: The newspaper places the accident on 21 August; his grave memorial gives his death as 25 August 1947.
