EXTRA.name: Doaksville
EXTRA.title: Doaksville: the biggest town in Indian Territory
EXTRA.hook: A trading post by the Kiamichi grew into the busiest town in the Choctaw Nation, then faded within a lifetime.
body: Doaksville took its name from Josiah Stuart Doak, co-owner of a trading post. He and his brother first set up at the mouth of the Kiamichi River, then moved about a mile west after the U.S. Army founded Fort Towson in 1824. Choctaw people relocated from Mississippi settled here, and steamboat access on the Red River made it a principal town of the Nation.

By 1840 it had several stores, a gristmill, a blacksmith and a hotel. In 1842 the Indian agent William Armstrong called it one of the most orderly and quiet towns in the West. A post office opened in 1847, and by 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, with more than thirty buildings and two newspapers, one printed in Choctaw.

The Army left Fort Towson in 1854 and the town's importance began to slip. The Civil War wrecked the plantation economy around it, an 1870 railroad bypassed it, and most businesses moved to Fort Towson. The post office closed in 1903. Only the Fort Towson-Doaksville Cemetery remains; the Oklahoma Historical Society acquired the site in 1960 and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 29, 1975.
This is the town and neighborhood of the Cedar, Towson and Kiamitia county families, framed here as the place they lived near, not as a record of any one relative.

quotes.t: one of the most orderly and quiet towns that you will find in the west
quotes.c: Agent William Armstrong, 1842, as quoted in Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation

EXTRA.note: Place history from secondary sources; not tied to a named relative. The 1870 date for the railroad that bypassed Doaksville comes from Wikipedia and is doubtful: the Frisco right-of-way plat at Fort Towson is dated 1903, and Joel Thompson remembered the family still trading at Doaksville in his boyhood in the 1890s.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation; Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture (Fort Towson, Choctaw County)

EXTRA.name: Doaksville Constitution
EXTRA.title: The 1860 constitution written at Doaksville
EXTRA.hook: A convention at Doaksville set the framework that governed the Choctaw Nation until its government ended in 1906.
body: The Choctaw and Chickasaw nations formally separated in 1855, and in 1860 a convention at Doaksville ratified the Doaksville Constitution, which guided the Choctaw Nation until 1906. Doaksville, a river-and-trading town that had been the largest settlement in Indian Territory since about 1850, served as the capital in this period; sources differ on the exact dates, and the capital later moved to Chahta Tamaha in 1863. Vincent B. Tims, partner of the town's founder, Josiah Doak, had been trading there since the late 1830s.

The constitution organized the Nation into counties inside its districts. Cedar County, for example, took its name from Big Cedar Creek (the Choctaw word for cedar is Chuala), was bounded by the Kiamichi River on the west and the Little River on the east, and had its seat at Sulphur Springs. Each county elected members to the National Council and also a county judge, a sheriff and a ranger to two-year terms. The judge ran county administration, the sheriff collected taxes, watched for intruders and took the census, and the ranger advertised and sold stray livestock.

For families in the Kiamichi country this was everyday government: the people holding these offices were their neighbors. Edward Ward Tims lived under it for decades. He was a district trustee in the early 1880s and a long-serving county judge of Towson County, and in 1887 he was made postmaster of Doaksville itself. The same constitution and the same county offices were still in force when the Dawes Commission came to enroll the Nation. Cedar County and its neighbors ceased to exist on 16 November 1907, when Oklahoma became a state.
EXTRA.note: Capital dates are inconsistent between sources; stated loosely on purpose. The constitution's own text has not been found online.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation; Wikipedia, Cedar County, Choctaw Nation

EXTRA.name: Doaksville, June 1865
EXTRA.title: The last Confederate general lays down arms near Fort Towson
EXTRA.hook: The Civil War ended in Indian Territory in the Choctaw Nation, a few miles from where these families lived.
body: After the Army abandoned Fort Towson in 1854, the post saw a brief resurgence during the Civil War when Gen. Samuel Bell Maxey chose it as headquarters for Confederate forces in Indian Territory.

On June 23, 1865, Cherokee Brig. Gen. Stand Watie surrendered his First Indian Brigade at Doaksville, near the fort, signing with two Union commissioners. He is generally called the last Confederate general officer to surrender. Some sources place the signing at Fort Towson itself; the date is consistent. Some writers call it the Battle of Doaksville, but no fight by that name is documented.
Doaksville was a fitting place for the war to end. A few weeks into the conflict, in June 1861, a Confederate flag was flying over the town, where the family's Vincent B. Tims lived out his life.

The war had wrecked the plantation economy around Doaksville, and the town never recovered. In 1870 a railroad went through somewhere else, most of the stores moved to Fort Towson, and the post office closed in 1903. The Doaksville site was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 29, 1975. Archaeologists dug there in 1995, 1996 and 1997, and a walkway and signs went in during 2001. For Choctaw families of the area the surrender was the end of four years in which their homeland was a Confederate district.
EXTRA.note: Place and event history; no specific family member is documented here. Whether a relative served is a lead to check in Confederate Choctaw rolls.
EXTRA.src: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Fort Towson entry; Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation

EXTRA.name: Fort Towson
EXTRA.title: Fort Towson: the army post built to receive the Choctaw
EXTRA.hook: The Army established Fort Towson in 1824, before the forced removal of the Choctaw from Mississippi.
body: In May 1824 a company of the Seventh Infantry pitched camp on Gates Creek, near where the Kiamichi runs into the Red River. The soldiers called it Cantonment Towson, after Gen. Nathan Towson, the army's paymaster general and a hero of the War of 1812. They had a long list of jobs: watch the boundary with Mexican Texas, keep the peace, and stand between the Plains tribes and the Choctaw who were expected to arrive from Mississippi.

Much of the work was unglamorous and unpopular. The troops enforced the federal law of 1802 against hunting and unlicensed trading on Indian land, moved off Anglo settlers who believed they were living in Miller County, Arkansas, and cut roads to Fort Smith and to Fort Jesup in Louisiana. The post was abandoned in 1829.

After the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek it reopened in 1830 as Camp Phoenix and was soon renamed Fort Towson, this time with solid barracks and officers' quarters. It was meant as a buffer for the Choctaw slated for removal to the area, and for several years it served as a terminal on the Choctaw Trail of Tears. A trader named Josiah Doak, who had first set up at the mouth of the Kiamichi, moved about a mile west to be near the soldiers, and his store grew into Doaksville. Vincent B. Tims, Doak's partner and an ancestor of this family, signed as a witness when the Choctaw and Chickasaw met at Doaksville, near Fort Towson, in January 1837.

The fort was a staging ground for troops headed to the Mexican War in 1846-48. A young Lieutenant Jefferson Davis served there, and Sam Houston is known to have visited. Troops left for good in 1854. During the Civil War General Samuel Bell Maxey made the old post his headquarters for Confederate forces in Indian Territory. The state acquired the property in 1967 and a visitor center and sutler's store are open to the public.
EXTRA.note: Institution history only.

EXTRA.name: Atoka Agreement
EXTRA.title: Allotment and the persistence of Choctaw government
EXTRA.hook: The Thompson family’s enrollment and land selections unfolded as Choctaw leaders faced federal pressure to divide the Nation’s land.
body: On 23 April 1897, representatives of the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations and the Dawes Commission signed the Atoka Agreement. It set terms for dividing tribal lands into individual allotments and reserved coal and asphalt lands. The agreement treated Freedmen and their descendants unequally, assigning them smaller allotments.

The agreement scheduled the end of the tribal governments for March 1906. The Choctaw and Chickasaw governments ratified it in November 1897, but Chickasaw voters rejected it in December, as Chickasaw law required a popular vote. The Curtis Act of 1898 required resubmission, and the agreement passed in a joint election on 24 August 1898.

The Dawes Commission had been established in 1893, before the agreement. Its enrollment process later reached the Thompson, Tims and Pisachubbe families. Betsy Tims Thompson applied with her family in 1899, and her son Simon’s birth that May required sworn statements from Betsy and his grandmother Emeline Tims.

In 1902 Choctaw and Chickasaw leaders and the federal government negotiated a supplemental agreement. A Choctaw executive committee circulated information and invited citizens to raise concerns before the vote. That October, Choctaw voters also chose a principal chief in a contested race; Green McCurtain was declared the winner. How any member of the Thompson family voted is not known.

Allotment changed the relationship between families and land. In 1903 Joseph Thompson selected tracts for Betsy and their children, including a homestead for Simon. Tribal land was divided into individual holdings, while federal restrictions governed transactions in many allotments. Allotment made it easier for Choctaw land to pass out of Choctaw hands.

The Nation did not disappear when federal policy reduced the government’s authority. Choctaw community members continued to meet and organize, and an advisory council emerged in the 1930s. In 1971 Harry J. W. Belvin became the first elected principal chief in decades to serve without the required presidential appointment. In 1978 a Choctaw council formed to develop a new constitution and restore representative government. Simon Thompson lived through these changes; his own political activities are not known.
EXTRA.note: Choctaw Nation history provides context for the Thompson family’s records. No evidence here identifies how a family member voted or whether they participated in the later organizations.

EXTRA.name: Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.place: Morgantown, Butler County, KY
EXTRA.title: A monument for both armies
EXTRA.hook: On the courthouse lawn in Morgantown stands a Civil War monument that honors soldiers from both sides.
body: Butler County, Kentucky, was created by the General Assembly on January 18, 1810, from parts of Logan and Ohio counties, and named for Major General Richard Butler, who died at the Battle of the Wabash in 1791. Its county seat, Morgantown, began in 1791 as a two-acre tract belonging to Christopher Funkhouser, and for a while it was called Funkhouser Hill. Salt-making was the first industry, and from 1833 a lock-and-dam plan made the Green River a way to market, with towns at Lock and Dam 3 (Rochester) and 4 (Woodbury).

The county was strongly Union but sent men to both armies, and it felt the war directly. Fighting broke out near Morgantown on October 29, 1861, and a skirmish followed the next day where Confederate forces were encamped. The war slowed the county's growth.

After the war, veterans of both sides raised money together for a monument on the courthouse lawn. The Confederate-Union Veterans' Monument, dedicated in 1907, is made of zinc, lists county residents who fought on each side, and is described as one of only two Kentucky Civil War monuments honoring soldiers from both sides, a sign of how neighbors and kin had been divided and then lived side by side.

The county reached its largest population, 15,896, in 1900, and about 1907 the Satterfields left Butler County for Franklin County, Texas. The river locks that had once carried the county's goods were washed out or abandoned later, in 1965 and 1980.
EXTRA.note: Place story. It describes the county where Smith and Satterfield kin lived, and the Satterfields' move to Franklin County about 1907 is from the family's own story. It does not claim a named ancestor served in either army.

EXTRA.name: Scottsville, Allen County, KY
EXTRA.place: Scottsville, Allen County, KY
EXTRA.title: Allen County and its county seat
EXTRA.hook: Allen County was cut out of Barren and Warren counties in 1815 and named for a colonel killed in the War of 1812.
body: Allen County was established in 1815 from parts of Barren and Warren counties. It honors Colonel John Allen, a state senator and soldier killed at the Battle of Frenchtown in Michigan during the War of 1812. Today it covers 352 square miles on the Tennessee line, adjoining Macon and Sumner counties in Tennessee.

The county seat began as a settlement on Bays Fork in 1797 that grew into a stagecoach station. The town was laid off in 1816, established in 1817 and named for Charles Scott, Kentucky's fourth governor. Early on it was also called Allen Court House and Scottville. It was incorporated in 1860.

A fire at the courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records, which is why some Allen County families are hard to trace in local papers. The county's population has grown from 14,628 in 1990 to 20,588 in 2020, and it was a dry county until voters approved legal alcohol sales in 2023.
EXTRA.note: Place story. The 1902 fire is a fact about the county, not a record of a particular family.

EXTRA.name: Hagansport, Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.title: A crossing on the Sulphur River
EXTRA.hook: Hagansport began as a river crossing, and its post office came and went over 70 years.
body: Hagansport grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port, named for an early settler. The spelling Hagansport was in use by 1857, when F. M. Sims was postmaster. The post office closed in 1866, reopened in 1876, and closed for good in 1929. The village sits on a divide between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, about eleven miles northwest of Mount Vernon.

By 1884 the community had about 150 people, four churches, a school, a mill and a cotton gin. In 1896 its one-room school had 69 pupils. The U.S. Bureau of Soils, which surveyed the county in 1908, found the cotton land around the village on a clay loam and warned that the river bottoms below were "more or less subject to overflow." John B. Smith farmed land he owned there in 1900; a tenant such as John C. Satterfield, who rented a farm at Hagansport in 1910, usually kept half the crop.

Emma Smith was buried in Hagansport Cemetery in 1905. By the 1930s the center had moved south onto Farm Road 71, with a sawmill, two churches, a school and 125 people, and later it shifted again, to its present spot at the junction of Highway 37 and Farm Road 71. About 40 people lived there in 1985, and the Handbook of Texas says the estimate was still 40 through 2000.
EXTRA.note: The Smith and Satterfield families lived in the Hagansport area.

EXTRA.name: Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.place: Franklin County, TX
EXTRA.title: Cotton, rails and tenant farms in Franklin County
EXTRA.hook: Between 1879 and 1929 the county's cotton acreage grew more than fourfold while yields fell by more than half.
body: Franklin County was created in March 1875 and named for Benjamin C. Franklin, and Mount Vernon won the county-seat election on 30 April of that year. White settlers had come from the late 1830s, mostly from Tennessee and the upper South, along the old Cherokee Trace. The county is small, 294 square miles of post-oak and blackjack woods, bounded on the north by the Sulphur River, with Big Cypress Creek running through the south.

For its first dozen years the county had no railroad and no navigable water. The East Line and Red River Railroad reached the southeast corner in 1876, and in 1887 the St. Louis, Arkansas and Texas Railway crossed the middle of the county and became the main route to market.

Cotton was the cash crop and corn fed the family; together they made up about three of every four harvested acres in 1880. In 1879, 706 farms planted 8,660 acres of cotton. By 1929, 1,678 farms planted 37,969 acres. Yields fell from about half a bale per acre to about one-fifth. Tenants were 34 percent of farmers in 1880 and 62 percent in 1930. Farm values fell from $4,172 in 1920 to $2,085 in 1930, and the first paved roads came only after voters approved a $200,000 bond issue in 1916.

John C. Satterfield reached the county from Kentucky about 1907 and in 1910 rented a farm at Hagansport, near the high-water mark of the county's population, which peaked at 9,331 in 1910. It fell to 8,494 in 1930 and bottomed at 5,101 in 1960, as the Depression and the shift to livestock took hold. Cotton fell to 16,582 acres by 1940. Oil found near Talco in 1936 reached northeastern Franklin County, but a 1939 local paper judged it not large enough to disturb the way of living.
EXTRA.note: Context for families who moved from Kentucky to Franklin County around 1900-1910. Only the Satterfield household is tied to it here (a rented farm at Hagansport in 1910); no other named ancestor is said to have been a tenant or an owner.

EXTRA.name: Grant, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.place: Grant, Choctaw County, OK
EXTRA.title: Grant began as a railroad stop in the Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.hook: Grant grew from a store of about 1885 into a station on the Frisco line, when the land was still part of the Choctaw Nation.
body: Grant was founded as a station stop on the St. Louis and San Francisco Railroad, which opened through Indian Territory in June 1887, though the town may trace to a store Basil Gooding opened about 1885. It was named for President Ulysses S. Grant.

A post office opened at Grant, Indian Territory, on January 31, 1889. At its founding the town lay in Kiamitia County, part of the Pushmataha District of the Choctaw Nation (some accounts say Apukshunnubbee).
The town counted 289 people in 2010 and 190 in 2020.

Charles Oscar and Artie Smith are buried at Grant Cemetery. A Red River ferry six miles south connected residents with Texas markets, and when the Arkansas & Choctaw laid its track five miles north, business drifted to Hugo. Grant had 416 people in 1910 and 296 in 1930, with a cotton gin, bank, hotel and a newspaper, the Grant Graphic. By 1930, 73 percent of Choctaw County's farmers were tenants.
EXTRA.note: Place story. It does not claim a Choctaw citizenship record for a named ancestor.

EXTRA.name: 42nd Indiana Infantry
EXTRA.title: From Evansville to Perryville and Stones River
EXTRA.hook: Raised in October 1861 from six southwestern Indiana counties, the 42nd was in the field at Perryville within a year and at Stones River by New Year's.
body: The 42nd Indiana Infantry was organized at Evansville and mustered in for three years on October 9, 1861, under Colonel James Garrard Jones. Its men came from six counties of southwestern Indiana.

In the autumn of 1862 the regiment moved into Kentucky, pursued Bragg's army from October 1 to 15, and fought at the Battle of Perryville on October 8. One of its lieutenant colonels, Charles Harvey Denby, left after Perryville to command the 80th Indiana.

The regiment then returned to Nashville and advanced on Murfreesboro on December 30, 1862. At Stones River (December 30, 1862 to January 3, 1863) Lieutenant Colonel James M. Shanklin commanded and was surrounded and captured on 3 January 1863.
From January 1863 the regiment belonged to the XIV Corps, Army of the Cumberland.

The Perryville losses were plain. On the morning of 8 October 1862 the regiment "numbered less than five hundred effective men. The entire loss, officers and men, killed, wounded and missing, was 166, or fully one-third of the entire command." Company G, one of the largest, had 52 rank and file in the fight and lost 22 killed and wounded. The regiment's actual fighting, a veteran wrote, "was not to exceed two hours." It was "the first general engagement the regiment was in, and its loss was by far the greatest of any of the succeeding ones."

At Stones River, on the morning of 31 December 1862, the regiment fought in the cedar woods beside the 15th Kentucky, whose colonel was killed. Company F's captain, William M. Cockrum, was wounded in the right shoulder.
At Chickamauga (September 19-21, 1863) the regiment was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel William T. B. McIntire. In November 1863 it fought at Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge.

At Chickamauga the regiment lost "eight killed, fifty-three wounded, and thirty-two missing, making a total of ninety-three," nearly all the missing taken prisoner; Company F's captain was among them. The reenlistment followed: the government "offered inducements to the men to re-enlist, or veteranize, on the first day of January, 1864," and "there were but few in the 42d Indiana who did not re-enlist." The regiment reached Indianapolis on 28 January 1864, where Governor Morton and others addressed a public reception, and the soldiers "became recruiting officers" to fill the ranks.

The 42nd reenlisted on January 1, 1864, and served in the Atlanta Campaign from May 1 to September 8, 1864: Resaca (May 14-15), Kennesaw Mountain, Peachtree Creek (July 19-20), the Siege of Atlanta (July 22 to August 25) and Jonesboro (August 31 to September 1).

Company F paid for the Atlanta campaign in names: David W. Johnson (killed 14 August 1864), John Warick (7 August 1864) and David W. Wallam (31 May 1864, at Altoona or Allatoona). The regiment's losses for the campaign could not be given by name, because "the day's and month's losses were reported in the aggregate, and not in detail." The last of Company F's dead, Lt. John Q. A. Steele, fell at Bentonville on 19 March 1865.

It went on to the March to the Sea, the siege of Savannah and the Carolinas, fighting at Bentonville March 19-21, 1865, and marched in the Grand Review at Washington on May 24, 1865. It mustered out at Louisville on July 21, 1865.
Total losses were 310: 113 killed or mortally wounded, and 197 dead of disease.
EXTRA.note: Regimental facts are documented. The connection to this family rests on Daniel O'Neal's service in the 42nd, covered in his own story.

EXTRA.name: Wright City, McCurtain County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: A company town built around a sawmill
EXTRA.hook: Wright City began about 1909 as a Dierks lumber company town, with the mill, houses, stores, bank and hotel all owned by the company.
body: The town had two names before it had its present one. When the post office was chartered on March 24, 1910, it was Bismark, after a Nebraska town the Dierks brothers knew. During World War I it became simply Wright, to shed the association with the German chancellor, and on May 18, 1920 it was renamed Wright City for William Wiley Wright, the county's first war casualty. The Choctaw Lumber Company, a subsidiary of Dierks Lumber and Coal, founded the town about 1909 beside a large timber-processing plant. Its first log was cut July 13, 1910.

The company supplied a sawmill, planer, railroad shops, housing, stores, a bank, a hotel, an ice factory and fire and police protection, and donated land for a school and churches. A company railroad ran from Valliant to De Queen, Arkansas.

This was the country the Hulsey family came to. By 1920 George Washington Hulsey, a farmer the family remembers as a preacher, had moved his wife Sarah and their six children from Arkansas to tenant-farm in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County. In 1930 the household of ten was renting near Wright City, with the mill and its company railroad close by.

Together the Wright City and Broken Bow mills could cut nearly 250,000 board feet of pine and 60,000 of hardwood a day. Workers struck for two months in 1947 and won an eight-cent hourly raise. Wright City had fewer than 500 people in the 1920s, 1,121 in 1950 and 1,068 in 1970.

Dierks Forests sold its non-core properties in August 1965, the town incorporated in 1966, and in 1969 Weyerhaeuser bought the mill complex that still anchors the town's economy. Its Little Cheyenne Rodeo, a rodeo, barbecue and dance started by local cowboys in 1933, is still held every July.
EXTRA.note: Place history for the family's McCurtain County years. The Hulsey household lived in Sulphur Township in 1920 and rented near Wright City in 1930, but no record names a Hulsey who worked in the mills.

EXTRA.name: Families of the Regulators
EXTRA.title: The Oath, the Burned Fields, and the Road West
EXTRA.hook: For the families who stood at Alamance, the battle lasted an afternoon. What came after lasted years.
body: Governor William Tryon's militia of about 1,000 won the field on May 16, 1771. Casualty figures are disputed: one account has the governor's side losing 9 killed and 61 wounded, others run to 27 government dead, and the Regulators carried off their own casualties, so perhaps 100 or more is only an estimate.

James Few was hanged at the camp the next day without a court. Of fourteen captives tried at a special term of the superior court at Hillsborough, twelve were convicted of treason and sentenced to hang. Six were pardoned at the last minute by King George III on Tryon's recommendation, and six were hanged at Hillsborough on June 19, 1771, among them Benjamin Merrill, Robert Matear, James Pugh and Captain Robert Messer.

Tryon then marched across Regulator country, burning homes and destroying crops. Residents were made to surrender their firearms, and he offered a pardon to nearly everyone who would swear an oath of allegiance to the Crown; within six weeks 6,409 people had done so.

Many Regulators and their families moved west. A few settled on the Mississippi near the site of Memphis and moved on again when some of Tryon's former militiamen turned up. Others went to Tennessee, where the Watauga Association formed in 1772 and the State of Franklin in 1784. Later study found that of 883 known Regulators only 34 became Loyalists, while 289 were Whigs.

quotes.t: Many Regulators and their families migrated westward, beyond North Carolina.
quotes.c: Summary of the aftermath of Alamance

EXTRA.note: Frames the westward chain the family followed. Whether a specific Moffitt signed the oath should be checked against the 1771 oath lists.

EXTRA.name: Hugo, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.rel: Choctaw County Oklahoma home area (place story)
EXTRA.title: A Town Born at a Railroad Crossing
EXTRA.hook: Hugo did not grow from a farm or a fort. It sprang up where two railroad lines crossed in the Choctaw Nation.
body: The Frisco built a north-south line through the area in 1887. In 1901–03 the Arkansas and Choctaw Railroad, later taken over by the Frisco, built an east-west line from Hope, Arkansas, toward Ardmore. The territorial town that sprang up at the crossing became Hugo.

It was founded in late 1901 in Kiamitia County, part of the Pushmataha District of the Choctaw Nation, and named for the French novelist Victor Hugo. The name was suggested by the wife of surveyor W. H. Darrough, a fan of his books.

Hugo grew fast. By 1910 it had 4,582 people, two newspapers, four banks and a creosoting plant, and in 1920 it had 6,368. The Depression closed three of its banks and the 1930 count dropped to 5,272, though by 1940 it was back to 5,909, with 111 retail businesses. The Frisco depot was built in 1914 and is a museum today. Agriculture, timber and ranching have been mainstays of the local economy since the start, which fits the family's timber work in Choctaw County.

The Al G. Kelly and Miller Brothers Circus moved its winter quarters to Hugo from Kansas in the early 1940s (sources give 1941 and 1942), and fifteen different shows have used the town as headquarters, at times about twenty wintering there. Showman's Rest at Mt. Olivet Cemetery was set aside for performers in 1960. In 1974 the Corps of Engineers finished Hugo Dam and made Hugo Lake.
EXTRA.note: No particular sawmill has been tied to the family's timber work. The year the circus came to Hugo differs between sources (1941 and 1942).

EXTRA.name: Etowah County, Alabama
EXTRA.title: The County That Had Two Names
EXTRA.hook: Etowah County was created under one name and renamed two years later, so the same ground carried two names within a few years.
body: Before 1866 the area was split mainly between DeKalb and Cherokee counties.
On December 7, 1866, the first postwar legislature created Baine County, named for David W. Baine, a politician and Confederate officer who died in battle in 1862. Gadsden was made the county seat.
On December 1, 1868, after the 1868 constitutional convention abolished Baine County, the same boundaries became Etowah County, from a Cherokee-language word.
So the same ground was DeKalb or Cherokee before 1866, Baine from 1866 to 1868, and Etowah afterward.
EXTRA.note: Place story with a practical research tip for the family; no named ancestor is tied to it here.
EXTRA.src: Wikipedia, Etowah County, Alabama (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etowah_County,_Alabama)

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Four documents, one name: William Moffitt in 1768
EXTRA.hook: In a single spring and autumn, William Moffitt's name went onto a petition, a committee list and the Governor's list of men too dangerous to pardon.
body: The Regulators kept their papers, and so did the royal government. William's year can be followed in print. On 30 April 1768 the Regulators issued their eighth Advertisement, and "William Maffet" is among the signers, alongside nearly the whole leadership. The meeting agreed to "send 12 men that we have chosen to meet on the said 11th day of May at Thomas Lindley's," the mill on Cane Creek.

The ninth Advertisement, the petition on public fees, carries roughly 450 names. "Wm Moffit" signs on page 734; a "James Moffitt" signs on page 737, probably a relative. Then on 21 May 1768, at George Sally's house, the Regulators chose a committee to collect their grievances and carry them to the Governor. The list begins "Wm Maffit." His name is first.

In September, while the Governor’s troops were on the march from Salisbury to Hillsborough, James Hunter delivered a letter to Tryon signed for the Regulators by four men: Peter Julian, James Evans, Abraham Teague and William Moffitt. It protests loyalty, saying the Regulators “will when occasion requires fight for and defend him to the last drop of blood” for King George, and that they bear “no ill-will to any but our cruel Oppressors from which number we exclude your Excellency.” It then turns: “But will nothing propitiate but our blood, we are determined at all events to fall like men, and sell our lives at the very dearest rate.” The last line is a plea: “We beseech you Sir not to drive us to despair.”

When the Regulators were assembled at Hillsborough, they sent "The humble Address of the Inhabitants of several Counties called Regulators." They were "desirous to submit ourselves to the clemency of your Excellency, and to lay aside all method of redress of our grievances, but by a due course of Law," and they begged that the Governor "will forgive all our past offences by your gracious Proclamation." It is "Signed in behalf of the said Counties," and the first name in the list of twenty-two signers is William Moffitt's, ahead of Peter Julian, Lewis Lowry, Christopher Nation, Samuel Low, John Marshill and the rest.

The court of the same month showed the other side. At the Hillsborough Superior Court on Thursday the 29th, the clerk wrote: "The indictment preferred against James Hunter, Ninion Hamilton, Isaac Jackson, John Philip Hartso, William Moffitt, John Pile & Francis Dossett, for a Rout, having been returned by the Grand Jury 'a true bill as to all except John Pile,' it is ordered by the Court that the bill be Quashed, by reason of the irregularity of the return, and that the Attorney General prepare a new bill." Two more bills against other Regulators were quashed the same day. No later bill against him is known.

The Governor's answer came on 3 October 1768 at Hillsborough. His proclamation pardoned the insurgents except thirteen men, and "William Moffitt" is on the Council's list between Malachi Fyke and Christopher Nation. A general pardon of 9 September 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection" and listed no exceptions; the pardon text does not say outright that it reached the thirteen.

His name does not appear in 1771. The reward proclamation outlawed only four men, and the sixteen men excepted from the June 1771 pardon include no Moffitt. Whether he stood on the field at Alamance on 16 May 1771 is not recorded.
In 1901 the boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators printed Tryon's list, with "William Moffat" on it, as the names of "the patriots of upper Carolina in the opinion of William Tryon."

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: What William did after Alamance
EXTRA.hook: The records leave William out of the 1771 outlaw lists, and family accounts say he fed the Patriots rather than fought in the Revolution.
body: After the Regulators were beaten at Alamance in May 1771, the Governor outlawed four leaders and named sixteen more for exception from pardon. William is on neither list. Where he lived afterward is not recorded beyond the Deep River neighborhood of his 1768 papers.

A family history says he took the oath that followed Alamance, never to bear arms against the King, and stayed neutral in the Revolution because of it. No militia service for him has been found. Instead, family accounts and a battleground memorial book say he supplied provisions to the Patriots, and a pay voucher is cited for provisions furnished.

The mill is where the sources disagree. The community of Moffitt, North Carolina, takes its name from the mill on Richland Creek, and a post office called Moffitt's Mills ran from 1823 to 1935. Hugh Moffitt, William's probable brother, is credited with the first mill. Family histories say William and Hugh built it together, and a Patriot record credits a James Moffitt of Brush Creek with "supplied sundries to the militia; ran Moffitt's Mill." That is likely another brother, and which Moffitt the vouchers name is not known.
A Patriot named Robert Moffitt, born 1762 of Brush Creek, is a different man from William's son Robert.

The Randolph County militia's first court met on 16 September 1801. Governor Caswell commissioned John Collier, Richard Owen and Joseph Shepherd as the regiment's officers, and the nine company captains were Shubal York, Joseph Smith, Dobson Burrow, Robert Redding, Samuel Moffitt, Colon Steed, John Brown, Charles Duncan and John Craven. Governor Caswell is credited with the commissions, but he died in 1789, so the commissions and the 1801 date cannot both be right. A Samuel Moffitt among the captains may or may not belong to William and Mary's household or to Hugh Moffitt's.
kv: Said by family history to have sworn after 1771; not seen in a record
EXTRA.note: The provisions claim rests on a family account and a compiled record; the voucher itself has not been seen. Whether William or Hugh or James ran the mill is unsettled. The Alamance book's statements about his birth in Donegal and burial at Richland Creek carry no citation.

EXTRA.name: William and Mary (Davies) Moffitt
EXTRA.title: A wagon, a still and 250 acres: two Moffitt wills
EXTRA.hook: William's will of 1796 and Mary's of 1820 show a working farm: a wagon, a still, a new field on the river, and eight grown or growing children.
body: William's will begins "I William Moffitt of Randolph County in the province of North Carolina, being weak in body." He gave his sons Robert, William and David land, and his daughters Naomi (Neomi Macky), Catharine Cox, Hannah Cox, Mary Wilkinson and Margaret £3 each, with Margaret also getting cows, sheep and a bed.

Robert received the 250 acres William had bought of William Cox, except "the new field that is cleared upon the River," which his mother kept for life. William got the 225-acre plantation where his father lived, with a share reserved for Mary while she was a widow. David, who was clearly under age, got land on Tibs Run, wagon iron "brought from Pig River," and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown in Cumberland County. If David died young, his brothers inherited and each sister would get £15.

"My Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt" received the wagon, the still, the plantation tools and the stock, and was named executrix with "my son Robart Moffitt" as executor. The witnesses were Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt.

Mary outlived him by more than twenty years. She dated her own will "the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820," in the Quaker style, naming the same five daughters and "my three sons," Robert, William and David. Her daughter Margaret was executrix and David executor, and William Cox and Stephen Cox witnessed. It was filed in 1822. Robert, her son and our ancestor, was alive in 1820.

quotes.t: my Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt Executrix & my son Robart Moffitt Executor
quotes.c: Will of William Moffitt, Randolph Co., N.C.

EXTRA.note: The last digit of William's will date is faint: one reading gives 1790, but the 1796 reading fits Robert as executor. Online trees give his death as 10 August 1797 or 1799; no record settles it. Mary's death is given as February 1822.
EXTRA.src: Will of William Moffitt (1796), Randolph Co. Will Book 2, pp. 30-31 (FamilySearch film 007640058); will of Mary Moffitt (1820, filed 1822)

EXTRA.name: Chamness, Norton, Moffitt and Davies
EXTRA.title: Two weddings at Cane Creek, sixteen days apart
EXTRA.hook: In the spring of 1763 the Cane Creek meetinghouse saw Joseph Chamness marry Margaret Norton and William Moffitt marry Mary Davies. Their children would marry each other in 1797.
body: Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized in 1751, with Anthony Chamness named its overseer. By 1763 the Chamnesses had been in North Carolina for fourteen years, since a transfer from Monocacy in Maryland to Carver's Creek Meeting in 1749, followed by a 490-acre grant on Cane Creek dated 24 June 1751.

On 17 March 1763 Anthony's son Joseph, born in Baltimore County, Maryland, married Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton, who had arrived from Virginia in 1762. Joseph became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Margaret bore eleven children and died in 1784.

Sixteen days later, on 2 April 1763, William Moffitt, 23, married Mary Davies, 22, at the same meeting. Her father Charles Davies had crossed the Atlantic as a bound youth, married Hannah Matson of Merion in Pennsylvania in 1732 or 1733, and followed the Quaker migration south. He was recorded as a minister at Cane Creek in 1761 and was disowned by the meeting five years later, after complaining that the women's minutes were "mixed with an untruth." He bought 187 acres in Orange County on 2 August 1758 and died on 13 May 1801; Hannah died on 25 October 1812.

Margaret's daughter Martha was born in 1778. On 20 September 1797 she married Mary's son Robert at Providence, under Center Monthly Meeting, and the Chamness and Moffitt lines joined. Their son Nathan carried the Moffitt name to Arkansas.

The Chamness-Norton marriage certificate reads: "Whereas, Joseph Chamness, son of Anthony Chamness and Sarah, his wife, of Orange County, in the Province of North Carolina, and Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County; and Province aforesaid; having declared their intentions of Marriage with each other before several Monthly Meetings of the people called Quakers, held at Cane Creek, in Orange County, and Province aforesaid, according to the good order used amongst them, and having consent of parents, or parties concerned, their said proposals of marriage were allowed by said meeting." The day was "the Seventeenth day of the Third Month in the Year of Our Lord One Thousand Seven Hundred and Sixty-three," when the two stood up "in a public meeting of the said people, held at their meeting house at Cane Creek" and each promised "with Divine Assistance" to be a faithful and loving spouse until death.

Beneath the signatures of "Joseph Chamness" and "Margaret Chamness," twelve witnesses signed: "John Marshall, Joseph Pike, William Piggott, John Stout, John Davis, William Marshall," and, in the second column, "Thomas Branson, Anthony Chamness, Edward Norton, Sarah Chamness, Elizabeth Norton, Elizabeth Chamness." A family historian remarked: "We note, also, the parents of Joseph and Margaret and his oldest sister all signed the certificate." So the page carries the names of all four grandparents of Martha Chamness, who would marry Robert Moffitt in 1797: Anthony and Sarah Chamness, and Edward and Elizabeth Norton. It is added that Joseph was made recorder of marriage certificates in 1764 and that the meeting's records from then until 1769, when he moved into Providence Meeting in Randolph County, "must be" in his writing.

One Find a Grave account places his birth in Luton, England and says he was indentured to a Quaker family in Philadelphia, while the Cane Creek family account says only that he was "sold to pay his passage." A note on that memorial suggests the disownment may be tied to a Deep River marriage dispute; the 1766 minute, since examined (see “The charge against the women's minutes”), says only that he charged the women's minutes with an untruth and does not name the entry, so that remains a possibility.

EXTRA.name: Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness
EXTRA.title: Robert and Martha: nine children in Randolph County
EXTRA.hook: Married at Center Meeting in 1797, Robert and Martha Moffitt raised nine children in Randolph County, and two of them left North Carolina for Missouri.
body: Robert Moffitt's marriage is in the Quaker record as "1797, 9, 20. Robert, s William & Mary, Randolph Co., m Martha Chamness." Martha, born 6 October 1778 in Guilford County, was the daughter of Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton and the granddaughter of Anthony Chamness.

Robert had been named executor of his father William's will the year before and inherited the 250 acres his father had bought of William Cox. He was alive when his mother made her will in 1820, and appears in the 1830 and 1840 censuses of Randolph County.

Their children, all born in Randolph County, were Naomi (1800), Sarah (1801), David (1802), William C. (1803), Aaron (1805), Hannah, Lydia (1811), Nathan (1814) and Robert (1815). Robert, the youngest, died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Missouri, in 1872. Sarah died at Lorimor, Iowa, in 1860, so Nathan was not the only child to leave. Martha lived to 1865.
kv: Naomi, Sarah, David, William C., Aaron, Hannah, Lydia, Nathan, Robert
EXTRA.note: The marriage and Robert's parentage come from the Quaker record. The children's list and Martha's parents come from compiled Quaker abstracts. Online memorials give Robert's birth as 6 October 1778 and his death as 6 October 1844, which is Martha's birth date copied over; as executor in 1796 he was probably born by about 1775. Martha's death is given as 11 October or 11 November 1865. Two other Robert Moffitts lived nearby and are not him.

EXTRA.name: Nathan H. Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Nathan the wheelwright, and a son in blue
EXTRA.hook: Nathan’s census trail runs from North Carolina through Arkansas to Missouri; a Union cavalryman of the same name may have been his son.
body: Nathan married Rebecca Williams on 13 October 1835 in Randolph County, North Carolina, and in 1840 he was in the county's South Division. A son, Calvin, was born there on 4 December 1841. By 1850 the family was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas.

Lawrence County in the 1850s was a mix of small farms, a county seat at Smithville, and 494 enslaved people among 8,875 white residents in 1860. By then Nathan was a wheelwright with $1,200 in land. Patrick was born in May 1853 and Henry in 1855. The war brought jayhawkers and bushwhackers to the county, though no major battle. A Calvin V. Moffitt served as a private in Company L, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), but whether that soldier was Nathan's son is unconfirmed. Family profiles place Nathan's son later at Duncan, Oklahoma, where he died on 13 February 1913.

By 1870 Nathan and Rebecca were in Dent County, Missouri, farming with no land of their own. Oregon County, where they next lived, was largely pro-Southern and suffered raids; its Alton courthouse burned in October 1863, and the historical marker adds that Lee's surrender "did not end the Civil War in Oregon County." Rebecca died there in 1871. That year Nathan married a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole.
Nathan died on 23 December 1873 in Oregon County. That August his son Patrick had married Alice Ann Cole there. A photograph labeled "Nathan Moffitt," shown with children, is kept in the family tree.

Nathan's brothers and sisters spread widely: Sarah and Naomi to Iowa, Robert to Strawberry Township and then Howell County, Missouri, and Hannah, Lydia, Aaron and William C. stayed in Randolph County. Aaron's son Veno Moffitt died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira.

The 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863, and Company L, where a Calvin V. Moffitt served, was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. Whether that soldier was this Calvin is uncertain.
EXTRA.note: The NPS record documents a soldier named Calvin V. Moffitt; identifying that soldier with Nathan's son remains a lead. Patrick is given as born 11 May 1853 at Sylamore and as dying on 20 December 1905 at Mountain View in one source, and as dying in November 1904 and buried at Sallisaw in another. Who burned the Alton courthouse is disputed: the marker says Union troops, a 2024 survey says Southern partisans.

(1835); Missouri Marriages (1871); NPS Civil War Soldiers database; Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Lawrence County'; Alton marker (HMDB 179894); WikiTree Moffitt-107, Moffitt-400

EXTRA.name: Henry and Hannah (Grimes) Moffitt
EXTRA.title: 1901: a death in Mountain View and 22 years of widowhood
EXTRA.hook: Henry died at 46 in the Stone County hills. Hannah, who could not read or write, kept the family together for another two decades.
body: Stone County was only 28 years old when Henry died. It was created in 1873, and Mountain View, its seat, had 99 residents in 1880, was incorporated on 14 August 1890, and got its first wooden courthouse in 1888. Henry, a farmer who owned his land free and clear in 1900, died there in 1901 at 46. Family accounts give the date as 9 September. No grave has been found and he has no memorial anywhere; Arkansas did not register deaths in Stone County until 1914.
The same spring, on 26 May 1901, Henry's brother Patrick lost his wife, Alice Ann (Cole) Moffitt, who is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery in Stone County.

Hannah stayed. In 1910 she was renting a house in Franklin Township with Tom, who worked as a railroad section hand, and Grady, who made barrel staves. She had borne seven children and six were living: among them Josephine, Jesse, Gimsa, Bertha, Tom and Grady. Jesse Gee Moffitt went to Texas and died in Amarillo in 1957; Tom died in Paris, Texas, in 1953.

She spent her last years at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou community six miles east of Mountain View with a grist mill, cotton gin, stave mill and sawmill by the early 1900s. Its post office opened in 1907, and the Herpel Missionary Baptist Church laid its cornerstone on 5 March 1923. Hannah died there on 4 April 1923, about a month later, and is buried in Herpel Cemetery, where her stone reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
kv: Hannah, Herpel Cemetery; Henry's grave not found
EXTRA.note: Henry's exact death date comes from family records and no original has been seen. The Stone County Record newspapers for September 1901 would be the likeliest check. Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930), buried at Herpel, may be a daughter but is not proved.

EXTRA.name: Grady and Mary Moffitt
EXTRA.title: A timber camp and a rented house in Hugo
EXTRA.hook: Grady and Mary raised their family in Oklahoma and Texas and buried three of their children.
body: Grady and Mary married about 1914. Their first son, Alvin, was born in September 1915. In 1917 Grady was at Ervin, Oklahoma, a place that existed only from 1904 to 1922, as a timberman for C. D. Neese. Which sawmill that was is not known. The county's biggest one was the Pine Belt Lumber Company at Fort Towson, begun in 1902.

Hugo was a young town. It was founded in 1901 where the Frisco's north-south line crossed the Arkansas & Choctaw, and the Frisco depot went up in 1914. Grady's family rented there at 411 North H Street by 1940.

Their children were Alvin B. (1915-1994, U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II), Odas Eugene (1918-1995; "Odis" in 1940, "Ottis" in 1920), Dois L. (1921-1947), Jimmie Gaynell (1923-1926), John Winfred (1925-1990), the twins Alton V. (1928-1975) and Eldon Herman (1928-2014), Donald K. (1931-2014) and Henry Wayne (1934-1937). The two toddlers who died were three years old.

In 1930, with six boys, they were living with Mary's parents, John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford, in Martin County, Texas. That is the county where Mary's father is buried. In 1940 Grady, 48, had been out of work for 50 weeks and earned $100.

Grady's brother Tom farmed beside him in 1920 and later lived in Paris, Texas, where he died in 1953, with a stone marked WW I and WW II. Their brother Jesse is buried at Tahoka, Texas. Grady and Mary lie at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo.
The full dates for the two children who died young are Jimmie Gaynell, 17 January 1923 to 26 October 1926, and Henry Wayne, 13 January 1934 to 12 May 1937.

EXTRA.name: John Morgan and Lizzie (Newton) Shackleford
EXTRA.title: Mary's people: from Etowah County to Texas and Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: An Alabama marriage in 1889, a Texas household in 1930, and Lizzie’s later home near her children at Apache.
body: John Morgan Shackleford was born on 30 September 1862 in Alabama and married Catherine Elizabeth "Lizzie" Newton on 1 December 1889 in Etowah County. Etowah County had been created only 21 years before, and for two of those years, 1866 to 1868, it was called Baine County. In 1900 at Gilbert, John was 37 and Elizabeth 28, with five living children. Mary, born 4 June 1895, was the "May, 5."

Her siblings were Balis Anthony (1892-1982, who died in Los Angeles County), Robert Yates (1897-1961), John Newton (1906-2002), Hazel Marzee King (1908-1980), Edward Richard (1910-1988) and Helen Elizabeth Josey (1915-1997).

By 1930 John Morgan was in Martin County, Texas, with his wife and children; Grady and Mary and their six boys were living with them. John died on 22 May 1930 and is buried at Evergreen Cemetery in Stanton. Lizzie died on 8 November 1951 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache, Caddo County, Oklahoma. In 1933 Lizzie moved from Dawson County, Texas, to Apache. She spent her final years near several of her grown children, and died at son Ed’s home southwest of town.

The Shackelfords of Virginia trace to an immigrant, Roger, who received a grant in Gloucester County in 1658. A Shackleford family history of 1940 says the family had no coat of arms, and Mary's descent from Roger is not proved.

In 1900 the household at Gilbert held John, 37, Elizabeth, 28, and five children: "Balous" 8, Myrtle 6, May 5, Robert 3 and Eddie 8 months. Notices of 1961 and 1981 name sisters Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins who do not fit that list. Hazel was born at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family was in northeast Texas about 1908 before reaching Martin County.

Lizzie’s marriage papers preserve a family moment just before the wedding. On 28 November 1889, her father, Balas Newton, gave permission for her to marry John. John carried that consent into the probate office and, two days later, certified that he had written and signed it at her father’s direction. A separate sworn statement names her as Lizzie Newton.

EXTRA.name: John Winfred Moffitt
EXTRA.title: ARD-19: the drydock that could not sail
EXTRA.hook: John's first ship had no engines, was 488 feet long, and was hit by a Japanese fighter while it held a damaged destroyer.
body: ARD-19 was a floating drydock built by the Pacific Bridge Company at Alameda, California, in 1943-44. It was about 488 feet long, 81 feet wide and 5,200 tons, with two 40 mm and two 20 mm gun mounts. It had no engines, so it was towed. Its work was to lift destroyers, minesweepers and landing ships out of the water at forward bases so their hulls could be repaired close to the fighting.

It was commissioned on 22 March 1944, the day John's muster rolls begin. It was towed across the Pacific in stages to join Service Squadron 10, the Navy's mobile base force, and reached Seeadler Harbor at Manus in the Admiralty Islands at the end of August 1944. In November it moved up to San Pedro Bay, Leyte.

The destroyer USS Ross had hit two Japanese mines off Dinagat and Homonhon on 19 October 1944, killing three men and leaving twenty missing. She was docked in ARD-19 on 24 November. Shortly before noon on 27 or 28 November (the two ship histories differ), a Japanese Army fighter crashed into the dock, starting gasoline fires that spread to Ross. Gunfire from ARD-19, Ross and LST-556 shot down a second fighter that was strafing them. The damage was heavy but kept the dock busy with its own repairs "for only a brief time." ARD-19 earned one battle star for Leyte, for 10-29 November 1944.

ARD-19 then carried on repair work at Subic Bay on Luzon "until after the end of World War II." Later its life was long: it was recommissioned in 1963 as USS Oak Ridge to dock ballistic-missile submarines and served until 2001.

On a crew of about 130 there was usually no doctor, and one or two corpsmen ran sick call. On a repair dock that meant burns, crushed hands and welding-flash eye injuries. That was general practice for such ships. John's rate and duties aboard ARD-19 are not known; on USS Chief in November 1945 he was rated F1c, fireman first class, so he may not have served as a corpsman at all.

EXTRA.name: John Winfred Moffitt
EXTRA.title: USS Chief: minesweepers, Nagoya and home
EXTRA.hook: John's second ship had already swept the mines ahead of Saipan, then spent the first postwar winter keeping Japanese waters clear.
body: USS Chief (AM-315) was an 890-ton Auk-class minesweeper commissioned on 9 October 1943. In June 1944 she swept mines ahead of the Saipan and Tinian landings. She was at Okinawa from late May to late August 1945. In September she swept minefields at Wakayama, Japan, ahead of the occupation forces and helped salvage the minesweeper YMS-418.
John joined Chief after the war, on occupation duty at Nagoya and Sasebo, which lasted until March 1946. Where he joined her is unknown; he may have come aboard in the Philippines or in Japan.
In March 1946 Chief sailed for San Francisco and arrived in April. John was discharged on 9 May 1946. In 1947 he married Faye Smith, on 12 June at Paris, Texas.
Chief went out of commission in reserve at San Pedro on 17 March 1947, was recommissioned for the Korean War, and was sold to Mexico in 1973 as ARM Jesus Gonzalez Ortega.
EXTRA.note: The muster index labels this ship MCM 14, which is a 1990s ship named after her; a 1946 roll can only be AM-315. The photograph is the ship in 1952, not in John's time.

EXTRA.name: John C. and Samantha (Johnson) Satterfield
EXTRA.title: From Morgantown to Soper: the Satterfield road
EXTRA.hook: Samantha Johnson married a widower with three children at about 20, raised eight more, moved the family to Texas, and ended her life in Choctaw County, Oklahoma.
body: Samantha D. "Mantha" Johnson was born on 28 March 1872 in Kentucky, a daughter of Melvina (Clark) Johnson. In 1892 she married John C. Satterfield, a widower with three children: Henry B. (born May 1883), Martha A. (August 1884) and John W. (January 1887).

The first six of their eight children were born in Kentucky. Wavey Lincoln arrived at Morgantown, in Butler County, on 28 December 1895 by his own draft cards (his stone says 9 January 1896); Artie Pearl followed in August 1898. In 1900 they were farming at Horse Mill. Joseph, an early son, died before 1910.

About 1907 the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. In April 1910 John, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport with Wavey, Pearl, James, Ira and Stella, and a last child was born there in 1912. John died in Franklin County between 1912 and 1916; no grave is known.

On 28 July 1917 Samantha married Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens, a widower, at Mount Vernon, Texas, and they crossed the Red River into Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Wavey Lincoln served as a private in the Army in the first World War and died at Soper in 1952. Samantha died on 1 October 1928 and is buried as Samantha D. Stephens at Soper Cemetery. Her daughter Artie Pearl married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914, and they lie at Grant Cemetery.
kv: About 1907, Butler Co., Ky. to Franklin Co., Tex.
EXTRA.note: John's death is given as 1919 in family trees but a family biography places it between 1912 and 1916, and he is absent by Samantha's 1917 remarriage. Most details about Samantha come from a Find a Grave biography written by a Stephens family member; the 1892 marriage record itself has not been seen.

EXTRA.name: Joel J. Thompson
EXTRA.title: Joel Thompson tells it in Hugo, 1937
EXTRA.hook: At 45, Joel Thompson sat down with a WPA interviewer and described the log house, the deer, the court and the schools of his boyhood.
body: On 28 August 1937 a Works Progress Administration field worker, Hazel B. Greene, took down Joel Thompson's story at his home on North G Street in Hugo. Joel was born on 29 January 1892, 'about 2 miles west of High Hill Methodist Church,' the son of Joseph P. Thompson and Betsy Tims. He said his father 'was second of nine children.'

He named the brothers and sisters who lived to be grown: Alex B., then himself, Peter Pitchlyn, Simon W., Joseph W., Jincy, who married Wilson Aaron, a full-blood Choctaw, and Marietta, who married Stephen Caldwell, also a full-blood. The family also raised an orphan boy, Wister Davis, from the time he was twelve. Our Simon is the fourth name on that list.

His picture of the place is plain and specific. The family finished school and Sunday school in the High Hill church house, and Joel got through the seventh grade there. The 1901 house had chimneys at each end, made of 'mudcats, or stick and dirt above the fireplaces which were made of native rocks.' Doaksville, where they got their mail and did their trading, was eight miles south by a very sandy road. Corinne was three miles north 'over the mountain,' which was easier once a store opened there.

He also remembered what his people did when someone was sick. Before white doctors came, and sometimes after, the family used Choctaw healers, who boiled tobacco in a pot set in a hole, spread a sheet over it, and laid the patient across the steam with the aching place directly above the pot.

Joel was 45 and said plainly what he could not recall, such as the maiden names of his grandmothers. Where his account can be checked against other records, it mostly holds up. Where it cannot (his father's years as judge and senator, the Massachusetts college), it is still the only account.

EXTRA.name: The Thompson allotments
EXTRA.title: Choosing the land, 1903
EXTRA.hook: Joseph Thompson went to Atoka in 1903 and picked out the family's homesteads, including a 160-acre quarter for his four-year-old son Simon.
body: The family applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899 and the Secretary of the Interior approved it on 12 December 1902. The next step was land. In the fall of 1903 Joseph P. Thompson gave testimony at Atoka, where the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes took the selections, naming tracts for his wife and children.

For Betsy he selected a homestead of Lots 3 and 4 and the south half of the northwest quarter of Section 4, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, about 160 acres valued at $519.71. In November 1903 he added the northwest quarter of Section 9 in the same township, another 160 acres valued at $520.

Simon, then four years old, received his homestead on 2 October 1903: the northeast quarter of Section 11, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, 160 acres valued at $520. Further tracts were selected for him in November 1903, March 1904 and October 1907, and his citizenship certificate was issued at Hugo on 6 December 1907. A younger child enrolled as a 'new born' under the Act of 3 March 1905 was enrolled separately. Ella, who died in May 1899, was dismissed from the roll and received no land.

Allotments were held under federal restrictions, so the owners had to ask permission to sell or free their land. Joseph's petition was filed on 27 August 1908, when he was at Fort Towson. He filed again from Corinne on 10 September 1915, and the Secretary of the Interior approved removal of restrictions on 28 March 1916. Betsy's report was filed on 29 March 1920 from 'R.F.D. #1, Box 45, Corinne'; it was approved on 30 April and the order removing restrictions was mailed to her on 11 May 1920.

EXTRA.name: Ella N. Thompson
EXTRA.title: Three weeks in the spring of 1899
EXTRA.hook: The family applied for enrollment on 1 May 1899. Simon was born on 4 May and his five-year-old sister Ella died on 22 May.
body: Ella was the third child of Joseph and Betsy Thompson to be listed on the Choctaw rolls. In 1896 she was 'Ella' in Cedar County, and in 1899 'Thompson, Ella N.,' a daughter, age 5, three-quarter blood.

The family made its application on 1 May 1899. Three days later Betsy gave birth to Simon, with her mother Emeline as midwife. On 22 May, Ella died. Her enrollment records say so in plain words: 'Died May 22, 1899.' The proof of her death was not filed until 18 April 1901.

Because she had died before the enrollment was approved, her name was struck. Her name was dismissed from the rolls under an order of 31 March 1905. She received no allotment, but she stands in the family's enrollment with her parents and brothers.

Sworn statements about her death survive. On 13 April 1901 at Doaksville, Joseph P. Thompson, then 39, swore that he was the father of "Ella N. Thompson" and that she "died on 22 day of May 1899." A second affidavit, as an acquaintance, was sworn the same day by Robert Tims, 26, her mother's brother; both were sworn before the notary R. L. Carter of Doaksville. The Commission had written to Joseph on 9 March 1901 that it "has information of the death of your daughter" and sent a blank form, and on 18 April it acknowledged "your affidavit and that of Robert Tims, relative to the death of your daughter, Ella N. Thompson, which occurred May 22, 1899."

EXTRA.name: James Brown "Jimmie" Tims
EXTRA.title: Betsy's brother on Merchants Row
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's brother sat in the Choctaw Council, and in 1937 he described his grandfather's store at Doaksville, in front of the old rock jail.
body: James Brown Tims, called Jimmie, was a son of Vinson and Emeline Tims and Betsy's elder brother. Joel Thompson remembered that when his father Joseph served as county judge and then senator, 'James Brown Tims was a Representative in the Choctaw Council.' Joel said the Tims family was 'quite prominent in public affairs.'

Jimmie was interviewed in 1937, the same year as his nephew Joel, and is said to have described his parents, Vinson and Emeline, and the stand of V. B. Tims on Merchants Row in Doaksville, in front of the old rock jail, whose foundations can still be seen. (It is not clear whether he meant his grandfather Vincent or his father Vinson.) An article on Cedar County's Choctaw name, Chuala, 'cedar,' from Big Cedar Creek, also cites his interview.

The jail is still there in outline. Visitors to the Doaksville site today walk past capped stone wells, a few foundations and the outlines of three jail cells. His brother Mitchell Tims (1869-1950) is buried at High Hill Cemetery near the old home place. By 1910 a James Tims household, probably his, was among the Thompsons' nearest neighbors in Wilson Township.

After he died, the Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma printed his memoir in the minutes of its September 1941 session at Ware's Chapel, near Anadarko: "James Brown Tims was born eight miles north of Ft. Towson, in what was then known as Doaksville, Indian Territory, on June 25, 1864. He was seventy-seven years of age at the time of his departure." That puts his death between 25 June and the conference of 12-14 September 1941. The memoir was signed by the Rev. Johnson W. Bobb, superintendent of the Choctaw District.

"Brother Tims was better known among the Choctaws as J. B. Tims. Of him it can be said: He loved everybody and everybody loved him." He began as a class leader and later became a local deacon in the Methodist Church, "preached to and led his people in the Christian way for about forty-five years," and served the Antlers Circuit for eleven of them. "Very influential among his people, Brother Tims always stood for right living and for Christian Education. At one time he was a member of the Choctaw Council." That last line is the same office his nephew Joel Thompson gave him in 1937.

He was still at work in 1940: James B. Tims was a local deacon of the Choctaw District in 1934, 1935 and 1936, and in 1940 was listed as "Tims, J. B., L.D., Rt. 1, Ft. Towson." A later memorial roll puts his death under 1940, but it warns that it contains errors, and the memoir's age of 77 fits 1941.

In 1899 Jimmie's household was enrolled: "Tims, James B.," age 36, one-half Choctaw, of Towson County, post office Alikchi, whose parents were "Vinson W. Tims," dead, and "Emeline Tims." He had been "Jas. B. Tims" in 1896. His wife, "Mary J.," 31, full-blood, was the daughter of Dixon Willis and Elizabeth Willis, both dead. Their children were Evelyn, Dixon and Rufus (Rufus an infant of five months when they applied on 18 April 1899).

Twins followed. On 27 August 1901 the Commission wrote that it had the application for "Lewie Tims and Lula Tims, twin children of James B. and Mary J. Tims, born July 19, 1901," and sent two forms because each child needed a separate application. Lula died on 19 January 1902 at about six months. On 30 October 1902 the Commission acknowledged "your affidavit and that of Mary J. Tims relative to the death of your minor daughter, Lula Tims," and her enrollment was canceled in 1904. Lowie was enrolled.

In 1919 he was among the Indian pastors the Southern church helped to support. In the Board of Missions' appeal, "J. B. Tims, Bruno Circuit (part support)" appears with a grant of $40 a year, in a list that also includes Wewoka, Chickasaw, Jesse, LeFlore and McCurtain circuits. The memoir of 1941 says he later spent eleven years on the Antlers Circuit.

EXTRA.name: Doaksville to Corinne
EXTRA.title: Where the Thompsons got their mail
EXTRA.hook: Joseph and Betsy's addresses on the records move from Doaksville to Fort Towson to Corinne as the post offices changed around them.
body: In 1899 the family's post office was Doaksville, Indian Territory, in Cedar County. Joel Thompson said Doaksville was about eight miles south of the home place, and that the family did 'all of our trading' there. A faint pencil note added in April 1905 changes it to 'Ft. Towson, I.T.' The Doaksville post office had closed in 1903, when the name became Fort Towson.

Corinne, three miles north 'over the mountain,' was more convenient. Its post office opened on 24 August 1904 and ran until 1958; it was named for Corinne Estill Lesueur, the daughter of a Confederate officer who later became Missouri's secretary of state. By September 1915 Joseph was writing from Corinne. In September 1918 Simon, 19, gave his work on his draft card as farmer for his father at Corinne. In 1920 Betsy's address was 'R.F.D. #1, Box 45, Corinne.'

In 1910 the family was in Wilson Township of Choctaw County, which was formed at statehood in 1907 from parts of Cedar, Towson and other old counties. They had not moved far; the county and post office names changed around them.

EXTRA.name: Peter Pitchlynn Thompson
EXTRA.title: Peter, the brother just older than Simon
EXTRA.hook: Joel's interview lists his brother as 'Peter Pitchlyn,' the same name as a famous Choctaw principal chief.
body: Joel Thompson's list of his brothers includes 'Peter Pitchlyn,' and in 1899 the boy was enrolled as 'Peter P.,' age 2, three-quarter blood; in 1896 he had been 'Peter B.,' probably a clerk's slip. He was the brother just older than Simon.
The name matches Peter Pitchlynn, a principal chief of the Choctaw Nation during Joseph's boyhood. The interview does not say whether the boy was named for him.
Peter P. Thompson (1896-1979) lies in High Hill Cemetery, near the church where the family worshipped and went to school.

A Peter Thompson of Fort Towson appears in Methodist Indian Mission records for nearly thirty years. In 1938 he was among the church school superintendents for the Choctaw District, "Peter Thompson, Ft. Towson, Okla.," and, a line below, "Mitchell Tims, Ft. Towson, Okla.," Peter's uncle. In 1940 Peter Thompson was a lay delegate for the Rufe Circuit, in 1947 and 1948 "High Hill . . . Pete Thompson, Fort Towson," and he was still a lay delegate in 1952, 1955 and 1965.
No middle initial is given, so this is probably, not certainly, Joseph and Betsy's son. The Fort Towson address, the High Hill church and his burial at High Hill all point to him.

EXTRA.name: High Hill
EXTRA.rel: The Thompsons' church, school and cemetery
EXTRA.title: High Hill: church, school and cemetery
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's parents are remembered at the old place, the Thompsons went to church and school in the High Hill church house, and several of the family are listed in the cemetery.
body: Joel Thompson remembered High Hill as a Methodist church where 'they had school in the church house for many years.' His father sat on the school board and the children went to school and Sunday school there 'all of our lives.' The 1901 house stood within 300 yards, and in camp-meeting weeks the Thompsons had 'lots of company,' with whole deer, hogs and turkeys barbecued for the crowd.

Betsy was married at her parents' home about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville, in Towson County, the place later known as the Charley Blankenship place. Joel said his grandparents Vinson and Emeline Tims were 'buried there at the old place.' High Hill Cemetery, three miles east of the junction of the Spencerville Road and State Highway 147 and half a mile south, holds Peter P. Thompson (1896-1979), Mitchell Tims (1869-1950), and Emeline Steadman Tims (1842-1918). Vinson's marker there is a cenotaph.

The name is a puzzle. Another High Hill, two miles south of Alderson in Pittsburg County, appears in a different interview, and the two should not be confused. For this family, High Hill rests on Joel's memory and on the graves of Emeline, Vinson and Peter.

High Hill was a church of the Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma, on the Rufe Circuit. In 1941 the Choctaw District listed the churches "in Choctaw county: High Hill, Hampton Chapel, Honey Spring, Pecan Groves, Kullichito," and from 1942 to 1948 High Hill's church school was led first by Willie S. Tims and then by Pete Thompson, both of Fort Towson. The 1943 minutes call the burying ground the "High Hill Indian Cemetery, north of Fort Towson."

Its neighbor, Hampton's Chapel, which the minutes call "the Church in the Wild Woods," ten miles north of Fort Towson, hosted the whole conference on 13-15 September 1940, with the Rev. Edgar Tims as host pastor. The same book lists Betsy's brother Mitchell Tims of Fort Towson among the Choctaw District's church school superintendents, as the 1938 and 1939 lists do, and puts Betsy's brothers J. B. Tims and Robert J. Tims on the roll of local deacons.

EXTRA.name: The Choctaw names on the cards
EXTRA.title: The Choctaw names
EXTRA.hook: Ata-sa-ha-bi, Lotima, O-we-na, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, Brazil and Siney were the parents of our enrolled ancestors.
body: The enrollment of 1899 named parents who did not themselves enroll, because they were dead. Legion Austin's father was Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County; Molsey Austin's parents were Brazil and Siney, both dead, of Red River. Emeline Tims's mother, O-we-na, was Choctaw of Towson County, and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi is the Mississippi-born name on another line of the family.

The names tell something about the Choctaw naming practice. A linguist, Ovid Vickers, wrote that in old Mississippi names were 'nearly always connotative,' earned by deeds, and that 'a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination abi signifying killer.' Surnames such as Thompson, Austin and Gardner were adopted after 1830, often from the given name of a respected white man.

Pisachubbe, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi and Ata-sa-ha-bi all look like names of this kind, ending in the war-name element. Their exact meanings are not recorded, and the Choctaw Nation's language staff cautions against reading the ending 'killer.' O-we-na is a Choctaw given name, meaning unknown. Joel Thompson said his father's mother's family 'had some sort of a Choctaw name' and 'never adopted a white man's name,' the same pattern from another line.

Molsey Austin; parents Brazil and Siney (dead, Red River)

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: The Act nobody could find
EXTRA.hook: In the Regulators' own account of how their movement began, William Moffit is the man who went through the laws and found no such Act as the deputy sheriff claimed.
body: In May 1768 the Regulators' committee wrote out a plain account of their quarrel with the Orange County officers, to carry to the Governor with their petition. It was Regulators' Advertisement No. 11. Midway through comes a scene at a tax meeting on Deep River, William Moffitt's own neighborhood.

The High Sheriff, Mr. Harris, had published an advertisement citing an Act of the Assembly as the authority for the tax, and many paid but disputed the authority of the Act. At the meeting, the committee wrote, Deputy Sheriff John Wood, "being questioned about the Act confidently persisted in the affirmative. Upon which William Moffit on examining the Laws, no such Act could be found, Wood now finding his knavery was detected, no less confidently denied the Advertisement to be Harris's." The sentence is clumsy in print, but its sense is plain: William looked through the laws, the Act was not there, and the deputy then denied that the advertisement was the sheriff's at all.

The committee drew its own moral. "This unprecedented Effrontery, convinced the Spectators that there was Knavery, and Collusion," and, judging the whole business of a piece, they "formed themselves into Bodies under the denomination of Regulators." By the committee's account, it was this scene that led the neighborhood to organize.

William's name is at the foot of the document. It closes "Signed in behalf and by Order of the Regulators by us the Committee," over eight names: John Low, James Hunter, Rednap Howell, Harmon Cox, John Marshel, W. Cox, W. Moffitt and George Hendry. A second paper, dated at Thomas Cox's mill on Monday 30 May 1768, orders the narrative carried to the Governor and Council by James Hunter and Rednap Howell, and William Moffitt signs that one too.

He had known the Cox family on Deep River for years. Court records cited in a Cox family history show William Moffitt proving a deed from Thomas Cox to Jacob Grigg for 179 acres in May 1765, and witnessing the will of William Cox, dated "the 20th Day of the first month 1767," together with John Cox and John Allen. When the Orange County court sat at Hillsborough in February 1767, the clerk recorded that "this Will was Exhibited in Open Court & Duly proved by the Oaths of William Moffitt, & John Allen." Years later two of his daughters, Catharine and Hannah, are named in the family wills as Cox wives, and the 250 acres he left his son Robert were land he had bought of William Cox.
The name is spelled Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt for the same man. The 1765 deed and the 1767 will are known only at second hand, through a Cox family history.

EXTRA.name: William Moffitt
EXTRA.title: September 1768: a letter, an address and an indictment
EXTRA.hook: As Tryon's troops closed on Hillsborough, William Moffitt signed a letter to the Governor, headed the signers of the Regulators' plea for pardon, and was named in a riot indictment the court threw out.
body: In 1768, while the Governor's troops were on the march from Salisbury to Hillsborough, James Hunter delivered a letter to Tryon signed for the Regulators by four men: Peter Julian, James Evans, Abraham Teague and William Moffitt. It protests loyalty, saying the Regulators "will when occasion requires fight for and defend him to the last drop of blood" for King George, and that they bear "no ill-will to any but our cruel Oppressors from which number we exclude your Excellency." It then turns: "But will nothing propitiate but our blood, we are determined at all events to fall like men, and sell our lives at the very dearest rate." The last line is a plea: "We beseech you Sir not to drive us to despair."

When the Regulators were assembled at Hillsborough, they sent "The humble Address of the Inhabitants of several Counties called Regulators." They were "desirous to submit ourselves to the clemency of your Excellency, and to lay aside all method of redress of our grievances, but by a due course of Law," and they begged that the Governor "will forgive all our past offences by your gracious Proclamation." It is "Signed in behalf of the said Counties," and the first name in the list of twenty-two signers is William Moffitt's, ahead of Peter Julian, Lewis Lowry, Christopher Nation, Samuel Low, John Marshill and the rest.

The court minutes of the same month show the other side. At the Hillsborough Superior Court on Thursday the 29th, the clerk wrote: "The indictment preferred against James Hunter, Ninion Hamilton, Isaac Jackson, John Philip Hartso, William Moffitt, John Pile & Francis Dossett, for a Rout, having been returned by the Grand Jury 'a true bill as to all except John Pile,' it is ordered by the Court that the bill be Quashed, by reason of the irregularity of the return, and that the Attorney General prepare a new bill." Two more bills against other Regulators were quashed the same day.

So within a few weeks William was a signer of letters for the Regulators, the first name on their plea for pardon, a man indicted for riot whose bill failed on a technicality, and then, on 3 October, one of the thirteen named in the Governor's proclamation as excepted from pardon. No later bill against him is known.

quotes.t: We beseech you Sir not to drive us to despair.
