EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: A postmaster's letters, August to November 1864
EXTRA.hook: The Confederate Post Office Department's surviving papers include letters signed by V. B. Tims, postmaster at Doaksville, and the last is dated 1 November 1864.
body: Doaksville was the end of two Confederate mail routes, and in 1862 and 1863 its postmaster was J. P. Kingsbury. By 1864 the office was in the hands of V. B. Tims.

On 16 August 1864 he wrote to Dr. James H. Starr, the Post Office Department's agent at Marshall, Texas, that he had advertised for bids to carry the mail on Route 410 from Doaksville to Fort Washita, "the time having expired, I have now to inform you that there was but one bid given in and that was by Thomas M. Arnett." On 9 September, signing himself in full as "Vincent B. Tims, P. M.," he sent back the contract and oath executed by Arnett, with the news that Arnett's application for exemption from army service had been refused by the district headquarters at Fort Towson, so he could not start work. The contract then went to the second-best bidder, and an October letter from Tims reports the new contractor, James M. Nunn, at work on the route.

The last letter is the plainest. "Doaksville C. N., Nov 1st 1864," it begins: "I herewith enclose you my accounts current from January 1st to Sept. 30th 1864 inclusive which shows a balance of Twenty cents due to you. I herewith enclose you Ten Dollars new issue from which please deduct my account and send the balance in postage stamps." It is signed "V. B. Tims P. M." His accounts for the first nine months of 1864 left a balance of twenty cents. The volume of mail handled at Doaksville in 1862 and 1863 "was quite small."

These letters bear on the date of his death. The family accounts give 14 or 17 June 1864, and his great-grandson Joel Thompson remembered him as the first postmaster at Doaksville. But the postmaster who signed in September and November 1864, with the same name and initials he used on the Chickasaw treaty of 1837, was alive and in office months after that date. The June 1864 date cannot stand, and the 1871 postmaster-roll entry for a 'V. B. Tims,' which seemed to conflict with it, may simply be Vincent himself.

One more signature is on a petition of 1 July 1864 from the postmasters along the Washington-to-Doaksville mail route, who complained that since the army courier line had stopped "we are deprived of all means of hearing from our friends and relatives in the army." It was signed by R. D. Wright of Netra Bok, Arkansas, William K. McKean of Ultima Thule, Arkansas, P. P. Pitchlynn at Eagle Town and "V. B. Tims, P. M., Doaksville, C. N." General Maxey forwarded it from Fort Towson on 30 July, and on 8 August Dr. Starr replied that the contractors had been ordered to resume service or the route would be readvertised.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Elam Stevenson
EXTRA.title: In his own words, 1869
EXTRA.hook: At 81, too old and nervous to write, the Rev. Elam Stevenson dictated his memories of early Methodism in Giles County to his son Augustus, and a church historian printed them.
body: In 1869 the Methodist historian John B. McFerrin asked old Elam Stevenson for what he remembered of the first Methodists in Giles and Lincoln counties. The answer is dated "Elkton, Giles county, Tennessee, July 28, 1869." It came through Elam's son John, and was written down by another son, Augustus, "as I am too old and nervous to write now." McFerrin printed it in 1871.

Elam is frank about his health. "My memory is failing me, and I am much afflicted with asthma, and I am not able to be out of my bed more than half my time. I have come down to the edge of the last river, and expect soon to cross over and join those who have gone on before." Of the people who came to the country when he did, "not one is now left; they are all gone, and I am left with only my wife as survivors of a past generation." He lived six more years, and Lydia three.

He remembers the move in 1813. The preacher Philip Bruce, he says, "came to my house and asked me to bring a part of his books in my wagon, as he had no conveyance but a one-horse sulky. I agreed to do so, and accordingly brought the books." Bruce's brother had married a sister of Elam's wife, and Bruce "made our neighborhood his home, after coming to Tennessee." This is Elam's own word on the journey, and it speaks of a wagon, which sits badly with the family story of a pack-horse crossing because there were no wagon roads.

He writes about his church as someone who helped build it. "Our Church at Bee Spring (so named because it was famous as a place for coursing wild bees, in the early settlement of the country) was organized in 1814. The society now numbers about two hundred, and worships in a large frame-church, and is in a prosperous condition. The present is the fourth house of worship we have had." In 1814, he adds, "Brothers Coleman Harwell, Meshach Boyce, and myself, began to preach in Lincoln county, in what is now called the Shiloh neighborhood, in private houses," and in 1815 the first society there was formed at the house of Seaborn Bruce.

McFerrin follows the letter with a short sketch of the writer: "Elam was the third son, and the first of the family to join the Methodist Church. He professed religion in 1804, and joined the Church in 1806. He was much opposed by his parents, who were Presbyterians... He was licensed to preach in 1813, and the same year removed to Tennessee." His house "was a welcome home" to every preacher on the Richland Circuit. "All his children are members of the Church, and four of his sons are preachers of the gospel; one of them, the Rev. J. B. Stephenson, once of the Tennessee, but now of the North Alabama Conference, is an itinerant." The sketch also calls his father James "a Captain in the Revolutionary war," a title the family later repeated and the militia record does not support.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Elam Stevenson and his sons
EXTRA.title: News of the Stevenson preachers, 1875-1885
EXTRA.hook: A weekly Giles County newspaper printed Elam Stevenson's death notice in 1875 and kept naming his preaching sons for the next ten years, including one who talked of moving to Texas.
body: Giles County, Tennessee, had a weekly paper, the Pulaski Citizen, and its neighborhood columns noted who was preaching where, who was sick and who had come home. The Stevenson preachers turn up in it again and again between 1875 and 1885.

On 18 March 1875 the Citizen printed a death notice: "Died, at the residence of W. M. Stevenson, near Bethany, on the 13th inst., Rev. Elam Stevenson, in his 88th year." It called him "this venerable minister of God," who "died as he had lived, with perfect Christian resignation," and said he left "a large line of descendants—children, grand children, and great-grand children, who will ever revere his memory." The 13th of March matches the date on the family's own record of his death. The W. M. Stevenson whose house it was is most likely his son Willis M., who is on the family roll of Elam's eleven children.

Three years later a writer visiting Bee Spring church walked through its graveyard and wrote: "Here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort, and many others, the founders and upholders of Methodism at Bee Spring." No first name is given, but Bee Spring was the church Elam founded in 1815, and Elam and Lydia were its founders.

Elam's son Abner appears as a working circuit preacher. When the Mt. Pisgah circuit preachers published their monthly appointments on 21 November 1878, the list read "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m., Abner Stevenson." In February 1878 a neighborhood correspondent, after listing the sick of the community, added: "We are informed that Rev. Abner Stevenson has a cancer cure. If true, come over." In August 1879 the paper's account of a revival at Bee Spring, where 41 people professed faith in seven days, listed him among the ministers who "aided in other services." In May 1884 a column reported: "We had two sermons at Rocky Point last Sunday, one by Abner Stevenson and one by W. H. Dixon," and said the fourth Sunday in June was his.

Texas comes into the story in 1881. On 27 January the Friendship column reported: "Rev. Abner Stevenson has abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living." On 5 May the Bee Spring column added: "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." A George W., the same age as Gilbert, was in Abner's household in 1870, so this is probably that son; why he went or how long he stayed is not said. Abner stayed in Giles County, and it was his son Gilbert, known as Frank, who later took a preacher's family west. Frank's seven children were born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.

One more brother is in the paper. On 20 August 1885 the county correspondent wrote of visiting "our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson," who "speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October." James C. is the third of Elam's children, and a family letter of 1932 remembers "Uncle Jimmie" as having preached 63 years.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Robert James Tims
EXTRA.title: A circuit preacher near Idabel
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's brother preached for forty years in the Choctaw country, and a memoir written by his nephew in 1944 names his parents as Vincent and Emiline Tims.
body: Robert James Tims was a brother of Betsy (Tims) Thompson. The Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma printed his memoir in the minutes of its September 1944 session at Salt Creek Church, near Holdenville, signed by his nephew, the Rev. Edgar Tims. It begins: "Robert James Tims was born six miles north of Fort Towson, Oklahoma, being the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims."

He stayed in the Fort Towson community until he entered Spencer Academy and finished his schooling there, and "upon leaving school it was his good fortune to meet Fannie Weesley, and they were married." The marriage lasted 48 years, until she died a few months before him. They had no children, "but a mighty host of friends."

In 1904, the memoir says, he was converted and licensed to preach, and he was later ordained a deacon. He was pastor of the Rufe Circuit, whose churches in the 1940s included High Hill and Hampton Chapel, for two years, and then of the Idabel Circuit for six, until failing health made him retire to a home five miles west of Idabel. He was among the clerical members in 1934 and 1935, pastor of the Idabel Circuit in 1936, and in 1940 "Tims, Robert J., L.D., Idabel."

"He preached his last sermon at Thomas Chapel on Sunday just before his triumphant passing on Tuesday." He died on Tuesday, 12 September 1944, and was buried in the Idabel cemetery. The memoir closes: "The name of Robert Tims will always be affectionately mentioned in the churches where he ministered."

Robert was enrolled at Doaksville on 25 April 1899 for Cedar County: "Tims, Robert," age 25, three-quarter blood, with his wife "Fannie," 18. His parents were "Vincent Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," and hers "John Wesley," dead, and "Winnie Wesley," both of Cedar County; the memoir spells her family name Weesley. In April 1901, aged 26, he swore a statement as an acquaintance on his niece Ella's death, signing his name "Robert Tims."

quotes.c: Memoir by Edgar Tims, Minutes of the Indian Mission of Oklahoma, 1944, p. 31

EXTRA.name: Noble Shaw
EXTRA.title: Noble Shaw's land, advertised at Oak Ridge in 1857
EXTRA.hook: In the spring of 1857 Sicily Shaw and J. H. Leak put Noble Shaw's 268-acre farm up for sale in the Greensboro newspaper.
body: In March 1857 a notice headed "Land Sale" appeared in a Greensboro, North Carolina, newspaper. It read: "Having qualified as Administrators on the Estate of Noble Shaw, deceased, with a will annexed, at the dwelling of said deceased, we will expose to public vendure on the 16th April next, a tract of land, consisting of 268 acres, well timbered and well watered, convenient to the Oak Ridge Institute, and on the direct road from Danville, Va., to Salisbury. The land will be sold on a credit." It is signed "J. H. Leak, Sicily Shaw, Administrators," at "Oak Ridge, P. O., March 24th, 1857." The same notice ran again in the issue of 2 April 1857.

"With a will annexed" is the old legal phrase for administrators who carry out a written will when the executor it names cannot or does not act. So Noble left a will, and Sicily, then 66, was one of the two people the court trusted to settle his estate and sell his land.

The farm lay near the Oak Ridge Institute, the academy in northwestern Guilford County, on the road that runs from Danville, Virginia, down to Salisbury. That fits the Guilford County home of the Shaw and Nordyke families. Noble was born on 22 April 1787 and Sicily on 2 August 1790; she outlived the sale by four years.

EXTRA.name: Dennis Garrett
EXTRA.title: "The jurors doe present John Oldton": the death of Dennis Garrett
EXTRA.hook: The court's indictment for Dennis Garrett's death names his son-in-law John Cole and his widow Barbara among the witnesses.
body: Dennis Garrett of Baltimore County died on 2 September 1691, weeks after a sword blow to the forehead. The Provincial Court's record of the case reads: "The jurors . . . doe present John Oldton late of Baltemore County taylor for that he the said John Oldton the 31st of July 1691 at Baltemore County . . . with force and armes in and upon the body of one Dennis Garrett then and there . . . an assault did make and him the said Dennis with one sword of the value of twenty shillings being the proper sword of the said John Ouldton upon the forehead of the said Dennis one blow did give of which said blow the said Dennis immediately from the 30th day of July aforesaid till the 2nd day of September did languish on which 2nd day of September in the year and at the place aforesaid the said Dennis Garrett of the said blow did dye."

The witnesses were "Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, John Cole (son-in-law of the deceased), Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett (the widow)." John Cole is the husband of Dennis's daughter Johanna, and Barbara is the widow who later deeded land to her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole. Oldton "was condemned to be hanged; but 'afterwards the said John Oulton was graciously pardoned by their Majesties pardon in usuall forme.'" A later writer put it more briefly: Oldton "was found guilty of the murder of Dennis Garrett of Baltimore County, and was condemned to be hanged, but received a royal pardon in time to save his life."

The Governor and Council of Maryland, meeting at St. Mary's on 11 April 1692, had already ordered the same stay of execution for "One John Olton a Taylor convict and under Sentence of Death for Murder" that they gave another condemned prisoner that day. Oldton went on to be appointed captain of the county's rangers in 1694/5, and it was remarked that "the onus of a verdict of murder in the first degree" did not stop him from "guarding the frontiers of a province."

A note on the record describes Dennis himself: "Dennis Garrett, an early settler on the site of Baltimore, has many descendants through the Cole, Gorsuch and Ensor families. With Thomas Stone he purchased 'Long Island Point,' a tract surveyed for William Poultney on the site of Fell's Point. His widow, Barbara Garrett, married (2nd) Thomas Broad." Other records give her second husband's name as John Broad.

A 1916 account of the Gorsuch and Lovelace families tells the same story. Oldton, it says, "got into serious trouble as the result of an affray with Dennis Garrett, a prominent planter, which caused Garrett's death. . . . The occurrence took place July 31, 1691, and Garrett languished away, dying Sept. 2".

EXTRA.name: John Cole
EXTRA.title: Cole's Choice, Cole's Addition and Cole's Adventure
EXTRA.hook: Three Baltimore County tracts were surveyed for John Cole between 1694 and 1706, and in March 1737/8 he stood on the ground himself and gave his age as about 67.
body: The Cole tracts lay along the old Baltimore County rangers' roads. "Coles Choice" was "surveyed for John Cole July 28th, 1694, but never patented" and was later taken up again under the name "Orange"; the same survey appears again as "Cole's Chance," with a deed from John Cole to Robert Green dated 1702. "A tract of 67 acres called 'Cole's Addition' surveyed for John Cole May 29th, 1698," lay "on the north side of Patapsco River in the woods," beside the path called Darley Path, where Chase Street and the Bel Air Road now cross in Baltimore.

"Cole's Adventure" was "surveyed for John Cole in the year 1706" and sat "on a run called Gwins Run." When Thomas Demmett held a land commission on it in March 1737/8, a note records that "John Cole, Senior, aged about 67 years, testified before the same commission that the beginning tree of 'Cole's Adventure' stood about a hundred yards to the eastward of Gwinn's Run". An age of about 67 in 1738 puts his birth around 1670.

A second land commission, held in August 1750 on Cole's Addition, took the depositions of men who had known him. John Ensor, Sr., aged 55, said that "about eighteen years ago the aforesaid John Cole (referred to elsewhere in the same deposition as the deponent's father-in-law) came with him this deponent to the place where he now stands" and showed him where the boundary oak of Cole's Addition must stand. William Green, aged 58, told the same story, "the aforesaid John Cole said there should have been a bounded tree of Coles Addition." Ensor was born about 1695, and the Ensor family is counted among the descendants of Dennis Garrett, John Cole's father-in-law.
The tracts lay north of the Patapsco on ground that is now in and around Baltimore, a generation before the town was laid out in 1729.

EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: Thirteen cents a ration: the Doak & Tims contracts, 1838-1839
EXTRA.hook: A House report of 1843 prints the army's signed contracts with Doak & Tims to feed Chickasaw emigrants at Doaksville, at thirteen cents a ration.
body: The Doaksville trading firm of Josiah Doak and Vincent B. Tims shows up in a report to the House of Representatives of 25 February 1843 on "Frauds upon Indians." The report reproduced a run of army subsistence contracts from the removal years, and four of them are with "Doak & Tims." The report charges the firm with nothing; the contracts are printed as exhibits among those of other suppliers.

No. 41 is "an extract from a contract made January 1, 1838, between Captain R. D. C. Collins, United States army, and Doak & Tims." It reads: "That the said Doak & Tims shall furnish complete rations to a party of about two hundred Chickasaw emigrants, and all such of said tribe who may join said party, to be supplied at this place from time to time . . . for the term of twelve months from the date of this contract; the ration to consist of one pound of beef or pork, or three-quarters of a pound of salt pork or bacon, a pint and a half of corn meal, and one gallon of salt to the hundred rations." For each ration "the said Doak & Tims shall receive from the United States the sum of thirteen cents".

No. 42, of the same date, has them feed up to two hundred horses belonging to the emigrants, "one gallon of good sound merchantable corn" a ration, again at thirteen cents. No. 44 renews the arrangement on 1 January 1839: "the said Doak & Tims shall furnish and deliver, to the Chickasaw Indians, at the depot at Doaksville, Choctaw nation, west, all rations of subsistence that shall be required at said depot, be the same more or less, for one year from the date hereof," at "thirteen cents" a full ration.

Elsewhere in the report, the notes to a witness summary say the Fort Towson issues for the twelve months "appear to have been made by David Folsom and Doak & Tims"; the witness, the Chickasaw interpreter Stone Love, "thinks satisfactory" those twelve months' issues. A letter from the officer settling the Chickasaw accounts mentions "a small party subsisting for the year, by Doak & Tims, under a contract with Captain Collins". Another contract, between the removal contractors Glasgow & Harrison and the army, carves out "the party of emigrants now at 'Doaksville,' and being subsisted by Doak & Tims".

These are the contracts behind the thirteen cents a ration that a missionary later remembered for the Doaksville trading establishment of Doak and Tims. They put the firm at Doaksville, feeding Chickasaw families as they arrived from Mississippi, at the start of 1838, before the town had a post office.

EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with": a clerk's letters from Doaksville, 1841 and 1843
EXTRA.hook: A young Connecticut clerk at the Doaksville trading house wrote his mother that Mr. Tims was in New York buying goods; two years later Tims was still making the trip for him.
body: Two letters from Charles Fanning Stewart of Connecticut to his mother, printed in 1931, tell of Doaksville. Stewart, born in 1814, had gone west "after having been engaged to clerk in a trading establishment at Doaksville, a thriving village in the Red River region of the Choctaw Nation." His letter of 17 April 1841 is headed "Doaks Ville, Choctaw Nation West." It describes the place: "Doaks Ville is some sixty miles west of the Boundary line between the United States and the Indian country. It is six miles north of the Red River which forms the line between us and Texas. Fort Towson is only half a mile from us . . . Our trade which is verry extencive is confined to the Red Men of the forrest."

Tims comes in near the end. "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with is now in New York purchasing a stock of goods," Stewart tells his mother. He had sent fifty dollars with him to leave with her friends in New York, and asked him to collect fifty more that was owed him in New Orleans. Stewart had meant to come home that summer, "but Mr. Tims trip to New York prevented it".

Stewart married Tryphena Wall on 9 May 1842 and opened his own store at Mayhew, on the road between Fort Towson and Fort Washita, with goods bought from his old employer in New Orleans. On 19 April 1843 he wrote that the stock he had brought the previous spring was sold and that he had "sent by my friend Mr. Tims last week for another stock of goods he will be in New York sometime in May." So Tims made the buying trip east in the spring of 1841 and again in 1843, and Stewart, who had clerked in his house, still trusted him to carry his orders and money.

Stewart does not give the firm's name or Tims's first name. The Mr. Tims of the Doaksville trading house in those years is almost certainly Vincent B. Tims of Doak & Tims, whose partnership with Josiah Doak was dissolved in February 1844.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Elam Stevenson
EXTRA.title: "A Methodist preacher all his life": a neighbor remembers Elam Stevenson, 1884
EXTRA.hook: In September 1884 the Pulaski Citizen printed a boyhood neighbor's recollection of Elam Stevenson settling near Bee Spring church, and of his sons and the families they married into.
body: On 25 September 1884 a Giles County newspaper carried a column headed "Old Times in Giles," signed "By F. T. M'Laurine." The writer walks through the families who settled his neighborhood on Little Bradshaw Creek, naming each in turn, the teachers he went to school to at Bee Spring, and the preachers who held the community together. One paragraph is about the Stevensons.

"Elam Stevenson and family settled 1½ miles south of us near Bee Spring church in 1815 or 1816; he soon after obtained license to preach and was a Methodist preacher all his life; died a few years since a very old man. He had one daughter, Catharine, who married a Mr. Hamilton. His sons were William, James, Coleman, John and others; James and John and one other were Methodist preachers, all good, industrious citizens. William married a Miss Malinda Rowe, a daughter of Joseph Rowe who lived near by. She was a beautiful young lady. James married a daughter of Mr. Duncan Brown, sister of ex-Gov. N. S. and J. C. Brown. John is a noted Methodist preacher."

The Browns he names are Neill S. Brown, governor of Tennessee from 1847 to 1849, and John C. Brown, governor from 1871 to 1875, both Giles County men. So the Rev. James Stevenson of this paragraph married into the family of two governors. The unnamed "one other" preacher among the brothers fits Abner.

The memory is a neighbor's, written seventy years on, and it differs in detail from the family's own record. Elam's 1869 letter says Bee Spring church was organized in 1814, and a sketch of his grandson says the family came to Giles County about 1813, a little earlier than the 1815 or 1816 given here. That sketch's list of the children has a daughter Katherine, which matches Catharine, but no son Coleman; William P., James C., Abner A., Willis M., John B., Thomas C., Elam A. and Gilbert are the sons it names. What the column adds is how the family looked from the next farm: a settled preaching family, with a license to preach early and a long ministry, whose sons married local daughters and, in three cases, took up the pulpit too.

EXTRA.name: Willie Jane (Maxwell) Tims
EXTRA.rel: 3rd great-grandaunt by marriage (wife of Judge Edward Ward Tims)
EXTRA.title: Sworn at Tuskahoma: Willie Tims on her marriage, 1902
EXTRA.hook: In December 1902 Willie J. Tims told the Dawes Commission she had lived sixteen years in the Choctaw Nation and had married Edward Tims near Doaksville in 1888.
body: On 8 December 1902 the Dawes Commission took testimony at Tuskahoma from "Willie J. Tims," who gave her age as thirty-two and her post office as Grant, Indian Territory. She was a white woman, born Willie Jane Maxwell, and she was asking to be enrolled as a citizen by intermarriage through her husband, Judge Edward Ward Tims of Doaksville. The Commission asked her the plain questions the law required: how long she had lived in the Nation, whether her husband was enrolled, when and where they married, and who had been married before.

Her answers put the marriage in 1888, "Close to Doaksville," performed by a minister named Frazier, without a license. Edward had been married once before, to a woman whose "given name was Polly," and Polly was dead by then. Willie said the two had lived together continuously, "No" separation, abandonment or divorce, as residents of the Nation.

The Commission's written decision, dated 9 December 1903, gave the date of the wedding as 29 April 1888. A certified copy of the marriage certificate survives, written in the Choctaw Nation's own court style: "Tonson County C. N. April 29th A. D. 1888." It is signed by R. S. Frazier, who wrote that he had that day "Joined the holy Estate of Matrimony, Hon. E. W. Tims and Mifs Wille Maxful all of Tonson County C. N." The clerk copying it in December 1906 kept the old spelling.

She was enrolled as "Willie J.," age 29, an intermarried white citizen; her father, Maxwell, is marked dead and a non-citizen. Her children with Edward were Lucy, Minnie J., Edmond, Benjamin W., Mertle (a baby of two months when the family applied on 8 May 1899) and Abel E., born 14 December 1901 and enrolled on 14 February 1902. Edward also had a ward, Adam Nanomantubbe, a boy whose dead parents are written as Tobias and Susan Nanomantubbe. In July 1903 the Commission answered a neighbor from Oscar, O. W. Seay, who had written that "Mr. Tims has a grandson named Adam Nonomatubi who is an orphan," and told him the boy was already enrolled with the family; the Secretary of the Interior had approved the whole group on 12 December 1902.
Willie Jane Tims was born on 27 July 1870 and died on 8 October 1922, four months before her husband. She is the mother of Private Edmond Tims, killed in France in 1918.

EXTRA.name: Mitchell Tims
EXTRA.title: Mitchell and Mildred Tims, and the baby daughter lost in 1900
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's brother Mitchell and his full-blood wife Mildred lost their baby daughter Else before the rolls were made.
body: On 25 April 1899 Mitchell Tims, age 30, one-half Choctaw, of Towson County, post office Doaksville, was enrolled. The clerk wrote his parents as "Benson Tims," dead, of Towson County, and "Emiline Tims," still living in 1896. His father's first name was spelled Vinson, Vincent and, here, Benson, but the family is the same.
His wife Mildred, 19, full-blood, had been "Mildred Billy" in 1896. Her parents were "Nuck-a-masha" and "Me-ley," both dead, of Jacks Fork County.

Their first daughter, Else, was born on 9 November 1899, after the application, and was added to the enrollment on 11 July 1902, though she had already died. On 5 December 1902 the Commission wrote to Mitchell at Doaksville acknowledging "your affidavit and that of James Wilson relative to the death of your daughter, Else Tims," which "occurred November 25, 1900." James Wilson was the husband of Mitchell's sister Rosie. Her enrollment was canceled on 8 July 1904, because she had died before the roll was made.

A second daughter, Agnes E., was born on 21 December 1901 and enrolled on 3 January 1902. A son, Vincenta W. Tims, was born on 28 July 1904. On 25 April 1905 the Commission wrote to Mitchell at Fort Towson that it had received "the affidavits of Mildred and Emeline Tims to the birth of Vincenta W. Tims," so his own mother, Emeline, again vouched for a grandchild's birth, as she did for Betsy's children. Two months later Mitchell wrote to ask whether the birth certificate had arrived, and the Commission confirmed it. The boy was entered on the roll of newborn children.

Mitchell Tims is buried at High Hill Cemetery. In 1938 the Methodist Indian Mission lists Mitchell Tims of Fort Towson, with his nephew Peter Thompson, among the Choctaw District's church school superintendents.
The James Wilson who swore with Mitchell in 1902 is probably his brother-in-law: Mitchell's sister Rosanna married a James Wilson of Cedar County, who was enrolled at Doaksville on 1 May 1899.

EXTRA.name: Willie Tims and Mary (Lewis) Tims
EXTRA.title: A letter to the Principal Chief about a baby who had died
EXTRA.hook: Willie Tims, Betsy's brother, was enrolled with his wife Mary and a baby son in 1901; in 1905 he had to correct the rolls for a second baby who had died.
body: On 1 May 1899 "Tims, Willie," age 23, three-quarter Choctaw, of Towson County, post office Doaksville, was enrolled, his parents "Vincent Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," living in 1896, the same pair named for Betsy Thompson. His wife Mary, 21, full-blood, had been "Mawey Lewis" in 1896; her parents were "King Lewis" and "Nancy Lewis." Their first son, Roberson, was born on 18 February 1901 and enrolled on 17 May 1901.

The jacket then follows the family for years. A second son, Wilson Tims, was born on 11 May 1904 and was entered when the Secretary of the Interior approved the roll of newborn children on 22 July 1905. But the child had died before the cutoff date of 4 March 1905, though the sworn statement had said he was living. In September 1905 Green McCurtain, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation, wrote to the Commission from Kinta that "Willis Tims," of Fort Towson, had told him the child "was at that time deceased" and wanted the name struck from the rolls. The Commission wrote on to the land office to stop any allotment for the dead child.

A daughter, Etline Tims, was born on 6 July 1905. On 19 May 1906 the Commission acknowledged "the affidavits of Mary Tims and Nancy Lewis," her mother and grandmother, to her birth. She was enrolled among the minor children, a girl of seven-eighths Choctaw blood.
A Willie Tims of Fort Towson later appears in Methodist Indian Mission minutes as a church officer at High Hill, but it is not said whether he is this Willie.

quotes.t: when in truth and in fact said child Wilson Tims, was at that time deceased, and that he made this mistake in the affidavit ignorantly
quotes.c: Green McCurtain, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation, to the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes, Kinta, 25 September 1905 (Choctaw New Born 1424)

EXTRA.title: The man on the card before Joseph's: Henry W. Thompson
EXTRA.hook: Henry W. Thompson was enrolled the same day as Joseph P. Thompson, and his parents were Simon and Lucy Thompson, not John and Betsy.
body: Henry W. Thompson and Joseph P. Thompson both applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899. They lived in Cedar County with the same post office, Doaksville. In 1910 a Henry W. Thompson was among the Thompsons' nearest neighbors in Wilson Township.

Henry was written down as "Thompson, Henry W.," age 25, full-blood, with his parents "Simon Thompson" and "Lucy Thompson," both dead, of Cedar County. Joseph's parents, by contrast, were John and Betsy Thompson. On the enrollment Henry is not Joseph's brother.

A note says he was "now the husband of Illie Thompson," with evidence of marriage filed on 16 July 1902. In 1903 the Commission returned to him at Doaksville the "certificate of marriage of Henry Thompson and Mrs. Eli Pesahombi, dated July 11, 1900." Illie, 18, was enrolled with a one-year-old son, Hampton Thompson, born on 12 November 1901, along with a Pisahambe youth and the Aaron family. When the baby's application reached the Commission through a notary at Doaksville in February 1902, it was sent back with a request for the mother's maiden name, since no one of her name had been listed.

quotes.t: In compliance with your request the certificate of Marriage of Henry Thompson and Mrs. Eli Pesahombi, dated July 11, 1900, is herewith returned to you.
quotes.c: Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes to Henry W. Thompson, Doaksville, 3 July 1903 (Choctaw 7-1282)

EXTRA.name: Joseph W. Thompson
EXTRA.title: Joseph W.: a sworn birth in 1905, and Emeline the midwife again
EXTRA.hook: Joseph and Betsy's son Joseph W. was born on 5 March 1903 and enrolled under the 1905 act; his grandmother Emeline Tims swore to his birth, as she had for Simon.
body: Joel Thompson's list of his brothers includes Joseph W. How he got on the roll can be followed. The Act of Congress of 3 March 1905 allowed children born after September 1902 and living on 4 March 1905 to be enrolled, so the family had to swear to his birth and to the fact that he was alive on that date.

In a sworn statement of 29 April 1905 at the Central District, "Betsy Thompson," of Fort Towson, said she was the lawful wife of Joseph P. Thompson, "who is a citizen, by Blood, of the Choctaw Nation," and that a male child "born to me on 5th day of March 1903" had been named "Joseph W. Thompson" and "was living March 4, 1905." On the same page, as "midwife," Emeline Tims swore that she had attended Betsy on the same day and that the child was living on the cutoff date. The notary for both was Thomas Fennell. It is the same arrangement as in 1899, when Emeline attended Simon's birth and swore to it.
He was entered separately among the newborn children enrolled under that act.

EXTRA.name: Armstrong Academy and Choctaw schools
EXTRA.title: A family name on the Armstrong school list
EXTRA.hook: A school list preserves William Harrison Pisachubbe's name and points to a Choctaw education system built and funded by the Nation.
body: On 22 August 1899, a list of Armstrong Academy students was sent to the enrolling Commission. It included Harrison Pisachubbe. Twelve years later, a federal official identified him as William H. Pisachubbe, son of Eunice and brother of Robert, the family's direct ancestor. The school list had given him a second enrollment under his middle name, and in 1911 the correction was made. Nothing says what he studied or how long he attended.

Armstrong Academy had opened in 1845 as part of the Choctaw Nation's school system. The Choctaw Council funded schools, often contracting with religious mission boards to operate them. The Civil War interrupted instruction, and the academy building later served as a Choctaw government meeting place before the Nation's capital moved to Tuskahoma.

In 1883 the Choctaw General Council passed an act establishing a school for orphan boys at Armstrong and appropriated money for its reopening. A separate act set a planned enrollment of fifty boys there and fifty girls at the Choctaw orphan school. The acts show the Nation making educational policy; a place on a later student list does not by itself explain a child's family circumstances or whether a parent was living.

The Oklahoma Historical Society dates the reopened orphan boys' academy to 1884. In 1898 the federal Curtis Act placed Choctaw Nation schools under United States government control. William's 1899 listing therefore belongs to a period when control over an institution begun by the Choctaw Nation was being transferred to the federal government. His own experience at the school is not known.

EXTRA.name: William Harrison Pisachubbe
EXTRA.title: One man, two names: William Harrison Pisachubbe enrolled twice
EXTRA.hook: A boys' school list in 1899 put "Harrison Pisachubbe" on the Choctaw rolls, and he was already there as William H. In 1911 the Interior Department sorted it out.
body: When Eunice Pisachubbe's family was enrolled on 10 May 1899 for Kiamitia County, post office Goodland, her son "William H.," 16, full-blood, was among them, noted as "William Harrison" in 1896. His father, Joseph Pisachubbe, is written as dead.

Three months later, on 22 August 1899, a list of students at Armstrong Academy, a Choctaw school, was sent to the Commission, and it included "Harrison Pisachubbe." That name was also put on the final roll, approved on 4 February 1903. In the meantime William H. had received a complete allotment under his first number, and in 1905 the Commission, not knowing about the doubling, made a second, arbitrary allotment in the name of Harrison. The certificates were mailed to Academy, Oklahoma, and came back marked "unclaimed."

On 2 August 1909 William H. testified at Hugo that he had told the postmaster to send the certificates back, as he already had his allotment as William H. Pisachubbe. Eunice, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter also gave testimony. On 1 August 1911 the Commissioner at Muskogee wrote to the Secretary of the Interior that Harrison Pisachubbe was "a duplicate enrollment of William H. Pisachubbe." The Secretary's office approved a notation on the roll on 16 August 1911: "Duplicate enrollment of No. 4466; not entitled to land or money under this number."

William H. had a son, Colbert, born on 26 June 1906 at Hugo, whose mother Mamie signed her application with a mark and whose birth was attended by a midwife, Cassie Davis. His enrollment was refused: the Commissioner decided on 27 November 1906 that, because Colbert "was not living March 4, 1906," the cutoff in the Act of 26 April 1906, he had no authority to consider it, and the Secretary affirmed on 26 February 1907. Mamie is called a non-citizen in the decision.
William Harrison Pisachubbe died in May 1937, and the family's account of the removal from Mississippi in 1832 was given at his death.

EXTRA.name: Edward Pisachubbe
EXTRA.rel: Ward of Eunice Pisachubbe, listed with Robert and William H. on Card 1580
EXTRA.title: Edward Pisachubbi's land letter, 1903
EXTRA.hook: Edward, Eunice's ward, wrote to the Commission in January 1903 about land he had picked for himself and his wife Frances.
body: Among Eunice Pisachubbe's household was one who was not her son. "Edward," 17, full-blood, was her ward, and his dead parents were "Simpson Pisachubbe" and "Sallie Pisachubbe," of Jackson County. He was the husband of Frances Byington.

On 31 January 1903 the Commission wrote to him at Hugo, answering his letter of 16 January, "in which you state that you have selected certain lands for the allotments of yourself and your wife, Frances Pisachubbi." He had added that part of the land he described was claimed by another citizen. The Commission told him it had "no means of recording the selections of citizens" and could not settle disputes about possession; the matter would be heard when land offices opened in the Nation, which it expected between the first of March and the first of April. A follow-up letter said admission to the land office would be by tickets handed out on or after 16 April 1903.
His letters show how the land was chosen in the Choctaw Nation in 1903: families walked the ground first and wrote to the Commission, and then had to apply in person at the land office.

EXTRA.name: Vincent B. Tims
EXTRA.title: Doak & Tims in the Texas Supreme Court, 1849
EXTRA.hook: A Doaksville store's unpaid account from 1840 to 1844 ended up before the Supreme Court of Texas, in a case titled Love v. Doak & Tims.
body: Doak & Tims, the Doaksville trading firm of Josiah Doak and Vincent B. Tims, appears in the law reports of Texas. (The report gives Doak the middle initial L.; the 1837 treaty he witnessed has Josiah S. Doak.) The case, Love v. Doak & Tims, was decided at the December 1849 term.

The court summarized the suit this way: it "was brought in the names of the appellees as copartners, trading as merchants, for the use and benefit of Josiah L. Doak, one of the said copartners." It was an action on a store account against a man named Love who lived across the Red River in the Choctaw Nation. The first item in the account was dated 1840 and the last 30 July 1844; the suit was begun in Grayson County, Texas, on 24 January 1848. A witness testified that he had sold Love goods up to 28 August 1840, "that at the time said account was made the defendant was a resident of Mississippi," and that Love "did remove in 1841" to the Choctaw Nation. A second witness said that in 1844 he had presented the account for payment and asked Love for an order on a Colonel Upshaw, or his note, and Love said he would settle it himself.

The trial jury found for Doak & Tims. On appeal, Chief Justice Hemphill reversed and dismissed the case on the law of limitations: the debt was more than two years old, and nothing in writing acknowledged it. This is the same partnership that held the army ration contracts of 1838 and 1839 and kept the store described in letters of 1841; the suit of 1848 came four years after the partners dissolved their business by mutual agreement in 1844, and it is brought for the use and benefit of Doak alone.
The account shows the store selling goods on credit over four years, with the bill pursued years later in a Texas court.

EXTRA.name: Judge Edward Ward Tims
EXTRA.title: Edward Tims on the ballot for Principal Chief, August 1886
EXTRA.hook: In August 1886 a wire from Little Rock named Edward Tims among four candidates for Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation.
body: In 1940 Judge Tims was remembered as "once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation." A newspaper dispatch of the time shows how far it went. Headed "Choctaws Hold an Election" and dated Little Rock, Ark., 5 August 1886, it read: "The election for principal chief of the Choctaw Nation was held yesterday." It names four men: Ben Smallwood, Thompson McKinney, J. P. Folsom (printed Fulsom) and Edward Tims. It adds that a large vote was cast and that unofficial returns pointed to the election of McKinney.

Edward Tims was then in his mid-forties, a county judge of Towson County and, since the early 1880s, a trustee of Apukshunnubbee District. The Doaksville post office came to him the next year. The dispatch gives no vote totals; Thompson McKinney went on to serve as Principal Chief, so Edward Tims was a losing candidate in a four-man race for the highest office in the Nation.
He is the same Edward Tims whose 1888 marriage near Doaksville is documented, and who named his father as Vincent B. Tims.

EXTRA.title: Nancy Pisachubbi, daughter of Te-hol-ba-ta-bi
EXTRA.hook: Nancy Pisachubbi's parents were written down in 1899, but nothing connects her to Joseph Pisachubbe.
body: In May 1899 "Pisachubbi, Nancy," age 69, a full-blood woman of Eagle County, post office Luk-fa-tah, Indian Territory, was enrolled, alone, and her enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902.

Her parents were two names: her father was "Te-hol-ba-ta-bi," dead, of Eagle County, and her mother was "Malindy," dead, with Mississippi written as her county. Her stated age suggests a birth around 1830, but her birthplace is not given.

One family tree gives Joseph a mother named Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, born about 1825 in Mississippi. The Nancy Pisachubbi whose father was Te-hol-ba-ta-bi has no husband or children listed, and nothing establishes that she was Joseph’s mother or that the two Nancy entries are the same person. A Case Pisachubbi enrolled beside her had a father called Pisachubbi and a mother called Noise; their relationship to Nancy is not established.

EXTRA.name: Rosanna "Rosie" (Tims) Wilson
EXTRA.title: "Rosey Ann Tims": a notary's letter and a grandmother who delivered the babies
EXTRA.hook: Betsy's sister Rosie married James Wilson. In October 1900 a Doaksville notary wrote to the Dawes Commission to say who she was, and her mother Emeline attended her children's births.
body: Rosie does not appear under the Tims name on the roll. She was enrolled on 24 April 1899 with her mother as "Rosanna Tims," and when she married James Wilson she was moved to his enrollment. On 1 May 1899 at Doaksville (the same day as Henry W. Thompson and Joseph P. Thompson), "Wilson, James," age 24, full-blood, of Cedar County, with parents "Simon Wilson" and "Melissie Wilson," both dead, was enrolled; his wife "Rosanna," 18, three-quarter blood, with her parents written "Benson Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," of Towson County; and a baby son. A note says Rosanna was "transferred to this card with her husband, Oct. 26, 1900."

How she was found is on record. In September 1900 the notary R. L. Carter of Doaksville sent in an application for the baby, Islam Wilson, born on 10 August 1900. The Commission sent it back because it could not identify the mother, who gave her age as eighteen and had clearly been married since she was listed. On 19 October 1900 Carter replied: "Rosey Wilson the wife of James Wilson was registered as Rosey Ann Tims and has been married since she was registered. Her mother name is Emaline Times her father died before he was registered." The Commission wrote back on 27 October that it had identified her as "Rosanna Tims the daughter of Emiline Tims, who was listed for enrollment April 24th, 1899." It still wanted the marriage certificate, and on 19 August 1902 acknowledged one between "James Wilson and Rosa Tims."

Two more children are on the jacket. A son was born on 23 March 1903, and Rosanna swore to the birth on 25 March 1905 with her mark, her husband James Wilson and John Aaron as witnesses. The midwife's statement, sworn on 19 April 1905, is signed "Emeline Tims," Rosanna's mother, who swore the same kind of affidavit for her grandson Joseph W. Thompson ten days later. A daughter, Candace, was born on 16 June 1905; in May 1906 the Commission acknowledged "the affidavits of Rosanna Wilson and Emeline Tims to the birth of Candace Wilson."
Rosie's husband is probably the James Wilson who swore with her brother Mitchell Tims in 1902 to the death of Mitchell's baby daughter.

quotes.t: Rosey Wilson the wife of James Wilson was registered as Rosey Ann Tims and has been married since she was registered. Her mother name is Emaline Times her father died before he was registered.

EXTRA.name: James Austin
EXTRA.place: Fowlerville, Towson County, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.src: Dawes Card 1363 (front and back) and jacket 7-1363, NARA Dawes Enrollment Jackets (Choctaw by Blood)
EXTRA.title: The boy who died before the roll was taken
EXTRA.hook: Born 15 November 1898, dead by April 1899, and still on a federal roll until 1904 when the Department struck him off.
body: James Austin was the second child in his parents' household. His father Legion swore at Fowlerville in early May 1899 that the boy was born on 15 November 1898 and was "now living." He was enrolled at age 1, with a note: "died April 1899."

The boy's birth proof is as plain as such papers get. The form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" is crossed out and "Father" written over it, and Legion signed by mark as a 33-year-old citizen by blood. The second statement, normally for a doctor or nurse, was sworn by a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who "knew" of the birth and also made his mark.

Proof of the death reached the Commission on 2 December 1902. The Secretary of the Interior approved the other four on 12 December 1902, with James marked "Died prior to September 25, 1902." The Department did not cancel his enrollment until 16 September 1904.

EXTRA.name: Adline (Austin) Pisachubbe
EXTRA.place: Fowlerville, then Speer, Choctaw County
kv: Choctaw by Blood No. 3740, Card 1363, enrolled 4 June 1901
EXTRA.src: Dawes Card 1363 and jacket 7-1363 (letters of 9 Oct. 1900 and 5 June 1901; birth affidavit of 19 Apr. 1901); 1940 U.S. census.
EXTRA.title: A baby on a card that was nearly closed
EXTRA.hook: Born 5 August 1900, a year after her family applied, and added by a letter and an affidavit signed with two marks.
body: Adline was born on 5 August 1900, a year after her parents' application and two years before the roll was approved. Her father wrote to the Commission from Garvin that October; on 9 October the Commission replied with a blank infant application and the instruction that if the mother or the midwife could not write, two disinterested witnesses must attest each mark.

Her mother, "Mulcy Austin," swore on 19 April 1901 that she was 25, a citizen by blood and "the lawful wife of Leageon Austin," and that a girl was born 5 August 1900 and named Adline Austin. The midwife, Sinie Hall, swore the same. Both signed with a mark before the notary William Swink at Fowlerville, with two witnesses, one of them Sallie Johnson.

The Commission acknowledged it on 5 June 1901, "the same being in proper form," and listed the child as Choctaw by Blood. The roll was approved on 12 December 1902. Adline later married William Harrison Pisachubbe, whose younger brother Robert had married her sister Lizzie, and died at Speer in 1929.

EXTRA.name: Towson, Red River, Blue and Kiamitia
EXTRA.place: Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory
kv: Legion and Molsey Austin, Emeline Tims; 1896 census Nos. 199-201, 12116
EXTRA.src: Dawes Cards 778, 1363, 1580; Constitution and Laws of the Choctaw Nation (1894), archive.org constitutionand00watkgoog.
EXTRA.title: Four Choctaw counties
EXTRA.hook: The grandparents' counties were Choctaw counties, not Oklahoma ones.
body: In 1899 the clerks recorded where each person had been counted in 1896, and where their dead parents had lived. For this line the answers are four Choctaw Nation counties: Towson for Legion and Molsey Austin and for Emeline Tims; Kiamitia for Eunice Pisachubbe, her sons and the ward Edward; Blue for her parents Jackson and Viney Gardner; and Red River for Molsey's parents Brazil and Siney.

Under the Choctaw constitution and its acts, Towson belonged to the Apukshunnubbee District, while Blue and Kiamichi were counties of the Pushmataha District, each sending one senator. In 1886 the Council cut Jackson County out of Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka, which is why Edward Pisachubbe's dead parents, Simpson and Sallie, are written as of Jackson County in 1899 while he was counted in Kiamitia.

Each person had both a county and a post office. The Austins were Towson County people with a Fowlerville post office, renamed Valliant in 1902, and Eunice was a Kiamitia County woman at Goodland. The old counties vanished at statehood in 1907, and the families that had been counted in four of them came together in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Simon and Frances settled at Jeter.

EXTRA.name: Calvin Vestal Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Born in Randolph County, N.C.; raised in Lawrence County, Ark.; died at Duncan, Stephens County, Okla.
kv: Index entries: Pvt., Co. G, 25th Arkansas Infantry (Confederate) and Pvt., Co. L, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union); identification probable
Widowed head of household, Reyno, Randolph Co., Ark.
EXTRA.title: Calvin Moffitt, from North Carolina to Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: Nathan and Rebecca’s son moved through Arkansas to Oklahoma; a Union soldier of the same name may have been him.
body: Calvin, born 4 December 1841 in Randolph County, North Carolina, was the second of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt's sons, after Miles H., 9, and was eight years old when the family was counted at Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850. He was still in the same township in 1860, a year after his parents' twin daughters were born, and when Henry was a child of four.

A "Calvin V. Moffitt" (also written Moffett) served as a private in Company L of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment, aged 22 in 1864. A Calvin V. Moffitt of Lawrence County is also said to have served in two Confederate units and then tried three times for a Union pension, and a Calvin V. Moffitt served in Company G of the Confederate 25th Arkansas Infantry; with the Lawrence County household that makes the identification probable. By 1870 he was married and living at Lebanon Township, Sharp County, Arkansas. His wife was Matilda Dailey (born 23 January 1849 in Polk County, Missouri).

He had six children. Andrew Webster was born in Sharp County on 17 January 1869 and died 24 December 1899. Sarah A. (born 1874 in Missouri) died 11 September 1883, and John W. (born 1877 in Missouri) died 7 February 1885, both as children. Milburn Green (1880-1956) lived and died in Arkansas. Wilson Cornelius, born at Golden City, Missouri, on 14 January 1889, farmed in Stephens County, Oklahoma, later lived in Johnson County, Arkansas, and died at Norco, California, in 1971.

The last child, Girdy Emalah, is shown as born and dying on 19 July 1891. Matilda died the next day, 20 July 1891, at New Pocahontas, Arkansas. In 1900 Calvin, a widower, was head of a household at Reyno, Randolph County. By 1910 he was at King Township, Stephens County, Oklahoma, near his son Wilson, and he died in nearby Duncan on 13 February 1913. A Civil War pension was claimed from Oklahoma.
