Moffett (Moffitt), Co. L, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), NARA M399, NAID 45422928: https://catalog.archives.gov/id/45422928
EXTRA.note: The NPS soldier record names a Calvin V. Moffitt; whether that soldier was Nathan's son is unconfirmed. The family-tree profiles and the Strawberry Township household establish a separate family lead. The dates of Matilda's and the infant's deaths come from a tree import and no certificate has been seen. An 1880 census entry at Janes Creek, Randolph County, attached to him in that profile does not fit his children being born in Missouri through 1889, so it is not used here. Update, 3 Nov 2026: the Union enlistment of 20 April 1864 (NARA M399, NAID 45422928) gives Calvin V. Moffitt's birthplace as Randolph County, North Carolina, his trade as wagon maker and his credit as Strawberry, Lawrence County; see "Two uniforms, two pension claims."

EXTRA.name: Patrick Green Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Born at Sylamore, Ark.; married in Oregon County, Mo.; lived and died at Mountain View, Stone County, Ark.
kv: Aug 1873, Oregon Co., Mo., to Alice Ann Cole (1857-1901)
20 Dec 1905, Mountain View (one source: Nov 1904, buried Sallisaw)
EXTRA.title: Patrick: the brother who stayed in Stone County
EXTRA.hook: Patrick married in Missouri the year his father died, then lived on in Mountain View, where Henry settled, and buried his wife four months before Henry died.
body: Patrick Green Moffitt was born on 11 May 1853, at Sylamore in the Ozark hills along the White River, though the family was in Lawrence County in 1850 and 1860. He was two years older than Henry. After the family went north into Dent and Oregon counties, Missouri, he married Alice Ann Cole there in August 1873, four months before Nathan's death on 23 December.

Alice Ann was born on 18 December 1857 in Missouri. Nathan's second wife was a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole, whom he married in 1871. It is likely, though unproved, that Alice was a Cole child of that household, which would make Patrick's bride his stepsister.

The couple returned to Arkansas and settled at Mountain View, where Henry's family was by 1889. Their daughter Lillian was born in 1894 and died in 1988. Alice Ann died on 26 May 1901 and is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery; Henry died that September.
Patrick's death is given two ways: 20 December 1905 at Mountain View, or November 1904 with burial at Sallisaw, Oklahoma. The 1905 date is the more widely repeated.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-106 (Patrick Green Moffitt), Cole-3005 (Alice Cole), Moffitt-105 (Lillian); Missouri marriages 1750-1920 index entry for Nathan Mofit, 1871; Find a Grave (Levisy Flat Cemetery)
EXTRA.note: Alice as Nancy Cole's daughter is a guess from the surname; no record names her parents.

EXTRA.name: Robert Moffitt (Nathan's youngest brother)
EXTRA.place: Born in Randolph County, N.C.; farmed in Henderson County, Tenn., and Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Ark.; died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Mo.
kv: 9 Nov 1872, Hutton Valley, Howell Co., Mo.
EXTRA.title: Uncle Robert in Strawberry Township
EXTRA.hook: Nathan's youngest brother followed him to Strawberry Township, Arkansas, by 1860, buried most of his early children, and ended up in the Missouri Ozarks.
body: Robert was the youngest of Robert and Martha (Chamness) Moffitt's nine children, born 19 June 1815, a year after Nathan. He married Cynthia Gardner, born in North Carolina on 29 April 1815, and in 1850 they were in District 17 of Henderson County, Tennessee, with seven children: John 17, Mary Ann 12, Malcy 10, Alzia 8, Henry P. 6, James H. 3 and Martha E., a baby.

By 1860 Robert, 45, and Cynthia, 45, were in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, where his brother Nathan was a wheelwright. The household had shrunk to Alzira 18, Parker 15, James 13, Martha 10, Jane 8 and Franklin 5. John, Mary Ann and Malcy are not found again, and Parker is last seen in 1860.

The family moved on into Missouri. Robert died on 9 November 1872 at Hutton Valley, Howell County, and was buried in what is now called Moffitt Cemetery near Willow Springs. Cynthia lived until 9 October 1895.

Four of the children have traceable lives. Alzira Adelaide (1842-1923) married James Thomas Loving in 1867, bore seven children and is buried at Willow Springs. James Henderson Moffitt (1848-1916) became a physician at Redford, Reynolds County; in January 1916 it was reported, "We were greatly pained to hear of the death of Dr. Moffitt which occurred at Redford the evening of the 7th." Martha Elizabeth (1850-1931) died at Springfield and Margaret Jane (1852-1923) at Montier, Missouri.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1932 (Robert Moffitt), Moffitt-1957, -1965, -1964, -1963, Gardner-25214; 1850 U.S. Census, Dist. 17, Henderson Co., Tenn.; 1860 U.S. Census, Strawberry Twp., Lawrence Co., Ark., p. 224; Ellington Press (Ellington, Mo.), 20 Jan 1916, p. 4; Missouri death certificate for J. H. Moffitt, 1916

quotes.t: We were greatly pained to hear of the death of Dr. Moffitt which occurred at Redford the evening of the 7th.
quotes.c: The Ellington Press, Ellington, Mo., 20 Jan 1916, p. 4 (as transcribed on WikiTree)

EXTRA.note: The census citations are given in the WikiTree profile; the census pages themselves were not viewed. Cynthia Gardner is from North Carolina and no link to the Choctaw Gardner family on the maternal side has been found.

EXTRA.name: Veno (Zeno) Moffitt
EXTRA.rel: Cousin of the 2nd great-grandfather (nephew of Nathan)
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C.; died as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira, N.Y.
kv: Aaron C. Moffitt and Mary "Polly" Brady
Co. F, 24th N.C. Infantry (CSA), enlisted 8 Apr 1863
Enlisted July 1862, Randolph Co., per muster rolls (8 Apr 1863 per Roll of Honor); Elmira grave No. 658
EXTRA.title: Nathan's nephew, who died in the Elmira prison camp
EXTRA.hook: From Randolph County, North Carolina, Veno was captured in Virginia and died at Elmira; a soldier with his cousin Calvin’s name served the Union in Arkansas.
body: Nathan's older brother Aaron C. Moffitt (6 December 1805 to 20 June 1877) stayed in Randolph County, North Carolina. He married Mary "Polly" Brady on 7 August 1827 and was with her in 1850 and 1870. Their son Veno, called Zeno in 1860, was born about 1828.

Veno married Charlotte L. "Lottie" Gardner (1824-1904), and they had Mary Jane (1860-1920) and the Rev. James Alfred Moffitt (1864-1926). At 34 he enlisted in the Confederate army on 8 April 1863 and joined Company F, 24th North Carolina Infantry.

He was captured near Drewry's Bluff, Virginia, on 16 May 1864. He was sent to the prison camp at Elmira, New York, where he died of chronic diarrhea on 11 October 1864. He is buried in Woodlawn National Cemetery at Elmira.

The war touched Moffitt families in several places. A Union cavalryman in Arkansas shared the name of Veno's cousin Calvin, though the identification remains unconfirmed. Lydia Moffitt Rains lost two sons in the war in North Carolina.

The road from Randolph County to Elmira can be followed, though the records disagree about how it began. The company muster rolls say he enlisted for the war in Randolph County in July 1862 under Major Mallett, while another roll gives 8 April 1863, age 34, and calls him a volunteer. He was present on every roll through December 1863. Captured near Drewry's Bluff on 16 May 1864, he was taken to Fort Monroe on 17 May and Point Lookout, Maryland, on 19 May, and was received at Elmira on 18 August. He died there on 11 October 1864 of chronic diarrhea, with no effects. Two later accounts disagree: one says he was captured at Petersburg on 17 June 1864 and died at Elmira on a date unknown, and another says he died there in November 1864. His name was also written onto a roll of sick prisoners paroled from Elmira on 11 October 1864, the day he died, and the entry was struck out with the word "Dead."

Company F had begun as the Cumberland Plough Boys, farm boys from Cumberland County, and its own history, written long afterward, remembers the loss of the first men the company ever had captured: twelve or fifteen taken at Petersburg in mid-June 1864 when Lieutenant Gainey's detachment held the line too long. That would fit the later account that has Veno taken at Petersburg on 17 June, but his passage to Fort Monroe on 17 May says May, and the company's memory may be a month off, or it may be telling of a different group. The date of his capture stays unsettled between mid-May and mid-June 1864.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1958 (Veno Moffitt), Moffitt-1959 (Aaron C. Moffitt), Gardner-25498; 1860 U.S. Census (Zeno Moffitt); U.S. Register of Confederates and Civilians Who Died in the North, 1861-1865; Find a Grave memorial 66301062 (Woodlawn National Cemetery); Compiled service record, Zeno (Veno) Moffitt, Co. F, 24th North Carolina Infantry, NARA M270, roll 309, National Archives Catalog NAID 168483033, card images read 3 Nov 2026: https://catalog.archives.gov/id/168483033; "The Cumberland Plough Boys, Company F, 24th Regiment N.C. Troops," submitted by William Bullard, NCGenWeb Cumberland County (https://ncgenweb.us/cumberland/ploughboys.html), read 4 Nov 2026
EXTRA.note: The prison record and burial are from the cards cited on WikiTree and Find a Grave; the originals were not viewed. Update, 3 Nov 2026: the service-record cards have now been read in the National Archives catalog. They support capture near Drewry's Bluff on 16 May 1864 and death at Elmira on 11 October 1864, but conflict on the enlistment date (July 1862 against 8 April 1863) and include stray cards giving Petersburg and November 1864.

EXTRA.name: William Cornelius Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C.
kv: Thalitha Williams (m. 7 Aug 1827); Elizabeth Fesmire (m. 1866); Araminta Hicks (m. 1873)
Milo, Dennis, Reuben, Mahala, Marshall, Mary Delphina, John Tyler; Hannah V., William Dufoe
EXTRA.title: William C. and his three Randolph County wives
EXTRA.hook: Nathan's brother stayed in North Carolina, married three times, and lost two sons by 1873; his first wife was a Williams, like Nathan's.
body: William Cornelius Moffitt, born about 1802, married Thalitha (Aletha) Williams on 7 August 1827, the same day Aaron, his brother, married Polly Brady. Thalitha was born 16 September 1804 at Deep River, Randolph County, and died before 1866. In 1850 and 1860 they had children at home.

Their children were Milo (1828-1881, died in Chatham County), Dennis (1830-1886), Reuben Elwood (1833-1915), Mahala Adeline (1835-1903), Marshall (1839-1863), Mary Delphina (1842-1898, died at Decatur, Indiana) and John Tyler (1843-1873). Marshall died in 1863, which fits the Civil War, but his service is not known.

William married Elizabeth Fesmire on 2 September 1866; she appears in the 1870 census and died about 1873. On 7 October 1873 he married Araminta Hicks (1844-1932), and in 1880 they had two young children, Hannah V. (born 1875) and William Dufoe (born 1876). He died in 1884 aged about 82; the birth date on his memorial is doubtful.
Nathan's wife was Rebecca Williams, also from Randolph County. Whether Rebecca and Thalitha were sisters is not known.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-922 (William Cornelius Moffitt), Williams-38370, Fesmire-258, Hicks-22845; North Carolina county marriages, Randolph Co., 7 Aug 1827 (FHL film 418,149); 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 U.S. censuses
EXTRA.note: The Williams sister idea is only a lead.

EXTRA.name: Sarah and Naomi (Moffitt) Barker
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C.; Union County, Iowa
kv: 21 Apr 1800 - 18 Dec 1860, Lorimor, Iowa; m. 1821 Rev. Beeson Barker (1802-1873)
b. c.1800; m. 5 Mar 1822 Robert Barker
Groesbeck Cemetery, Lorimor, Union Co., Iowa
EXTRA.title: Two sisters who went to Iowa with their Barker husbands
EXTRA.hook: Nathan went west to Arkansas; his sisters Sarah and Naomi married two Barkers and settled in Iowa, where Sarah died on a sled being hauled home.
body: Sarah and Naomi were the oldest of Robert and Martha Moffitt's children. Naomi married Robert Barker on 5 March 1822, and Sarah married the Rev. Beeson Barker in 1821. Both families left Randolph County for Union County, Iowa.

A family memory of Sarah's death survives: "Mrs. Beeson Barker was born in 1800 and died in 1860 in the early winter. She took sick at the home of her son, Jerry, in Winterset. She wanted to come home so Marion Carey took a yoke of oxen hitched to a pin sled with a wagon box on it and putting a feather bed in it, brought her home. She lived only a few days. This broke up the active home of Rev. Barker." She is buried at Groesbeck Cemetery, Lorimor.

Sarah and Beeson had eight children: Aaron Dennis (1824-1881), Jeremiah Harmon (1826-1885), Robert Moffitt (1830-1834), Martha Jane (1831-1838), David Pearce (1834-1918), Mary Rahab (1838-1891), Sarah Ann (1841-1850) and William Beeson (1842-1926).

Naomi and Robert Barker's daughters Mary D. (1823-1899) and Deborah L. (1824-1907) both married their Moffitt cousins, Solomon C. and Stancil, sons of Charles Moffitt and Mary Beeson, and both died in Union County, Iowa.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1914 (Sarah Mary Moffitt Barker), Moffitt-1915 (Naomi Moffitt), Barker-20885, Barker-20899, -20900, -20901; NC marriages 1759-1979; 1850 and 1860 U.S. censuses; Find a Grave memorial 9344842 (Groesbeck Cemetery)

quotes.t: She wanted to come home so Marion Carey took a yoke of oxen hitched to a pin sled with a wagon box on it and putting a feather bed in it, brought her home.
quotes.c: Family account quoted on WikiTree, Moffitt-1914

EXTRA.note: The deathbed account is an undated family account; the census and burial records are as cited on WikiTree.

EXTRA.name: Lydia (Moffitt) Rains and Hannah (Moffitt) Craven
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, N.C. (Coleridge and Ramseur)
kv: 11 Dec 1806 - 24 Jan 1888; m. Isaiah Craven (1799-1885); Concord Cemetery, Coleridge
19 Jun 1811 (WikiTree: 18 Jun) - 2 Mar 1885; m. 29 Jun 1833 (30 Jun in the Chamness history) Alfred Rains (8 Feb 1811 - 25 Sep 1888)

Nathan (25 Jul 1834 - 18 May 1862, Raleigh), Mary (1836-1912, m. Simon Pickett), Susanna E. (1838-47), William A. (1840-59), Daniel (b. 15 May 1842; d. Raleigh, May 1862), Alfred E. (1844-1917; paroled 1865), Robert M. (1853-1918)
EXTRA.title: The sisters who never left: Hannah and Lydia
EXTRA.hook: Nathan's sisters Hannah and Lydia stayed in Randolph County, and Lydia lost two sons, Nathan and Daniel, at Raleigh in 1862.
body: Hannah Moffitt, born 11 December 1806, married Isaiah Craven and in 1850 lived in his household in Randolph County. They had at least Hiram Peter (1835-1900), Peter W. (1837-1861), Molcy, and Lewis Pickett (1846-1924). Hannah died on 24 January 1888 and is buried at Concord Cemetery, Coleridge.

Lydia, born in June 1811, married Alfred Rains on 29 or 30 June 1833 and appears in the censuses of 1850 through 1880. Her seven children were Nathan (25 July 1834), Mary (15 April 1836, who married Simon Pickett), Susanna E. (1 September 1838), William A. (15 October 1840), Daniel (15 May 1842), Alfred E. (4 September 1844) and Robert M. (29 March 1853). Three of the seven died before their parents. Susanna was eight when she died in February 1847, and William A. was nineteen when he died on 22 October 1859, a year and a half before the war began, so the statement that Nathan and William Anderson "died in the Civil War" cannot be right for William. The two sons who died in uniform were Nathan and Daniel. Both enrolled on 5 March 1862 in the Randolph Rangers, later Company G of the 46th North Carolina Infantry, and both died of disease at Raleigh, Nathan on 14 May (18 May in a hospital register) and Daniel on 17 May 1862. Alfred Evans served in Company G of the 38th North Carolina from August 1864 and was paroled at Greensboro on 19 May 1865.
Lydia died on 2 March 1885 and is buried in the Rains-Caveness family cemetery at Ramseur. Her brother Nathan, far away in Missouri, had died twelve years earlier.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1398 (Hannah Moffitt Craven), Moffitt-1913 (Lydia Moffitt Rains), Craven-2765, Rains-1897; NC marriages (Alford Rains and Lydia Moffitt, 29 Jun 1833); 1850-1880 U.S. censuses; Find a Grave memorials 29673064 and 133480891; Compiled service records of Nathan and Daniel Raines (Rains), Co. G, 46th North Carolina Infantry, and Alfred E. Raines, Co. G, 38th North Carolina Infantry, NARA M270, National Archives Catalog NAID 93953857, 93953852 and 93845046; Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922), pp. 90-91 (Lydia's birth and marriage, Alfred's dates, and the seven children's birth and death dates), Internet Archive historygenealogy00hans, read 4 Nov 2026
EXTRA.note: Lydia's children come from WikiTree and from Hanson's 1922 Chamness history, which prints the dates without a source (Daniel is "n. f. d." there, no further data, and the 1845 birth year that WikiTree gives for him is replaced by Hanson's 1842). The service files match the names and Randolph County birthplace of Nathan, Daniel and Alfred Evans, but no card names a parent, so the identification is probable. Hanson's William A. is taken to be WikiTree's William Anderson, and his death in 1859 is Hanson's only.

EXTRA.name: Thomas Berry "Tom" Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Born at St. James, Stone County, Ark.; farmed beside Grady in Choctaw County, Okla.; died at Paris, Texas.
kv: 17 Feb 1889, St. James, Stone Co., Ark.
Farming next to Grady, Wilson Twp., Choctaw Co.
21 Mar 1953, Paris, Texas; stone marked WW I and WW II
EXTRA.title: Tom, the brother next door
EXTRA.hook: Tom was born at the old Buck Horn settlement, worked the railroad, and followed his brother Grady to Choctaw County.
body: Thomas Berry Moffitt was born on 17 February 1889 at St. James in Stone County, Arkansas, the first of Henry and Hannah's children known to be born in Stone County. In 1910 he was living with his widowed mother in Franklin Township and working as a railroad section hand.

By 1920 he was farming next door to Grady in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma. His wife, Vesta, was born in Arkansas on 2 March 1892 and died at Holdenville, Hughes County, Oklahoma, on 15 October 1930.

Tom later lived at Paris, Texas, where he died on 21 March 1953. His grave marker is carved with World War I and World War II service, He was the son of Henry H. Moffitt and Hannah Grimes and the brother of Grady.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-1137 (Thomas Berry Moffitt), Moffitt-1138, Grimes-4049; 1910 U.S. Census, Franklin Twp., Stone Co., Ark.; 1920 U.S. Census, Wilson Twp., Choctaw Co., Okla.; Find a Grave (Thomas Berry Moffitt)
EXTRA.note: The WikiTree profile does not give his military record; the marker wording is from Find a Grave. Henry's death date appears on WikiTree as 9 September 1901.

EXTRA.name: Josephine, Jesse Gee, Gimsa and Bertha Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Randolph and Stone counties, Ark.; West Texas
kv: Born about 1877; age 3 in Janes Creek Twp., Randolph Co., 1880
Born Aug 1883 by the 1900 census, when she was at home in Franklin Twp., Stone Co.
Born Mar 1886 by the 1900 census, when she was at home; Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930) is possibly the same
EXTRA.title: Grady's older brothers and sisters
EXTRA.hook: Four of Henry and Hannah's seven children are known only by a census line or a gravestone, and one of them went to the Texas plains.
body: In 1880 at Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, Henry and Hannah had Josephine, 3, and Jesse, 1. Hannah said in 1910 that she had borne seven children and six were still living, so one died young and has left no trace.

Jesse Gee Moffitt (1879-1957) went to the Texas plains; he is buried at Tahoka in Lynn County, and family notes place his death at Amarillo. In 1900 Jesse, Gimsa and Bertha were with their parents at Franklin Township, Stone County, along with Tom and Woodford (Grady); Josephine, who would have been about 23, was not in the household.
A Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930) is buried at Herpel Cemetery, near her mother, and may be the Bertha of the household. That is not proved.
EXTRA.src: 1880 U.S. Census, Janes Creek Twp., Randolph Co., Ark.; 1900 and 1910 U.S. Censuses, Franklin Twp., Stone Co., Ark.; Find a Grave (Jesse Gee Moffitt; Bertha May Barham, Herpel Cemetery)
EXTRA.note: Little is recorded for these siblings. Gimsa is the spelling transcribed from the 1900 census and may be a misreading of a given name.

EXTRA.name: Alvin, Odas, Alton, Eldon and Donald Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Choctaw County, Okla.; Paris, Texas
kv: Twins born 1928; Alton d. 1975, Eldon d. 2014
Dois L. (1921-1947, Navy ship's cook) and John Winfred (1925-1990, Navy)
'Vernon Moffitt, 24, Grant, Okla.', Air Force basic course, Lackland, Sep 1953; father's initials printed W. E.
EXTRA.title: Grady and Mary's sons
EXTRA.hook: Grady and Mary raised five more sons to adulthood beside John and Dois, and lost two toddlers and Dois himself.
body: Alvin B., born in September 1915, was the first of Grady and Mary's children, arriving about a year after their marriage. When Grady signed his draft card in June 1917 as a timberman at Ervin, Oklahoma, supporting a wife, his mother and one child, that child was Alvin, the only one yet born. Alvin later served in the U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II and died in 1994.

Odas Eugene was born in 1918 and was "Ottis" on the farm in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, in 1920, where he and Alvin lived beside Grady's brother Tom, and "Odis, 21" in 1940. He died in 1995. No service dates have been found for Alvin or Odis beyond Alvin's Air Corps service, though two of their younger brothers, Dois and John, served in the Navy and have their own stories.

The youngest sons were the twins Alton V. and Eldon Herman, born in 1928, and Donald K., born in 1931. By April 1930 the family had six boys and was living with Mary's parents on a farm near Stanton, Martin County, Texas, with Grady out of work. By 1940 they were renting at 411 North H Street in Hugo, where the twins were 11 and Donald 8, and Grady, 48, reported twelve weeks of work in 1939 and an income of $100.

A "Vernon Moffitt, 24," of Grant, Oklahoma, finished Air Force basic training at Lackland, Texas, in September 1953. The age fits one of the twins, probably Alton, but the father's initials are printed W. E. rather than W. G. and no twin is named, so it is only a lead.

Two small children never grew up with them: Jimmie Gaynell, who lived from 17 January 1923 to 26 October 1926, and Henry Wayne, from 13 January 1934 to 12 May 1937, both three years old. Of the seven sons who grew up, Dois was the first to go, in 1947, after breaking his neck in the Red River. Alton died in 1975, John in 1990, Alvin in 1994 and Odas in 1995, and Eldon and Donald both in 2014. The two toddlers and Dois lie at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo, with their parents.
EXTRA.src: 1920, 1930 and 1940 U.S. censuses (Choctaw Co., Okla.; Martin Co., Tex.; Hugo); Find a Grave family links (Shoat Springs Cemetery); family-tree dates; WWI draft registration, Grady Moffitt, 5 Jun 1917; Shoat Springs Cemetery, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, transcription by Tammy Sharp and Karla K. Willis Sharp (USGenWeb Archives); Texas death record of Dois L. Moffitt, 1947; Air Force basic course notice, Sep 1953 (as cited in 'Woodford "Grady" Moffitt')
EXTRA.note: The dates listed for these children come from census records and family-tree entries; some exact dates need independent confirmation.

EXTRA.name: John Grimes and Penelope "Penny" Blackshear
EXTRA.place: Williamson County, then Wayne County, Tenn. (Hardin Creek, near Waynesboro)
kv: Born c.1775 in South Carolina; died 14 Jun 1844, Wayne Co., Tenn.; buried Haggard Farm
Born 6 Jun 1789, Jones Co., N.C.; living after 1850 (one list: after 1864)
James B., Elisha S., John Anderson, William Jasper, and probably David H.
EXTRA.title: The Grimes farm on Hardin Creek
EXTRA.hook: A Blackshear daughter from Jones County, North Carolina, married a South Carolina Grimes and raised a family at the Haggard farm near Waynesboro, where David H. Grimes was born.
body: John Grimes was born in South Carolina about 1775. Penelope, called Penny, was the daughter of Jesse and Hannah (Huggins) Blackshear of Jones County, North Carolina, and she was born there on 6 June 1789. Jesse took his family to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810. John and Penelope's first known child, James B., was born in Williamson County about 1807.

In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of Jesse Blackshare, deceased: his widow had remarried as Hannah Mairs, and the balance was due to "Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare" and the other heirs. Penelope's first child was born about 1807, so she was already married by then; the court may simply have used her maiden name for the share due to her.

The Grimes family later moved to Wayne County. John died there on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm. Their children were James B. (about 1807), a daughter (1810-1815), Elisha S. (about 1817), a daughter (1820-1825), John Anderson (born October 1823), an unnamed son (1825-1829) and William Jasper (born 1826). David H. Grimes, born in 1829 in Wayne County, fits the unnamed son, and a family tree names a John Grimes as his father.
A Blackshear family history lists "A dau., m. Grimes" as the first child of Jesse Blackshear of Jones County and Williamson County. Penelope is shown still living after 1850.
EXTRA.src: Grimes Family Genealogy, "Our Grimes Line" (descendants of John Grimes and Penelope Blackshear); Genealogy.com Grimes forum, Pamela Bryant, 17 July 2003; Williamson Co., Tenn., Probate Court Wills vol. 2, p. 109 (Oct. 1814), as cited on WikiTree Blackshear-160; P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954); Ancestry family tree for David H. Grimes
EXTRA.note: David H. Grimes is not named in the Grimes family website; he fits the unnamed son of 1825-1829. The tree that names John Grimes as his father calls him "John Jasper" born 1784, which does not match the site's John, born about 1775. WikiTree gives Penelope an 1814 death date that cannot be right if she was living in 1850 or 1864. The family tree in this archive gives Penelope's birth as 6 July 1789 rather than 6 June.

EXTRA.name: William Jasper, John Anderson and the other Grimes brothers
EXTRA.place: Wayne County, Tenn.
kv: Born 1826; will probated 1 Jul 1872; wives Malaha Keaton, Tennessee Ann McClanahan
Born Oct 1823; wife Mary C. Arnett; 1860 farmer worth $4,000 land and $3,500 personal
Born c.1817, Williamson Co.; Haggard Farm
EXTRA.title: "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor"
EXTRA.hook: In 1872 William Jasper Grimes made a will leaving his land to his second family and his first wife's children, and named his brother John executor.
body: John Anderson Grimes, born in October 1823 in Wayne County, married Mary C. Arnett about 1852. In 1860 he was a farmer, 37, with $4,000 in land and $3,500 in personal property, with Mary, 27, and children Nancy E., 7, George (Kearney), 5, Sarah F., 3, and John, 1. They were still on the family farm in 1900, run by their son George.

William Jasper Grimes was born in 1826. He married first Malaha Keaton and had twelve children between 1844 and 1868, among them Sarah J., Margaret G., John Q. A., Lucinda, Mary P., William Jasper K., Sevilla, Nancy C., Jasper Wayne, Benjamin Stout (a Blackshear name), Fannie and Mahulda Vista. His second wife was Tennessee Ann McClanahan.

His will was probated on 1 July 1872. It leaves his wife Tennessee Ann the home farm for her life and the land bought from John H. Cole, requires that "each of our children at the age of 21 years or at marriage" receive "one good horse, Bridle and Saddle, one cow and calf, one bed, bedstead and furniture," gives his two sons John A. and W. J. Grimes the tract bought from John B. Rutledge, and ends: "I nominate and appoint John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor to this my will."
James B. (born about 1807) and Elisha S. (born about 1817) both lived in Wayne County, Elisha on the Haggard farm.
EXTRA.src: Genealogy.com Grimes forum: "Will Abstract of William Jasper Grimes, Wayne Co. Tennessee" (P. Bryant, 16 Oct 2002); "Grimes in Wayne Co., Tn. 1860 census" (17 July 2003); Grimes Family Genealogy, Our Grimes Line

quotes.t: I nominate and appoint John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor to this my will.

EXTRA.name: Jesse Blackshear and the 1814 heirs
EXTRA.place: Jones County, N.C.; Williamson County, Tenn.
kv: About 1767, Jones (or Craven) Co., N.C.; father Elisha Stout Blackshear
Williamson Co., Tenn.; WikiTree gives 26 Jul 1803
Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob, Jesse, Penny and James
EXTRA.title: A Williamson County estate and a daughter named Penny
EXTRA.hook: The 1814 court order dividing Jesse Blackshear's estate is the paper that names Penny Blackshear, who married John Grimes.
body: Jesse Blackshear was born about 1767 in Jones County, North Carolina, son of Susannah and Elisha Stout Blackshear. He moved to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810; two of his sons remained in North Carolina until after 1810.

In October 1814 the Williamson County court heard the settlement of "Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd." Hannah, his widow and administrator, was by then "Hannah Mairs, wife of Isaac Mairs," and the "balance of $227.30" was divided between "Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees," Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob and Jesse. Hannah died on 4 June 1829 and is buried in Brown Cemetery, Wayne County.

The sons can be traced. Ezekiel (born 13 July 1792) lived in Williamson County in 1820, in Haywood County in 1830, and died at Brownsville on 23 April 1837; his widow, Isabella Dobson, was "bur. in the Ozarks" in 1882. Elisha (about 1794) farmed in Marshall County in 1840. Jacob (born 26 January 1802) moved to McNairy and Obion counties. The first child is "A dau., m. Grimes."
EXTRA.src: Tennessee Probate Court Books, Williamson Co., Wills 1812-1819, vol. 2, p. 109 (Oct. 1814), as cited on WikiTree Blackshear-160 and Blackshear-2; P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954), entries for Jesse, Ezekiel, Elisha, Jacob; WikiTree Huggins-10
EXTRA.note: WikiTree gives Jesse's death as 1803, which does not fit an estate settled in 1814 with a guardian; the settlement could follow years after his death. Penelope's place as the "dau., m. Grimes" rests on the name Penny and the Grimes family site.

EXTRA.name: Elijah Blackshear of Waynesboro
EXTRA.rel: 4th great-granduncle (probable brother of David H. Grimes's mother)
EXTRA.place: Waynesboro, Wayne County, Tenn.
kv: 29 Mar 1830, before Isaac G. Grimes, J.P.
EXTRA.title: A militia oath before a Grimes justice of the peace
EXTRA.hook: Penelope's brother Elijah swore never to fight a duel, in front of a Wayne County Grimes.
body: Elijah Blackshear was born on 9 June 1800, the son of Jesse Blackshear. He lived in Waynesboro, Tennessee, and married Dicena McMahon about 1820. Their children were Lucinda (1823), the twins Jesse Marion and James Newton (1826), and Hannah Permelia. James Newton married a Grimes, Elizabeth Anne, daughter of Isaac G. Grimes, on 11 April 1847.

On 29 March 1830 Elijah signed two oaths: "I do solemnly swear that I will support the Constitution of the U. S., and the State of Tenn.," and "I, Elijah Blackshear do solemnly swear that I will not give or accept a challenge either written or verbal to fight a duel, nor will I be the bearer of a challenge for such purpose." Both were sworn before Isaac G. Grimes, J.P., the same man who is the father of his son's later wife.
Isaac G. Grimes's relationship to John Grimes is not known.
EXTRA.src: P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954), entries for Elijah and James Newton Blackshear (archive.org blackshearianage00blac)

EXTRA.title: The oldest of the ten Hulsey children
EXTRA.hook: Eldest of ten, he was about six in 1910 and about thirty when his father died.
body: William Roy was the eldest of the ten children, born in 1904, three years after his parents married on 22 December 1901. By April 1910 he was about five or six and the family was in Mountain Township, Garland County, Arkansas, with his parents and two younger brothers, John W. and Noah, before Oscar was born in October of that year at Hot Springs.

He was the child who saw the whole move. His father was a laborer on the Camp Pike construction job near Little Rock in September 1918 and living at Story in Montgomery County; by 1920 the household was in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, farming as tenants, and in 1930 it was near Wright City. When his father died on 5 August 1935 William Roy was about 30 or 31, the oldest of the ten children (the youngest, George Paul, was 9 or 10).

Four of Oscar's seven brothers survived him in 1982, so three had died by then, Louis Daniel among them. Whether William Roy was one of them, whom he married and where he lived as an adult are still open. A Roy Hulsey, 34, married Bonnie Meredith, 15, in Montgomery County, Arkansas on 22 January 1938; that age fits William Roy (b. 1904), but nothing names his parents.
EXTRA.note: The birth year and parentage come from the family listing of the ten children; the dates of death, marriages and later homes have not been confirmed from a certificate or census page and are marked lead where given.

EXTRA.title: John Wesley, the second son
EXTRA.hook: The second son, three years old in 1910 in Garland County.
body: John Wesley, called John W. in 1910, was born in 1906 and was the second son. In April 1910 he was three or four years old in the Mountain Township, Garland County household with his father George, mother Rebecca and brothers William R. and Noah. His father, then farming in Garland County, is remembered in the family as a preacher.

He was twelve when his father, whose home was at Story, registered for the draft in September 1918, and about fourteen when the family moved west over the line to McCurtain County, Oklahoma, a county then filling with sawmill and railroad work. His brother Oscar later worked government relief jobs and lumber towns in the same corner of the state.
His marriage, children, death and burial are not known. Four of Oscar's brothers were still living when Oscar died in 1982; whether he was one of them is unknown.

body: Noah was born in 1908, two years before Oscar and the third of the ten. He is the youngest child named in the April 1910 household in Mountain Township, Garland County, where he would have been one or two years old beside William R. and John W.
He grew up as the family moved from Garland to Montgomery County, Arkansas (where the family lived at Story while his father worked at Camp Pike in 1918) and on to McCurtain County, Oklahoma.
Noah's adult life, spouse and death are not known.

body: Fred was born in 1913, three years after Oscar, and was five years old when his father, whose home was at Story, registered for the draft in September 1918.

He was about seven in 1920, the year the household was recorded as tenant farmers in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma with six children at home. By 1930, when the household of ten was renting a farm near Wright City, he was about sixteen or seventeen.
Fred's marriage, military record and death are not known.

body: Ruby Ellen was the first daughter after five sons, born in 1915 when her mother Rebecca was about thirty. She married a Stipe. Two sisters survived Oscar in 1982, and Ruby and Grace were the only daughters, so Ruby was evidently one of them.
She was a girl of five in 1920 in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, and fourteen or fifteen in 1930 near Wright City. She was about twenty when her father died in August 1935.
Her husband's first name, the date and place of the marriage and her death are not known.

EXTRA.hook: Born in 1918, the year his father was building Camp Pike.
body: Grady was born in 1918, the year his father, whose home was at Story, Montgomery County, registered for the draft while working for Stewart-McGehee on Camp Pike. He was the seventh child and probably the last born in Arkansas.

He was about two in 1920 in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, and about twelve in 1930. He was about seventeen when his father died in 1935, and in 1940, at 21 or 22, he was old enough for the first peacetime draft registration of 16 October 1940.
His marriage and death are not known.

EXTRA.title: A gunshot near his mother's farm, January 1948
EXTRA.hook: Louis Daniel Hulsey, 27, a World War II veteran and timber worker, was found dead near Mena, Arkansas, on 13 January 1948; his death was ruled a suicide.
body: Louis Daniel Hulsey was born at Bethel, Oklahoma, on 11 May 1920, a son of George Hulsey and Rebecca Graves. He was a World War II veteran, single, a timber worker, and had lived 13 months in the Acorn community by Mena, Polk County, Arkansas, on his mother's farm.

He died on 13 January 1948. The cause of death was written "Gun shot wound. Self inflicted bullet entered right temple going thru front part of head. Was found dead about 1/4 mile from his mother's farm house in the Acorn community at 6:30 AM Jan-13-1948." It was ruled a suicide, and the coroner O. R. Wood of Mena signed on the same day. His mother Rebecca Hulsey gave the information. He was buried on 15 January 1948 at Storey, Arkansas.
The next day's Idabel paper carried the headline "Gunshot Wound Is Fatal for Former Wright City Man" over an article naming him.
EXTRA.note: His birth date and place, death and burial come from his Arkansas death certificate, which spells the burial place Storey; the 1948 Gazette article is known from its headline only.

body: Grace Irene was born in 1923, the ninth child and second daughter, when her mother was about 39. She married a Dunagan, and the family list records her under that name.

She was about seven in 1930 in the renting household of ten near Wright City, and about twelve when her father died in August 1935. Her mother, Sarah Rebecca, later left Oklahoma and died at Bandon, Coos County, Oregon on 23 December 1972; whether Grace lived near her in Oregon is not known.
Her husband's first name, her marriage and her death are not known. She and Ruby Stipe appear to be the two sisters who survived Oscar in 1982.

EXTRA.hook: The youngest of the ten, nine or ten when his father died.
body: George Paul was the youngest, born in 1925 when his father was 48 or 49 and his mother Rebecca 41. He shared his first name with his father, George Washington Hulsey.

He was four or five in 1930 near Wright City and nine or ten when his father died on 5 August 1935 and was buried at Breashears Cemetery near Story. At seventeen, in 1942, he would have been of age for the draft within the following year, in the middle of the Second World War.
His adult life is not known.

EXTRA.title: Margaret Crumpton and the Graves family
EXTRA.hook: Margaret Crumpton married Jesse Graves in Garland County in 1884; how she connects to Sarah Rebecca is not settled.
body: In 1880 a widowed Margarett J. Crumpton, age 25, of Mountain Township, Garland County, lived in a household with Rebecca Cornett, age 69, and John W. and William H. Crumpton, ages four and two. The matching name, age and county make her a possible match for the 1884 bride, not a proven one. A Graves family genealogy identifies Rebecca as Margaret's mother and the boys as Margaret's sons, though nothing in the household itself says so.

A Margaret Cornett, age six, was in Searcy County in 1860 with Edward and Rebecca Cornett. That is promising, but linking her to the woman in the 1880 household needs more evidence: Rebecca's ages differ substantially between the two, and the 1860 household stated no relationships.

On 31 January 1884, a Jesse Graves married Margaret Crumpton in Garland County. The register records Margaret as 28 and Jesse as 38. A family account of 1977 names Margaret as a wife of Jesse Graves and Sarah Rebecca as his daughter, but does not say which wife bore Sarah. That age conflicts with the age given for Jesse in 1871, so whether both concern the same man is unresolved.

The Graves family identifies Margaret as Sarah Rebecca's mother and reports that Margaret died on 5 May 1884, the day Sarah was born. Nothing directly confirms the parentage or the death. The genealogy gives two possible maiden names, Speer and Cornett, without resolving the conflict.
EXTRA.note: The identification of the 1880 and 1884 Margaret Crumptons, Margaret's maiden name, the identity of the 1860 Margaret Cornett, and Sarah Rebecca's mother are unresolved. The 1884 groom's age differs substantially from that cited for Jesse in 1871. The family genealogy's account of Margaret's death has not been independently verified.

EXTRA.title: Married at fifteen in a neighbor's house
EXTRA.hook: Jesse Graves's first wife was 15 when they married at Jack Phillips's house in 1871.
body: Emma was a daughter of Nicholas Fisher, and her probable mother was Sarah L. Garrett, who married William Gray, a man named Kirkland, Nicholas Fisher and Jack Phillips, whose home in Mountain Township was where Emma married.
Jesse was "18 years old and Emma was 15." They married on 2 April 1871 at the residence of Jack Phillips.

They lived in Garland County, and the family was there in June 1880. The children born by then were Abraham Nicholas, Catherine Eunice and Greenbury H. as the children born by then, and a son Vestal born in 1881. Emma is not found after that. A 1977 family account names Margaret Crumpton as another wife of Jesse, though whether the Jesse of the 1884 marriage is the same man is unverified.

EXTRA.title: Nancy Cutter and the Graves household
EXTRA.hook: Jesse Graves married Nancy Cutter in Garland County in 1889, and family accounts give Nancy different surnames.
body: A Jesse Graves married Nancy Cutter in Garland County on 19 September 1889, the groom 38. A 1977 family account names Nancy Wilborn Sutton as a wife of Jesse Graves, while the Graves family calls her Nancy Wilborn Kyle Cuttler. The different names keep the records from being tied together with confidence.

The Graves family says Nancy had earlier married John B. Kyle and Samuel B. Cuttler, and names children Isaac and Prince. It also lists Lucinda, William Vestal, Pearl Mae and Cora Ellen as children of Nancy and Jesse. These relationships are unconfirmed.

The family places Nancy in Garland County in 1920 and 1930, says Jesse died in 1910 and says Nancy died on 20 November 1932. The 1977 account names Sarah Rebecca as Jesse's daughter but not which wife was her mother; the relationship between Sarah and Nancy is not established.
EXTRA.note: The 1889 marriage index names Nancy Cutter; the 1977 query uses Nancy Wilborn Sutton, while the family genealogy uses Nancy Wilborn Kyle Cuttler. The connection between these names and Sarah Rebecca requires independent verification.

Original names Robert without a middle initial; infant indexed as Selatha G., handwriting uncertain.
EXTRA.title: A possible route from Georgia to Arkansas
EXTRA.hook: Robert in Salathiel’s Georgia household may be the Robert Hulsey recorded in Arkansas in 1860; the connection remains open.
body: In 1850 Robert, 17, was in the Union County, Georgia, household of Salathiel, 43, and Elizabeth, 35. The other young Hulseys include Maryan, 19; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl transcribed Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. A published extract gives Robert a middle initial R. and reverses the ages of Benjamin and the girl above him.

In 1860, in Carouse Township, Hempstead County, Arkansas, Robert Hulsey, 27, born Georgia, was a farmer with $240 in real estate and $80 in personal estate. Sarah A., 20, born Mississippi, and a one-year-old male born Arkansas lived in the same dwelling. Robert has no middle initial on this page. The infant’s name is indexed as Selatha G.; its handwritten spelling is uncertain, and the published extract’s reading Salathel G. should not be treated as a secure match to Salathiel. No relationships are recorded, and Benjamin is not listed in this household.

If this is the same Robert, he was in Arkansas by 1860. The shared 1850 household suggests that he and Benjamin may have been brothers, but it does not state their relationship. The identity of the Benjamin F. Hulsey on the 1864 Union roster also remains unconfirmed.
EXTRA.note: Neither the 1850 Georgia page nor the 1860 Arkansas page gives Robert a middle initial. His age and Georgia birthplace fit a possible match, but the infant’s uncertain name supplies no secure additional identification. The Georgia-to-Arkansas identity and the proposed relationship to Benjamin remain leads.

EXTRA.src: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242 (https://www.graves-fa.org/gen-histories/gens/gen242.html), Gilliam Graves (no. 1), citing the 1853-1861 Montgomery Co. tax and guardianship records and the 1860 census.
EXTRA.title: Gilliam Graves and the orphans of Samuel and Sarah
EXTRA.hook: In 1854 Gilliam Graves was named guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves; one of them, William Riley, died without a will in 1861.
body: In January 1854 Gilliam Graves was appointed guardian for the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves of Montgomery County, Arkansas. The parents are thought to be Samuel Graves and Sarah Cole, who were married on 30 March 1837 in Randolph County, North Carolina, by Moore Graves.

Gillum and Moor Graves were both in Cherokee County, Georgia, in 1840, and "it is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s." The widow Sarah appears on the Montgomery County tax lists from 1851 and bought a 40-acre tract, the NW SE of section 11.

In 1860 the children were a household of their own: William (Riley), 22, farmer, and Alley, 17, Ursa, 15, Alison, 14 and Madison, 11, all born North Carolina. In April 1861 Gilliam is again named guardian for the minor heirs Alley, Ultha, Alison and Madison. William Riley died intestate on 1 November 1861.
How these children were related to Gilliam, whether nephews and nieces or otherwise, is not established.

quotes.t: It is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s.
quotes.c: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242

EXTRA.note: Names are spelled Alley, Ursa, Alison, Madison in the 1860 census and Alley, Ultha, Alison, Madison in the 1861 guardianship; Ursa and Ultha are probably the same child.

EXTRA.name: Mary (Polly) Gray Washburn Graves
EXTRA.rel: Third wife of Gilliam Graves, stepmother of Jesse Graves
EXTRA.place: Hot Spring Co. and Cedar Glades, Arkansas
kv: William Andrew Gray and Sarah L. Garrett
Franklin W. Washburn, 1 Feb 1859, Hot Spring Co.
c.1879, Cedar Glades; buried beside Gilliam, Mountain Valley Cemetery
EXTRA.src: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242 (https://www.graves-fa.org/gen-histories/gens/gen242.html), Gilliam Graves (no. 1) and children by Mary Gray (nos. 16 ff.).
EXTRA.title: Married at nineteen, then to a man twice her age
EXTRA.hook: Polly Gray was 19 when she married Franklin Washburn in 1859; by 1864 she had a daughter by Gilliam Graves.
body: Polly Gray was the daughter of William Andrew Gray and Sarah L. Garrett, a woman who married four times (Gray, Kirkland, Fisher and Phillips). She was born about 1840 in Hot Spring County and, on 1 February 1859, married Franklin W. Washburn: the record lists him as 21 and her as 19.

By 1864 she was Gilliam Graves's wife, and their daughter Mary Elizabeth was born on 13 August 1864, two months before Gilliam deserted from the Union army (12 October 1864) and returned on Christmas Day. In 1880 the Graves children by Polly were living with Andrew Washburn, her son by Franklin, and his wife Amanda.
Polly died about 1879 at Cedar Glades. Gilliam, who is supposed to have been killed by robbers in January 1876, is buried next to Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery, once called Mt. Pleasant Cemetery.
EXTRA.note: The genealogy gives the 1859 ages as 21 for Washburn and 19 for her. The date of her death is given only as about 1879.

Named in the Sep 1893 Garland County bond and license; age fifteen

Hulsey family query, Arkansas Family Historian 15:4 (Dec 1977), p. 218, https://argensoc.org/wp-content/uploads/afh/AFH154Dec1977.pdf#page=26; Garland County marriage bond and license, Benjamin F. Hulsley and Lucy Morgan, Sep 1893, https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HT-65TS-YYW?i=615&groupId=1417439&lang=en; FamilySearch index F7SC-WLQ, https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:F7SC-WLQ.
EXTRA.title: The women named in the Hulsey records
EXTRA.hook: Different names survive for the women in the Hulsey family; each stands on its own until the connections can be established.
body: In June 1880, B. F. Hulsey’s wife was Sarah G., thirty, born in Arkansas. Three children, Margaret M., George W. and Charles F., were in the household. She is called the wife of their father, but nothing says she was their biological mother.

A family account of 1977 calls Benjamin’s wife Margaret Partain. Other family accounts use Sylvania Susane Partin. Neither name has been linked securely to Sarah G. Similar surnames and a recurring Benjamin are clues, but they do not establish a mother for George Washington.

A September 1893 Garland County marriage bond and license name Benjamin F. Hulsley and Lucy Morgan. The license, issued on 25 September, calls Lucy fifteen. The century printed on the bond was corrected to 1893 by hand, and no ceremony is readable. This shows the couple's application for marriage, while their relationship to the 1880 family remains open.
EXTRA.note: No woman in this account is substituted for another. The records do not yet establish George Washington Hulsey’s biological mother or prove that the 1880 father and 1893 groom were the same man. The license issue date is not a confirmed ceremony date.

EXTRA.name: Cedar Glades, Montgomery County
EXTRA.rel: Place the family lived (home of Gilliam Graves, 4th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Cedar Glades, Montgomery County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: "Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down": a Union petition, March 1864
EXTRA.hook: Weeks after Gilliam Graves joined the Union cavalry at Cedar Glades, Union men from the same county begged the army for help against murder and plunder.
body: Gilliam Graves, 45, volunteered for the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864. Less than two months later, on 10 March 1864, a letter went from Little Rock to Col. C. C. Andrews, who commanded the post. It was signed by Oliver Adair "and others" who called themselves "citizens of Montgomery County, Ark., and members of Company L, Fourth Arkansas Cavalry." The printed letter reads Company L, which may be a misprint for D, the company raised at Cedar Glades; the family's own man is on the roster of Company D.

The men wrote that "Deeds of cruelty and barbarity that would shame Indians are of daily occurrence." They gave three cases from a single day: "On the 1st instant the wife of Mr. James Dosier was shot through the shoulders, and her child (one year old) shot through the arms. On the same day Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down, mortally wounded, and his brains then blown out. William Gray (citizen) was shot in a brutal and cowardly manner on same day."

They added that "the plundering of houses, breaking and burning of cotton cards, wheels, &c., belonging to Union citizens is of common occurrence," and asked that about 100 cavalry be sent into the county, where forage and mills were plentiful. Because "our company is not armed," they suggested that guides be taken from among themselves. A "Skirmish at Cedar Glade, Ark." is listed for 1 March, the same day as the shootings, with no circumstantial reports.

The letter does not name Gilliam Graves, and nothing says he or any Hulsey signed it. What it shows is the neighborhood he enlisted from: Union families in the Ouachita hills in the winter of 1864, with their cavalry company still unarmed while their neighbors were being shot at home. Gilliam's later death, "supposedly killed by robbers" in Garland County in 1876, came in the same kind of country.
EXTRA.src: The War of the Rebellion: Official Records, Series I, vol. 34, part 2 (1891), p. 631, Oliver Adair and others to Col. C. C. Andrews, Little Rock, 10 March 1864; vol. 34, part 1, p. 3 and Index (Skirmish at Cedar Glade, Ark., 1 March 1864). archive.org full text of vol. 34.

quotes.t: Deeds of cruelty and barbarity that would shame Indians are of daily occurrence.
quotes.c: Oliver Adair and others, Montgomery County, 10 March 1864

quotes.t: On the same day Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down, mortally wounded, and his brains then blown out.
quotes.c: Official Records, vol. 34, pt. 2, p. 631

EXTRA.note: The event and the petition are proven by the printed Official Records. That Gilliam Graves or B. F. Hulsey took part in it is not shown; the OCR text reads "Company L".

EXTRA.name: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry in Montgomery and Hot Springs counties
EXTRA.rel: Place and regiment of Gilliam Graves and B. F. Hulsey
EXTRA.place: Montgomery County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Scouts "to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers," 1864
EXTRA.hook: The orders and reports that sent the 4th Arkansas Cavalry back through Montgomery County in 1864, with the wounded and missing it cost.
body: A Union company recruited at Cedar Glades had to be used somewhere, and the army's papers show where. On 11 April 1864 Col. A. H. Ryan, commanding the 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Lewisburg, was ordered to send 2nd Lt. John N. Jones with 75 men to Hot Springs County. The general "wishes the detail to start at the earliest practicable moment. He orders that no houses be burnt by them and no property destroyed, but he wishes them to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers who may fall in their way."

On 11 June 1864 an expedition was organized "to make a scout in Saline, Hot Springs, Montgomery, and Perry Counties," with 100 men of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, four companies of the 3rd U.S. Cavalry and part of Merrill's Horse, under Maj. G. Harker, "to be gone six or eight days." Fifteen days later, on 26 June, Capt. Joel Brown of Company A wrote General Steele about the loyal families crowded into Dardanelle: "mostly soldiers' families," "without medical aid, and not enough of men in town to bury the dead."

The army's monthly summary for August 1864 records the result: "14th, a battalion of the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry returned from scout through Saline, Hot Springs, and Montgomery Counties. Fought with small bands of the enemy daily until arriving at Farr's Mill. Captain Green, with twenty-five men of this battalion, engaged Cook's and Crawford's companies, numbering about 100 men, drove them and killed 4 and wounded 6 of the enemy." The battalion itself lost "1 private killed, Captain Quin and Lieutenant Spiva and 6 privates wounded, and 3 men missing."

Nothing in them names Gilliam Graves or Benjamin Hulsey. They show the war they were in: a cavalry that was short of arms and horses, scouting the hills it came from, with soldiers' wives sheltered in river towns and bushwhackers threatening to burn out Union households. Deserters were a constant trouble for the regiment; in the fall a scout at Helena arrested one Company I man at his home. Gilliam's own absence from 12 October to 25 December 1864 fits that same autumn, but the reason for it is not recorded.
EXTRA.src: Official Records, Series I, vol. 34, pt. 3 (Hdqrs. Detachment Seventh Army Corps, 11 April 1864); vol. 34, pt. 4, pp. 322-323 and 561 (11-12 June, 26 June 1864); vol. 41, pt. 1, Chap. LIII, Itinerary of the Seventh Army Corps, August 1864 (archive.org full text).

quotes.t: to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers who may fall in their way
quotes.c: Order for a scout to Hot Springs County, 11 April 1864

EXTRA.note: Page numbers are from the OCR text of the volumes and should be checked against page images. No document seen names Gilliam Graves or Benjamin Hulsey.

EXTRA.name: Company F, 42nd Indiana: the eleven who starved at Andersonville
EXTRA.rel: Comrades of Daniel W. O'Neal (3rd great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Oakland City, Gibson County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: "Starved to death at Andersonville": the Company F monument, 1893
EXTRA.hook: Daniel O'Neal's company raised its own limestone shaft at Oakland City and carved on it the names of eleven men who died as prisoners.
body: The monument stands on a small triangle of ground beside the railroad in Oakland City. A 1913 booklet says it was put up by the surviving members of Company F, 42nd Indiana, "as a loving tribute to the memory of their comrades who gave up their lives in defense of the flag." It was built in the summer of 1893 and dedicated that September, with an address by Capt. A. J. McCutchan of Company A.

A committee of Col. W. M. Cockrum, John W. Corder, James T. Bell, John P. Simpson and Washington Strickland raised the money, and Cockrum deeded the lot to the county. The contract went to William Kelley of Oakland City for nearly $1,000. The shaft is of oolitic limestone, twenty-eight feet tall, with a carved soldier on top. "On the several sides of the dies are the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number." That should include Daniel W. O'Neal, who is on the company roll, though no one has confirmed his name on the stone.

On one side is a scroll reading "Starved to death at Andersonville," and beneath it eleven names: Chesterfield P. Dill, Alford Farmer, J. M. Hunter, H. H. Hunter, John H. Martin, Adam Canon, Wm. A. Reavis, W. W. Oliver, A. H. Mariner, Jacob Strickland and A. C. Coleman. The booklet adds: "These all were taken prisoners at the battle of Chickamauga and died at Andersonville." Most can be matched on the company roll, though spelled a little differently: Christfield P. Dill, Alfred Farmer, Henry H. Hunter, Adam Cannon, William A. Revis, William W. Oliver, Adolphus H. Marriner and Andrew C. Coleman.

The shaft also lists the company's battles: Perryville, Stone's River, Stevenson, Flint River, Chickamauga, Lookout Mountain, Mission Ridge, Ringgold, Buzzard Roost, Big Shanty, Snake Creek Gap, Chattahoochee River and Bentonville. Whether Daniel was present for all of them or left in March 1862 is the open question about his service; the men who built this stone, his neighbors from the same few townships, would have known.
EXTRA.src: Gil. R. Stormont, Gibson County in the Civil War (Princeton, 1913), "Co. F, 42nd Indiana Monument" (archive.org, gibsoncountyinci00stor); S. F. Horrall, History of the Forty-second Indiana (1892), roll of Company F, pp. 64-67.

quotes.t: Starved to death at Andersonville.
quotes.c: Inscription on the Company F monument, Oakland City, 1893

EXTRA.note: That Daniel W. O'Neal is among the 143 names has not been confirmed by a reading of the stone.

EXTRA.name: The first legal hanging in Gibson County
EXTRA.rel: Place the O'Neal family lived (Gibson County, Indiana)
EXTRA.place: Princeton and Haubstadt, Gibson County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: William Thomas Camp, hanged at Princeton, 22 November 1872
EXTRA.hook: A murder over a $75 note ended with Gibson County's first execution, while Daniel and Vashti O'Neal were raising their young family in the county.
body: An 1884 county history calls it "the first legal execution in this county." William Thomas Camp and J. R. Bilderback, both of Pike County, walked and rode to Haubstadt on 31 July 1871 and, finding no lodging, lay down to sleep in a piece of woods near the village. Camp had picked up a hickory club to use as a cane. As Bilderback slept "with his head on the roots of a tree," Camp "struck him on the head several times and killed him."

"There had been no grudge or quarrel between them, but the motive for the crime was shown by the larceny of a note for seventy-five dollars which Bilderback held on Camp." Camp threw the body into a fallen treetop, took some of the dead man's clothes and rode his horse to New Harmony, where the dead man's brother William had him arrested. Back at Haubstadt he showed where the body lay; a coroner's jury found it "horribly mangled by hogs," and Camp confessed under oath.

Jailed at Princeton, he escaped before trial and hid near his mother's home, was later picked up in Kentucky for horse-stealing and jailed at Owensboro, and was brought back. He was convicted of first-degree murder in July 1872 and sentenced to hang on 4 October. Gov. Baker gave him a respite until Friday, 22 November 1872, "when, at 2 o'clock p.m. of that day, he was executed by Sheriff F. W. Hauss." His lawyers were Col. Charles Denby, who had left the 42nd Indiana to become colonel of another regiment, and C. A. Buskirk.

Daniel O'Neal's household was then on its farm in Columbia Township, with Parsis (born 1868) a small child; the case was the talk of the county but is a place story, not a family one. No O'Neal is named in the account.
EXTRA.src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (Chicago, 1884), "First Legal Hanging," in the chapter on the county courts (archive.org, historyofgibsonc0000jast).

quotes.t: There had been no grudge or quarrel between them, but the motive for the crime was shown by the larceny of a note for seventy-five dollars.
quotes.c: History of Gibson County, 1884

EXTRA.note: Page number not recorded from the OCR text. Stormont's booklet says Denby was transferred from the 42nd Indiana and commissioned colonel of another Gibson County regiment after Perryville.

EXTRA.name: The Princeton cyclone
EXTRA.rel: Place the O'Neal family lived (Gibson County, Indiana)
EXTRA.place: Princeton, Gibson County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: A Sunday-evening cyclone, 27 February 1876
EXTRA.hook: The worst storm in Gibson County history took the roof off a church at "church time" and carried a house thirteen feet.
body: An 1884 county history says that "on Sunday evening, Feb. 27, 1876, the most severe cyclone which ever passed over Gibson County struck Princeton." It came from the southwest and "destroyed almost the entire southern part of Princeton, doing damage to the extent of over fifty thousand dollars." It "happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes." The roof and steeple of the C. P. Church were taken off.

The Sutton family's two-story frame house was "large," "comparatively new." "The wind lifted the house and it came down over the fence, distant thirteen feet from the foundation," breaking it "into three parts, one part going north, another east and another west." Ten persons were inside, "Mrs. Sutton and seven children, a son-in-law and his children." A two-year-old was found "hanging by its hands to a rafter on top of the fallen house"; a nine-year-old blown out of an upstairs window walked about four hundred feet to a neighbor's door and knocked, "remarking 'his house was blowed.'" Eight of the family were found huddled in a space about ten feet square, saved by a bureau, and "crawled out" through a hole sixteen inches across.

Parsis O'Neal, Katie Stevenson's mother, had been born at Princeton in 1868, and the family's farm was in Columbia Township a few miles south. No O'Neal is mentioned in connection with the storm; it is told here as the county's worst disaster of the years they lived there.
EXTRA.src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (Chicago, 1884), chapter on climate and natural events ("Cyclones") (archive.org, historyofgibsonc0000jast).

quotes.t: It happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes.
quotes.c: History of Gibson County, 1884

EXTRA.note: The O'Neal link to this storm is by place only. The text says the storm "passed out northeast of Oakland" in the OCR, which may be misread.

EXTRA.name: Coleman L. Stevenson (b. 1832)
EXTRA.rel: First cousin of Frank Stevenson (2nd great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Ninth District, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: A Stevenson cousin in the 32nd Tennessee, 1862-1865
EXTRA.hook: While Daniel O'Neal wore Union blue in Indiana, a first cousin of his future son-in-law wore Confederate gray from Giles County.
body: In 1886 Coleman L. Stevenson was described as "a first-class farmer and stock-raiser" of the Ninth Civil District of Giles County, born 26 December 1832. He was the eldest son of William P. Stevenson, a brother of Rev. Abner A. Stevenson, and so a first cousin of Frank Stevenson.

It says: "In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war. He participated in most of the principal battles, and was a brave and gallant soldier." The 32nd was a Confederate regiment. His family was large: two wives, who were sisters (Louisa and Dorcas Jackson), his own children, and "three orphan children to raise," Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J. Jackson, daughters of his wife's dead brother and sister-in-law.

The same sketch gives the family's own roll of Rev. Elam Stevenson's children, and records that William P. "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel." Coleman held 265 acres at home and 400 more elsewhere in Giles County in 1886, was a Democrat, and belonged, like his uncles, to the Methodist Episcopal Church South.
The Stevensons were Giles County people, and Frank's O'Neal in-laws were Indiana Unionists, so the two sides of the family met only after the war, in Frank's marriage to Parsis O'Neal.
EXTRA.src: Goodspeed Publishing Co., History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County Biographical Appendix, sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 871-872 (archive.org, historyoftenness00good).

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee, 1886

EXTRA.note: Goodspeed does not say the 32nd was Confederate; that is from the regiment itself. Whether Abner or his own sons served is not known.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Philip Bruce (1765-1825)
EXTRA.rel: Preacher who made his home with the family of Rev. Elam Stevenson (4th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Bee Spring, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: "I saw him die, and closed his eyes": Elam Stevenson and Philip Bruce
EXTRA.hook: The old itinerant whose books Elam hauled in his wagon died among the Stevensons' neighbors, and Elam shaved and shrouded him.
body: In 1869 Elam Stevenson, then 81 and housebound, dictated to the Methodist historian John B. McFerrin his memories of the preacher Philip Bruce, who came to Giles County in 1813 and "made our neighborhood his home." Bruce, in Elam's telling, was a Virginia Conference man who never married, who had once been offered a rich young Charleston woman's plantation and declined it ("he thought she had about money enough to send him to ruin"), and who after his health failed lived with his brother Joel and taught a day school for the neighborhood's children, giving to the poor every dollar the Conference sent him.

Elam was at the deathbed. "I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him. His death was calm and peaceful; there was not a struggle nor a groan. He did not move a muscle, only a slight quiver of the upper lip when the last breath left the body." A few days earlier the circuit preacher had preached to him: "It was a high day with him. He was very happy, and spoke in raptures of heaven." Bruce died in May 1825.

He was buried in the country graveyard "about two miles distant from our church (Bee Spring), by the side of his sainted mother and two of his brothers." His stone, Elam says, was put up by the Virginia Conference and reads: "To the memory of the Rev. Philip Bruce, an itinerant Methodist preacher nearly fifty years. He was born December 25, 1765, and died May, 1825. He loved God and the souls of mankind, many of whom became seals to his ministry."

The same letter records the cost of the Civil War to Elam's church. The first Methodist church in Giles County, Rehoboth, was replaced "by a large frame-church, which was destroyed by the Federal soldiers during the late war." It also tells of Meshach Boyce's son William, who "went to Arkansas at an early day as a missionary, and was drowned in a small stream, the second year of his labors."
EXTRA.src: John B. McFerrin, History of Methodism in Tennessee, vol. 2 (Nashville, 1871), pp. 180-190, letter of Rev. Elam Stephenson, Elkton, 28 July 1869 (archive.org, historymethodis00mcfegoog).

quotes.t: I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him.
quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson, 1869

quotes.t: a large frame-church, which was destroyed by the Federal soldiers during the late war
quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson on Rehoboth church, 1869

EXTRA.note: McFerrin prints the name as Stephenson. Page numbers are approximate from the OCR text (182-183 for the Bruce passage).

EXTRA.name: Salathiel Hulsey's household in 1850
EXTRA.place: Union County, Georgia
EXTRA.title: Ten Hulseys in one house: Union County, Georgia, 1850
EXTRA.hook: The census puts Benjamin at three, with a six-year-old girl above him; a published extract had reversed their ages.
body: On 11 November 1850 the household of a Georgia-born blacksmith, Salathiel Hulsey, 43, stood in District 85, Union County, Georgia. It included Elizabeth, 35; Maryan, 19; Robert, 17; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl transcribed Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. Arminda Burnett and J. C. Bell were also living there.

The original resolves an age discrepancy in a published extract: Benjamin is three, and the girl immediately above him is six. Those ages had been reversed in the extract. Three is consistent with the family’s 1847 birth year for Benjamin, although the census does not give his exact birthday. It also has no relationship column, so it cannot establish that Elizabeth was each child’s biological mother or prove this child became the later Arkansas Benjamin.

The compiler of that extract suggested that Robert in this household was a man recorded in Hempstead County, Arkansas, in 1860. The Arkansas record does show a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, but no middle initial. It lists Sarah A., 20, and an infant male whose name is indexed as Selatha G.; the handwriting is uncertain. The extract’s Salathel G. therefore cannot be used as a secure naming link to Salathiel. The identification of the two Roberts, like Benjamin’s connection to Arkansas, remains open.
In 1840 Salathiel was counted in Hall County, and in the 1830 Hall County Hulsey list he is one of seventeen men named Hulsey, living among the Hulseys of Charles and Adler.
EXTRA.src: San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000), "1850 Union Co., GA" and "1860 Hempstead Co., AR" census extracts (archive.org, sdgsfamilies64); 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga. Original downloaded and independently read; Benjamin is 3 on line 34, girl immediately above him is 6 on line 33. Original 1860 U.S. census, Carouse Township, Hempstead County, Arkansas, Albany post office, dwelling/family 961, lines 18–20, NARA M653 roll 42, RG 29, indexed p. 830; enumeration date fields blank. Independently read and downloaded image 12 of 30: https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/7667/images/4211301_00318?pId=13097887 ; index and citation https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/records/13097887 . Original names Robert without a middle initial; infant indexed as Selatha G., handwriting uncertain.
EXTRA.note: The original page has now been independently examined and preserved. Benjamin’s age is three, not six. The household relationships and its proposed connection to the later Arkansas family remain inferred.

EXTRA.name: The Hulsey cluster of Hall County, Georgia
EXTRA.rel: Possible kin of Salathiel Hulsey (proposed 4th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Hall County, Georgia
EXTRA.title: Seventeen Hulsey households in Hall County, 1830
EXTRA.hook: In 1830 Hall County had seventeen Hulsey households; Salathiel’s relationship to the others remains unknown.
body: In 1830 Hall County, Georgia, a county formed in 1818 from the Cherokee cession, had seventeen households headed by a Hulsey, among them Charles, Adler Jr., Joel, Elija, Demsey, William, Sarah, Pleasant, James, Adler Sr., Armistead, Hiram, Micajah, Jesse, Salathiel, Charles F. and Vincent. The 1832 Cherokee land lottery also carried Hall County names: “Charles Hulsy” and “Alder Halsey, Jr.” of Hamilton’s District, and “Pleasant T. Hulsey” and “James Halsey,” a soldier, of Dobbs’s District. Earlier, on 31 October 1820, Franklin County, Georgia, taxed James Hulsey Sr., Joel Hulsey and Pleasant Hulsey. None of these has been tied to Salathiel.

The senior line runs: Charles Hulsey and his wife Hannah, married about 1752, lived in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, in the 1770s, near the North Carolina line, then in Greenville County, South Carolina. A Greenville deed of 1792 names their sons "James, Charles, Jesse, Adonijah and Adler." The article says the family name was spelled "interchangeably Huddlesy, Hulsey, Huldsey."

A Georgia memoir gives the family’s origin. The sketch of Col. William Hulsey, born in DeKalb County on 1 October 1839, says: “JENNINGS HULSEY, native of Virginia, immigrated to South Carolina with his parents while he was a child. Came to Georgia, married REBECCA PATE” and died in DeKalb County, and adds: “The pioneer Hulsey from England.” So the best account of the surname is Virginia, then the South Carolina upcountry, then north Georgia, a path that matches the Hulseys of Franklin and Hall counties. Salathiel named a son Jennings, which may be a clue to a connection and is no more than that; the memoir’s Jennings is the grandfather of a DeKalb County man, not a proven ancestor.

Where Salathiel fits is unknown. Some family trees give him a father Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and a mother Mary Tharp, but nothing supports it; the Hall County Jesse of 1830, and the Jesse among Charles's sons, are both possible fathers by name alone. Salathiel was born about 1807 in Georgia, which puts a South Carolina-born parent in Hall County at the right time.

In 1850 Hall County still held a Charles Hulsey, 55, farmer, real estate $2,000, born in South Carolina, with Hannah, 52, also born in South Carolina, and a widow, Sally Hulsey, 33, with children. None of this ties to Salathiel, but it is the neighborhood he came from.

Arkansas came next. In 1860 a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, with no middle initial, lived in Hempstead County, Arkansas, with Sarah A., 20, and an infant son whose name is read as Selatha G.; the handwriting is uncertain. This may be Salathiel’s son Robert, but the link is not proved. Benjamin F. Hulsey, then 16 or 17, is on the roster of Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment raised in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863-64; so was Gilliam Graves, the grandfather of the woman George Washington Hulsey, probably Benjamin’s son, would marry in 1901. Montgomery County had been organized on 9 December 1842, and a history of the Ozark region says its settlers “came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties.”

EXTRA.name: 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)
EXTRA.rel: Regiment of Gilliam Graves (4th great-grandfather) and of a Benjamin F. Hulsey, possibly the 3rd great-grandfather; a Calvin V. Moffitt in it may be the 2nd great-granduncle
EXTRA.place: Montgomery County and Little Rock, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills
EXTRA.hook: A Union regiment raised in Arkansas included Gilliam Graves and soldiers named Benjamin F. Hulsey and Calvin V. Moffitt.
body: The 4th Regiment Arkansas Volunteer Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863 and mustered out on 30 June 1865. Its companies were raised among Arkansas Unionists. Company D was recruited in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863–64, and on 14 January 1864 Gilliam Graves volunteered at Cedar Glades, at 45, a farmer, five feet ten inches tall with black eyes. The roster of the same company has a private "Hulsey, Benjamin F." A Calvin V. Moffitt also served in Company L, but whether he was the son of Nathan Moffitt is uncertain.

The regiment's actions read like a calendar of small, hard marches. A skirmish on the Saline River on 15 February 1864. A move to Cedar Glade on 1 March, which is also listed as a skirmish that day (no report was filed). A scout from Little Rock to Benton on 27–31 March, led by Capt. E. H. Vance, who arrested three women hauling cotton for guerrillas and wrote that "the bushwhackers made a desperate rally to get the captured wagon and their fair friends, but they failed to get either." Mount Elba on 30 March. Then the Camden expedition of April 1864, which took in Jenkins' Ferry. In mid-May the regiment was at Dardanelle, and from 25 September to 13 October it took part in an expedition from Little Rock to Fort Smith.

The regiment's own story had darker edges. Union men in Montgomery County were hunted by neighbors, and the March 1864 petition from Company L names a wife and child shot and a doctor killed at Cedar Glades. In September 1864 a detachment out of Helena went looking for "deserters from the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry" and took one, Benjamin Davis of Company I. Gilliam Graves's own roll entry reads that he "deserted on 12 October 1864 and returned on 25 December 1864." No reason is given, and nothing places Company D on any particular march that month.

In November 1864, Maj. Harris S. Greeno led 130 men of the regiment out of Devall's Bluff, where the regiment had its cavalry depot, toward Batesville and Searcy and reported that Price's army had been "badly whipped at every point." The regiment finished the war at Little Rock, scouting to the Saline River and Bayou Metoe in April and May 1865, and was mustered out on 30 June.
