EXTRA.name: Buck Horn, Stone County
EXTRA.rel: Place the family lived (Henry and Hannah Moffitt's Stone County, Arkansas)
EXTRA.place: Buck Horn, Stone County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Buck Horn, March 1864
EXTRA.hook: Two Union reports name Buck Horn: one orders cavalry to "kill, capture, and destroy" a camp there, the other says the farmers wanted "peace on any terms."
body: Buck Horn, in what is now Stone County, Arkansas, is the old settlement near St. James where Henry and Hannah Moffitt's son Tom was born in 1889. Twenty-five years earlier it appears twice in the Union record of the war. On 12 March 1864 the district headquarters at Batesville wrote to Lt. Col. William Baumer, First Nebraska Cavalry, to take men across White River at Ramsay's Ferry and go to Round Bottom, near Sylamore, for forage, protecting the steam transport Miller. The order goes on: "You will endeavor to hunt up the enemy reported to be in camp at McDermott's, near Buck Horn, and kill, capture, and destroy them."

The order shows the care its writer thought necessary. Baumer was to recapture any mules taken from the Union train that he found with local people, "leaving the women and children of the family undisturbed and in possession of their household goods and such work-cattle as they need to cultivate their farms." He was told to be "kind and courteous in your dealings with the defenseless citizens," to give receipts for everything he took, and to "prevent your men from entering houses, pillaging, or burning any houses or fence rails." "Incendiarism or unnecessary severity," the order says, "you are strictly charged to prevent."

A week later Maj. Lewis C. Pace of the Eleventh Missouri Cavalry reported from Batesville on a seven-day scout of 206 miles (15–21 March 1864) after a Confederate force under Rutherford. On the last day he marched "down the river through Buck Horn. Here I could gain no information of Rutherford." His men were out of rations and many horses barefooted. He added a note on the country that fits the hills the Moffitts later farmed: "a rough, rocky, and mountainous country, destitute of forage excepting in the valleys and coves of the mountains," where "the farmers generally are busily engaged preparing their ground for planting, and express a great desire for peace on any terms."
These are two glimpses, not the story of a battle. The county's bloodiest fight of the war came at Buck Horn in May 1864, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers.

EXTRA.name: Company D, 142d Infantry, 8 October 1918
EXTRA.rel: Edmond Tims's company (son of Judge Edward Tims; 1st cousin, 4× removed)
EXTRA.place: St. Etienne-a-Arnes, Champagne, France
EXTRA.title: The runner's morning: Company D at St. Etienne
EXTRA.hook: Edmond Tims's company got lost in the French sector that day, but his battalion lost its commander and half its runners to a single shell.
body: The 36th Division's history, printed in 1920, describes the morning of 8 October 1918 from the front. The 142d Infantry was ordered forward at 5:15 a.m. to take the village of St. Etienne-a-Arnes, in Champagne, after the Marines in the 2d Division had taken the ridge. The Second Battalion jumped off from Hill 140 and went through machine-gun fire. The First Battalion, Companies A through D, followed in support. Companies A and B were in the first wave and C and D in the second.

To reach the jumping-off place, the history says, the men of the First Battalion had to pass "in squad columns, or single file, through the trees down the northern slope of Blanc Mont and through the barrage placed by the enemy's batteries to cut off the supporting troops from the fight." They suffered heavy casualties from shell fire and lost their commanding officer, Capt. Charles Kuhlman: "The burst of a shell wounded half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners." Edmond Tims was a company runner, and a company runner's job was to carry messages between the company and the battalion.

Company D's morning went wrong in a different way. "In this advance the men of Company D failed to follow the wake of Company B and wandered into the French sector to the left, where they remained through the balance of the day." Captain Kuhlman was so badly hurt that his loss "did not become known to his company commanders until the middle of the afternoon." The high-explosive shells were mixed with gas, and many gas casualties followed later in the day. Company B, whose wake Company D had been told to follow, lost its first lieutenant, Arthur J. Matheny, "killed instantly just after he had crossed the last belt of wire," and the second lieutenant, Thomas F. Collins; "more than thirty men in Company B had been killed and more than fifty wounded."

The honor roll at the back of the book lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date 8 October 1918. The regiment's own report, written in January 1919, says a fellow runner spoke to him at 8 a.m. on the 9th and found him killed an hour later. The two dates are a day apart and both fall inside the 142d's fighting at St. Etienne. Before the war he had served in Company L of the First Oklahoma Infantry, the National Guard regiment that the history says was assembled at Fort Sill in the spring of 1917, after months of border duty the year before.

quotes.c: Ben H. Chastaine, Story of the 36th (Oklahoma City, 1920), p. 117

EXTRA.name: Camp Pike, September 1918
EXTRA.rel: Place Rev. George W. Hulsey worked in 1918 (2nd great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Camp Pike, near Little Rock, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: The camp where George Hulsey was working when the influenza came
EXTRA.hook: George W. Hulsey signed his draft card on 12 September 1918 as a laborer at Camp Pike, and eleven days later the camp's base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a day.
body: On 12 September 1918 George Washington Hulsey, 42, filled out his draft card at Story in Montgomery County. It gave his employer as the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company at Camp Pike, the Army training camp near Little Rock. The camp had been established on 18 July 1917 and was the mobilization point for the 87th Division.

The Army's medical commission that studied pneumonia and influenza in the camps reached Camp Pike on 5 September 1918. Its report says the camp's death rate from lobar pneumonia, over its whole history, was third among the 32 camps in the country, and from bronchopneumonia fourth. The report adds that "beginning September 1 there had been a gradual increase of the number of patients admitted with the diagnosis of acute bronchitis." On 23 September, 214 cases of influenza were admitted to the base hospital in a single day, and that is the day the commission dates the epidemic.

"The epidemic was at its height from September 27 to October 3, during which period there were in the neighborhood of 1,000 new cases daily." By 31 October it was over, and a second, milder wave came at the end of November. Counting from 1 September to 31 October, the commission recorded 12,393 men reporting sick with influenza and 1,499 cases of pneumonia, with 466 deaths. These are figures for soldiers; the report says nothing about the civilian construction crews working on the camp.
Nothing says whether George Hulsey was working at Camp Pike during those weeks, or whether he was ill. By 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma.

quotes.c: Opie, Freeman, Blake, Small and Rivers, Epidemic Respiratory Disease (St. Louis, 1921), p. 52

EXTRA.name: Draft registration days, 1917–1942
EXTRA.rel: The men of the family at four registrations (Grady Moffitt, Simon Thompson, Oscar Hulsey, Charles Oscar Smith)
EXTRA.place: Choctaw, Montgomery and Pushmataha counties
EXTRA.title: Four registration days and the men who signed
EXTRA.hook: On 5 June 1917, 12 September 1918, 16 October 1940 and 27 April 1942, the family's men lined up to give a clerk their name, age and employer.
body: The first World War registration was on 5 June 1917 for men aged 21 to 30. Grady Moffitt was 25, a timberman at Ervin, Oklahoma, married and supporting his wife, his mother and a child; he was tall and stout, with gray eyes and dark hair. Robert Pisachubbe, 28, farmed for himself at Speer, black eyes, black hair, medium height, slender. By age Joel Thompson (b. 29 January 1892), Peter P. Thompson (b. about 1896), Wavey Lincoln Satterfield (b. 28 December 1895, at Morgantown, Kentucky) and Edmond Tims (b. about 1893) all fell into the same registration. Nothing shows that Joel or Peter was inducted. Wavey served as a private in the Army, and Edmond served first in Company L, First Oklahoma Infantry.

The third and widest registration, on 12 September 1918, took in men aged 18 through 45. Simon Thompson, 19, signed as a farmer working for his father at Corinne. George Washington Hulsey, 42, signed at Story, Arkansas, as a laborer at Camp Pike. Edmond Tims died on the fields of St. Etienne less than a month later.

The World War II draft began on 16 October 1940 with men aged 21 to 35. Oscar Franklin Hulsey, 30, registered that day at Mount Ida, Montgomery County. When the war began, Congress required all men aged 18 through 64 to register. The fourth registration, on 27 April 1942, was for men 45 to 64, and was nicknamed "The Old Man's Draft." Its purpose was an inventory of skills and available labor; those men were not liable for service. Charles Oscar Smith, 52, signed as "Charlie Oscar Smith" of Forney, Choctaw County, working on a farm, with mail at Hugo Route 1, naming "Mrs. Pearl Smith" as the person who would always know his address. Robert Pisachubbe, 53, signed at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.

Their sons went in different ways. Dois Moffitt enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942, aged 21, and served as a ship's cook until 27 January 1946. John Winfred Moffitt enlisted on 17 December 1943, at 18, and served on the floating drydock ARD-19 and the minesweeper USS Chief. No service dates are known for their older brothers Alvin and Odis, or for the Hulsey brothers of Oscar's generation.

EXTRA.name: James H. Satterfield and the 9th Kentucky
EXTRA.place: Allen and Butler counties, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: Three months in the 9th Kentucky
EXTRA.hook: James Satterfield joined the Union army in 1861 and left after three months; the regiment he joined lost 357 men, 250 of them to disease.
body: In 1885 James H. Satterfield said that "in 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service." He was 23, a young farmer in Allen County, and his father, Henry, died that same year.

The 9th Kentucky Infantry was organized at Camp Boyle, Adair County, and mustered in for three years on 20 November 1861. Its first winter was spent in camp at Columbia, Kentucky, until February 1862. If James joined in the autumn of 1861, the three months he describes would have ended about the time the regiment marched to Bowling Green and then Nashville, leaving camp on 15 February. His own account does not say whether he was discharged, detailed or transferred.

The regiment was in the rest of the war. It was at Shiloh on 7 April 1862, the siege of Corinth, Perryville (in reserve), Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge, the Atlanta campaign and Jonesboro. It mustered out on 15 December 1864. Its dead number 357: 8 officers and 96 enlisted men killed or mortally wounded, and 3 officers and 250 enlisted men dead of disease. In the 9th Kentucky, disease killed more than twice as many men as the enemy.
Butler County, where James settled in 1876, put up a veterans' monument in 1907 on the courthouse lawn to the soldiers of both armies. It is described as one of two such Kentucky monuments.

quotes.t: In 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service.

EXTRA.name: Sidney Rufus Satterfield & Eliza "Ancie" (Johnson)
EXTRA.rel: 2nd great-granduncle (brother of John C. Satterfield) and his wife, Samantha's first cousin
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky; buried at Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson
EXTRA.title: Two brothers' wives from one Clark family
EXTRA.hook: John C. Satterfield's brother Sidney married a Johnson girl whose mother was a sister of Samantha Johnson's mother.
body: Sidney Rufus Satterfield was born on 2 September 1865 in Kentucky, the third son named in his father's 1885 account ("Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C."). His parents were James Henry Satterfield and Malissa A. Gibson, so he was John C. Satterfield's full brother. He died on 19 November 1949 at Richardsville, Warren County, and was buried at Satterfield Cemetery, near Jetson in Butler County.

His wife was Eliza "Ancie" Johnson, born 19 July 1871, died 27 December 1951. Her parents were James P. Johnson (1840-1884) and Martha J. Clark (1839-1923), and Martha J. was an older sister of Melvina (Clark) Johnson, the mother of Samantha "Mantha" Johnson. That makes Ancie a first cousin of the woman who married Sidney's brother John C. in 1892. Two Satterfield brothers married into the same Clark-Johnson family.
Sidney and Ancie had at least three children: Walter, born and died in 1890; Mary Cecil (Woosley), 1891-1989; and Lillie (Embry), 1893-1946. All of them are buried at Satterfield Cemetery.
kv: Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson, Butler Co., Ky.

EXTRA.name: James Doiser Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born in Allen County, Kentucky; died at Hickoria, Clay County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: The brother who went to Arkansas
EXTRA.hook: James D. Satterfield, born in Allen County just before the family left for Minnesota, ended up in Clay County, Arkansas.
body: James Doiser Satterfield was born in February 1867 in Allen County, Kentucky, a son of James Henry Satterfield and Malissa Gibson. He is "James D." among the six children of the first marriage in his father's 1885 account. He was born the year his father says the family "removed to Dakota County, Minn."

He married in 1889 a wife recorded as Iverson Embry Satterfield (1871-1926), with five children: Laura Myrtle Hooper (1890-1951), Juvanda McKinney (1892-1922), Claud Edward (1899-1963), Fannie Esther Dobbins Tisdal (1902-1977) and James Ralph (1909-1983).

He died on 10 July 1929 at Hickoria, Clay County, Arkansas, and is buried at Redenbo Cemetery in that county. That is a different part of the Mid-South from his half-brothers at Texarkana, and from John C., who went to Franklin County, Texas.

EXTRA.note: The wife's name as given on Find a Grave looks like a transcription of a maiden name (Embry); not checked.

EXTRA.name: A. M. (Satterfield) Coots
EXTRA.place: Born in Minnesota; buried at Butler Phelps Cemetery, Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: A daughter born in Minnesota, dead at twenty-one
EXTRA.hook: One Satterfield child was born during the eight years the family spent in Dakota County, Minnesota, and died in Kentucky a year after her wedding.
body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography says that "in 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky." One child is known to have been born there. A. M. Satterfield was born on 23 July 1870 in Minnesota, a daughter of James Henry Satterfield and Malissa Gibson and a full sister of John C. Satterfield.

She married Calvin H. Coots (1869-1932) in 1891 and died on 25 May 1892, aged 21. She is buried at Butler Phelps Cemetery in Butler County. Her mother had died in 1877, soon after the move back, and her father had remarried in 1878 to Lucinda Belle Phelps, a Butler County woman.
Her Minnesota birth bears out the Minnesota years in her father's 1885 account.
kv: Butler Phelps Cemetery, Butler Co., Ky.

EXTRA.name: Lucinda Belle (Phelps) Satterfield and her nine children
EXTRA.rel: Step-3rd-great-grandmother; her children are half-siblings of John C. Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky, then Bowie County, Texas
EXTRA.title: James Satterfield's second family
EXTRA.hook: After Melissa died in 1877 James H. Satterfield married a 21-year-old neighbor and had nine more children, most of whom ended up around Texarkana.
body: Lucinda Belle Phelps was born on 30 May 1857 in Butler County, a daughter of Solomon Phelps and Sarah J. (Deweese). She married James H. Satterfield on 2 June 1878, a year after Melissa Gibson's death. They had nine children: Martha Belle (born Nov 1879), Alonzo Thomas (1882), Minnie E. (1884), Joe Griffin (1886), Laura E. (1887), Charles J. (1890), George Franklin (1892), Grover C. (1894) and Effie J. (1899). Lucinda died on 5 June 1917.

By 1909 the grown children were marrying in Bowie County, Texas, or across the Arkansas line: Charles J. to Alma Morgan on 5 December 1909; Alonzo to Zoda Mae Slader Reed in September 1914; Grover to Norah Walker on 28 May 1917 at Maud; Joe Griffin to Lennia Champion on 11 November 1917; George to Eula Viola Martin on 2 September 1917 at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas. Laura married a Douglas Henry and died in October 1975.
Minnie E. is said to have married a "(?) Smith." That could be a coincidence of a common name, and nothing links her husband to Charles Oscar Smith's family.

James himself died in Bowie County on 28 November 1922 (another account says 24 November 1922 or 1924) and is buried at Reed Cemetery. His 1885 biography already credits him with 1,340 acres in Butler County and another 425 acres in Tennessee.

Three of Lucinda's sons left fuller records. Alonzo Thomas, born 6 June 1882 in Butler County and one of the three children named in his father's 1885 biography, married Zoda Mae Slader Reed in Bowie County, Texas, in September 1914 and died there on 18 December 1950. George Franklin, born at Brooklyn on 10 May 1892, married Eula Viola Martin at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas, on 2 September 1917, served in World War I (his stone reads “ARKANSAS CPL CO E 3 TRAINING REGT WORLD WAR I”), and died at Texarkana on 4 January 1958; he is buried at Odd Fellows Cemetery, Lockesburg, Arkansas. Grover Cleveland, born 5 April 1894, married Norah Walker at Maud, Bowie County, on 28 May 1917 and died at Maud on 13 December 1966.

EXTRA.name: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born at Morgantown, Butler County, Kentucky; died at Soper, Choctaw County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: A headstone that gets the birthday wrong
EXTRA.hook: Artie Pearl's older brother was a private in the Army in the First World War; his Oklahoma stone and his draft cards disagree about his birth date.
body: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield was the oldest surviving child of John C. and Samantha Satterfield. His stone at Soper Cemetery gives his birth as 9 January 1896, but his World War I and World War II draft registrations both give 28 December 1895 at Morgan Town, Butler County, Kentucky, so the stone is probably the error.

The stone is marked "TEXAS PVT. U.S. ARMY World War I." That fits the family's move to Franklin County, Texas, about 1907. In 1925 he married Jewel Dale Weems (1908-1984), and they later lived in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Samantha and her second husband had settled.
He died at Soper on 24 March 1952, aged 56, and is buried there in plot E4, the same plot as his mother Samantha.

EXTRA.name: James Bethel Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born in Kentucky; died at Paris, Lamar County, Texas; buried at Soper, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: The brother who married a Riddle
EXTRA.hook: James Bethel Satterfield and his sister Stella both married into the Riddle family.
body: James Bethel Satterfield was born on 12 May 1901 in Butler County, Kentucky, and was about six when the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. He married Alice Elizabeth Riddle (1900-1976), and they had seven children born between 1922 and 1940, one of whom, Charlie, died in 1940 at about ten.
His sister Stella had married Clifford Calvin Riddle (1898-1975). Whether Alice and Clifford were brother and sister is not known.
James died on 7 December 1964 at Paris, Texas, and is buried at Soper Cemetery in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, near his mother.

EXTRA.name: Stella (Satterfield) Riddle
EXTRA.place: Born in Franklin County, Texas; buried at Chillicothe, Hardeman County, Texas
EXTRA.title: Stella, dead at seventeen
EXTRA.hook: Artie Pearl's youngest sister married a Riddle and died at 17.
body: Stella B. Satterfield was born on 6 October 1907 and was one of the two children John C. and Samantha had after the move to Texas (in 1910 she was about two). Her mother married again in 1917 and moved with Stephens to Oklahoma.

She married Clifford Calvin Riddle (1898-1975). She died on 25 January 1925, aged 17, and is buried at Chillicothe Cemetery, Hardeman County, Texas, far from Soper and Hugo where her mother and sister lie. No cause of death is given.
In April 1910 she was "little Stella" in the Hagansport household.

EXTRA.name: Ira L. and Jewel Thompson Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Ira born in Kentucky; Jewel born at Talco, Titus County, Texas; both ended in Choctaw County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: The two youngest Satterfield boys
EXTRA.hook: Ira served in the Army in the Second World War; Jewel was born at Talco, Texas, five years before his mother remarried.
body: Ira L. Satterfield was born in 1905 in Kentucky and was five in April 1910 at Hagansport. He is buried at Grant Cemetery, the same cemetery as his sister Artie Pearl and Charles Oscar Smith, with a stone marked "AMRY WWII." He died in 1977.

Jewel Thompson Satterfield, the last child, was born on 3 May 1912 at Talco in Titus County, Texas. He married Marie Nabors in 1929, when he was 17, and had five children. He died at Hugo on 13 January 1995 and is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery there.

EXTRA.name: Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens
EXTRA.place: Born in Tennessee; Oaks Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, in 1920; died at Mount Pleasant, Texas; buried at Bridges Chapel Cemetery
EXTRA.title: The widower Samantha married in 1917
EXTRA.hook: Samantha Satterfield's second husband was a 59-year-old widower whose first wife was part Choctaw and who went back to Texas after Samantha died.
body: Billy Alexander "Bird" Stephens (Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens in the family's other records) was born on 16 February 1858 in Tennessee, a son of Calaway "Cal" Stephens (1824-1863) and Sarah Ann Little (1822-1913). He was the youngest of six children.

He is said to have married Martha Adeline Liles (born 1861) in Newton County, Arkansas, on 28 March 1878, and she was said to be one-quarter Choctaw. She died in 1916 and is buried at Old Saltillo Cemetery in Hopkins County, Texas. They had eight children, of whom seven are known: John Harvey, Nancy Ann (Brown), Mary Adeline (Simmons), Joseph Carroll, Wiley Alexander, Francis Henry and Tomie Delmane, who died at 10 in 1907.

On 28 July 1917 at Mount Vernon, Franklin County, the 59-year-old widower married 44-year-old Mrs. M. D. Satterfield. They moved to Oaks Township, Choctaw County, and were there in the 1920 census. After Samantha died in October 1928 he went back to Titus County, Texas, and died at Mount Pleasant on 23 January 1944. He is buried at Bridges Chapel Cemetery.

The Choctaw claim finds no support in the enrollment of the Choctaw Nation: no Martha Adeline, no Bird or Alexander Stephens, and no Liles appears among those enrolled. The one-quarter Choctaw statement stays a family tradition.

EXTRA.name: Newton Jasper Clark & Polly Clark (maiden name unresolved)
EXTRA.place: Brooklyn, Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: The Clarks of Brooklyn, Kentucky
EXTRA.hook: Newton’s 1850 household includes Polly; Melvina’s death record names her parents as Newton Clark and Mary Dunn.
body: Newton Jasper Clark was born on 6 August 1817 and died on 3 April 1878 in Butler County. His parents are said to be William Clark (1785-1856), born in Granville County, North Carolina, and Levina Willis (1785-1877). William is credited with service in the War of 1812; that is not checked.

Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms took out a license on 20 January 1839. William Anderson joined them in marriage on 24 January and signed the return on 25 January. These are three different events; the 20 January date repeated in family accounts is the license date.

Polly’s age was proved by Moses Elms and Newton’s age was sworn to; neither age in years is given, and how Moses was related to Polly is not stated. Melvina’s 1929 death record names Newton Clark and Mary Dunn as her parents. The marriage gives the bride’s name as Polly D. Elms but does not reconcile Dunn and Elms or establish an earlier marriage. That the bride was the Polly in Newton’s 1850 household and Melvina’s mother remains probable.

Family memorials place Newton’s burial at Newton Clark Cemetery, Brooklyn, and give Polly’s death as 16 February 1888 and burial at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown. They link Martha J., Stanford C., Beverly L. "Belva" and Melvina as children. These family links are not independently proved, since the 1850 household states no relationships; Stanford’s age of 8 in 1850 also conflicts with the later 1844 birth date attributed to him.

Newton's stone at the Newton Clark Cemetery near Brooklyn, in Butler County, reads: "Newton Clark was born August the 6 1817 d[ie]d April the 3 1878." Polly's grave in the Clark Cemetery at Morgantown is marked by an uncut fieldstone with no legible inscription, so her death date of 16 February 1888 rests on family accounts rather than on the stone.

Three of the Clark children left records of their own. Martha J., the eldest, born 1 February 1839, married James P. Johnson; their children included Eliza “Ancie,” who married a Satterfield. James died in 1884 and Martha lived on as a widow for 39 years, dying in Butler County on 13 February 1923; both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson. Stanford C., born 6 June 1844, served as a private in Troop A of the 12th Kentucky Cavalry, a Union regiment, as his headstone at Belmont General Baptist Church Cemetery, Morgantown, says, and a Stanford Clark is listed as a Union private in Company A of the 12th Kentucky Cavalry. He married Serenia Hunt in 1867 and died on 12 June 1913. Beverly L. “Belva,” born 2 October 1850, married Margaret Ann Coots in 1877, raised eight children mostly in Kentucky, and went west: he died at Cushing, Payne County, Oklahoma, on 18 February 1939 and is buried at Fairlawn Cemetery there.

EXTRA.name: Stanford C. Clark
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: A Union cavalry private
EXTRA.hook: Samantha Johnson's uncle Stanford Clark rode with the 12th Kentucky Cavalry.
body: Stanford C. Clark was born on 6 June 1844 in Kentucky, said to be a son of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. His headstone at Belmont General Baptist Church Cemetery, Morgantown, is marked "PVT TRP A 12 REGT KY CAV CIVIL WAR." The 12th Kentucky Cavalry was a Union regiment.

On 9 February 1867 he married Serenia Hunt (1851-1918) in Butler County. He died on 12 June 1913 at age 69. By then his niece Samantha and her husband John C. Satterfield had left Butler County for Texas.

A Stanford Clark served as a Union private in Company A of the 12th Regiment, Kentucky Cavalry, entering and leaving as a private. That matches the troop and regiment on his headstone, though no age or residence is given. The regiment was organized at Caseyville and Owensboro and mustered in on 17 November 1862; it chased Morgan's raiders in July 1863, served in the Knoxville campaign that winter and mustered out on 23 August 1865.

EXTRA.name: Beverly L. "Belva" Clark
EXTRA.place: Born in Butler County, Kentucky; died at Cushing, Payne County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: The Clark brother who went to Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: Melvina’s reported brother Belva Clark died at Cushing, Oklahoma, at 88, with eight children behind him.
body: Beverly L. "Belva" Clark was born on 2 October 1850 in Butler County, Kentucky, said to be a son of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. In 1877 he married Margaret Ann Coots (1861-1944).

He had eight children: Palvena (Smith), Sardena (Flener), William Pearl, Fannie Ellen (Coots), Purnie Dee (Noteware), Carrie (born and died in 1891), Martha D. (Fulkerson) and David Carl. Most were born in Kentucky; the Clark family was in Oklahoma by the time he died.
He died on 18 February 1939 at Cushing in Payne County, Oklahoma, and is buried at Fairlawn Cemetery there.

EXTRA.name: Martha J. (Clark) Johnson & James P. Johnson
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Kentucky; buried at Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson
EXTRA.title: Melvina's older sister
EXTRA.hook: Martha Clark married James P. Johnson; their daughter Ancie married a Satterfield and is buried at the cemetery that carries the Satterfield name.
body: Martha J. Clark was born on 1 February 1839 in Butler County, said to be the eldest child of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. She married James P. Johnson (7 January 1840 - 30 June 1884). Three of their children were Mary Isabella "Isey" (Phelps), 1868-1936; Eliza "Ancie" (Satterfield), 1871-1951; and William Miligan Johnson, 1875-1950. Two more were Oliver P. and Drucilla.
James died in 1884 and Martha lived on as a widow for 39 years. She died on 13 February 1923 in Butler County. Both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson.
James P. and Melvina's husband, who is not named, shared the surname Johnson; whether they were brothers or cousins is not known.

EXTRA.name: Charlie Johnson
EXTRA.place: Born at Brooklyn, Butler County, Kentucky; died at Welchs Creek, Butler County
EXTRA.title: Samantha's brother who stayed
EXTRA.hook: Samantha went to Texas and Oklahoma; her brother Charlie lived and died within a few miles of where they were born.
body: Charlie Johnson was born on 27 April 1885 at Brooklyn in Butler County, a son of Melvina Clark Johnson, 13 years after his sister Samantha. He died on 14 February 1959 at Welchs Creek, Butler County, and is buried at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown, with his mother's Clark family.

He had two wives. The first was Martha Alice Satterfield (27 August 1886 - 22 July 1918), buried at Clark Cemetery; she died at Riverside, Warren County, aged 31. The second was Pernie Brooks (1905-1944). Eight children included Carlie, Cooper F., James Wallace, Artie Mae Roberts, Cevil, Golda Marie Hunt, Chester and Cova Myrl Felty.
Martha Alice's parents are not named, so whether she belonged to the same Satterfield family as her husband's brother-in-law John C. is unknown.

EXTRA.name: Hazel Marzee (Shackleford) King
EXTRA.rel: Great-grandaunt (sister of Mary Tinsley Shackleford Moffitt)
EXTRA.place: Born at Rattan, Delta County, Texas; died at Paris, Texas
EXTRA.title: Hazel Shackleford King and her brothers and sisters
EXTRA.hook: Hazel's family stretched from Texas to Oklahoma and California, and three Moffitts carried her casket.
body: Hazel Marzee Shackleford was born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, and died on 22 December 1980 at Paris, Lamar County. At her death it was printed: "Mrs. King was born in the Rattan community of Delta County, a daughter of John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton. She attended schools in Delta County and married John Wesley King who preceded her in death in 1968."

Her brothers and sisters were named: "four sisters, Mrs. Joe Haskell, Mrs. Beula [sic] Hutchings and Mrs. Helen Josey, all of Apache, OK, and Mrs. Eular Tillman of Lawton, OK; three brothers, Balis Shackleford of CA, John S. Shackleford and Edward Shackleford, both of Apache, OK." Mary Moffitt had died in 1962, and Robert Yates in 1961.

Three of the six pallbearers were Moffitts. Two of them, Donald and Odis Moffitt, were very likely sons of Grady and Mary and so Hazel's nephews, though the paper gives no relationships. She is buried at Meadowbrook Memorial Park, Paris.

quotes.t: Mrs. King was born in the Rattan community of Delta County, a daughter of John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton.

EXTRA.name: Balis Anthony Shackleford
EXTRA.place: Born in Alabama; died in Los Angeles County, California
EXTRA.title: Mary's oldest brother, who went to California
EXTRA.hook: In 1900 the Shackleford children were at Gilbert, Alabama; Balis, the oldest, spent his last decades in Los Angeles County.
body: Balis Anthony Shackleford was born on 5 February 1892 in Alabama. In 1900 at Gilbert, Etowah County, his father John, 37, born September 1862, married 10 years, born in Alabama of a Georgia parent, and his mother Elizabeth, 28, had "5 children born, 5 living": "Balous" 8; Myrtle, 6 (Aug 1893); May, 5 (Jun 1894); Robert, 3 (Oct 1896); and Eddie, 8 months (Sep 1899).

That list holds two children not in the later notices. Myrtle (born Aug 1893) and Eddie (born Sep 1899) do not appear among the survivors named in 1961 and 1981. They may have died young or may be known by other names. The Edward Richard Shackelford who lived to 1988 was born in 1910, a different child.

Balis married Bertha Mae Fox (1895-1970); a daughter, Jewell Irene Denman, lived 1914-1978. He died on 9 January 1982 in Los Angeles County and was buried on 2 February at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes. The California death record gives his name as Balis Anthony Shackelford.

EXTRA.name: Robert Yates Shackleford
EXTRA.place: Born at Gadsden, Etowah County, Alabama; died at Oroville, California
EXTRA.title: A death in an Oroville hospital
EXTRA.hook: His death notice named all his brothers and sisters, including 'Mamie Moffett' of Oklahoma.
body: Robert Yates Shackleford was born on 25 October 1897 at Gadsden, Etowah County. In June 1961 it was reported: "Robert Y. Shackleford died early this morning in an Oroville Hospital. He was 63. Born in Alabama, he was a resided of Gridley for 10 years... He was a veteran of World War I."

The survivors were: "three brothers. Bayles of Los Angeles and Ed and John of Oklahoma; six sisters, Mrs. Josephine Haskell, Mrs. Helen Josey, Eulah Tillman and Mamie Moffett, all of Oklahoma; Beulah Hutchins and Mrs. Hazel King, both of Texas, and 16 grandchildren." Mamie Moffett is Mary Tinsley Shackleford Moffitt, who died the next year. His widow was Mae and he had eight children.
He is buried at Gridley-Biggs Cemetery in Butte County, California; the stone carries a World War II marker, while the paper says World War I.

EXTRA.place: Oklahoma and Texas
EXTRA.title: Three sisters known only by married names
EXTRA.hook: Notices of 1961 and 1981 list sisters of Mary Moffitt who do not appear in the 1900 household.
body: The notices of 1961 and 1981 together name three sisters of Mary Shackleford Moffitt who are not in the earlier list: Mrs. Josephine (Mrs. Joe) Haskell, Eulah (Eular) Tillman of Lawton, Oklahoma, and Beulah (Beula) Hutchins (Hutchings). Both also name Helen Josey and Hazel King.

In 1900 John and Elizabeth had five children, the youngest born in 1899. Josephine, Eulah and Beulah were therefore born after 1900, between about 1901 and 1915, or Myrtle (born 1893) may be one of them under another name. This cannot be settled.
The family lived in Delta County, Texas, around 1908, in Martin County, Texas, by 1930, and later in Caddo County, Oklahoma, where Lizzie is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache.
kv: Chico Enterprise-Record 23 Jun 1961; Lamar County Echo 1 Jan 1981
EXTRA.src: The Chico Enterprise-Record, 23 Jun 1961, p. 3; The Lamar County Echo, 1 Jan 1981 (both as transcribed on Find a Grave)
EXTRA.note: Lead: no vital record seen for any of the three.

EXTRA.name: Hagansport Cemetery
EXTRA.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas
EXTRA.title: Where Hagansport buried its dead
EXTRA.hook: The cemetery where John B. Smith and Emma Langley lie holds about 250 graves, begun in the 1880s.
body: A county history describes the cemetery: "Hagansport Cemetery is in the Hagansport Community and has around 250 graves. Burials probably started in the 1880's. The people of the community had probably used the Pierces Chapel Cemetery previous to the start of Hagansport Cemetery."

The earliest marked grave is Laura Terry's, born 13 June 1870 and died 13 October 1876. Smaller family burying places nearby, now lost, include the Cannon cemetery two miles south of Hagansport and the Singleton cemetery two miles northeast, where "there were once about ten wooden stakes marking gravesites."

Emma Langley Smith, who died on 15 March 1905, and John B. Smith, who died in 1918 and whose grave was marked with a wooden stob, were buried here. Some of John B. and Emma's children also grew up here: Charles Oscar Smith and his sisters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie and brother Jimmie are the children recorded in 1900.
EXTRA.src: Historical Records of Franklin County, Texas (B. F. Hicks and Doris Meek, 1967-72), cemetery descriptions at https://www.txgenwebcounties.net/franklin/cemetery.htm; 1900 U.S. Census, Franklin Co., Tex.

EXTRA.name: Satterfield Cemetery, Jetson
EXTRA.place: Jetson, Butler County, Kentucky
EXTRA.title: A Butler County burying ground with the family's name
EXTRA.hook: At least five of the Satterfield and Johnson kin are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson, Kentucky.
body: Satterfield Cemetery lies at Jetson, Butler County. Among those buried there are Sidney Rufus Satterfield (1865-1949), his wife Eliza "Ancie" Johnson (1871-1951), their infant Walter (1890), Ancie's father James P. Johnson (1840-1884) and her mother Martha J. Clark Johnson (1839-1923).

The cemetery is the burial place of those who stayed. John C. and Samantha moved to Texas about 1907; Sidney and Ancie stayed on the farm country of Butler and Warren counties, and Sidney died at Richardsville, Warren County, in 1949.
The Satterfields buried here are the sons and daughters of James H. Satterfield, who farmed in Butler County from 1876 and, by his own 1885 account, owned 1,340 acres there.
kv: Sidney R. and Ancie Satterfield; James P. and Martha J. Johnson; Walter Satterfield
EXTRA.src: Find a Grave memorial 19774914, 19774910, 19786592 and 19786602; Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), p. 676

EXTRA.name: Wheelock Cemetery, Millerton
EXTRA.rel: Place the family buried Oscar Hulsey
EXTRA.place: Wheelock, near Millerton, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, the old Choctaw mission ground where Oscar Franklin Hulsey was buried in June 1982.
kv: Wheelock mission ground, 2 miles northeast of Millerton, McCurtain Co., Okla.
Oscar Franklin Hulsey, funeral at 2 p.m. on the Sunday, reported in the McCurtain Gazette of 20 Jun 1982
No Wheelock transcription is posted in the McCurtain County USGenWeb cemetery files, so Oscar's stone is not confirmed by a published listing
Missionaries of the 1830s-1850s, e.g. Rev. Alfred Wright, d. 31 March 1853
EXTRA.src: R. E. Flickinger, The Choctaw Freedmen and the Story of Oak Hill Industrial Academy (1914), p. 22 (archive.org/details/choctawfreed00flick); Chronicles of Oklahoma 25:3 (Autumn 1947) and 26:3 (Autumn 1948); McCurtain Gazette, 20 June 1982 (obituary of Oscar Hulsey, quoted in his entry); McCurtain County cemetery files, USGenWeb Archives (files.usgwarchives.net/ok/mccurtain/cemeteries/, no Wheelock file)
EXTRA.title: Buried among the missionaries at Wheelock
EXTRA.hook: Oscar Hulsey's funeral in 1982 was held at a mission graveyard where stones from the 1850s still stand.
body: Wheelock was a Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws. Its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, who removed to the Choctaws' new land in October 1832, and the buildings stood about two miles northeast of the later town of Millerton. A 1914 book on the neighborhood says what remained: 'the two mission school buildings, a strongly built stone church 30 by 50 feet, a two story parsonage and cemetery.'

The same book copies one stone from the graveyard: 'Sacred to the memory of the Rev. Alfred Wright who entered into his heavenly rest March 31, 1853, age 65 years. Born in Columbia, Connecticut, March 1, 1788. Appointed Missionary to the Choctaws 1820. Removed to this land October, 1832. Organized Wheelock Church December, 1832. Received to its fellowship 570 members.' In 1947 the Oklahoma Historical Society's journal listed Wheelock among the state's 'historic old cemeteries ... that offer much fine material.'

Oscar Franklin Hulsey died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71. His funeral was held at 2 p.m. at Wheelock Cemetery with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was laid there in a graveyard where, a teacher at the mission school wrote of a three-year-old's burial there in the 1890s, the child was placed 'beside missionaries who had passed away half a century before.'
His wife Katie is buried at Mount Olivet in Hugo.

EXTRA.name: Mount Olivet Cemetery, Hugo
EXTRA.rel: Place the family buried Frank, Parsis and Katie
EXTRA.place: Hugo, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Frank and Parsis Jane Stevenson and their daughter Katie Hulsey are buried.
kv: 1907, as Burgoyne Cemetery (Choctaw County cemetery list; Association for Gravestone Studies newsletter)
Main entrance at 8th Street and Trice, Hugo; Sec. 29, T6S, R17E
STEVENSON Frank N. 1860-1950; STEVENSON Parsis Jane 1887-1956, Block 2
Buried here after services 2 Feb 2009; too recent for the 2000 canvass
EXTRA.src: Choctaw County, Oklahoma, Mount Olivet Cemetery, Block 2 (Upper and Lower), canvassed 2000 by Ron Henson (USGenWeb Archives, files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/mtolivet/block2.txt); Cemeteries of Choctaw County Oklahoma, Ron Henson, USGenWeb Archives (files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/cemchoc.txt); Newsletter of the Association for Gravestone Studies (Showmen's Rest article), archive.org/details/newsletterofasso1422asso; obituary of Katie Hulsey, 2009
EXTRA.title: Two Stevenson stones in Block 2
EXTRA.hook: Frank and Parsis Stevenson lie side by side at Hugo's Mount Olivet, with one birth year on a stone listing that cannot be right.
body: Mount Olivet is Hugo's old municipal cemetery. It was 'Originally called Burgoyne Cemetery' and dates to 1907, 'very nearly to the town's beginning.' It is better known as the home of Showmen's Rest, the circus performers' section dedicated in 1961, with its granite dancing elephant at the entrance.

A listing of Block 2 made in 2000 reads: 'Stevenson  Frank N.  1860  1950' and 'Stevenson  Parsis Jane  1887  1956.' These are stones for Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' Stevenson, who died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, and for his wife Parsis Jane.

Two points need care. The listing gives Frank's birth as 1860, while his family record and a photograph of his stone have 17 November 1861; his 1870 and 1880 census ages fit 1861 or 1862, and the middle initial N is not in his known name. Parsis Jane's death year, 1956, matches the family record, but a birth in 1887 is impossible for the mother of children born from 1884; a photograph of her stone reads 1868, so the listed 1887 is a misreading or comes from another marker. It gives no inscriptions beyond names and years.
Their daughter Katie Cornelia Hulsey died on 30 January 2009, with burial at Mount Olivet. That is nine years after the listing, so her stone is not in it.

EXTRA.name: Shoat Springs Cemetery: the Moffitt graves
EXTRA.rel: Place where Grady and Mary Moffitt and three of their sons are buried
EXTRA.place: South of Hugo, Choctaw County, Oklahoma (3 miles east of SH 93 on US 70, then 2.75 miles south on Fallon Road).
kv: Feb 16, 1921 - Aug 25, 1947; OK SC1C USNR WWII
EXTRA.src: Shoat Springs Cemetery, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, transcription by Tammy Sharp and Karla K. Willis Sharp (USGenWeb Archives, files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/shoatesprings.txt); Cemeteries of Choctaw County Oklahoma, Ron Henson, USGenWeb Archives (files.usgwarchives.net/ok/choctaw/cemeteries/cemchoc.txt)
EXTRA.title: Five Moffitt stones at Shoat Springs
EXTRA.hook: The cemetery list confirms the dates of Grady, Mary and three of the boys they buried.
body: Five Moffitt entries stand in a row at Shoat Springs: 'Moffitt, Dois L. -- Feb 16, 1921 - Aug 25, 1947; OK SC1C USNR WWII', 'Moffitt, Jimmie Gaynell -- Jan 17, 1923 - Oct 26, 1926', 'Moffitt, Henry Wayne -- Jan 13, 1934 - May 12, 1937', and 'Moffitt, Woodford Grady -- Nov 6, 1891 - Jun 21, 1972; Mary Tinsley -- Jun 4, 1895 - Aug 26, 1962.'

These match the dates already in the family record. Dois's date of 25 August 1947 is the date on his Texas death record, four days after the Red River accident of 21 August. The rating on his stone, SC1C, is Ship's Cook First Class in the U.S. Naval Reserve, the job he held through the war.
Jimmie Gaynell and Henry Wayne were each three; their parents joined them in 1962 and 1972. The cemetery lies in the community of Hugo.
Only names and dates are recorded, with no epitaphs.

EXTRA.name: Cane Creek Friends burial ground
EXTRA.rel: Place the Chamness and Moffitt Quaker ancestors worshipped
EXTRA.place: Cane Creek Meeting, Snow Camp, Alamance County, North Carolina.
kv: 26 acres and a house, 14 Feb 1764, 'for the use and benefit of Cane Creek Meeting' (trustees Peter Stout, Jeremiah and Benjamin Piggott, David Vestal)
Large stone placed 1975 for Anthony and Sarah Chamness
Not individually confirmed: early Friends graves were unmarked and no grave list for William Moffitt, Mary Davies or Sarah Cole appears in this source
EXTRA.src: From Whence We Came: Cane Creek Meeting Sesquibicentennial Reunion (Snow Camp, N.C., c. 2000), archive.org/details/fromwhencewecame00cane
EXTRA.title: The meeting ground where the Chamness stone stands
EXTRA.hook: Anthony Chamness has a 1975 memorial in the Cane Creek cemetery, placed by descendants, not a stone of his own day.
body: On 14 February 1764 William Marshall transferred 26 acres on Cane Creek, next to Simon Dixon's mill dam, to the trustees Peter Stout, Jeremiah Piggott, Benjamin Piggott and David Vestal 'for the use and benefit of Cane Creek Meeting.' The account adds: 'This is the property where the Meeting House and burial grounds are presently located.' A separate Marshall account says William and Rebecca Marshall gave the 26 acres and the house on it.

Of Anthony Chamness it is said: 'In 1975 friends and family erected a large stone in the Cane Creek Meeting's cemetery to commemorate these early pioneers and their devoted service to the Cane Creek congregation.' It dates him 'circa 1713-1777,' says he and Sarah Cole 'were among the first overseers of the Cane Creek Meeting,' and notes that his will was made on 24 November 1776. 'Chamness descendants still come yearly to stroll between the quiet graves.'
The same book says British troops took over the meeting-house during the Revolution and 'some English soldiers are buried in the cemetery.'

The memorial stone is a modern commemoration. It is not said where Anthony, Sarah, William Moffitt or Mary Davies lie, and Quaker burials of that time were commonly unmarked, so those graves remain unlocated.

EXTRA.name: Breashears Cemetery, Story
EXTRA.rel: Place the family buried Rev. G. W. Hulsey
EXTRA.place: 1.25 miles east of Story, Montgomery County, Arkansas, on Red Ridge Road, a quarter mile off Highway 298.
kv: 1.25 miles east of Story on Red Ridge Road, in a fenced field
Online list (2008, 139 names); Montgomery County Cemetery Records (1986, 117 names; 1998 edition); 106 graves unmarked
Four Hulsey headstones counted; the posted photo study does not list which
EXTRA.src: Montgomery County ARGenWeb, 'Breashears Cemetery, Story' (argenweb.net/montgomery/breashears_cemetery.htm; photo study, June 2020); Find a Grave index (Breashears Cemetery), as cited in the entries for Benjamin F. and G. W. Hulsey
EXTRA.title: A small graveyard with four Hulsey stones
EXTRA.hook: Both Benjamin and George Washington Hulsey are said to rest at Breashears, but no list names them.
body: Breashears Cemetery lies east of the Montgomery County town of Story, in a field off a gravel road, 'fenced, with a bench under the shade of an old tree.' It has been transcribed at least three times, most recently with 139 names, and an earlier count recorded 117 names and 106 unmarked graves.

The stones are counted by surname: 'Breashears (15), ... Holmes (7), Hulsey (4), ... Kilby (10), Lamb (12), Lenderman (9) ...,' with the majority belonging to eight families. The Hulsey stones are not itemized.

Rev. George Washington Hulsey (d. 5 August 1935, age 58) and Benjamin Franklin Hulsey (d. 16 December 1924), whom family accounts make his father, are the two Hulseys the family has placed here. The four-stone count is consistent with that, but nothing confirms either name. Other burials listed there show the kind of neighbors who surround them: Rev. H. H. Holmes (July 2, 1863 - May 15, 1935, 'The Lord is my shepherd'), M. R. Lenderman (1858-1935) and Gertrude A. Breashears (1881-1952, 'Mother is Resting').
No church is named for the cemetery.

EXTRA.rel: Place the Stevenson preachers were buried
EXTRA.place: Bee Spring Methodist church, about 3 miles northeast of Bryson and 15 miles southeast of Pulaski, Tennessee.
kv: 1815 by Rev. Elam Stevenson, with Stephen Loyd, Meshack Boice and James McCowan
1855, a frame church 36x50 ft; building committee included J. G. Stevenson
Night of 29 April 1909 by a tornado
'All that remains of this today is the cemetery, sadly neglected'
Bee Spring Cemetery list, Giles Co. TNGenWeb: about 75 Stevenson entries (not in the Giles County USGenWeb archive index, which lists Campbell, Diana, Doster and Shane only)
EXTRA.src: History of Methodist Churches and Institutions in Middle Tennessee, 1787-1956 (1956), 'Bee Spring Memorial' by Sterling E. Stovall, historian (archive.org/details/historyofmethodi00cart); Rev. Elam Stevenson in McFerrin, History of Methodism in Tennessee, vol. 2 (1871), account of Bee Spring (archive.org/details/historymethodis00mcfegoog); Giles County Archives index (usgwarchives.net/tn/giles/gilcems.html); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); The Pulaski Citizen, 30 May 1878, p. 1
EXTRA.title: What is left of Bee Spring is the graveyard
EXTRA.hook: The church where Elam Stevenson preached for decades was blown down in 1909; by 1956 only the cemetery survived, neglected.
body: The Methodist history of middle Tennessee says the original Bee Spring church 'was organized in 1815 by Rev. Elam Stevenson,' son of a Revolutionary captain (a rank the militia record does not support), who 'professed religion in 1804,' united with the church in 1806, was licensed to preach in 1813 and 'the same year moved to Tennessee.' The first house was logs; a larger log church followed in 1822 or 1823, and a frame church in 1855 whose building committee included J. G. Stevenson. Its members were 'largely the families of the McClaurines, Loyds, McGuires, Sherrills, Moseleys, Bruces, Rowes, and Stevensons.'

Elam's own 1869 account mentions the church-yard: Rev. Meshach Boyce, who helped build the first house, 'died in the faith, and his dust now sleeps in our church-yard at Bee Spring.' A visitor in 1878 wrote that 'here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort.' Elam had bought the fifteen acres for the church for $20 in 1815.

'On the night of April 29, 1909, the Bee Springs Memorial Methodist Church was totally destroyed by the memorable and terrible tornado which passed through this section of Giles and Lincoln Counties.' The congregation rebuilt at Bryson, three miles away. Of the old site the 1956 history says: 'All that remains of this today is the cemetery, sadly neglected.'

About seventy-five Stevenson graves are listed for Bee Spring. The tall stone over Elam and Lydia reads, on Elam’s side, “Erected to the memory of Reverend Elam Stevenson, born September 24, 1787, died March 13, 1875. Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life.” On the back: “Erected to the memory of Lydia Stevenson, born August 16, 1787, died March 6, 1872. Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church.”

Some years were hard. In the summer of 1854 Citty died on 20 June, Elam R. on 2 August and William B. F. on 19 August. In the winter of 1856 Louisa (Coleman’s young wife) died on 1 February, Joseph J. on 15 February, Ann Eliza on 2 March and James Elisha on 3 March. An “infant” is dated 6 October 1831 (the first child of William and Malinda), and several more are listed only as “child” or “infant.” No causes of death are given, and which Stevenson household each child belonged to is not always known.

Elam’s sons and their wives lie near him. Rev. Abner A. Stevenson (d. 1896) is listed with his wife Martha S. (Still Watson, 1823-1887, who died on 12 July 1887); his brother Rev. James C. (23 June 1813 to 23 February 1899) lies beside Margaret Caroline (8 December 1816 to 11 February 1886); Willis McKendree is there (18 January 1818 to 6 February 1900), as are Coleman L. (1832-1908), with Dorcas (1832-1892), and Thomas C. (1825-1906). The congregation buried a Stevenson as late as 1994.

EXTRA.name: Robert and Margaret (Stuart) Moffitt's sons
EXTRA.rel: The family 5th great-grandfather William Moffitt came from
EXTRA.place: Donegal, Ireland; Philadelphia; Chatham and Randolph counties, North Carolina
EXTRA.title: Six brothers and the road from Donegal
EXTRA.hook: Two family records agree that Moffitt sons left Donegal for Philadelphia and went on to the North Carolina Piedmont, and they disagree about which brother came first.
body: Two family accounts tell the Moffitt crossing, and they do not match in every detail. The Bible record of Abijah Moffitt says Robert Moffitt was born in Scotland, went to Ireland when young, and married Margaret Stuart there. It names eleven children: James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Mary, Catheren, Robert, Hugh, John and Patrick. In that record John crossed first, went back to Ireland, and returned to Philadelphia with five brothers.

A Moffitt genealogy of 1928 has the wedding of "Robert Moffat to Margaret Stuart at Moffat Wells, Scotland" about 1750, and then: "After their marriage, Robert and Margaret migrated to Donegal County, Ireland." It names the same eleven children and says "all but Catharine and Patrick emigrated to America." On the crossing it gives a different brother: "According to tradition, William came first, alone, and went back. Being pleased with the country, he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time. Later they went to Chatham or Randolph County, N. C."

The Donegal end has no parish or townland. The one piece of background that fits a bride named Stuart is an old history that says that in "eastern Donegal" the Cunninghams and the Stewarts "settled" colonists "from Ayrshire and Galloway." That places Scots-Irish Presbyterians of her surname in the county; it does not place Margaret's own family.

The Carolina end is on record. At Cane Creek Meeting in 1763 William married Mary Davies and, in the family's account, his brother Hugh married her sister Hannah, which shows the brothers had joined the Quaker neighborhood of Charles Davies rather than a Presbyterian one. The counties give a sense of how little the family needed to move. Orange was formed in 1752 from Johnston, Bladen and Granville; Chatham in 1770 from Orange; Guilford in 1770 from Rowan and Orange; and Randolph in 1779 from Guilford. A household on one stretch of the upper Deep River could have been written into the Orange court records in 1765, the Chatham records in the 1770s and the Randolph records in 1796, the year William made his will, without anyone leaving home, if the family stayed put.

The surname spelling is the family's own explanation. The 1928 book says the brothers agreed to end the name in -itt so that kin could recognize each other wherever it turned up. North Carolina papers of the 1760s write Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt interchangeably, so the story is tradition, not record.
EXTRA.src: Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt (quoted on WikiTree, Moffitt-65); Frank Moffitt, Moffitt Genealogy: Silas Moffitt and Hannah Wilkinson Moffitt (1928), pp. 1-3, archive.org/details/moffittgenealogy00moff; J. A. Hanna, The Scotch-Irish (1902), archive.org/details/scotchirishorsco01hann_0; D. L. Corbitt, The Formation of the North Carolina Counties 1663-1943, archive.org/details/formationofnorth00corb (Orange, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph entries)

quotes.t: According to tradition, William came first, alone, and went back. Being pleased with the country, he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time. Later they went to Chatham or Randolph County, N. C.
quotes.c: Moffitt Genealogy (1928), p. 2-3

quotes.t: Randolph was formed in 1779 from Guilford.
quotes.c: Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties

EXTRA.note: The two family accounts disagree on who crossed first (John in the Bible Record, William in the 1928 book) and on whether Robert's wife was Margaret or, in the Alamance Battleground book, Martha. No Donegal parish record has been seen.

EXTRA.name: Hugh Moffitt
EXTRA.rel: Possible brother of 5th great-grandfather William Moffitt
EXTRA.place: Chatham County, North Carolina; possible move to Ohio
EXTRA.title: Hugh Moffitt plans a move west
EXTRA.hook: In 1799 Hugh prepared to leave North Carolina with his family; a later family account says he died near Chillicothe, Ohio.
body: The Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt says "William and Hugh married Davis daughters of North Carolina," and the 1928 Moffitt Genealogy names the wives as Mary and Hannah. In an 1853 letter, Joseph Moffitt named his father Hugh, mother Hannah Davis, and Hugh's brother William. Joseph also said Hannah's sister Mary married a Moffitt; identifying that man as the William in our Randolph County line remains an inference.

A transcribed will dated 1 October 1799 identifies Hugh Moffit of Chatham County, names his wife Hannah and son Joseph, and says he had disposed of his affairs in order to move with his family to the Northwest Territory. It also names six of the brothers Joseph later listed in his letter. These overlapping details strongly support identifying the will and letter with the same Hugh, though neither the will nor the letter has been seen in the original.

The later Bible record says Hugh went to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and died near Chillicothe about 1800. The 1799 will supports an intended move and is consistent with a departure later that year, but makes a definite 1798 departure doubtful. Neither the will nor Joseph's letter establishes that Hugh completed the journey or died in Ohio; those details rest on family tradition.

In 1798 Westfield Monthly Meeting in Guilford County sought advice on members moving to the Scioto River, and Cane Creek certificates to Ohio began in 1804. This is context for movement west, but it does not name Hugh or establish his route.
EXTRA.src: Hugh Moffit will, 1 October 1799, Chatham County Will Book A, p. 189b, transcription: https://www.ncgenweb.us/chatham/court/wills_lmn.html; Joseph Moffitt letter, 4 August 1853, printed in The Nebraska and Midwest Genealogical Record, July 1924, p. 130: https://negenweb.net/NEHolt/The_Nebraska_and_Midwest_Genealogical_Re.pdf#page=139; Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt (WikiTree Moffitt-65); Moffitt Genealogy (1928), p. 3; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 256 and 265, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week
EXTRA.note: The 1799 will records a planned move, not a completed journey. The 1853 letter and the will identify the same immediate family, but the original documents and an Ohio death or burial record have not been seen. The connection to William Moffitt and Mary Davies is supported by family testimony and later genealogy, but remains a lead.

EXTRA.name: Silas and Hannah (Wilkinson) Moffitt
EXTRA.rel: Cousin of 4th great-grandfather Robert Moffitt; Hannah was Robert's niece
EXTRA.place: Randolph County, North Carolina to Hamilton County, Indiana
EXTRA.title: Silas Moffitt's wagon: Randolph County to Hamilton County, October 1823
EXTRA.hook: A first cousin of our Robert Moffitt rode ahead to Indiana in 1822, built a cabin, and brought his wife and two children north in a single wagon in the fall of 1823.
body: Silas Moffitt (1794-1873) was the son of Charles Moffitt, one of William Moffitt's brothers, and Mary Cox; our Robert Moffitt was William's son, so the two were first cousins. Silas married Hannah Wilkinson (1799-1886) in Randolph County, North Carolina, on 4 May 1820. Hannah was the daughter of William Wilkinson, an Englishman, and Mary Moffitt, William Moffitt's daughter, who married on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795 by the family's account. That makes Hannah Robert's niece, and Silas her first cousin once removed.

The 1928 genealogy says the son-in-law and father-in-law "both seemed to think the Northwest Territory offered them better opportunities, so two years after the wedding they started for Indiana on horseback in quest of their future homes." The land "was bought direct from the government, and so far as is known, most of it was bought in Wilkinson's name." They built "rude cabins" and went back for the families. Wilkinson, "unable to return the following year," died in Carolina before he could make the trip, and his family left soon after.

Silas and Hannah, "with their two children Mary and Charles, along with another family whose names have been lost, made the trip in the early fall and reached the site of their future home on the 8th day of the golden month of October, 1823." A county history says: "The family made the trip from North Carolina with a four-horse team and all their possessions in one wagon." Their eldest son Charles W. was born in North Carolina only weeks before they started.

They lived in the log cabin for three years. Then Silas built a brick house out of brick he made himself, the second brick house in the township. When he died on 28 August 1873, nearly 79 and a few weeks short of fifty years on the place, he owned several hundred acres and had served as county commissioner and for two terms as treasurer of the township trustees. It was said that he "lived and labored for half a century on the old Moffitt homestead." He and Hannah are buried in Carmel Cemetery. The Wilkinsons owned land, slaves and a tan yard, and the family left a slaveholding county for a free state, the same road hundreds of Carolina Quaker families took.
EXTRA.src: Moffitt Genealogy: Silas Moffitt and Hannah Wilkinson Moffitt (1928), pp. 3-5, quoting Haines, History of Hamilton County, Indiana, archive.org/details/moffittgenealogy00moff; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896)

quotes.t: The family made the trip from North Carolina with a four-horse team and all their possessions in one wagon.
quotes.c: Haines, Hamilton County history, quoted in the Moffitt Genealogy (1928)

EXTRA.note: Compiled 1928 family book quoting a county history; no North Carolina or Indiana deed has been checked.

EXTRA.name: Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies; Edward and Elizabeth (Brown) Norton
EXTRA.rel: 6th great-grandparents (Mary Davies Moffitt's parents) and 6th great-grandparents (Margaret Norton Chamness's parents)
EXTRA.place: Radnor and Goshen, Pennsylvania; Hopewell and Fairfax, Virginia; Cane Creek, North Carolina
EXTRA.title: Two Quaker families, one road: Davies and Norton to Cane Creek
EXTRA.hook: A Welsh-named indentured servant and an Irish Quaker's son took the same Pennsylvania-Virginia-Carolina road, twelve years apart.
body: Charles Davies and Hannah Matson were married in the twelfth month (February) of 1732/3 under a Radnor Monthly Meeting certificate, which places the wedding at the house of Charles Read, a Philadelphia justice of the peace. Charles Davies was an immigrant to Pennsylvania about 1725, and from there went to North Carolina. Hannah was "daughter of John Matson of Merion"; the family's own note in the back of the Cane Creek minute book says Charles "was brought over the ocean and sold to pay his passage." The Davies surname, with its alternate spelling Davis, is Welsh, and Radnor and Merion were Welsh townships in the Quaker settlement west of Philadelphia.

From Pennsylvania the couple went to Virginia. A certificate "having been made for Charles Davis and Hannah, his wife to Hopewell Monthly Meeting" is minuted, but the early Hopewell minutes were burned, so the exact year of the move is lost. Charles and Hannah were charter members of Cane Creek Monthly Meeting and moved "in or before 1750." Cane Creek was set up in the tenth month of 1751; Orange County, in which the land fell, was cut from Johnston, Bladen and Granville in 1752. Charles bought 187 acres from Henry McCullogh on 2 August 1758 and died in 1801.

Edward Norton's son, also Edward, was the other traveler. His 1739 marriage at West Nottingham Meeting names his father as "Edward Norton, dec., of the County & Parish of Armagh, in the Kingdome of Ireland." The Nortons are said to have moved to Hopewell in Virginia, then to Fairfax, and reached Cane Creek in 1762, the year before their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness. A Quaker historian describes exactly this stream: in 1754, the first year of New Garden Monthly Meeting, "we have settlers coming in from Pennsylvania, from Hopewell and Fairfax meetings, Virginia," and concludes that "the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants, not by the expansion of the native element."

Those two sentences are the family's story in small. The Davieses reached Cane Creek about 1750, the Chamnesses in 1749-51, and the Nortons in 1762. By 1763 the three families met at the meetinghouse for two weddings, sixteen days apart: Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton on 17 March, William Moffitt and Mary Davies on 2 April.
