EXTRA.name: Giles County in the Civil War
EXTRA.place: Pulaski and Bee Spring, Giles County, Tennessee
kv: Giles County, Tenn.; Pulaski, Elkton, Prospect, Lynnville
Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and wife Martha; son Gilbert b. 17 Nov 1861 near Pulaski
Bee Spring (listed in the Twentieth Civil District)
EXTRA.src: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, pp. 758-760 and church list in the district descriptions, p. 766 (archive.org: historyoftenness00good).
EXTRA.title: Soldiers on the road to Huntsville: Giles County, 1862-1863
EXTRA.hook: Abner Stevenson's son Gilbert was five months old when the first Federal troops marched into Pulaski.
body: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born near Pulaski on 17 November 1861, to Rev. Abner Stevenson and Martha. A county history says what the next four years were like around the family farm. "The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala. Pulaski, Lynnville, Elkton and Prospect were each visited by Federal troops in large numbers, and Pulaski and Lynnville were fortified." On Fort Hill above Pulaski "a formidable fort or earth-work was erected."

The first Federals to come in any number arrived in April 1862, when Col. Mark Monday brought a detachment of Gen. Negley's brigade from Columbia to drive off John Morgan's cavalry, who were plundering the Federal wagon trains. Gilbert was then about five months old. Monday camped at Pulaski until September 1862. In August 1863 Col. Hayes raided the county with a regiment of cavalry and camped a day and a night in Pulaski. In the same year, in the history's words, "Lynnville and Elkton were both raided by the Federals, the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain."

That October Gen. Wheeler retreated south through the county with Gen. Wilder after him, and in November "Gen. W. T. Sherman and his entire army passed through Giles County, en route to Chattanooga, making a short stop at Elkton." Bee Spring, the Methodist church Elam Stevenson helped found, stood in the Twentieth Civil District with Mount Pisgah and Mount Zion.

The history does not name Abner's household. It gives the setting: a Methodist preacher with a farm, a wife, and a new baby on a road that three armies used. Abner's nephews Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served the other side from their own farms nearby, in the 32nd Tennessee.

quotes.t: The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, p. 759

quotes.t: the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, p. 759

EXTRA.note: Place story. It describes the county, not any raid on the Stevenson farm; no source seen says what Abner's family lost or did.

EXTRA.name: John Milton Garrison and the Kentucky General Assembly
EXTRA.place: Warren, later Allen County, Kentucky
kv: 4 Oct 1788, Cowans Ford, Mecklenburg Co., N.C. (WikiTree)
6 Dec 1809, Wilson Co., Tenn., Patsey Cannon
One slave counted in the household (WikiTree transcription)
Act of the General Assembly, session of 1847-48, p. 410, sec. 6
EXTRA.src: Acts passed at the session of the General Assembly for the Commonwealth of Kentucky (1847-48), p. 410, sec. 6 and index (archive.org: actspassedatses72kentgoog); WikiTree Garrison-4365 (biography and census transcriptions) and Cannon-4655.
EXTRA.title: One enslaved person in 1810, and a divorce by act of the legislature in 1848
EXTRA.hook: John M. Garrison's household counted a slave in 1810. Thirty-eight years later the legislature ended his marriage, and he is said to have married the neighbor woman he had children with.
body: John Milton Garrison was born on 4 October 1788 at Cowans Ford in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, and came as a boy with his parents to Warren County, Kentucky. On 6 December 1809 he married Martha "Patsey" Cannon in Wilson County, Tennessee. Their daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield and is the Garrison link into the Satterfields.

Slavery. In 1810 "John M Garreson" in Warren County had a household of five that included one enslaved person, a man of about 21. In 1820, 1830 and 1840 his Allen County household (7, 11 and 7 people) held none. In 1850 he was 62, a farmer, with real estate valued at $2,250. Whether he held anyone after 1810 is not known.

The marriage ended in the legislature, by statute. The Kentucky legislature's act of 1847-48 read: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." It gives no reason.

One family account gives a reason, without a source. It says that during the marriage he "fathered children by Sarah Stamps who lived nearby," that he "had the KY legislature declare those children legitimate," and that after the divorce he married Sarah. In 1850 J. M. Garrison, 62, lived with an "S" aged 57 and three younger Garrisons aged 21, 19 and 6. The legitimation act has not been found, so that part is unconfirmed. He died in Allen County on 18 September 1860.

quotes.t: That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons.
quotes.c: Acts of the General Assembly of Kentucky, session of 1847-48, p. 410, sec. 6

EXTRA.note: The divorce is proven by the printed act. The 1810 slave count is a WikiTree transcription (probable). The Sarah Stamps children and their legitimation are a lead: WikiTree states them without a source and the act was not found.

EXTRA.name: Renting on shares at Hagansport, 1908
EXTRA.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas
kv: U.S. Bureau of Soils, Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas, 1908
Tenant furnishing everything: half the crop
EXTRA.src: A. E. Kocher and W. S. Lyman, Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas, in Field Operations of the Bureau of Soils, 1908 (USDA, 1909), pp. 931-947; archive.org: usda-soil-survey-of-franklin-county-texas-1908.
EXTRA.title: What a rented farm at Hagansport meant in 1910
EXTRA.hook: The government's 1908 soil survey says what tenants paid, what the land near Hagansport grew, and why the north end of the county was held back.
body: In April 1910 John C. Satterfield, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, and John B. Smith and Emma Liza Langley Smith had farmed there in 1900. The U.S. Bureau of Soils surveyed Franklin County in 1908 and wrote about farming in just that corner, without naming any family.

On renting, the survey says that "the rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops. When the tenant furnishes only the labor he is given one-third of the corn and one-fourth of the cotton." In 1900 only 44.1 percent of the county's farms were run by their owners, and the average farm was 77.9 acres. Most land could be bought for $5 to $10 an acre, more in the Sulphur River bottoms. The authors add that "since that date many of the tenants have acquired title."

On Hagansport itself: the town sits on a divide between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, with bodies of Wilson clay loam "in the vicinity of Hagansport and Lavada." The survey calls that soil "somewhat better adapted to cotton than to corn," says it was nearly all in cultivation, and gives the cotton yield as "from one-third to three-fourths bale per acre." The bottoms along the river were "more or less subject to overflow." Of the north end of the county, the survey says: "Other small centers in the northern part of the county are Daphne, Lavada, and Hagansport. In this part of the county development is seriously hindered by the absence of adequate shipping facilities."
This is a general portrait. It does not say whether the Smiths owned or rented, or whether the Satterfields farmed on halves or thirds, but it describes the terms on which families like them worked.

quotes.t: The rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops.
quotes.c: Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas (1908), p. 931

EXTRA.note: The soil survey describes the area, not an individual ancestor; the family details come from census records.

imgs.cap: Soil map, Franklin County sheet, Texas, from the U.S. Bureau of Soils survey of 1908 (Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas; Field Operations of the Bureau of Soils, 1908, published 1909). Hagansport lies in the north between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, with Mount Vernon to the south. U.S. government publication, public domain; Internet Archive scan, downscaled only

EXTRA.name: The fifteen children of Abner and Martha Stevenson
EXTRA.rel: Brothers and sisters of 2nd great-grandfather Frank Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee, with branches in Alabama, Arkansas and Texas
EXTRA.title: Fifteen children at Bee Spring
EXTRA.hook: Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a farming preacher, and a twin; eleven of them were under one roof in 1870.
body: Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson were married on 8 December 1838. Their fifteen children, all born in Giles County, were Lucinda C. (3 May 1840), William Elam Fletcher (9 April 1842), Lydia Mary Eliza (20 December 1843), Catherine M. Frances (10 January 1846), Augustus Summerfield (30 October 1847), Ellen Tillman and James Willis (twins, 30 January 1850), Larkin Henry (12 October 1852), Amanda Elizabeth (21 October 1854), Julia Ann Desdemona (July 1857), John Edward Thomas (16 September 1859), the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington (both 17 November 1861), Wilson McAlister (15 August 1864) and Manerva Jane (22 July 1866).

In 1870 the household in District 10 held A. A. Stevenson, 54, Martha, 47, and eleven children: Lucinda 28, James 20, Ellen 20, Larkin 18, Amanda 16, Julia A. 14, John E. 12, George W. 8, Gilbert 8, Mack 5 and Manerva J. 3. The two eight-year-olds are the twins. By 1880 the house was nearly empty: Abner, 63, "Farming Preacher," Martha, 56, Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16 and Jane M., 12, with three hired or fostered Whittaker children and a one-year-old grandchild named Berry Andrew, born in Alabama. The Andrew grandchild was probably the youngest son of Abner's daughter Eliza, who had died in November 1878.

Several of the dates agree with the Bee Spring graveyard. W. Mack Stevenson lies there, born 15 August 1864 and dead 30 June 1940, which matches Wilson McAlister. Nathan A. Stevenson, 12 November 1870 to 21 July 1936, is Abner's grandson Nathaniel, William's son. Werner W. Stevenson, 4 March 1880 to 23 June 1974, is James Willis's son. Abner himself lies there, as does Martha S., 19 February 1823 to 12 July 1887.

The children scattered. Lucinda married Perry Pittman Williams and died in 1920; Eliza Mary married John Newton Andrew on 20 December 1870 and died in 1878; Frances married J. M. Whitaker and died on 18 April 1889; Summerfield went to Arkansas and was buried near Crowley's Ridge; Ellen married James Marion Britton; Julia went to Texas as John Newton Andrew's third Stevenson wife; Edward died in El Paso; George, by family account, became a judge at Lubbock; James Willis became a Methodist minister; Manerva married Andrew R. Merrill and moved to Ardmore, Tennessee. Frank went to Indiana.
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com) for Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558), Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Daniel Waters O'Neal (O'Neal-2667), with the 1870, 1880 and 1910 census transcriptions printed there; Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Goodspeed list of Elam Stevenson's children, p. 872.
EXTRA.note: The Casey family history names the fifteen children and their births; the 1870 and 1880 census households and the cemetery dates fit it, but the family history has no sources for the exact days.

quotes.t: Farming Preacher
quotes.c: Abner A. Stevenson's occupation, 1880 U.S. census, 10th District, Giles County, Tennessee

EXTRA.name: George W. and Edward Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Texas
EXTRA.title: Two Stevenson brothers go to Texas
EXTRA.hook: One brother, by family tradition a judge at Lubbock and the father of thirteen; another died of smallpox at El Paso in June 1886, working for the railway.
body: Frank Stevenson had a twin. George Washington Stevenson was born on the same day, 17 November 1861, and in 1870 both were 8 years old in the same Giles County household. In May 1881 it was noted that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." It is said that George later lived at Lubbock, Texas, where he was a judge, and that he was the father of thirteen children. It names none of them. Lubbock County's county judges for those years (Shannon, Brown, Crump and Bean, 1891 to 1906) include no Stevenson, so if he held a bench it was not that one.

John Edward Thomas Stevenson, born on 16 September 1859, was "John E," 12, in 1870. It is said that Edward "moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway" and "died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886." He would have been 26. The Texas and Pacific reached El Paso in 1881, so the job fits the date.

The pull of Texas runs through this family. In January 1881 their father "abandoned the idea of going to Texas." Their sister Julia Ann followed her husband John Newton Andrew there, and by the 1870s their sister Ellen Britton's growing family was moving between Giles County and Texas. When Frank and Parsis lived there in the 1890s and 1900s, three of their children were born in Texas.

quotes.t: Edward Stevenson moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway. Edward Stevenson died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886.
quotes.c: Casey family history, Master Publication 3-109

quotes.t: Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week.
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2

EXTRA.src: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2 (Library of Congress); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); 1870 U.S. census, District 10, Giles County, as transcribed on the Frank Stevenson WikiTree page.
EXTRA.note: The El Paso death and the Lubbock judgeship come from the family history alone, which has no source for them. Lubbock County's list of county judges, 1891-1906, has no Stevenson; a G. F. Stevenson appears among the county's precinct commissioners in 1894-95, and nothing ties him to George. A Texas death record or a Lubbock court record would settle both. Source: https://www.lubbockcounty.gov/department/division.php?fDD=13-0, read 4 Nov 2026.

EXTRA.name: Julia Ann Desdemona (Stevenson) Andrew
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Rockwall and Wilbarger Counties, Texas
EXTRA.title: One widower, three Stevenson wives
EXTRA.hook: John Newton Andrew of Giles County married a Stevenson cousin, then a Stevenson sister, then Frank's other sister; the last wife took him to Texas.
body: John Newton Andrew was born in Giles County on 20 February 1841. His first wife was Mary Hamilton, a granddaughter of Rev. Elam Stevenson through Elam's daughter Catherine. His second, on 20 December 1870, was Eliza Mary Stevenson, Frank's sister, who bore him four sons (Baxter, Abner, Truman and Perry) and died on 16 November 1878. His third was Eliza's younger sister Julia Ann Desdemona Stevenson, born in July 1856 or 1857. Julia was thus "John's third marriage to a Stevenson woman."

Julia and John had four children, Ray, George, Tina Tisha and Alice. A son, Roy Jackson Andrew, was at Rockwall, Texas, on 30 July 1893 and died in Wilbarger County, Texas, in 1964. John died on 28 March 1909 and Julia on 3 July 1928 at Vernon, Wilbarger County, though one account gives 1925 as her death year, so the date is not settled.

Rockwall comes up again in this family. The possible first husband of Parsis O'Neal, Frank's wife, is said to have died in Rockwall County in 1901. If Frank and Parsis were among the Giles County Stevensons around Rockwall in the 1890s, the Texas births of their children Willie, Frank and Elisha would be explained, though this is only a guess.
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles Stevenson-5863 (Julia Ann Desdemona), Andrew-1921 (John Newton Andrew) and Andrew-1917 (Roy Jackson Andrew).
EXTRA.note: Julia's death year is given as 1925 and 1928 in different WikiTree fields, and her birth as 1856 and 1857. A Texas death certificate or Vernon cemetery record would settle it.

EXTRA.name: Ellen Tillman (Stevenson) Britton
EXTRA.place: Giles and Crockett Counties, Tennessee; Texas
EXTRA.title: Ellen Stevenson and the Brittons
EXTRA.hook: A twin born in 1850 who married a Giles County farmer, went to Texas and back, and raised seven children.
body: Ellen Tillman Stevenson was born on 30 January 1850, the twin of James Willis. On 24 December 1871 she married James Marion Britton, born on 3 March 1840 in Giles County, the son of Wilson Britton and Elizabeth Ragains. His brother John Frank Britton died in Collin County, Texas, in 1890.

Seven children are named: Logan Harwell, Sarah Beulah, Amanda Elizabeth, an infant daughter, Wilson Arrington, James Wilson Lafayette "Fate," and Carlos Erskine. In 1880 at Friendship, Crockett County, James and Ellen's household included son L. H., age seven, and daughters B. V., age five, and M. E., age three. Logan's birth is given as 17 September 1872 and Sarah Beulah's as 24 January 1873; these dates are only four months apart and cannot both be right. By 1900 Ellen and James were back in Giles County.

James died on 18 September 1913 in Giles County and Ellen on 4 March 1927 (another account gives 4 February); both lie at Mount Zion (New Zion) Cemetery near Pulaski. Their daughter Amanda married Eli Bascom Pitts on 2 March 1892 and had eleven children. Sarah Beulah married Samuel McNeese and had eight, including twins who died the day they were born, 10 June 1902.
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families, pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (https://www.rcasey.net/acrobat/ste0301b.pdf); 1880 U.S. census, Friendship, Crockett County, Tennessee (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MDQY-F5F); 1900 U.S. census, Logan Britton (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MSCB-B5Z); Sarah Bulah McNeece, Tennessee death record, 1957 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QKM9-KRS9); Find a Grave memorial 88644767; WikiTree profiles Stevenson-3637, Britton-1643 and Britton-2364.
EXTRA.note: Birthplaces and the month of Ellen's death differ between the sources. The family history's 17 September 1872 birth date for Logan and 24 January 1873 date for Sarah Beulah are only four months apart. The 1880 census records a son L. H., age seven, and daughter B. V., age five; Logan's 1900 census gives September 1872. Sarah Beulah's 1957 death record names her parents James Britton and Ellen Stevenson but estimates her birth year as 1873; her grave memorial gives 24 January 1872. The exact dates and the identification of B. V. with Beulah remain unresolved.

EXTRA.name: Rev. James Willis Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: A third-generation preacher with three wives
EXTRA.hook: Frank's brother James Willis, a twin of Ellen, became a Methodist minister, married three times, and lived until 1943.
body: James Willis Stevenson, born on 30 January 1850, was the twin of Ellen. He was a Methodist minister. His first wife was a cousin, Nancy J. Stevenson, and their only son was Werner Wesley, born on 4 March 1880. After Nancy died he married Elizabeth A., and then Beatrice, born in October 1870 in Alabama. In 1900 James and Beatrice were in Giles County, and he later lived at Ardmore, Tennessee.

His second and third marriages gave him another ten children: Bessie (1885), Bertha (1887), Coleman (1893), Cletis Z. (1897), Lydia M. (1898), and Nore, Clower, Elizabeth, Charlie and Talmadge Dewitt. He died on 9 November 1943 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his grandfather founded.

Werner Wesley (1880-1974) stayed in Giles County and married Lila Mitchell. Their daughter Nannie married Robert Hulsey, born in January 1904. No connection between this Giles County Hulsey and Katie Stevenson's husband Oscar Hulsey has been shown.
EXTRA.src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (James Willis Stevenson, Werner Wesley Stevenson); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); 1900 and 1920 censuses, Giles County, as cited in the family history.
EXTRA.note: The 1943 death date comes from the family history; the cemetery list used here has no matching entry for him.

EXTRA.name: Rev. William Payne Stevenson and Malinda (Rowe)
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: A preacher with soldier sons and a short-lived brood
EXTRA.hook: Elam's oldest son had nine children on a Giles County farm, buried six of them young, and sent two sons into the Confederate 32nd Tennessee.
body: William Payne Stevenson was born on 27 September 1810 in North Carolina, the oldest son of Rev. Elam Stevenson. On 14 October 1830 he married Malinda Rowe in Giles County. In 1886 it was said that he "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel," and that he settled on his farm in 1838. He lived to 14 January 1892; Malinda died on 21 January 1888. He is buried at Bee Spring.

His nine children were an infant son who lived and died in 1831; Coleman Lafayette (26 December 1832); Elam R. (1835); Joseph J. (1837); Sarah Ann P. (10 March 1840); Wilbur Marion (20 January 1841); Presley W. (8 September 1847); William F. (19 January 1853); and John Henry (1856). Six of the nine did not reach adulthood. Presley W. died on 30 June 1849 (the cemetery reads 30 July), Elam R. on 2 August 1854, William B. F. on 19 August 1854 and Joseph J. on 15 February 1856. Sarah died on 10 February 1846.

The two grown sons went to war. Coleman "enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers" in 1862 and "served until the close of the war," taking part "in most of the principal battles." The 32nd was organized at Camp Trousdale in the summer of 1861, with four Giles County companies, and went first to East Tennessee and Kentucky. The 32nd served in Brown's Brigade of the division of Gen. C. L. Stevenson (no kin), and was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi. Wilbur Marion served in the same regiment until the fall of 1864, "when left the service due to ill health."

Coleman raised not only his own sons but three orphaned Jackson nieces of his wife (Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J.). He died on 24 October 1908. Wilbur married Martha Jane Hampton on 9 November 1865. She died on 28 December 1918 and he died the next day, 29 December 1918, in Giles County. No cause is given, but their dates fall in the winter of the great influenza epidemic.

quotes.t: He has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles Co., sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 872

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, p. 872

EXTRA.src: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County, Biographical Appendix, pp. 871-872; Goodspeed, Giles County military chapter, p. 758-759; Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (William Payne Stevenson, Coleman Lafayette, Wilbur Marion); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page).
EXTRA.note: The influenza suggestion is only a guess from the dates. Neither source states a cause for the 1918 deaths.

EXTRA.name: Bee Spring Cemetery, the Stevenson burials
EXTRA.rel: Place the family lived and was buried
EXTRA.place: Bee Spring Methodist Church, near Bunker Hill and Bryson, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: The Stevenson row at Bee Spring
EXTRA.hook: Four Stevenson burials between 1 February and 3 March 1856, two more in August 1854: the graveyard Elam founded shows how hard those years were.
body: Elam Stevenson bought fifteen acres for $20 in 1815 to found Bee Spring church. About seventy-five Stevenson graves lie in the cemetery behind it. The tall stone over Elam and Lydia reads, on Elam's side, "Erected to the memory of Reverend Elam Stevenson, born September 24, 1787, died March 13, 1875. Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life." On the back: "Erected to the memory of Lydia Stevenson, born August 16, 1787, died March 6, 1872. Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church."

The graves show how the family's children died. In the summer of 1854: Citty on 20 June, Elam R. on 2 August and William B. F. on 19 August. In the winter of 1856: Louisa (Coleman's young wife) on 1 February, Joseph J. on 15 February, Ann Eliza on 2 March and James Elisha on 3 March. An "infant" is dated 6 October 1831 (the first child of William and Malinda). Several more are listed only as "child" or "infant." No causes are recorded.

The family also kept its dead close. Rev. Abner A. is listed there with his wife Martha S. (1823-1887); his brother Rev. James C. (23 June 1813 to 23 February 1899) lies beside Margaret Caroline (8 December 1816 to 11 February 1886); Willis McKendree is there (18 January 1818 to 6 February 1900), as are Coleman L. (1832-1908), with Dorcas (1832-1892), and Thomas C. (1825-1906). The congregation also buried a Stevenson as late as 1994. In 1878 a visitor noted that "Here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort."

quotes.t: Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life.
quotes.c: Elam Stevenson's gravestone, Bee Spring Cemetery, as quoted in the Casey family history, p. 3-98

quotes.t: Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church.
quotes.c: Lydia Stevenson's gravestone, same stone, reverse side

EXTRA.src: Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page) (burial dates for Stevenson entries); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (gravestone inscriptions, p. 3-98); The Pulaski Citizen, 30 May 1878, p. 1.
EXTRA.note: The cemetery list gives no cause of death and does not say which Stevenson household each child belonged to; only the names matched in the family history are placed.

EXTRA.name: Catherine A. (Stevenson) Hamilton
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Limestone County, Alabama
EXTRA.title: "They who bear the cross shall bear the crown"
EXTRA.hook: Elam's eldest child moved to Alabama with her husband, raised nine children, and is quoted on her gravestone; her sons went on to Texas and Arkansas.
body: Catherine A. Stevenson was born on 2 October 1808 in North Carolina, the oldest of Elam and Lydia's eleven children. She married William B. Hamilton, born in 1808 or 1809 in South Carolina. Their nine children were Lydia J. (1832), Mary A. (1834), James (1839), Elam Carr (1 February 1842), Clatinda I. (20 January 1844), George Worth (1846), Thomas C. (1848), Gilbert William (1850, in Alabama) and John Baxter (30 April 1853, in Limestone County, Alabama). The family was in Limestone County in 1860, 1870 and 1880.

William died on 8 September 1872 and was buried in the Wallace Cemetery in Limestone County. Catherine died on 2 December 1888, and the same cemetery has her stone: "Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown." A grandson, Robert J. Hamilton of Ripley, Alabama, described her as "a short, chubby, and very cheerful little lady."

Her children moved west. Her son George became a Methodist minister. Clatinda never married and died on 4 March 1892. Gilbert William married Martha J. Thorpe and lived in Greene County, Arkansas, where their daughter Bessie was born on 31 March 1880; Martha died on 19 May 1881, Gilbert on 6 June 1896, and both were buried at Pruetts Chapel. John Baxter married Mary Arantha Lynch in Kaufman County, Texas, on 31 January 1884 and had nine children there. Her daughter Mary A. became the first wife of John Newton Andrew, who later married two of Frank's sisters.

quotes.t: Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown.

EXTRA.name: Elam Augustus Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Arkansas; Winston County, Alabama
EXTRA.title: A doctor and preacher who moved to Arkansas in 1858
EXTRA.hook: Abner's younger brother carried the family trade to Arkansas, taught his sons the pulpit, and is buried at Booneville, not far from Danville where Frank later lived.
body: Elam Augustus Stevenson was born on 3 February 1829 in Giles County, the son of Rev. Elam and Lydia. He joined the Tennessee Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South. In 1858 the Conference recorded "Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference" (Ouachita, in Arkansas). A 1930 biography of his son says he "came to Arkansas and became pastor at El Dorado and Princeton" in 1858. His son James Baxter was born at Richmond, Arkansas, on 24 October 1860, and Thomas Elam's birth at Booneville is given as April 1857, a year before the transfer, so he may have been in Arkansas earlier than 1858.

Ten years later he was back in Tennessee, where in 1870 "E A Stephenson," 40, lived with Alabama-born wife H. S., 27, and sons Thomas, James and John. In 1875 he was listed as "readmitted" and then "transferred to White River Conference," and appoint "Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson," in the White River Conference of northeast Arkansas. In 1880 he was at Addison, Winston County, Alabama, aged 51 and married to Hannah, listed as a "Doctor & Preacher" with seven children at home. Hannah Celia Carolan, born in 1844 at Somerville, Alabama, died on 26 October 1884 at Carolan, Logan County, Arkansas. Elam A. died on 17 April 1886 and is buried at Oak Hill Memorial Cemetery, Booneville.

A 1930 biography says he "was a graduate of the Vanderbilt University" at Nashville. Vanderbilt did not open until 1875, when he was already 46, so the claim must be a family exaggeration. It also names his wife as "Earl (Cook)," which nothing else supports, so the sons by his first marriage and by Hannah are not yet separated.

quotes.t: Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, 1858 (archive.org item 27838123.1858.emory.edu)

quotes.t: Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences, MECS, 1875, appointments (archive.org item 27838123.1875.emory.edu)

EXTRA.name: Rev. James Baxter Stevenson
EXTRA.rel: First cousin of 2nd great-grandfather Frank Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Richmond, Booneville and Atkins, Arkansas; Oklahoma City
EXTRA.title: Frank's cousin the Arkansas Methodist
EXTRA.hook: A cousin of the Hulsey ancestor Frank preached in Yell County in 1883, was the first pastor of Oklahoma City's Methodist church, and is the Rev. J. B. Stevenson whose 1932 letter is quoted for the family's years of preaching.
body: James Baxter Stevenson was born on 24 October 1860 at Richmond, Arkansas, the son of Rev. Elam A. Stevenson. His 1930 biography says he "grew up in Tennessee, to which State his father had returned when he was six," and that at nineteen he "returned to Arkansas and settled in Booneville, Logan County" (the 1930 text is hyphenated across a line). He was licensed to preach on 21 September 1881. In 1883 "the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years" and then to the Mulberry Circuit and to Paris, Logan County.

He became "the first pastor of the Methodist church in Oklahoma City" and later served at Guthrie, Fort Smith, Conway, Batesville, Morrillton, Dardanelle, Fayetteville, Paragould, Russellville and Ozark. The Conference appointments confirm some of this: "Conway Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1892, "Van Buren Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1896, "Morrillton Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1900. From 1927 he was pastor at Atkins. He married Lulu Briggs on 14 May 1885. They had four children, among them Eugene Hendrix, a Rhodes Scholar who studied at Oxford and took a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania.

This is the J. B. Stevenson who wrote in 1932 that "Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years." The letter is said to have been to "Eugene Hendricks Stevenson," which fits his son Eugene Hendrix. His Yell County parish of 1883-85 is the county where Frank Stevenson was living at Danville in 1910, and his father's burial place at Booneville is in the next county.

quotes.t: Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years.
quotes.c: Rev. J. B. Stevenson, 1932 family letter, Giles County TNGenWeb

quotes.t: In 1883 the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years.
quotes.c: Arkansas and Its People (1930), vol. 4

EXTRA.note: The 1932 letter is attributed on the Giles County site to "Rev. J. B. Stevenson, Elam's grandson"; James Baxter, then 72, is the grandson of that name found in the Minutes and the Arkansas biography.

EXTRA.name: Rev. James Calvin Stevenson and Margaret Caroline (Brown)
EXTRA.place: Near Bryson, Giles County, Tennessee
EXTRA.title: Golden-wedding preacher, and a general in the family
EXTRA.hook: James Calvin Stevenson married into the family of two Tennessee governors, preached at Giles County weddings for decades, and was great-grandfather to the general for whom Andrews Field is named.
body: James Calvin Stevenson was born in North Carolina on 23 June 1813 and was brought to Giles County, Tennessee, as a babe, the son of Rev. Elam Stevenson and a brother of Abner. On 19 November 1835 he married Margaret Caroline Brown, who had been born on 8 December 1816.

Margaret came, it seems, from one of the best-known families in Tennessee. A neighbor, F. T. M’Laurine, remembered in 1884 that James “married a daughter of Mr. Duncan Brown, sister of ex-Gov. N. S. and J. C. Brown,” and her grave at Bee Spring remembers her the same way. Her brother Neill Smith Brown was the twelfth governor of Tennessee, from 1847 to 1849, and later United States minister to Russia; her brother John Calvin Brown was a Confederate major general, the nineteenth governor, from 1871 to 1875, and afterward president of the Texas and Pacific Railway. Both were born in Giles County to Duncan and Margaret Smith Brown. The kinship rests on that memory rather than on any will naming Margaret among Duncan Brown’s children.

James was a preacher. Through the 1850s and 1860s he married couples across Giles County, among them Swinney and Dyer on 19 January 1852, Young and Huff on 3 November 1852, Stovall and Stephenson on 3 September 1860, and Woodard and Barnfield on 25 August 1862.

Fifty years on, the couple were still together near Bryson. On 20 August 1885 a county correspondent called on “our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson,” who “speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October.” Margaret died a few months later, on 11 February 1886. James lived until 23 February 1899 and is buried beside her at Bee Spring.

They had ten children, among them Sarah, who married James Hollon, and Catherine Eliza, born in 1838, whom her husband called Eliza Catherine. In 1856 she married the Rev. William Thomas Andrews, who in his autobiography of 1912 remembered her as the daughter of James C. and Margaret C. Stevenson and named their son James David Andrews. James David’s son was Frank Maxwell Andrews, a major general by 1937, who rose to lieutenant general and gave his name to Andrews Field, now Joint Base Andrews.

quotes.t: speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 20 Aug 1885, p. 3

quotes.t: Frank Andrews was a general and died off the coast of Iceland.
quotes.c: Casey family history, p. 3-107

TNGenWeb cemetery page); Giles County marriage returns (Giles Co. TNGenWeb marriage index, grooms S-Y); Wikipedia, "Frank Maxwell Andrews," early life.; W. T. Andrews, Memorial Sketches (1912), pp. 340–341, https://archive.org/details/memorialsketches00andr/page/340/mode/1up; The Pulaski Citizen, 10 Mar 1937, https://tngenweb.org/gilestn/obituaries/GC1930-1939_Obits.html; Nashville Public Library, James D. Andrews Papers, https://assets.library.nashville.gov/documents/finding-aids/Special_Collections_Division_Finding_Aid_AndrewsSeries2.pdf; Goodspeed (1886), https://www.tngenweb.org/goodspeed/giles/bios.html; Elam Stevenson will, https://ahgp.org/tn/giles/wills/stev.htm. Elam Stevenson’s will and the 1886 Goodspeed sketch support the connection between James Calvin and his brother Abner, the direct ancestor.

EXTRA.name: The O'Neal brothers of Gibson County
EXTRA.place: Gibson and Pike Counties, Indiana; Missouri
EXTRA.title: Parsis's brothers stayed home
EXTRA.hook: Five of Daniel and Vashti O'Neal's sons and their youngest daughter lived out their lives in or near Gibson County, Indiana, while Parsis and Mary went west.
body: Daniel Waters O'Neal and Vashti Pearson had ten children, and eight of them reached adulthood: Parsis, her sister Mary and the six told here. William Allen was born on 15 April 1863 in Tennessee (though an 1880 listing says Indiana) and died on 11 September 1933 in Pike County, Indiana, with burial at Blackfoot Cemetery. His wife was Nancy Jane Mason, born in 1865 at Oakland City, who died there on 20 June 1923.

John Sherman was born on 15 January 1866, a few months after the regiment mustered out, and died at Somerville on 19 July 1940. He married Jane Minerva Mitchell. George Johnson was born on 16 August 1875; an 1880 listing says in Missouri, so the family may have spent some time there in the 1870s (another account says Tennessee). He lost his first wife, Adella Douglas (born 1875), on 27 February 1906, married Sarah Eleen Reed, and died at Somerville on 12 June 1965 at 89. Daniel Clinton, born 9 June 1878, married Flora Nellie McGregor and died on 3 March 1954. David Commodore, born at Somerville on 22 March 1881, married Birdie Viola Rembe and died at Evansville on 7 May 1955.

The youngest, Charity Louisa, born on 19 December 1887, was the only daughter besides Parsis and Mary to live to adulthood. She married Fred Skomp, born on 7 May 1884 in Greene County, Indiana. He died at Hobart, Indiana, on 5 August 1949, and she died at Valparaiso on 15 November 1979. Vashti's five living sons in 1919 were William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, and her daughters were Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville.
EXTRA.src: Obituary of Vashti O'Neal, Jan 1919 (Find a Grave 24711779); WikiTree profiles O'Neal-3565, 3566, 3567, 3568, 3569, 3570 and spouse pages; 1880 U.S. census, Columbia Twp, Gibson Co., Indiana, as printed on the Parsis O'Neal WikiTree page.
EXTRA.note: Death dates after 1900 are taken from WikiTree and are not checked against Indiana death certificates.

EXTRA.name: Mary Elizabeth (O'Neal) Farris Rinker Wilson
EXTRA.place: Gibson County, Indiana; Missouri; Arkansas; Tuttle, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: A hundred years from Indiana to Oklahoma
EXTRA.hook: Parsis's oldest sister married three times, raised her children in Arkansas, and was feted at 100 in Tuttle.
body: Mary Elizabeth O'Neal was born on 16 November 1860 in Gibson County, Indiana, the first child of Daniel and Vashti, ten months after their marriage. By 1878 she had married David Raliegh Farris, born in 1856 in Indiana. Their son Elmer Cooper Farris was born on 25 September 1878 at Princeton and died in Sequoyah County, Oklahoma, in 1948. A second son, Daniel Riley, born in Arkansas on 23 March 1881 and recorded as Fairce, died at Mead, Oklahoma, in 1968.

On 10 February 1884, in Arkansas, Mary married Joseph McConnell Rinker, 29, born in Iowa. Their children were Lydia Bell (1885, Sunset, Arkansas), Armenda Mae (1888), Cynthia Jane (1890), Joseph Jonathan (1892, Fayetteville), Vasha (1895, died 1897), Oscar Ashel (1897), Letha Agnes (1900) and Alta (1902, died 1906). Joseph was in Roger Mills County, Oklahoma, in 1910 and died on 27 May 1919 at Wapanucka.

When she died in December 1960, Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, 100, was remembered: she "was born in Gibson County, Indiana, near Evansville, and spent most of her early life in Missouri, and raised her children in Arkansas. She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926." She "celebrated her 100th birthday in Nov 16, 1960, and passed away at her home on Wednesday, Dec 14, 1960." Survivors included "3 sons, 3 daughters, 51 grandchildren, 150 great-grandchildren, & 73 great great grandchildren." She was buried in Fairlawn Cemetery. Her third husband was James Calvin Wilson, born in 1867 at Princeton, Indiana.
Katie's brother Eddie was born in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in July 1907, the same year Mary first came to Oklahoma.

quotes.t: She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926.
quotes.c: Tuttle Times, 22 Dec 1960, obituary of Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, as transcribed on WikiTree O'Neal-2666

EXTRA.note: Names and dates for her children and husbands are from WikiTree; the Rinker and Wilson marriages are not checked against a county marriage register.

EXTRA.name: Katie Stevenson's brothers and sisters
EXTRA.rel: Brothers and sisters of great-grandmother Katie (Stevenson) Hulsey
EXTRA.place: Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Seven children in 1910
EXTRA.hook: At Danville, Arkansas, in 1910, Katie was the baby, with six older brothers and sisters born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma.
body: On 18 April 1910 at Danville, Yell County, Frank Stevenson, 51, "Clergyman," and his wife Jane, 41, had these children at home: Delphia, 18, born in Indiana; Willie, 16, Texas; George, 12, Indiana; Frank, 8, Texas; Elisha, 6, Texas; Eddie, 2, Oklahoma; and Katie, under one year, Arkansas. Frank and Jane said they had been married 25 years and that seven children had been born. These are the seven.

Delphia was the oldest daughter. When Katie died in 2009 she was preceded in death by "daughters Delphia and Mary," so she named a daughter for her sister. Willie was born in Texas about 1894. George Sherman Stevenson died on 3 June 1978 at Kilgore, Gregg County, Texas, and his death record names his mother as Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson. Frank, born about 1902 in Texas, is "Frank Lester" in other trees, and one list calls the sixth child "Allen" where the household has Elisha.

The youngest brother, Horace Edward "Eddie," was born on 13 July 1907 in Garvin, McCurtain County, Oklahoma. He married Edith Marie Shunkey (born 29 July 1911 at Muskogee, died 2 April 2003 at King City, Oregon), and he died on 1 February 1998 at Portland, Oregon.

Other trees give a different list for the same parents: Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886), Nellie Vashti (1889), Frank Lester (1902), Horace Edward (1907) and Katie. Iva Myrtle, Adison and Nellie would have been 26, 24 and 21 in 1910, so they could have been grown and away; and their link to this family is not documented.
EXTRA.src: 1910 U.S. census, Danville, Yell Co., Arkansas, as transcribed on the WikiTree pages for Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558); WikiTree Stevenson-5100 (Horace Edward Stevenson); Texas death certificate 1978, George Sherman Stevenson, cited on WikiTree O'Neal-3514.
EXTRA.note: Delphia, Willie, George, Frank, Elisha and Eddie are the names on the 1910 census page; the later given names in other trees are not proven. The census is also the only record yet seen for Willie and Delphia.

EXTRA.name: Otho Louderback
EXTRA.rel: Possible first husband of 2nd great-grandmother Parsis O'Neal
EXTRA.place: Pulaski County, Arkansas; Illinois; Rockwall County, Texas
EXTRA.title: A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County
EXTRA.hook: A Parsis J. O'Neal, 16, is said to have married a 40-year-old Otho Louderbank on Christmas Day 1884, and her grave memorial still carries the Louderback name.
body: An Arkansas marriage record reads: "Parsis J O Neal and Otho Louderback were married 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Arkansas. Otho was 40, Parsis, 16 years old." The groom's name is spelled "Louderbank." Pulaski County is Little Rock. In 1880 Parsis, 11, had been in her father's household in Gibson County, Indiana. Parsis's sister Mary was also in Arkansas by February 1884.

William Ortho Louderback was born about 1836 to 1844 at Princeton, Gibson County, the same county as the O'Neals. He is said to have died in 1901 in Rockwall County, Texas, and a daughter, Henrietta Louderback, born in Illinois and dead in Texas in 1955, is listed as a child of Parsis and him.

Her memorial at Hugo is titled "Parsis Jane O'Neal Louderback (26 Mar 1868-26 Jan 1956)," so she was remembered under the Louderback name to the end, while her marriage to Stevenson has no record behind it. In 1910 Frank and Jane said they had been married 25 years, which would put that wedding in 1885, months after the Louderback record. Either the 1910 answer is loose, or the Stevenson household began without a recorded marriage, or the Louderback marriage ended early. Nothing settles it. Willie, Frank and Elisha Stevenson were born in Texas after 1894, where Otho Louderback died in 1901.
EXTRA.src: WikiTree O'Neal-3514 (Parsis Jane O'Neal), Louderback-86 (William Ortho Louderback) and Louderback-85 (Henrietta Louderback), quoting "Arkansas Marriages, 1837-1944," FamilySearch F73Z-LQF; 1910 census, Danville, Yell Co., Ark.
EXTRA.note: The marriage record itself has not been seen. Both the Louderback surname index and the bride's age should be checked against the Pulaski County, Arkansas, marriage register for 25 December 1884.

EXTRA.name: Gilliam Graves in Cherokee County, Georgia
EXTRA.place: Cherokee County, Georgia
kv: 10 May 1838, Gen. Winfield Scott at New Echota
Montgomery Co., Ark., tax lists by 1853; Union volunteer 1864
EXTRA.src: Gilliam Graves's Cherokee County jury service (Dec 1835 and 5 Nov 1838) as given on his own page; James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee, 19th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology (1900), "The Removal, 1838-39," pp. 130-133, and the note "Removal forts, 1838" (https://archive.org/details/mythsofcherokee00moon); Wikipedia, Cherokee County, Georgia (land lottery of 1832; Etowah, now Canton, county seat 1833)
EXTRA.title: A juror in Cherokee County, the year of the roundup
EXTRA.hook: In November 1838 Gilliam Graves sat on a county jury a few months after soldiers emptied the Cherokee farms of his county into a stockade.
body: Gilliam Graves served on Cherokee County, Georgia, juries twice, in December 1835 and on 5 November 1838. The county had been carved out of the Cherokee Nation's Georgia land, and the state gave that land to white men by lottery in 1832. Its seat, first called Etowah, is Canton today.

In May 1838 the rest of the story arrived. Gen. Winfield Scott set up at the Cherokee capital, New Echota, and on 10 May told the Cherokee that "before another moon had passed every Cherokee man, woman, and child must be in motion" for the West. About 7,000 regulars, militia and volunteers were used. Stockade forts were built to hold the people until they could be moved, and five stood in Georgia: Fort Scudder in Lumpkin County, Fort Gilmer in Gilmer County, Fort Coosawatee in Murray County, Fort Talking Rock in Pickens County and "Fort Buffington, near Canton, in Cherokee county."

A historian who gathered the story from people who had lived it wrote: "Families at dinner were startled by the sudden gleam of bayonets in the doorway and rose up to be driven with blows and oaths along the weary miles of trail that led to the stockade. Men were seized in their fields or going along the road, women were taken from their wheels and children from their play." Looters followed the soldiers, and many families, looking back from a ridge, "saw their homes in flames." A Georgia volunteer later said: "I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew."

When about seventeen thousand people had been gathered into the stockades the removal began. It is said that "hundreds died in the stockades and the waiting camps," mostly from the rations, and that "over 4,000" Cherokee died as a direct result of the removal.

Nothing says what Gilliam saw or did that summer. He was in the county, but not where he lived in it. But when he was called to serve on 5 November 1838, the Cherokee families of his county had been gone from their farms for some months. By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, and in January 1864 he volunteered as a Union private at the age of 45.

quotes.t: I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew.
quotes.c: A Georgia volunteer, quoted in James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), p. 130

EXTRA.note: Gilliam's jury service comes from the Graves family compilation cited on his own page; Mooney does not mention him or any juror. The page numbers are those of the Annual Report edition. This is a place-and-time story: nothing seen says Gilliam took any part in the roundup.

EXTRA.name: Doaksville, June 1861
EXTRA.rel: Place where Vincent B. Tims (4th great-grandfather) kept store
EXTRA.place: Doaksville, Choctaw Nation
kv: Wednesday of the first week of June 1861 (counting from the dates the witness gives)
Capt. Robert M. Jones, "the wealthiest Choctaw"
Rev. John Edwards, superintendent of Wheelock girls' seminary
Doak & Tims contracts 1838-39; sued in Texas 1849; "V. B. Tims, P. M." there in Sept 1864
EXTRA.src: John Edwards, "My Escape from the South in 1861," The Chronicles of Oklahoma 43, no. 1 (Spring 1965), pp. 58-89, esp. 70-73 and the editor's notes 13-15 (https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofokla4319okla); Chronicles of Oklahoma 41 (1963), Doaksville postmaster letters of 1864 (https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofokla4119okla); Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Choctaw County and Hugo (okhistory.org, entries CH051 and HU010)
EXTRA.title: "Hung up to the first limb": Doaksville, June 1861
EXTRA.hook: In the first week of June 1861 a Northern missionary learned that a meeting at Doaksville, the town where Vincent Tims kept store, had called for hanging men who would not take the South's side.
body: John Edwards, a Presbyterian missionary from New York, had taught at Spencer Academy and since 1853 ran Wheelock Seminary for Choctaw girls. In 1861, as the Choctaw Nation was pressed toward the Confederacy, he refused to pledge himself to take up arms for the South. His account of what followed was printed by the Oklahoma Historical Society a century later, with the editor's remark that a writer at Goodland had told her of the story, "It just would not do to print!"

A few weeks earlier, riding back from Pine Ridge, Edwards had come through Doaksville and found that "The Confederate flag was flying over the town." On 1 and 2 June the Principal Chief, George Hudson, and Peter Pitchlynn stayed with the Edwardses on their way to a special council at Doaksville. Hudson carried a message recommending neutrality; Edwards later heard "that he was compelled by a vigilance committee to change it recommending the Choctaws to join the South."

Then, he writes, "On Thursday afternoon I learned that on Wednesday a public meeting had been held at Doaksville, the capital, at which Capt. Robert M. Jones, the wealthiest Choctaw, took the ground that 'every man that was not with them must be hung up to the first limb between heaven and hell.'" The next morning a neighbor, Mrs. Dukes, came to say "the committee are to be here today to hang you." He handed his keys to a friend, had his pony Jerry saddled, prayed with his wife and was on the road "probably within 15 minutes of the time the word came." His plan was that Mrs. Edwards would follow with the children, and the editor credits her with managing the family's escape.

Jones, the editor's note says, owned about 500 enslaved people, plantations on the Red River and "a large store at Doaksville." His house, Rose Hill, stood east of present Hugo; the state encyclopedia says it burned in 1912.

Vincent B. Tims had been a trader at Doaksville since the late 1830s, in the firm of Doak & Tims, and in 1864 he signed Confederate mail contracts there as "V. B. Tims, P. M." The Edwards account never names him, and nothing says what Tims said or did that week. It records only the town where he did business and the climate in it.

quotes.t: every man that was not with them must be hung up to the first limb between heaven and hell.
quotes.c: Capt. Robert M. Jones, as reported by John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 72

quotes.t: The Confederate flag was flying over the town.
quotes.c: John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 70

EXTRA.note: Place story. The dates are worked out from Edwards's own "1st and 2nd of June" and "the following Monday"; he gives no date for the Doaksville meeting. The editor places Jones's home four miles southeast of Hugo; the encyclopedia says six miles east.

EXTRA.name: The Pine Belt logging train, 25 June 1915
EXTRA.rel: Place: the lumber company of Choctaw County where Grady Moffitt worked as a timberman
EXTRA.place: Fort Towson, Choctaw County, Oklahoma
kv: Clifford Riggs, log hauler, paid $2 a day
$6,000; compound fracture of right leg and ankle; 32 days in bed
Pine Belt Lumber Company, Fort Towson; logging railroad about 15 miles long
Oklahoma Supreme Court, 6 April 1920 (rehearing denied 14 Dec 1920)
EXTRA.src: Pine Belt Lumber Co. v. Riggs, 80 Okla. 28 (1920), Supreme Court of Oklahoma, on appeal from the District Court of Choctaw County (https://static.case.law/okla/80/); Grady Moffitt's 1917 draft card and the Pine Belt company as given on the family pages
EXTRA.title: The logging train that ran away, 25 June 1915
EXTRA.hook: A log hauler jumped from a runaway train on the Pine Belt Lumber Company's railroad near Fort Towson and broke his leg; the company said he had signed away his right to sue.
body: The Pine Belt Lumber Company ran a mill, dry kilns and planers at Fort Towson and a railroad about 15 miles north into the woods, along which it logged. Clifford Riggs hauled logs by wagon and team and was paid $2 a day. His petition says the company gave its workers passes to ride the train between Fort Towson and the woods.

On 25 June 1915, Riggs says in his petition, he boarded a train near his work and "the train in going down a steep grade got out of the control of the train men operating the same and ran away down the grade." He "believed that the only chance to save his life was by jumping." He landed with a compound fracture of the right leg and ankle, was in bed 32 days, and said his injuries were permanent. He sued in the Choctaw County district court for $6,000, charging that the air brakes and steam brakes were old, worn and insufficient, and had been for a long time.

The company answered that its track was only a tramway for hauling logs and not a common carrier, that Riggs had been careless and had accepted the risk, and that before boarding he had signed a paper releasing it from any claim for injuries on the train. A jury found for Riggs.

On 6 April 1920 the Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed. A contract, it said, "whereby the servant, in consideration of the employment, or of the wages, agrees to release and discharge his master from liability on account of injuries caused by the negligence of his master" is forbidden by the state constitution and "void as against public policy." The opinion does not state how much the jury awarded.

Two years after Riggs jumped, Grady Moffitt, 25, put "timberman" and "C. D. Neese, Ervin, Oklahoma" on his draft card in the same county. Which sawmill bought his timber is not known, and the county's biggest sawmill was the Pine Belt company's at Fort Towson. Nothing links Riggs to the family. The case shows what a timber hand's day could end in, and what a signed paper did not protect against.

quotes.t: the train in going down a steep grade got out of the control of the train men operating the same and ran away down the grade

EXTRA.name: J. P. Austin, killed near Hagansport
EXTRA.rel: Place: the Hagansport neighborhood where John B. and Emma Smith (2nd great-grandparents) farmed

H. J. Carbough; life in the penitentiary, affirmed 7 Mar 1906
Ella (Austin) Johnson, who testified that she had been in the plot
Charles Oscar born there 1889; the family on its own farm in the 1900 census
EXTRA.src: Wallace v. State, 46 Tex. Crim. 341 (8 June 1904); Wallace v. State, 48 Tex. Crim. 318 (31 May 1905); Carbough v. State, 49 Tex. Crim. 452 (7 Mar 1906), Court of Criminal Appeals of Texas, on appeal from the district courts of Franklin and Camp counties (https://static.case.law/tex-crim/46/, /48/, /49/); Handbook of Texas, Hagansport; Charles Oscar Smith's page for the Smith farm
EXTRA.title: A Sunday in August 1898: the Austin murder at Hagansport
EXTRA.hook: In August 1898 a farmer near Hagansport was shot on his way to his field by a man hired at the sawmill; the court cases ran until 1906.
body: On Sunday, 28 August 1898, J. P. Austin walked from his house toward his field in the bottom, "across the lake," and did not come home. His wife Ella took the children to church at Hagansport, a mile or a mile and a half away. That night he was still gone. On Monday morning she went back to Hagansport and asked a neighbor named Martin to look for him, and told him to try the trail from the lake to the field.

He was found there, killed. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals later said the killing occurred "twelve or thirteen miles north" of Mount Vernon. Ella Austin, by then Mrs. Johnson, told the jury why she knew where to send Martin. She said that H. J. Carbough "wanted me to take the life of my husband so that he and I could marry," and that she refused. Weeks later he said he would not do it himself, "but would get some one that would." In July he told her "there was a man at the sawmill by the name of T. C. Wallace and that he would be all right to do the work," for "seventy-five or a hundred dollars." The week before the killing, she said, Carbough warned her not to let the oldest little boy go with his papa.

On the evening of the killing, she testified, Wallace came to her house on foot, carrying a long bundle wrapped in a sack, and said: "Your man is down yonder; the work is done; the man is down yonder between the fields on the trail. You know me by Carbough."

Wallace was held in jail for months before he was indicted, and was tried in Franklin County five days after the indictment, some five years after the killing. The jury gave him death. On 8 June 1904 the Court of Criminal Appeals reversed, finding that he should have had a continuance to bring in witnesses and that the prosecutor had urged the jury that if he was not at the scene, "in God's name he should have told where he was." The case was moved to Camp County and tried again; on 31 May 1905 the court reversed that verdict too, for errors in instructing the jury about the testimony of accomplices. Carbough was tried in Camp County as an accomplice and given life in the penitentiary, and on 7 March 1906 the court affirmed.

What became of Wallace after the second reversal, or whether the widow was ever charged, is not known. The murder happened in the Hagansport neighborhood during the years the Smiths were farming there: Charles Oscar was nine in the summer of 1898, and by 1900 his father owned the farm. Nothing connects the family to anyone in the case.

quotes.t: Your man is down yonder; the work is done; the man is down yonder between the fields on the trail.
quotes.c: T. C. Wallace to Mrs. Austin, as she testified; Wallace v. State, 46 Tex. Crim. 341 (1904)

quotes.t: He wanted me to take the life of my husband so that he and I could marry.
quotes.c: Ella (Austin) Johnson, testimony quoted in Wallace v. State, 46 Tex. Crim. 341 (1904)

EXTRA.note: Court record, not a newspaper account. The widow's testimony is the account of an admitted accomplice, and the court twice reversed Wallace's conviction, so his guilt was never settled in these opinions. The family connection is the place and the years only.

EXTRA.name: Frogville, July 1912
EXTRA.rel: Place: where grandfather John Winfred Moffitt was born in 1925
EXTRA.place: Frogville, Choctaw County, Oklahoma
kv: Sloan Pool, keeper of the log scale at the Frogville sawmill
John Buxton, sentenced to hang (21-27 Nov 1912); his father A. F. Buxton acquitted

EXTRA.src: Buxton v. State, 11 Okla. Crim. 85, 143 Pac. 58 (22 Sept 1914), on appeal from the District Court of Choctaw County (https://static.case.law/okla-crim/11/); John Winfred Moffitt's birthplace as given on his own page
EXTRA.title: A quarrel over the log count at the Frogville sawmill
EXTRA.hook: In July 1912 a log cutter shot the scaler at the Frogville sawmill five times over a pay settlement, thirteen years before John Moffitt was born there.
body: Frogville, on the Red River in Choctaw County, was a place of about forty families when John Winfred Moffitt was born there in October 1925. Thirteen years earlier it had a sawmill, and the sawmill had a log scale. Sloan Pool kept it; a man named Wyrick was the sawyer. The log count in the scaler's book was what a cutter's settlement was figured from, so what he wrote was money.

On 18 July 1912 Pool went out to scale logs with Jess Allen and the old logger A. F. Buxton. A. F. Buxton's son John joined them. Allen, an eyewitness, said they all sat on a log while Pool showed John the book, with every log set down. John said he did not want it to be "like the last month's pay day," and the two argued about whether Pool had "figured" him out of money. Allen said that Pool replied, "in that way I mean to dispute your word," and "John shot him." Pool was hit five times. Allen swore that John stood over the body and said, "the next log you scale will be in hell," and shot him again. Then, Allen said, John took Pool's knife from his pocket, asked "how are you going to swear about this?", cut his own arm with it and pressed the knife into the dead man's hand.

Witnesses said Buxton had been talking for weeks. On the day, a man heard him say he would have his settlement from "those damned fellows over there." At the start of July another had heard him say that "the company was beating him" and that he meant to kill Pool. Buxton swore the opposite: that Pool had cut him once on the breast and twice on the arm with "a little old pocket knife," that he had been carrying the pistol because he was told two men were waiting in the woods to kill him, and that "I shot him to keep him from killing me." His sister, Mrs. Ruth Holden, said Allen had told her in jail that he had sworn falsely against her father.

The jury in the Choctaw County district court found John Buxton guilty of murder on 21 November 1912 and set his punishment at death; his father was found not guilty. The judge sentenced him on 27 November to be hanged. On 22 September 1914 the Criminal Court of Appeals affirmed. Because a new state law on executions had taken effect while the appeal was pending and the date fixed had passed, it sent the case back to Choctaw County to set another day. The opinion says nothing about what followed.

The Moffitts were not yet in the county in 1912; at the 1910 census Grady, 18 or 19, was in Stone County, Arkansas, making barrel staves. By 1917 he was a timberman at Ervin, in this same timber country. That day showed what work at a mill in Choctaw County could come to when the scale and the pay disagreed.

quotes.t: the next log you scale will be in hell
quotes.c: John Buxton, as testified by Jess Allen; Buxton v. State, 11 Okla. Crim. 85 (1914)

EXTRA.note: Court opinion; the quotations are testimony as summarized by the court. Nothing seen connects the Moffitt family to anyone in the case. Grady's 1910 stave-making and 1917 timber work are from his own page.

EXTRA.title: A family quarrel ends in a stabbing, January 1938
EXTRA.hook: Oscar Hulsey, 27, was arrested after a two-day search in the mountains north of Millerton for stabbing his wife's brother.
body: In the last week of January 1938, Oscar Hulsey and Eddie Stevenson of Millerton, named as his brother-in-law, had a family quarrel that ended with Stevenson stabbed. A local paper put it in six sentences under the headline "Oscar Hulsey Arrested on Assault Count."

It read: "Oscar Hulsey faces a charge of assault with attempt to kill after his arrest Monday night by Deputies James Houston and Bud Butler. He was charged in connection with the stabbing Saturday night of his brother-in-law Eddie Stevenson of Millerton. Stevenson is in the Sanitarium of Paris, where his condition was reported as satisfactory Monday afternoon. The stabbing followed a family quarrel, officers said. Hulsey was arrested in a remote mountain area 30 miles north of Millerton after a two-day search." By its dates the stabbing was Saturday night, 29 January, and the arrest Monday night, 31 January.

The charge did not go away quickly. The district court dockets of September and October 1938 list "the State of Oklahoma vs. Oscar Hulsey" as assault and battery with intent to kill for the October 1938 term, and the dockets of September 1939 list it again, set for Saturday, 14 October 1939. No sentence, plea or dismissal is known. By April 1940 Oscar was back in Arkansas at South Fork in Montgomery County, working on a government job, and in 1941 his marriage to Katie ended in divorce.

EXTRA.name: Bennie George Hulsey and the pickup truck
EXTRA.place: U.S. 70 two miles west of Hugo, Choctaw County, Oklahoma

Compound fracture of the skull and internal injuries

EXTRA.src: Undated family clipping of an obituary article, "Youth Killed While Riding Bicycle on Hiway Near Hugo" (shared on Ancestry as "Oscar's Son Obit"); matches the headline "Bennie G. Hulsey Dies After Accident Tuesday," The Southeast Oklahoman (Hugo), 24 Jul 1947, p. 1 (Newspapers.com image 904237818, headline index only); McCurtain Gazette (Idabel), 26 Jul 1947, p. 1, “Former County Youth Dies in Bicycle Mishap,” https://www.newspapers.com/image/665487680/.
EXTRA.title: Killed on his bicycle, July 1947
EXTRA.hook: Bennie George Hulsey, 13, turned in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo and died within the hour.
body: The report read: "Choctaw County's second highway fatality was suffered Tuesday night when Bennie George Hulsey, 13, died of injuries received when he turned in front of a pickup truck on his bicycle, the local highway patrol unit reported." Three eyewitnesses told the patrolmen that the boy turned directly into the path of a truck driven by Mack Flinn, 29, of Grant, on U.S. 70 two miles west of Hugo in front of Leon Griffin's store, about 7:30 p.m.

"The boy, son of Mrs. Katie Hulsey, Hugo Route One, was rushed to the Hugo hospital but he succumbed 45 minutes later from a compound fracture of the skull and internal injuries." The patrol said he was knocked 75 feet; Flinn's truck swerved off the road, jumped a four-foot fill and turned over once and a half. Flinn had only a few bruises and two other men in the truck were slightly hurt. The boy's death "marked the second road fatality in Choctaw County during 1947."

Services were set for 11 a.m. Thursday at the Coffey Funeral Home chapel, with burial at Mount Olivet. He was a member of the Assembly of God church and had been born in Danville, Arkansas, the paper says, and had moved with his mother and family to a place on Hugo Route One. The survivors named in the continuation are his mother, his father Oscar Hulsey of Wright City, two sisters, Mrs. Delphia Murphy of Oregon and Mary of Hugo, and four brothers, Leon, Glen, Charles and Willis, all of Hugo. Mary was his sister Mary Ellen, our grandmother, then eight years old.

The Idabel paper, where the Hulseys had lived, ran the story on its front page on Saturday, 26 July, under the headline “Former County Youth Dies in Bicycle Mishap.” It adds what the boys were doing. Pulling a home-made wooden sled and a toy wagon behind their bicycles, Bennie and the son of Leon Griffin had been riding back and forth between the Griffin home and the Griffin store. Bennie and the truck were both headed east when he turned north toward the store's driveway. Highway patrolman Cecil Snapp and Sheriff Bird Collins investigated. It names him as the son of Oscar Hulsey of Wright City and Mrs. Katie Hulsey of Hugo Route 1, and lists his injuries as internal injuries, a compound fracture of the skull and broken ribs.

quotes.t: The boy's death marked the second road fatality in Choctaw County during 1947.
quotes.c: Clipping of the Hugo newspaper, July 1947

EXTRA.note: The clipping does not show the newspaper's name or date. The date is inferred from the matching headline in The Southeast Oklahoman of 24 July 1947, which makes the accident Tuesday, 22 July. The clipping is a low-resolution photograph, so a few words in the second column are read from context. The McCurtain Gazette of 26 July 1947 confirms the Tuesday date, the place and both parents' names. It says he died about 9 p.m., 45 minutes after the collision; the Southeast Oklahoman clipping puts the collision about 7:30 p.m. The two times do not agree.

EXTRA.title: Two courthouses and a second wife
EXTRA.hook: Oscar and Katie were divorced in Arkansas in 1941 and he remarried five weeks later; Katie then sued in Oklahoma, and in January 1946 her divorce was one of a record 26 granted in a single day.
body: Oscar and Katie Hulsey were divorced on 26 September 1941 in Montgomery County, Arkansas. On 3 November 1941, five weeks later, Oscar Hulsey, 31, of Mount Ida, married Hester May Whittington; his birth date was given as 27 October 1910.

The two may have married again afterward. A marriage license was filed in McCurtain County on 27 February 1943 for "HULSEY, OSCAR F" and "STEVESON, KATIE," both named as applicants. It gives no ages or residences, and the paper license is held by the court clerk at Idabel, so whether it records a second marriage of the couple after the Arkansas divorce is not known. If it does, it would explain why Katie needed a divorce in Oklahoma as well.

Katie went back to Oklahoma and appears to have brought a second action there. The court docket of 10 October 1945 reads "Katie Hulsey vs. Os[car Hulsey], divorce," and from 24 November to 15 December 1945 a notice by publication was run in the district court with Katie Hulsey as plaintiff and Oscar Hulsey as defendant, addressed "To: Oscar Hulsey."

The suit ended in January 1946. On Saturday, 12 January 1946, the Idabel paper reported on its front page that a county record had been broken that Wednesday: District Judge George R. Childers had granted 26 divorces in a single day, one more than the previous record of 25, the court clerk, Buel Grinage, said. The paper printed every one of them, the first name of the spouse who filed followed by the other's full name: Addie from C. L. Mahon, Lorene from Jesse Ramage, Floyd from Mary Dimmitt, and so on down a column of twenty-six names. Near the bottom, between Rosa Bell from Lonnie Lewis and John from Dorothy Keiss, is "Katie from Oscar Hulsey." The same front page, a column over, carried the homecoming notices of local men just out of the Army and Navy, which may explain why the judge had so much to do.

By 1950, with both the Arkansas divorce of 1941 and the Oklahoma divorce of 1946 behind them, Katie, 40, was head of a household at Jeter in Choctaw County with her children Glen, Mary, Charley and Willis, "Separated" and "Keeping house." An Oscar Hulsey, "Divorced," lived alone as a farmer on the road between Wright City and Gloster in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, the township where his parents had farmed; he was 38, born in Oklahoma, so the match is probable, not certain.
No reason is given for either divorce.
EXTRA.note: The Arkansas index does not say who filed. The 1950 Oscar Hulsey in Sulphur Township is probable because the age and birthplace are slightly off (38, Oklahoma). The January 1946 list names the parties only as "Katie from Oscar Hulsey," but the 1945 notice in the same court names Katie Hulsey as plaintiff and Oscar Hulsey as defendant, so the identification is firm. The link between the postwar homecomings on the same page and the number of divorces is the paper's juxtaposition, not a stated cause. The 1943 license is probable for this couple (Oscar F. and Katie, clerk's spelling Steveson).

EXTRA.name: Edith Irene (Thompson) Slaton
EXTRA.title: Edith, the Thompson daughter who was proud to be Choctaw
EXTRA.hook: Junior's younger sister was the baby of the house in 1940, and she was proud of her Choctaw heritage all her life.
body: Edith Irene Thompson was born at Hugo on 27 December 1939, one of the children of Simon and Frances (Pisachubbe) Thompson, and grew up in the same crowded farmhouse at Jeter as her brother William “Junior” Thompson, the grandfather of this family. She was the baby of the household when the 1940 census taker arrived the next spring.

When she died in 2012 it was said that she loved her family very much, enjoyed spending time with them, and was “especially proud of her Choctaw Indian Heritage.” She married twice. Her first husband, Bert Jones, died before her; at her death she was married to Cleatus Williams. Her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren lived around Hugo and Blackwell.

Edith died at Durant on 12 April 2012, aged 72. By then she had buried both parents, her brothers Leonard and Junior, and her sisters Ethel Hamill and Norma Homer. Only one brother, Bernie of Grant, was named among her survivors. A color portrait accompanied the notice of her death.
EXTRA.src: Choctaw Nation, Biskinik, May 2012, p. 16, https://www.choctawnation.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/may-2012-biskinik.pdf#page=16.

EXTRA.name: Balas Newton
EXTRA.title: A father’s permission, preserved on paper
EXTRA.hook: Named as Lizzie Newton’s father in the original papers for her 1889 marriage.
body: In November 1889 Balas Newton gave written permission for his daughter Lizzie to marry John M. Shackleford in Etowah County, Alabama, and John swore to it.

In 1880 a Balus Newton lived in Etowah County with wife Mary and daughter Elizabeth, aged seven. Their uncommon names, location and Elizabeth’s age make them a probable match for the Balas and Lizzie of the 1889 marriage. Mary is called Balus’s wife, but nothing says she was Elizabeth’s mother.

The 1880 home held nine people. Balus was forty-four and farming; Mary, thirty-six, was recorded as keeping house. The seven children listed as Balus’s sons and daughters ranged from a twelve-year-old son, whose occupation was farm hand, to an eight-month-old daughter born in November. Between them were Ann, ten; Lindsey, nine; Elizabeth, seven; Hezekiah, four; and Amanda, three. Alabama was the birthplace of Balus, Mary and all seven children.
In March 1901 a Balus Newton made final proof on land before the county clerk, but no age or family names are given, so he may or may not have been Lizzie’s father.

Lizzie's father had fought for the Confederacy twice over: at twenty-five in Company E of the 1st Florida in 1861, and later in Company E of the 51st Alabama Cavalry, until he came home in April 1865. Born in Pickens District, South Carolina, in October 1835, he was still drawing an Alabama pension near Gadsden at seventy-five and signed his papers with a mark.

EXTRA.name: Catherine Elizabeth “Lizzie” (Newton) Shackleford
EXTRA.title: Lizzie’s road from Alabama to Apache
EXTRA.hook: Married in Alabama in 1889, she made her later home near her children in southwestern Oklahoma.
body: Lizzie Newton was born in Etowah County, Alabama, on 20 February 1873. She married John M. Shackleford there on 1 December 1889. Her father Balas Newton gave written consent to the marriage.

In 1880 seven-year-old Elizabeth was in the Etowah County household of Balus Newton and his wife Mary. The rare name, place and age make this a probable match for Lizzie and her father in the 1889 marriage. Mary Ann Dockery, who married a Bailus Newton in 1867, is a probable mother, though no record says so.

The family’s travels eventually took Lizzie to Texas. In 1933 she moved from Dawson County to the Apache community in Caddo County, Oklahoma. She belonged to the Baptist church, and several of her grown children also made their homes in or around Apache.
She spent her final days at the home of her son Ed, six miles southwest of town, and died there on 8 November 1951, aged seventy-eight. She was buried in Fairview Cemetery at Apache.

Her family had grown across Oklahoma, Texas and California. At her death it included nine surviving children, forty-two grandchildren and sixteen great-grandchildren. Sons Ed and John and daughters Mrs. Joe Haskell and Helen Josey lived at Apache; other children had settled in Lawton, Texas and California.
kv: 1933, Dawson County, Texas, to Apache, Oklahoma
8 Nov 1951, at son Ed’s home southwest of Apache
Balas Newton, named in the original 1889 consent and affidavit
EXTRA.note: The 1951 obituaries and her grave marker agree on 20 February 1873; the 1900 census gives February 1872. The newspaper spelling “Etowak” is normalized to Etowah. Both obituaries place daughter May/Mary Moffett at Granite; that place has not been silently changed to Grant. The funeral time was tentative when the notices were printed. Mary Ann Dockery is a probable mother, based on the 1880 household and the 1867 marriage; no record naming Lizzie’s mother directly has been located.
