EXTRA.name: John Winfred Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Moonshine and federal court in Hugo
EXTRA.hook: An October arrest report and later federal court notices preserve a different side of life in Hugo.
body: On a Saturday night in October 1961, two men looking for whisky visited John W. Moffitt in Hugo. They left without a purchase, but Moffitt later caught up with them in town and offered a half-gallon. When he handed it over, the buyers showed their badges: one was a federal alcohol-tax agent and the other worked for the state liquor board.
Moffitt, thirty-six, was arrested and brought before U.S. Commissioner Lon Kile on Monday. His bond was set at $1,000.

Oklahoma had been dry since statehood. Voters repealed prohibition on 7 April 1959 and allowed package sales, but they refused local option, and liquor by the drink stayed illegal until 1984. The "Cannon raids" of the late 1950s had already shut off most of the state's supply. In that Oklahoma a half-gallon sold in town was a crime.

The following spring, federal court news named John Winfred Moffitt of Hugo. In May 1962 he pleaded guilty to two counts of violating the federal liquor stamp law. A June sentencing list recorded John Winfred Moffitt of Choctaw County receiving two years’ probation for operating a still.
EXTRA.note: Identification as the family’s John Winfred Moffitt is probable: the 1962 reports give his full name and Hugo/Choctaw County; the October 1961 report gives John W. Moffitt’s age as 36, matching his 25 October 1925 birth. None names a wife, relative or street address. The court file has not been examined, so the 1961 arraignment and 1962 prosecution have not been proved to be the same case. The newspaper records establish what happened to the men they name; the remaining uncertainty is their identification with this family member and the link between cases.

EXTRA.name: B. F. Hulsey
EXTRA.title: A miner’s household in the Ouachitas
EXTRA.hook: In 1880 B. F. Hulsey worked as a miner and raised a young family in Montgomery County, Arkansas.
body: B. F. Hulsey was thirty-two in Center Township in June 1880. Born in Georgia, he was working as a miner in the Ouachita country of western Arkansas. His wife Sarah G., thirty, had been born in Arkansas.
B. F. was not the only miner on the page: William W. Gleason and C. W. Dyer also gave that occupation. Mining was part of the local community, though nothing shows the men worked together.

Three children were at home: Margaret M., six; George W., four; and Charles F., five months. The household offers a likely childhood home for the later George Washington Hulsey of Story. George’s own 1918 draft registration gives a December 1875 birth, consistent with the four-year-old.

Margaret M. is called a daughter and George W. and Charles F. sons of B. F. Margaret had been born about 1874, George about 1875–76, and Charles early in 1880. Sarah G. appears as B. F.’s wife. Those relationships establish the household, but they do not expressly establish that Sarah was every child’s biological mother.

A later family account connects a Benjamin F. Hulsey with a son George Washington and children named Charles, Mary and Francis. It also gives a wife named Margaret Partain and dates that conflict with other accounts. The overlapping names are useful clues, but it does not resolve the mother’s identity or prove that all the Benjamin Hulsey records concern one man.

Of Sarah G. herself there is little more than her age and her Arkansas birth: her father was born in North Carolina and her mother in Tennessee, which outlines her own family without naming either parent. Her maiden name and full given names are still unknown. She is not Sarah Rebecca Graves, whom George later married, and nothing yet identifies her with Sylvania Susane Partain, the name a descendant's photo caption gives for George's mother.
EXTRA.note: The original 1880 census records B. F. Hulsey, 32, born Georgia, with wife Sarah G., 30, born Arkansas, and son George W., 4, in Center Township, Montgomery County, Arkansas. George’s December 1875 birth in the 1900 Sulphur Springs census and 24 December 1875 birth on his 1918 draft card are consistent with the child’s age. A 1977 family query associates a Benjamin F. Hulsey with a son named George Washington. The connection remains probable: no record yet explicitly connects the adult George, husband of Sarah Rebecca Graves, to the named 1880 parents. This household has not been securely identified with the separate Benjamin Franklin Hulsey biography or with Sylvania Partain. The 1977 query is an unsourced family-research submission with conflicting names and dates; it calls the wife Margaret Partain and gives a 1921 death. It is supporting evidence, not proof of the connection or of a mother’s identity. Sarah G. is recorded as B. F.'s wife, not explicitly as George's mother, so she is a probable mother or stepmother. This story now includes the shorter entry about Sarah G.; its old link opens this page.

EXTRA.name: Sarah G. Hulsey
EXTRA.title: Sarah G., of Center Township
EXTRA.hook: Arkansas-born Sarah lived with a miner’s family and three young children in the Ouachita hills.
body: Sarah G. lived with B. F. Hulsey and three young children in Center Township, Montgomery County, Arkansas, in June 1880. She was thirty and Arkansas-born; she was his wife.

She was born about 1850 in Arkansas to a father from North Carolina and a mother from Tennessee, so her people had come west from the older states before she was born. Neither parent is named, and her own maiden name and full given names remain unknown.

Her husband, thirty-two and born in Georgia, gave his work as miner, and the house stood in the busiest season Silver City ever had. The crossroads, about six-tenths of a mile from the center of Center Township, had taken its name in 1876 and was said to hold more than a thousand people by 1880. Three children filled the house: Margaret M., six; George W., four; and Charles F., only five months old.

The household names Sarah as B. F.'s wife but not as the mother of each child. She may have been George's mother or his stepmother; if she was Charles's mother, she had a baby of a few months in the house that June.

The silver did not last. Every mine had closed by the end of 1882, when George was not yet seven. No record has been found that follows Sarah past the June 1880 count. A Benjamin F. Hulsley took out a Garland County marriage license with Lucy Morgan in September 1893, but nothing ties that man to this household, so what became of Sarah G. is not known. She should not be mistaken for Sarah Rebecca Graves, whom George married years later, nor for Sylvania Susane Partain, a name some family accounts give for George's mother and that has not been linked to her.
EXTRA.note: The original 1880 census lists Sarah G., 30, born Arkansas, as the wife of B. F. Hulsey, in the household containing his son George W., 4. She is a probable mother or stepmother of that child; the census names her as wife, not explicitly as his biological mother. The identification of this child with the later George Washington Hulsey remains probable. Hulsey is her married surname; her maiden name and full given names are unknown. She is not Sarah Rebecca Graves, George’s later wife, and has not been identified with Sylvania Susane Partain.

EXTRA.name: Lt. Gen. Frank Maxwell Andrews
EXTRA.title: The air commander behind the Andrews name
EXTRA.hook: From the Stevenson family in Tennessee came Frank Maxwell Andrews, a pioneer of American air power and the namesake of Joint Base Andrews.
body: Frank Maxwell Andrews was born in Nashville on 3 February 1884, the son of James David Andrews and Lula Adaline Maxwell. He graduated from West Point in 1906 and began his Army career in the cavalry. During the First World War he entered aviation and earned his pilot’s wings in 1918.

In 1935 Andrews took command of the newly organized General Headquarters Air Force. He argued for a modern long-range bomber force and supported developing and buying the Boeing B-17. By 1943 he was commanding United States forces in the European theater, where American and Allied forces were preparing for the campaigns ahead.

When his father died in 1937, Frank recalled how the family had traveled to a world’s fair by train under oil lamps when he was a boy. Years later he flew his father to the Chicago fair in an amphibious airplane, landing on Lake Michigan.

On 3 May 1943 Andrews was killed when the B-24 bomber Hot Stuff crashed in Iceland. In 1945 Camp Springs Army Air Field in Maryland was renamed Andrews Field in his honor; it became Andrews Air Force Base in 1948 and is now part of Joint Base Andrews.

The family connection runs through the Stevenson line. Elam and Lydia Stevenson’s sons included Abner Arrington Stevenson, our ancestor, and his brother James Calvin. James’s daughter Eliza Catherine married William Thomas Andrews; their son James David was Frank’s father. Elam and Lydia are the shared ancestors.

EXTRA.name: Rev. William Thomas Andrews
EXTRA.title: A minister’s memoir that connected two families
EXTRA.hook: In 1912 William Thomas Andrews set down the names of his wife’s parents and their children, preserving a link between the Stevensons and the Andrews family.
body: William Thomas Andrews grew up in Giles County, Tennessee, after his mother brought the family there from Limestone County, Alabama. He was licensed to preach in 1856. On 30 November of that year he married Eliza Catherine Stevenson, daughter of the Rev. James C. and Margaret C. Stevenson.

In a 1912 autobiography Andrews named their five sons and daughter. The first son named was James David Andrews of Nashville, the future father of Frank Maxwell Andrews. James David’s later memorial also named William Thomas and Eliza as his parents.

Andrews spent his first fourteen years in ministry as a local preacher, then joined the North Alabama Conference. His assignments took him to Limestone, Scottsboro, Florence, Gadsden, Talladega and other communities. His published account lists those appointments across decades of church work.
His portrait was printed as the frontispiece of the book.

EXTRA.name: Mary Ann Dockery Newton
EXTRA.title: Mary Dockery and the Newton household
EXTRA.hook: An 1867 marriage and an 1880 census offer a possible name for Lizzie Newton’s mother.
body: A license was issued in St. Clair County, Alabama, on 11 February 1867 for Bailus Newton and Mary Ann Dockery, and the ceremony took place at a Gibson residence; the day is not clear enough to settle the differing dates.

In 1880 Balus Newton and his wife Mary lived in Etowah County with children including Elizabeth, seven. The surname is Newton, though an index reads Keaton. Balus’s name, the county and Elizabeth’s age fit the father and daughter named as Balas and Lizzie in Lizzie’s 1889 marriage consent.

Mary’s work was entered as keeping house in a household of nine. The eldest boy, twelve, was already listed as a farm hand; the youngest child was an infant of eight months. Elizabeth stood between older children Ann and Lindsey and younger children Hezekiah, Amanda and the baby.

Mary was Balus’s wife in 1880, but nothing says she was Elizabeth’s mother. The earlier marriage to Mary Ann Dockery and the household make her a probable mother, but nothing directly names Lizzie’s mother. A death record for Oda Verbena Newton names parents Balous Newton and Mary Marzee Dockery; a similarly named young daughter appears in the 1880 home.

EXTRA.name: Betsy Tims
EXTRA.title: Betsy Tims, the Choctaw wife of the Doaksville trader
EXTRA.hook: Her son gave her name in one line: "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County.
body: On 8 May 1899, at Doaksville, Edward W. Tims, 58, was enrolled. The clerk wrote his father as "Vincent B. Tims," dead, "Non Citz," and his mother as "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. That line is the only record that names the Choctaw wife of the Doaksville trader.

Edward was entered as one-half Choctaw. Since his father was a noncitizen, that implies that Betsy was counted a full-blood Choctaw, though she was given no fraction, no age and no number. A history of Doaksville written from the Tims family's papers calls her Vincent's "full-blood Choctaw wife" and says the two stayed at Doaksville for the rest of their lives.

Three of her children are known: Vinson W., born in 1838, Edward Ward, born in 1842 by family accounts (58 in 1899), and a daughter, Phoebe, who died before the final rolls were made. Vinson's children were enrolled as Choctaws through him and through his wife Emeline Steadman, and his daughter Betsy, born in 1870, who married Joseph P. Thompson, carried her grandmother's name.

She married in the years when the Choctaw Nation was rewriting its marriage law. On 6 October 1836 the General Council abolished "the custom of not intermarrying with their own Iksa," the matrilineal clans, so that "all persons, without any distinction of Iksa, are left to make their own choice as to whom they shall marry." In October 1840 it ruled that no white man could marry in the Nation until he had been a citizen for two years, that he must take a license from a judge or the district clerk and be married by a minister, and that "no white man who shall marry a Choctaw woman, shall have the disposal of her property without her consent." A white man who left his wife "without just provocation" could be ordered to pay her damages and lose his citizenship. No marriage record for Betsy and Vincent has been found, so it is not known which of these rules applied to them.

Her husband's business ran through the removal years: Doak & Tims held the army contracts of 1838 and 1839 to feed arriving Chickasaw emigrants at thirteen cents a ration, and in January 1837 Vincent witnessed the Treaty of Doaksville. Family files give Betsy's birth as about 1800 in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi and her death as about 1860 at Doaksville. Nothing supports either date, and nothing gives her Choctaw name or her parents.

EXTRA.name: Samuel Garrison
EXTRA.title: Samuel Garrison's two tours: Stono, 1779, and Frederick, 1782
EXTRA.hook: Samuel Garrison was at Stono Ferry at sixteen, served again as the war wound down, and was granted a pension in Kentucky only months before he died.
body: Samuel Garrison was born on 24 August 1762, on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line by his family’s record, though perhaps in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. He was still a boy when the Revolution reached the Carolinas.

In 1779, at sixteen, he served four months as a private in Captain James Barr’s company of Colonel Charles McDowell’s regiment, in General John Butler’s brigade of North Carolina militia. In old age he remembered that “he was at the Battle of Stono,” the fight at Stono Ferry near Charleston on 20 June 1779, “in which Major Anderson was killed,” and that Colonel Roberts of the artillery was killed too. Stono Ferry was a British victory: General Lincoln’s attack on the British rear guard cost the Americans about 34 killed and more than a hundred wounded, and Colonel Owen Roberts of the South Carolina artillery was mortally wounded. Samuel kept his discharge, signed “Jas. Barr, Capt.” (a name sometimes read as Bass), which certified his service “from the 20th of March till ye 20th of July” and was dated “2nd July 1779 Near Stono”; the date, he said, should have read the 20th.

He served again as the war was ending: five months in Captain Thomas Beatty’s company of Select Militia, raised under a state act, until Lieutenant Conrad Doll discharged him at Frederick County, Maryland, on 14 January 1782. A family genealogist wondered whether Samuel helped guard the British prisoners marched to Frederick after Yorktown, and repeated a claim that he was at Yorktown itself. Samuel claimed nine months of service in all and said nothing of Yorktown.

By his family’s record, on 14 March 1786, in Mecklenburg County, he married Esther Alexander, a daughter of Hezekiah Alexander. He became a church elder there, ordained on 10 September 1793, and they had nine children. Their sixth child was born in Mecklenburg in September 1797 and the seventh at Bays Fork Creek in Warren County, Kentucky, on 1 April 1800, so the family moved west between those dates. Samuel is said to have been Allen County’s first member in the Kentucky legislature, in 1816.

In old age, living at Hickory Grove in Warren County, Samuel went before the court on 6 September 1832, aged 69, to ask for a pension. On the strength of his two original discharges, his certificate was issued on 6 November 1832, counting four months in 1779 and five in 1781–82, at $30 a year from 4 March 1831. He had little time to draw it. Samuel died on 27 March 1833, in Warren County by one account and in Allen County, at a daughter’s home near Scottsville, by another; Allen County was formed partly from Warren, so the two may describe one place. One family correspondent placed his grave on his old home place south of Scottsville; another did not know where it was.

Two questions remain open. The first is Samuel’s father. The family genealogist first named John Garrison (born 1744), a son of a Baptist minister of Monmouth County, New Jersey; later he preferred a different John Garrison, said to be a son of David Garrison Sr., who came to Mecklenburg from Salem County, New Jersey. He admitted that positive proof of that John’s relationship to David had never been found, and the link to Samuel is only “claimed,” so the family’s line stops, for now, at Samuel. The second is his service and Esther’s death. Some have made him a private in the Continental Line and placed Esther’s death in Coles County, Illinois, but his own discharges were from the militia, and the family record puts Esther’s death in Allen County, Kentucky.

That this Samuel is the husband of Esther Alexander and the father of John Milton Garrison rests on Stuart's family record and a second compiled list (DAR Magazine, August 1952), not on a county record. Stuart's text is inconsistent in places: it calls the service both Continental and Colonial troops in different passages, though the discharges name the North Carolina militia, and it gives Esther's death year as 1827 once and 1829 elsewhere. Samuel's father is unresolved.

EXTRA.name: Hezekiah Alexander
EXTRA.title: Hezekiah Alexander's will names a daughter, Esther Garrison
EXTRA.hook: A 1796 Mecklenburg will ties an Alexander daughter to a Garrison household and to a granddaughter named Caroline.
body: On 8 August 1796 Hezekiah Alexander of Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, made his will, and a codicil followed on 28 January 1797. It names his wife Mary; sons William Semple, James R., Silas, Hezekiah, Amos, Joel and Ozwald; and two daughters, Kezia Alexander and "Esther Garrison," with "her husband" and "dau. Caroline Garrison and other ch. of Esther." William Semple and James R. were to serve as executors with their mother. It does not name Esther's husband, and a later genealogy says only that she married "Unknown Garrison." So no printed account of the will names her husband. That name, Samuel Garrison, comes from the Garrison family record.

The Esther passage matters because it is a record made in Hezekiah's lifetime that ties an Alexander daughter to a Garrison household and to a child, Caroline, who matches the eldest child in Samuel and Esther Garrison's family record (born 9 January 1787). A family genealogist who had a copy of the will quotes the clause for Esther. It leaves a chest of drawers in trust for Caroline, and an enslaved woman named Jean with her children, whom the transcription lists as Siah, Frank and Nancy, for Esther's use for eighteen years, after which they were to be divided between Esther and her children, or, if she died first, among her children as her husband saw fit. His copy is partly garbled, so the names are as he read them. The same will gave four sons Hezekiah's tracts on the French Broad River, each to pay Esther 25 pounds as he reads it. The codicil gave Charles Polk the property that Hezekiah's "late beloved dau. Mary" took with her when she married him.

Hezekiah himself is well documented. He lived from 1728 to 16 July 1801, the son of James Alexander, a Cecil County, Maryland, magistrate and Presbyterian elder, and Margaret McKnitt. He married Mary Sample on 12 June 1752, settled in Mecklenburg, and was appointed a county magistrate in 1768. He sat on the Committee of Safety, was one of thirteen members of the provincial council of 1776, and as a delegate to the Halifax congress that year was placed on the committees that drafted North Carolina's bill of rights and constitution. The entry counts seven sons and three daughters and notes that he enslaved people. In June 1776 Richard Caswell, treasurer of the Southern District, paid Hezekiah Alexander 1,200 pounds for supplies furnished to the militia, and the family's stone house in Charlotte was built in 1774.

Hezekiah did not farm, forge and legislate alone. The 1790 census counts thirteen enslaved people in his household, and the tax lists of 1797 and 1798 show six "black polls," working-age men and women. In April 1791 he bought four more, a girl for 90 pounds 8 shillings, a man for 150, a girl for 136 and a woman for 163, along with livestock and household goods, at the estate sale of a neighbor, Agnes Allen. His will names eleven. Sam, Abram and Bett went to his wife Mary, with the land and the household goods; Jack went to his eldest son, William Sample; Anne to Silas; Hannah to Keziah; and Jean, with her children Siah, Frank and Nancy, to Esther Garrison. A girl named Mary had already been sold to John Parks Jr. through his son James R., and Hezekiah left James the value still owed. The codicil of January 1797 sent "Negro Nance," who had apparently lived with his daughter Mary since her marriage, to Mary's widower, Charles Polk.

Two more children, Nance and Rachel, turn up in the inventory of his estate on 16 October 1801, valued at 150 and 130 dollars, though neither is in the will. Mary Sample Alexander's will of 30 September 1803 left Bett to her son Joel and Bett's daughter, born on 5 September 1799, to Keziah; the faded handwriting has been read as Fanny and as Jenny. The 1800 census, which lists the household under his son Ozwald with Hezekiah and Mary apparently living in it, counts nine enslaved people. Nothing more is recorded of any of them: no surnames, no birthplaces, and no word of what became of them. Hezekiah's grandson S. P. Alexander remembered, in a letter to the historian Lyman Draper in 1874, how the children around 1825 used to gather around an old Black man who told of the wonders he and "Mas. Hezekiah" had seen during the war, so at least one of them was with Hezekiah through the Revolution.

The sources disagree on small points. One account gives Hezekiah's birth as 13 January 1722 and his death as 10 January 1801, against 1728 and 16 July 1801 in another. For Mary Sample it gives death on 17 May 1806 at 71, while another has 17 May 1805. It names three daughters, Esther, Mary and Keziah, and repeats the family account that Mary was killed by a gun accident while her husband cleaned his rifle; the will says only "late beloved dau. Mary." The 1796 will is the one contemporary record here, and it proves only that Hezekiah had a daughter Esther Garrison with a daughter Caroline. Identifying her with Samuel Garrison's wife, and John Milton Garrison as her son, rests on the family record.

EXTRA.name: Children of Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison
EXTRA.rel: 5th great-granduncles and aunts (siblings of John Milton Garrison)
EXTRA.title: Nine children from a family record: the Garrisons of Bays Fork Creek
EXTRA.hook: John Milton Garrison's brothers and sisters, from Mecklenburg County to Warren County, Kentucky, and on to Alabama.
body: Samuel Garrison kept a record book of births, marriages and deaths, and a family genealogy drawn from it lists nine children. The first six were born in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina: Caroline (9 January 1787), John Milton (4 October 1788), Hezekiah Alexander (February 1791), Mary (31 January 1793, who died on 26 October that year), Hannah (15 September 1794, born at her grandfather Hezekiah Alexander's home) and Samuel Young (September 1797). The last three were born at Bays Fork Creek in Warren County, Kentucky: Calvin Alexander (1 April 1800), Esther (22 February 1802) and Cynthia (19 April 1804). Caroline is the only one also named in a will: her grandfather's will of 1796 leaves a chest of drawers in trust for her.

The record follows several of them into adult life. Caroline married William Ray in 1814. On 10 June 1813 in Warren County, Hezekiah Alexander Garrison married Rebecca Lyle, a native of Loudoun County, Virginia. Nine of their children were born in Kentucky before the family moved to Morgan County, Alabama, where he died on 15 August 1846; she died near Moulton on 5 August 1873. Samuel Young Garrison married Eliza Pogue on 23 June 1829 and, in a second marriage, Chalia S. (Mitchell) Jones on 10 December 1840. Calvin married Mariah Neal and later Nancy Margaret Hawkins. Esther married Samuel Alfred Stubbins on 4 August 1825 and died on 13 December 1831, ten days after the infant son she had borne that November. Cynthia married John C. McPheeters on 22 June 1825.

John Milton Garrison was the first son, and Family informants place him on Trammell Fork Creek in Allen County. They also speak of his burial alone in a field by an old cemetery there, which may not agree with the flat marker at Mount Pleasant cemetery, so the grave is unsettled. Later corrections change an earlier date of 1814 for his marriage to Patsey Cannon to 1808 or 1809, in line with the 6 December 1809 Wilson County marriage, and date the legislature's divorce to 29 February 1848 (the approval date printed with the act) and his marriage to Sarah Stamps to 30 March 1848. The same pages show how unsettled his own children are. One descendant counted ten children, five by Sarah Stamps, and named Nancy, Sidney, John, Charles and William Thurston as hers; another says all of them were born before the divorce; a third list gives Patsey children called John Jr., Samuel Jr., Calvin, Abram and Mary C. The genealogist can neither prove nor disprove any of it.

Only that last list has a Mary, and nothing shows she is our Mary Cannon Garrison, born 17 October 1811; the list is unsourced and reached him through a chain of correspondents. The record that names John Milton as her father is her son James's own account of 1885. A lineage printed in 1952 gives a second compiled list of Esther Alexander Garrison's children: Caroline, Milton, Hezekiah, Hannah, Esther, John and Samuel. It matches the family record for six of the nine names, omits Calvin, Mary and Cynthia, and adds a John who is not in the family record. The two compilations may share a source, so they count as one line of evidence, not two.

EXTRA.name: Calvin V. Moffitt and David H. Grimes
EXTRA.rel: 2nd great-granduncle (Calvin, Henry's older brother) and 3rd great-grandfather (David H. Grimes)
EXTRA.title: Two uniforms, two pension claims: Calvin Moffitt and David Grimes
EXTRA.hook: A Lawrence County man made three failed tries at a Union pension, and a Confederate lieutenant's widow made a claim of her own.
body: Two cases of men who served the Confederacy and later sought Union pensions matter here. "Calvin V. Moffitt of Lawrence County served in two Arkansas Confederate units," but when he applied for a pension he "claimed a few months' service in a Union unit and tried three times unsuccessfully to qualify for a Union pension." The files made by that process were far more rewarding for descendants than for Calvin. The second case is "David H. Grimes," a third lieutenant in the 27th Arkansas Confederate Infantry whose widow applied for a Union pension, claiming he had briefly served in 1864 in a Union unit. No dates, wives or place are given for Grimes, and Calvin's father's name is not given either.

Calvin V. Moffitt is Nathan Moffitt's son, born in 1841 and raised in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County. A Calvin V. Moffitt was a private in Company G of the Confederate 25th Arkansas Infantry, and a Calvin V. Moffitt (also entered as Moffett and Moffat) a private in Company L of the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry. That pairing fits the account of two uniforms. Union pensions turned on the unit, not the man's residence, which bears on a puzzle: Company L was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. Company G of the 25th was enrolled at Pocahontas, in Randolph County, on 13 March 1862, and the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863. A C. V. Moffatt, private, Company K, 1st Arkansas Volunteers (30 days, 1861), could be the second Confederate unit, but nothing links him to Calvin.

David H. Grimes is harder. A D. H. Grimes rose from corporal to third lieutenant in Company I of the Confederate 27th Arkansas Infantry. That company was organized on 6 July 1862 at Richwoods, Izard County, one of the four parent counties of Stone County, where Henry Moffitt and Hannah Grimes later lived. That fits the rank and regiment, but a family tree has David Grimes living and dying in the Mississippi lowlands of southern Arkansas by 1876, and nothing puts a David Grimes in Izard County. Whether Hannah Moffitt's father is this lieutenant is unsettled.

A Union pension file is built from sworn statements, and a widow's claim has to prove a marriage and a death. If these two men are ours, such files could name Hannah's mother, and the children of both families, and could show where each man lived in the 1890s and 1900s. Calvin's three attempts may have left several sets of papers.

The service files settle much of this. The Confederate file for "Calvin V. Moffitt" shows him enrolled at Pocahontas on 13 March 1862 by Captain Turnbull for twelve months, in a company first carried as Company E of Turnbull's Battalion and then Captain Sloan's company of the 30th Arkansas before it became Company G of the 25th. A roll dated 30 June 1862 gives his age as 21. He is marked present on the rolls from late 1862 through October 1863, and the roll for January and February 1864 ends his Confederate service in four words: "Deserted his company Feb 8, 1864." A separate file for "C. V. Moffatt" puts him in Captain L. W. Robertson's company of 30-day volunteers, mustered on 17 November 1861 and discharged on 17 December, with transportation due "from Pocahontas to Smithville," the Lawrence County seat. That is very likely the second Confederate unit.

Ten weeks after leaving the 25th, on 20 April 1864, he enlisted in the Union army at DeValls Bluff for three years, signing the enlistment paper with his mark. The papers say he was born in Randolph County, North Carolina, was 22, and worked as a "Wagon Maker" ("Waggonmaker" on the enlistment), the trade of his father Nathan, the Strawberry Township wheelwright. He stood 5 feet 11 inches, with light eyes, dark hair and a light complexion. He was mustered in at Little Rock on 12 May 1864, paid a $25 bounty and $13 advance pay, assigned to Company L, and credited to the 1st Congressional District, Lawrence County, Strawberry. Every roll from the summer of 1864 onward repeats the same remark: deserted 20 August 1864 at Camp Fishback near Little Rock. In May 1909 the War Department pulled his records, which fits the later pension attempts.
The D. H. Grimes file adds a little to the lieutenant's side. He was 33 in 1862, born in Tennessee and living in Izard County, and he enlisted at Richwoods on 6 July 1862.

Moffitt of Lawrence County" and the index has the matching unit entries; with the 1850 Strawberry Township household already on this site, that is probable, not proved, because the guide does not name his parents and the index carries no age or place. The guide's page is a printed example, not a record. The index is one man in the Confederate 25th and one in the Union 4th, while the guide says two Confederate units; the second unit was not identified. For David H. Grimes only name, rank and regiment match, and the earlier note's family-tree placement in southern Arkansas does not fit Izard County, so the identification is unconfirmed. Update, 3 Nov 2026: the Union enlistment papers give Randolph County, North Carolina, as Calvin's birthplace, wagon making as his trade and Strawberry, Lawrence County, as the place he was credited to, which ties the Union soldier to Nathan's household far more firmly than the index did. The Confederate enrollment and the Union enlistment are still two files joined by name, age and place rather than by a statement that they are the same man. Ages conflict slightly: 21 on a Confederate roll of June 1862 and 22 in April 1864, while a December 1841 birth gives 20 and 22. The pension files themselves remain unexamined.

EXTRA.name: Dr. James R. Alexander and Dorcas Garrison
EXTRA.rel: 6th great-granduncle (brother of Esther Alexander) and his wife, a probable sister of Samuel Garrison
EXTRA.title: A brother and sister, a sister and brother: Dr. James R. Alexander and Dorcas Garrison
EXTRA.hook: Hezekiah Alexander’s son James, a Princeton student turned army surgeon, married Dorcas Garrison in York District, South Carolina, and went west to Kentucky a few years before his sister Esther.
body: James R. Alexander was born on 23 November 1756, on the line between Pennsylvania and Maryland, a son of Hezekiah Alexander, and he was living in Cecil County, Maryland, when the Revolution began; one family history has him born about 1761 instead. In 1776 he was a student at Princeton College.

When the alarm reached Nassau Hall that year, he went home to Cecil County and enlisted as a private in Captain Walter Alexander’s company of the Maryland “Flying Camp,” and he was soon made a sergeant. He fell sick at Elkton, then followed his company north by way of Philadelphia, Trenton, Princeton and Newark, and reached Fort Lee after dark on the eve of 16 November, so that, in his own words, he “saw the battle from Fort Lee but was not in it” when Fort Washington fell across the Hudson. He retreated with the army through New Jersey and was discharged on 1 December 1776.

He went back to medicine and joined his father in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. On 25 May 1780 Dr. Alexander volunteered again, this time as a surgeon. Four days later, on 29 May, Tarleton’s men cut down Buford’s regiment at the Waxhaws, and James nursed the wounded in a Presbyterian meeting house near the battlefield and then at Charlotte, until the British reached the town that autumn. He became surgeon to Colonel William Lee Davidson’s Mecklenburg regiment and stayed with it until Davidson was killed at Cowan’s Ford on the Catawba on 1 February 1781.

James and Dorcas Garrison were married on 26 November 1789, though where is disputed: Dorcas herself, in her widow's application, said Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, while Mark Garrison, testifying from Parke County, Indiana, in 1839, and the published marriage records say York District, South Carolina. A family record gives the day as the 6th. She had been born on 23 January 1766, perhaps a daughter of John Garrison. That page lists their ten children: Silas (10 May 1791), Amanda (6 February 1793), Charles Grandison (27 August 1794), Mary Sample (April 1796), Mark (29 December 1797), Abigail (8 November 1799), Hannah (19 August 1801), James Rankin (5 July 1803), John G. (March 1806) and Dorcas Reese (28 December 1807). When Hezekiah made his will in 1796, he named James twice, first with "his children," then as co-executor with his brother William Semple.

About 1795 or 1796 James and Dorcas moved to Kentucky, a few years ahead of Esther and Samuel Garrison. In old age James asked for a pension. He applied on 14 May 1833, giving his age as 76, and was allowed $103.33 a year from 1831 for four months as a private and four and a half as a surgeon. He died in Allen County on 11 March 1836, and on 9 May 1839, at seventy-two, Dorcas applied as his widow. She was still a widow in Allen County in 1850, and is said to have died in 1852. In 1856 their son Mark, writing for himself and for Silas, Charles G., Mary S., Abigail, James R., John G. and Dorcas R., called them the only surviving children, so Amanda and Hannah had died by then. Dorcas's widow's pension, allowed in the same amount as his, was granted under the act of 1838.

The Garrison family’s historian had a phrase for it: a brother and sister Garrison who married a sister and brother Alexander. He admitted that some doubt Dorcas was John Garrison’s daughter, but reasoned from dates and places that she was, and another family history names John Garrison as her father too; York District, where she married, is where Stuart placed John Garrison’s family in the years before about 1795. Whether Dorcas and Samuel were really brother and sister, and which John Garrison was their father, remain unsettled. What is clear is that the Alexander and Garrison families were joined twice, and that both couples ended their days in the same part of Kentucky.

EXTRA.name: Gardner men of Blue County in the 1891 sketches
EXTRA.rel: Possible kin of Eunice (Gardner) Pisachubbe's parents, Jackson and Viney Gardner (lead)
EXTRA.place: Blue County and Wheelock, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.title: Which Gardner was Eunice's brother? Five sketches from 1891
EXTRA.hook: An 1891 book prints sketches of five Choctaw men named Gardner. Only one names his father as Jackson Gardner, the name on Eunice Pisachubbe's Dawes card, and the book never connects him to her.
body: When Eunice Pisachubbe was enrolled at Goodland on 10 May 1899, she named her parents as Jackson and Viney Gardner, both dead, of Blue County. Nothing else has turned up about them. One place to look is an 1891 book of biographical sketches, the same book that prints Joseph P. Thompson's. It has sketches of five Choctaw men named Gardner, and they do not share a father.

Josiah Gardner was born at Wheelock in 1851, went to neighborhood schools until he was fifteen and lived with his parents until 1871, when he began farming for himself. At twenty-one he married Elizabeth Beajis, who was part Cherokee and lived three years. In 1877 he married Sallie Thunley, a Choctaw, and had no family by her. The sketch calls him "a fourth son of Jackson Gardner, of the Oklafalaya clan" and says he was a lawyer who practiced in the Choctaw courts. Eunice's card puts her birth about 1850, a year before Josiah's. If the two Jacksons are one man, Josiah would be her brother or half-brother.

James W. Gardner was born in Blue County, Choctaw Nation, in 1849, if the printed "18i9" is read that way, which fits his 1870 marriage. His father died while James was a child, so he stayed home to look after his widowed mother and never had schooling. In 1870 he married Emily Cornwell, the widow of Wm. Lawson, and by 1891 he had a four-hundred-acre farm near Wynne Wood (now Wynnewood), about thirteen hundred head of cattle, part of the town site and four children. His father is not named. A Blue County birth, a father dead early and a widowed mother are all consistent with a Gardner household whose parents were both dead by 1899, but they are consistent with many households.

The other three can be set aside as sons of Jackson. William Gardner, born in 1830 on the Tombigbee River in Mississippi (printed "Tom Bigby"), names his father as Jeremiah Gardner and his mother as Clarissa La Flore, and says the family reached Towson County in 1833. Judge G. W. (Green) Gardner, born at Little River in January 1844 (printed "18-14"), was also a son of Jeremiah, "who came to the Indian Territory in 1833." Judge Jeff. Gardner, born near Wheelock, was the eldest son of "Noll Gardner," at one time an interpreter for the missionaries; a 1941 life of him, as Principal Chief from October 1894, names his parents as Noel and Hannah Gardner, mixed-blood Choctaws from Mississippi, and gives his birth near Wheelock on 12 July 1847 from his tombstone. Wheelock thus had at least two Gardner households in these years, Noel's and Jackson's. William's sketch also mentions a Tims: before he opened his own store at Hamilton, in Blue County, he worked for "E. B. Tims, the sutler at Doaksville," probably Vincent B. Tims.

What this does not show matters as much. Every sketch is the man's own account, and none links Jackson Gardner to Viney, to Blue County or to a daughter Eunice. Wheelock was a mission and academy, and the sketch does not say which county it lay in. A history of the Tobucksy County courthouse at McAlester also names a Josiah Gardner, a full-blood Choctaw lawyer who could neither read nor write; whether he is the Wheelock-born Josiah is not known. Whether Josiah was Eunice's brother stays unsettled.

A Choctaw family researcher’s transcription of the 1855 census adds one candidate. In the Chickasaw District, a Jackson Gardner kept house with Mary Gardner, Simeon, Abiline, Alfred, Jesse, Josiah and Harriet. The Dawes cards, forty-odd years later, fill in some of the grown children. Jesse J. Gardner, 50, Alfred W., 51, and Josiah, 50, a full-blood, all named Jackson and Mary Gardner as their parents. Lon Gardner, 25, full-blood, named Simeon and Harriet. The 1891 sketch of the Wheelock-born lawyer Josiah Gardner calls him “a fourth son of Jackson Gardner” of the Oklafalaya clan; if Abiline was a daughter, Josiah is the fourth son in that census list, and the sketch fits.

The same transcriber also pointed to a Jackson, twelve, in the household of William Gardner, 34, on the removal-era lists of 1831, which would make a Jackson born about 1819, though the match is her own guess. A trees-only tradition puts Eunice’s father at about 1820 in Mississippi. They fit, and that is all they do.

The trouble is Eunice herself. She was about five in 1855 and is not among the children, and her card gives the mother as Viney, not Mary. Either she belonged to a different Jackson Gardner, or Jackson had had an earlier wife, Viney, and Eunice grew up under another roof, or the clerks wrote the names down differently in 1899. Until the cards themselves are opened, Jackson of the Chickasaw District is a candidate and not an ancestor.

EXTRA.name: Joseph Thompson and the Choctaw men who went to Roanoke
EXTRA.rel: Context for Joseph Perry Thompson (2nd great-grandfather): five Choctaw men with the same Virginia college in their sketches
EXTRA.place: Salem, Virginia, and the Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.title: Spencer Academy to Salem, Virginia: Joseph Thompson in company
EXTRA.hook: Joseph Thompson's 1891 sketch has him at Roanoke College until 1886. Five other Choctaw men in the same book name the same college, and three of the six went there from Spencer Academy.
body: Joseph Thompson's 1891 sketch says he was educated at Spencer Academy and at "Mount Harmon Institute, Northfield," and completed his education at Roanoke College in Salem, Virginia, "where he remained until 1886." He then taught school, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889 and was elected to the lower house of the Choctaw Council the next year. The only other account of his college years is his son Joel's memory, which gives a different order; a college catalog of 1881-82 does not list him.

The same volume shows he was not alone in making the trip. Jacob Jackson was born about 1845, went to Fort Coffee Academy and, after the Civil War, to an academy at Little Rock and King's College in Tennessee, and in 1870 to Roanoke College, "where he spent four years." He began practicing law in 1874, served as senator for Skullyville County and was National Secretary of the Choctaw Nation by 1889. Napoleon B. Ainsworth, born at Skullyville in 1856, entered Roanoke at fifteen, "graduated after four years, in June, 1880," and won the orator's medal that year; the dates do not quite agree with each other, since four years from fifteen would be 1875. He went on to law school at the University of Virginia, served the Nation as auditor and in 1883 married Miss Emily K. Thompson at Roanoke, Virginia. Nothing in the sketch ties her to this Thompson family.

Three more followed the Spencer-to-Salem route Joseph took. Solomon E. Hotema, born near Grant in 1854, went to Spencer Academy and had his education "completed at Roanoke College"; he was elected Kiamichi County clerk in 1881, county judge in 1884, 1885 and 1886, representative in 1887 and senator in 1890. The Rev. William H. McKinney, born in January 1861, was at Spencer until 1877, then spent five years at Roanoke, took his A.B. in 1883, went on to a divinity degree at Yale in 1886 and became a district school trustee and a Presbyterian minister. Don Juan Folsom, born in August 1866 in Atoka County, spent three years at Roanoke after Denison High School, returned to Atoka in 1884, and was elected Clerk of the House that year. His mother's maiden name was Thompson; no link to this family is known.

The pattern is the point. By 1891 a Spencer Academy education followed by college in Virginia was a recognized road to Choctaw office, and county clerk and then the House was a common first step; Hotema and Joseph both followed it. That makes Joseph's own sketch more believable. It does not confirm his years at Roanoke, which still rest on a sketch that Joseph supplied himself and on his son's memory, and the sketches of the other five are the same kind of source.

EXTRA.name: Rev. John Washington Hulsey (1864–1944)
EXTRA.rel: Another Hulsey family in Montgomery County, Arkansas; kinship to George Washington Hulsey not shown (lead)
EXTRA.place: Mount Ida and Montgomery County, Arkansas; Latimer County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: A Hulsey pastor at Mount Ida
EXTRA.hook: A Baptist minister named Hulsey served the Mount Ida church for twenty-two years while George Washington Hulsey lived and worked in the same county. Nothing ties the two families together.
body: A short life of the Rev. John Washington Hulsey was printed in 1952. He was born on 17 March 1864 at Arkadelphia, Arkansas, the son of Lucretia Overall Hulsey and Dr. James Carroll Hulsey, a country doctor who practiced around Cameron, Williams, Spiro, Hartshorne and Wilburton in what became Oklahoma. John had little schooling. He was converted in the summer of 1889, at twenty-five, near Bengal in Latimer County, and was ordained by the Harlan's Chapel Baptist Church on 1 September 1889. The article says he could hardly read when he began to preach.

His pastorates run through two states. In Indian Territory and Oklahoma he served Bengal, Cameron and Poteau, organized the First Baptist Church of Wilburton in 1898 and was moderator of the Short Mountain Baptist Association in 1895, 1896 and 1898. In Arkansas he served Waldron, Parks, West Hartford and Mansfield from 1908 to 1913, then Norman, Caddo Gap and Mount Ida in 1914-1917. From 1922 to 1944 he was pastor at Big Fork, Cherry Hill, Antioch and Mount Ida, and his second term at Mount Ida lasted twenty-two years, "until his death." In 1919 he directed the $75 Million Campaign in Montgomery and Polk counties. He died at Little Rock on 17 November 1944, where he had gone to attend the state Baptist convention.

The geography is the reason for interest. George Washington Hulsey, a boy of four in 1880 in Montgomery County, lived at Story in that county in 1918 and dying at Washita, in Montgomery County, in 1935, with his burial at Breashears Cemetery near Story. His son Louis Daniel died near Mena, in Polk County, in 1948. Mount Ida, Caddo Gap and Norman, where the Rev. John Hulsey was pastor, all lie in Montgomery County, and Big Fork, another of his churches, is in Polk County. Family usage calls George "Rev.," although his records name him a laborer and farmer. A family memory of a Hulsey preacher at Mount Ida may belong to this man and not to George, but nothing supports that.

A shared surname, a shared county and the middle name Washington are not evidence of kinship. Nothing connects Dr. James Carroll Hulsey of Arkadelphia to Benjamin F. Hulsey, born about 1848 in Georgia, or to the Salathiel Hulsey household in Union County, Georgia, in 1850.

EXTRA.name: The post offices on the Thompson, Tims, Austin and Pisachubbe cards
EXTRA.rel: Place story: the mail addresses on the Dawes cards of Joseph Thompson, the Tims brothers and the Austin family
EXTRA.place: Doaksville, Fort Towson, Alikchi, Fowlerville (Valliant) and Corinne, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.title: Five post offices and their dates
EXTRA.hook: Each household had a post office. The dates show when Doaksville, Fowlerville and Alikchi opened and changed their names around the family.
body: In 1899 each household had a post office: Doaksville for Joseph and Betsy Thompson and for Mitchell and Willie Tims, Alikchi for James B. Tims, Fowlerville for Legion and Molsey Austin and Goodland for Eunice Pisachubbe. The Postmaster General's records give the dates for most of them, though they show the offices "on paper" and not always as they ran on the ground.

Doaksville's office opened on 11 November 1847, when the Fort Towson office, which dated from 7 September 1832 with George C. Gooding as its first postmaster, took the Doaksville name. Joseph R. Bertholet (the Berthelet of the Doaksville store) was the first postmaster of Doaksville, appointed in 1847. That bears on a family memory. Joel Thompson said that "Venson Brown Tims" was the first postmaster at Doaksville, but the list gives that place to Berthelet. The two men are linked in the same year: at the Red River Raft Convention held at Clarksville, Texas, in the winter of 1847, two Doaksville citizens, Berthelet and Vincent B. Tims, "took a prominent part."

The office was not always open. It did not operate from 2 July 1866 to 28 May 1867 or from 15 September 1867 to 29 June 1869. A "V. B. Tims" was named its postmaster on 17 May 1871, after the second reopening, and Edward Tims was appointed in 1887. On 12 June 1903 the name was changed back to Fort Towson, which explains why in 1905 the family's address was changed from Doaksville to "Ft. Towson, I.T." Corinne's office, the one the Thompsons used after 1904, opened on 24 August 1904 with Pearl Wynn as its first postmaster.

Fowlerville was the Austin family's office. It opened on 7 July 1894 with Nathaniel M. Fowler as postmaster and was renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902, with Hosea L. Fowler as the first postmaster under the new name. Legion Austin swore to his son James's birth at Fowlerville in May 1899, his wife's 1901 statement for their daughter Adline was sworn there too, and he is said to have died at Valliant on 8 April 1903, less than a year after the change. Alikchi, James Tims's address, opened on 13 July 1888 with John Wooley as postmaster, almost eleven years before he applied. Spencerville opened on 17 May 1902, and Joseph Thompson is said to have died there in 1927.
Goodland, Eunice Pisachubbe's address, is the one gap: no Goodland office is listed, so which office served her household in 1899 is not known.

EXTRA.name: D. H. Grimes
EXTRA.rel: Possibly the 3rd great-grandfather (David H. Grimes, Hannah Grimes Moffitt's father)
EXTRA.title: Elected at Richwoods, dismissed at court-martial: D. H. Grimes, 1862–1863
EXTRA.hook: A 33-year-old Tennessean in Izard County was elected lieutenant within six weeks of enlisting and was dismissed by court-martial eight months later.
EXTRA.place: Richwoods and Camp Bragg, Arkansas; 27th (Shaler's) Arkansas Infantry, Hindman's Division
kv: 6 Jul 1862, Richwoods, by Capt. Riggs, for the war; 2nd corporal, Co. I
Camp Bragg, Ark., roll dated 31 Jul 1862; age 33
6 Apr 1863: age 33, county Izard, born Tennessee
body: D. H. Grimes of Company I, 27th Arkansas Infantry, left a short Confederate record, but it is the only description of him yet found. He enrolled on 6 July 1862 at Richwoods, in Izard County, under Captain Riggs, "for the war." The muster-in roll, made at Camp Bragg, Arkansas, on 31 July 1862, lists him as second corporal of Company I in what was then the 1st Regiment of McBride's Brigade, and gives his age as 33. The regiment was also known by its colonel's name, as Shaler's Regiment.

Six weeks later his company chose him as an officer. He was promoted to junior second lieutenant on 18 August 1862, and in April 1863 he was recorded as elected on 18 August 1862, aged 33, from Izard County, Arkansas, and born in Tennessee. Rosters of Hindman's Division for February 1863 list him as third and second lieutenant, and the second of them marks him "Absent sick." A company roll dated 28 February 1863 says instead "Absent without leave."

By March and April 1863 he was present but "In arrest," and his record closes: "Dismissed Court Martial Apr. 4, 1863." The charge is not given. It may be connected with the absence without leave noted a few weeks earlier.

Whether this lieutenant is Hannah Moffitt's father is still open. David H. Grimes of the family tree was born in 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, which fits a man of 33 in 1862 who was born in Tennessee, and Hannah herself gave Tennessee for both her parents in 1900. Against that, the same tree places David in the lower Mississippi country of Arkansas in the 1850s and has him dying there in 1876, far from Izard County, and nothing names a wife or child. A widow of a David H. Grimes of this regiment later sought a Union pension; that file, if it can be found, would be the record most likely to settle the question.

body: William C. Moffitt's son Marshall died in 1863, and his service can now be told. A Confederate record for "Marshall D. Moffitt" places him in Company E of the 44th North Carolina Infantry, a company raised in neighboring Chatham County and known as "The Turtle Paws."

The company's muster-in and descriptive roll, made at Camp Mangum near Raleigh on 3 April 1862, says he was born in Randolph County, was 23 years old and stood 5 feet 10 inches. He had enrolled in March, at Lows Store according to that roll and at Pittsboro according to the muster rolls, for three years or the war, and he signed the oath of allegiance to the State of North Carolina himself, as "M. D. Moffitt." He was present on the company's rolls from March through August 1862 and again on the roll for January and February 1863, last paid to 31 December 1862.

A register of Confederate soldiers who died of wounds or disease records his death on 28 March 1863 at Greenville, North Carolina. The state's Roll of Honor gives his county as Randolph, his entry into service as 4 March 1862 and his age as 21, and says simply that he "Died April 1863 of Disease."

His age of 23 in 1862 fits the birth year of 1839 given for William C.'s son Marshall, and the Randolph birthplace and the 1863 death agree, so the identification is probable. Nothing names his parents. His file also holds a stray card for a "W. D. Moffitt," captain of Company H of the same regiment, who resigned on 16 July 1862, and the regiment had another Randolph-born private, Milo M. Moffitt, 18, in the same company; neither is identified here, and Milo is too young to be William C.'s son of that name, born in 1828.

EXTRA.name: Nathan, Daniel and Alfred E. Rains
EXTRA.rel: Cousins of the 2nd great-grandfather (sons of Nathan's sister Lydia Moffitt Rains)
EXTRA.title: Three days apart at Raleigh: the Rains brothers of the Randolph Rangers, 1862
EXTRA.hook: Two of Lydia Moffitt Rains's sons enrolled on the same day in March 1862 and died of disease at Raleigh within three days of each other that May.
EXTRA.place: Holts and Camp Mangum, N.C.; Raleigh; 46th and 38th North Carolina Infantry
kv: Capt. O. W. Carr's Co. (Randolph Rangers), later Co. G, 46th North Carolina Infantry
Born Randolph Co.; farmer; 5 ft 11 1/2 in; enrolled 5 Mar 1862 at Holts; died 14 May 1862 at Raleigh (hospital register: 18 May)
Born Randolph Co.; farmer; 5 ft 9 3/4 in; enrolled 5 Mar 1862 at Holts; died 17 May 1862 at Raleigh
Co. G, 38th N.C.; enlisted 19 Aug 1864, Camp Holmes; paroled Greensboro, 19 May 1865
body: A family tree says that two of Lydia Moffitt Rains's sons, Nathan and William Anderson, "died in the Civil War." The Confederate service records tell a somewhat different story: a Nathan Rains and a Daniel Rains, both born in Randolph County, enrolled together and died within days of each other in the spring of 1862.

Both men enrolled for active service on 5 March 1862 at Holts, in Randolph County, in Captain O. W. Carr's company, the "Randolph Rangers," which became Company G of the 46th North Carolina Infantry. The company's muster-in and descriptive roll, dated at Camp Mangum near Raleigh on 16 April 1862, lists each as a farmer born in Randolph County; Nathan stood 5 feet 11 1/2 inches and Daniel 5 feet 9 3/4. Each signed the state oath of allegiance, "N. Rains" and "D. Rains." No ages are given.

Neither left Raleigh. The North Carolina Roll of Honor says Nathan "Died May 14 1862 of Disease at Raleigh" and Daniel died there of disease on 17 May. The Confederate register of deaths agrees on both dates, and a Raleigh hospital register puts the death of N. Rains on 18 May 1862. The illness is not named.

A third brother came later and came home. Alfred E. Rains (also carded as A. Rains and A. C. Rains) was enlisted for the war at Camp Holmes on 19 August 1864 by Colonel Mallett, and served as a private in Company G of the 38th North Carolina Infantry. He drew clothing in November and December 1864, signing by mark, and he was paroled at Greensboro on 19 May 1865 as one of the men surrendered with the Army of Northern Virginia. No service for a William Anderson Rains was found, and none is needed: a brother William A. died on 22 October 1859, before the war.

EXTRA.name: Hezekiah Alexander Garrison & Rebecca (Lyle)
EXTRA.rel: 5th great-granduncle (brother of John Milton Garrison) and his wife
EXTRA.place: Married in Warren County, Kentucky, in 1813; moved between 1830 and 1832 to Cotaco Creek, about six miles east of Somerville, Morgan County, Alabama.
EXTRA.title: From Bays Fork to Cotaco Creek: the Garrisons who went to Alabama
EXTRA.hook: John Milton Garrison's younger brother took his family south to Morgan County, and the family Bible he left kept their story.
body: Hezekiah Alexander Garrison was born at Cowan's Ford on the Catawba River in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, in February 1791, and went with his parents, Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison, to Warren County, Kentucky, about 1798 or 1799. On 10 June 1813 he married Rebecca Lyle there. The family list gives her birth as 25 October 1796 in Loudoun County, Virginia, and names her parents as Manasseh Lyle and Sarah Chaney (also written Chemey), who were first cousins; the Lyles had moved from Loudoun to Bedford County, Virginia, and then to Warren County. Rebecca's obituary gives her birth as 18 August 1796 instead.

Their first nine children were born in Kentucky, in the part of Warren County that became Allen County: Esther Lyle, Samuel Newton (1816), Hillery Y. (1818), Simon Peter (1820), William Calvin, Hannah A., Nancy B., Sarah H. (1828, who died the next year) and Andrew Jackson (April 1830). Then the family went south. Morgan County, Alabama, was opened to settlement in 1830 and Cynthia C., the tenth child, was born there on 3 April 1832, so the move fell between those dates, and a county history shows a Garrison among the settlers who filed land claims in 1830. The obituaries date the move about 1831 (Hillery's) and 1832 (Simon Peter's, and Rebecca's, which adds "I think"). An old section plat puts the family on a half-section of land straddling Cotaco Creek, about six miles east of Somerville, the county seat, near the Old Center Springs camp ground. The last child, Mary Rebecca, was born in Morgan County on 23 June 1835.

Samuel Newton, the eldest son, died in Morgan County on 27 July 1837, at twenty-one, and E. Welch wrote a long poem on his death "in his Mother's stead" that was kept with the family papers. Hezekiah died on 15 August 1846, the date set down in the family Bible; when Rebecca died, she was remembered only as having lost him "about the year" 1846. In 1850 Rebecca, 55 and born in Virginia, headed a Morgan County household with Andrew Jackson, Cynthia and Mary R., and her married sons Simon Peter and William Calvin lived beside her with their families. Cynthia married W. S. McClanahan on 4 January 1854 and died on 11 November 1856.

Rebecca outlived her husband by twenty-seven years. She was a Methodist for fifty years; until she gave up keeping house, "her house was the preacher's home," and two of her sons became preachers. During the Civil War she saw at least one son side with the Union while her youngest son was killed fighting for the Confederacy; the Union son is not named. She died on 5 August 1873, after nine days in bed, at the home of her son-in-law S. W. Shackelford near Moulton, Alabama.

Nearly all of this comes from one book, Hezekiah's Bible, with handwritten births, marriages, deaths and burials and with newspaper obituaries pasted into its record pages. It passed to his youngest daughter, Mary Rebecca, and then to her daughter Minnie, who gave it before her death to a great-granddaughter of Hezekiah's living in Decatur, and its pages were copied for a Garrison genealogy in 1979.

EXTRA.name: Rev. Hillery Y. Garrison & Rev. Simon Peter Garrison
EXTRA.rel: Sons of Hezekiah Alexander Garrison; first cousins of Mary (Garrison) Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born in Allen County, Kentucky. Hillery preached in the Helena District of the Arkansas Conference and died in Phillips County, Arkansas; Simon Peter stayed near Old Center Springs, Morgan County, Alabama.
EXTRA.title: Two preachers from Center Springs: Hillery and Simon Peter Garrison
EXTRA.hook: Two of Hezekiah Garrison's sons became Methodist preachers: one rode Arkansas circuits through the Civil War, the other never left the neighborhood of the old camp ground.
body: Hillery Y. Garrison was born in Allen County, Kentucky, on 22 January 1818 and came with his father to Morgan County, Alabama, about 1831. He professed religion at Barret's Camp-ground in the fall of 1837 under the Rev. William H. Johnston, was licensed to preach in 1842, joined the Tennessee Conference that fall, was transferred to the Alabama Conference and placed on the Coosa Circuit, and "located" (left the traveling ministry) when the year was out. He also studied and practiced medicine. In 1848 he married Jane Alexander, daughter of the Rev. Aaron Alexander of Lincoln County, Tennessee. Jane died at her father's home on 10 October 1850, in her twenty-third year, a few weeks after her sister Martha, her father and her baby of about five months. Hillery's obituary prints her death year as 1830, an evident slip.

He married again, to Eliza C. Beale of Madison County, Alabama, and moved to Arkansas. The family dates that marriage 28 December 1852; his obituary puts it in 1854, with the move soon after. In the Arkansas Conference, Hilary Y. Garrison (so spelled) was a preacher on trial in 1862 and 1863 and was received into full connection at Jacksonport in October 1864. He worked in the Helena District each year: at Prairie after the conference of November 1862, on the Helena Circuit after October 1863, on the Prairie Circuit after October 1864 and at Clarendon after the conference of 1865. The church kept its minutes through the war in the Confederacy, and they place him at work in the same district through all four years.

He died in Phillips County, Arkansas, on 8 December 1868, after about twenty-four hours of quinsy. He left a wife and one child in Arkansas, "an aged, widowed mother in Alabama," and several brothers and sisters.

Simon Peter Garrison, born in Allen County on 10 January 1820, moved with his parents to Morgan County in 1832 and, as his son Simon R. Garrison wrote, "settled near Old Center Springs' Camp ground." He joined the church at seventeen. On 18 December 1844 he married Louisa Glover, born in Northampton County, North Carolina, on 9 July 1828, whose widowed mother had moved to Morgan County near the same camp ground. They had seven children. Louisa died near Somerville of consumption in February 1874; two of her sons had just entered the ministry. In 1875 Simon Peter married Annie E. Orme, and they had three children, two of whom died as infants.

Simon Peter was an exhorter and class leader for years before he was licensed to preach in 1862. He was ordained deacon at Florence and elder at Decatur, the latter in 1876, and his preaching stayed mostly in his own neighborhood and county; his son called him one of the "old-time" Methodist local preachers. He was a wealthy farmer. He died at Somerville on 13 May 1896 after a long illness and lived to see his two oldest sons preach. He and Louisa are buried in a family cemetery near Center Springs Methodist Church.

EXTRA.name: Mary Rebecca (Garrison) Shackelford & S. W. Shackelford
EXTRA.rel: Youngest child of Hezekiah Alexander Garrison; first cousin of Mary (Garrison) Satterfield
EXTRA.place: Born in Morgan County, Alabama; lived at Moulton and at Hartselle; buried in Hartselle cemetery.
EXTRA.title: The youngest child, a carriage shop at Hartselle, and the Bible she kept
EXTRA.hook: Mary Rebecca Garrison married a Morgan County wagon maker, lost a brother in the last weeks of the war, and handed her father's Bible down to her daughter.
body: Mary Rebecca Garrison, the youngest of Hezekiah and Rebecca Garrison's eleven children, was born in Morgan County, Alabama, on 23 June 1835. She was still at home with her widowed mother in 1850, in 1850. On 29 September 1858 she married S. W. Shackelford. Her mother died in August 1873 at the Shackelfords' home near Moulton; S. W. Shackelford also lived at Moulton, but the couple's longer home was Hartselle, in Morgan County, where both were buried.

In March 1887 a trade paper noted that "S. W. Shackelford is building a wagon and carriage shop at Hartselle, Ala." The notice says nothing more about him, but the name, the initials and the town agree with the family record.

The family list in the Bible names four Shackelford children. Fannie Laura, born on 10 March 1863, died on 1 April. Robert James, born on 28 August 1864, married Sallie C. Bennet at Zion, Kentucky, on 12 July 1886 and made his home in Nashville. Hillery Sather, born on 12 May 1873, was living at Wynnewood in the Indian Territory when his mother died. Minnie Ann Emma, born on 6 August 1876, married R. L. Cox of Hartselle and lived to be 102; she died in 1978 in a nursing home at Athens, Limestone County, and was buried beside her husband in the Shackelford lot at Hartselle.

Mary Rebecca's brother Andrew Jackson Garrison, born in Allen County, Kentucky, in April 1830, married Sarah Sanders in Morgan County on 30 January 1862. The Bible records in longhand that he "was killed by our Federal Enemys, April 1865, near Crutchers shop, Madison Cty., Ala.," and that he was "a member of Col. Meads Confederate Guerillers." No service record for him was found. An Andrew J. Garrison served as a sergeant in the 1st Alabama Reserves, but nothing ties that man to this one.

Mary Rebecca died at Robert's home in Nashville. Her death notice, clipped from a Hartselle paper and kept in the Bible, says her body was brought home on a Sunday, her funeral was held at the Methodist church, and she was buried in Hartselle cemetery beside her husband. The date of the notice is not given. She had inherited her father's Bible, with its handwritten records and pasted obituaries, and it passed to Minnie, who gave it to a Garrison cousin in Decatur.

EXTRA.name: James H. Satterfield in Marshan Township, Minnesota
EXTRA.place: Marshan Township, Dakota County, Minnesota, just south of Hastings.
EXTRA.title: School District No. 95, Marshan Township, 1874
EXTRA.hook: A James H. Satterfield sat on a new school board in Marshan Township in 1874, bearing out his own account of the family's years in Dakota County.
body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography says he moved from Allen County, Kentucky, to Dakota County, Minnesota, in 1867 and went back to Kentucky in 1875. His daughter A. M. was born in Minnesota in 1870.

A county history of 1881 tells how School District No. 95 of Marshan Township began. The district was organized on 31 March 1874 at a school meeting at the house of W. B. Mather, which voted to raise $400 for a schoolhouse; the building went up on the northeast quarter of section 8, on land owned by Peter Huneicker. "The first trustees of the district were elected at this meeting, and were as follows: James H. Satterfield, director; L. D. Massey, clerk; William R. Mather, treasurer." Ella Gilkey taught the first term, four months in the winter of 1875-76, to about twenty-seven pupils. A later history repeats it with the same names.

Marshan was bounded on the north by Nininger, Hastings and Ravenna, on the east by Ravenna, on the south by Douglass and on the west by Vermillion. Its soil was mostly sandy, and the Vermillion River crossed its western sections.

The name, the county and the years agree with his own account, and the school meeting falls a year before he says he left. The clerk's name is a second point of contact. James's sister Ruth M. Satterfield married a Massey and is buried, as Ruth Melissa Massey (1840-1935), at Amarillo. Whether L. D. Massey was her husband is not known. If the director was James, he did not stay to see the first term taught: by his own account he was in Warren County, Kentucky, in 1875.

EXTRA.name: Joseph Perry Thompson in the Choctaw General Council
EXTRA.place: Cedar County and the General Council, Choctaw Nation
EXTRA.title: Proposed by J. P. Thompson: Joseph in the council records, 1890–1904
EXTRA.hook: Joel remembered his father as a lawmaker for years, and one line in the printed acts of the October 1904 session may be his: 'Proposed by J. P. Thompson.'
body: In 1891, while he was still under thirty, it was written of Joseph that he began as a schoolteacher, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889, and "the year following he was elected representative to the lower House," where he was "one of the youngest members of the legislature." His son Joel later added that he served as county judge and about six years as a senator. None of this has been matched to a record of the General Council itself.

The council Joseph joined in 1890 passed several laws for his own county. Among them were an act approved 31 October 1890 that redrew the line between Cedar and Nashoba counties along Ward's Creek, an act approved 15 October 1891 that set up an election precinct "at or near the Gilbert Cooper place" in Cedar County, to be called Lick precinct, and an act approved 3 December 1891 that moved the Cedar County court ground from Pine Hill to Sulphur Spring, the court ground Joel later remembered his father presiding over. It is not printed who proposed these acts or how anyone voted, so they show what Joseph's council did, not what he did in it.

The clearest entry comes at the end. The acts of the General Council for the October 1904 session open with a run of resolutions giving each committee a clerk. One authorized the chairman of the Committee on Petitions to appoint a clerk "to make and keep a full record of the work of said committee," at four dollars a day, paid by warrant of the National Auditor. It closes: "Proposed by J. P. Thompson." Like the bills around it, it took effect "by statute of limitation" on 13 October 1904 (the printer set the year as 1604), over the name of Principal Chief Green McCurtain, attested by J. W. Conser, recording secretary.

Only initials are given. The only adult Choctaw citizen named Thompson whose given names begin with J. P. is Joseph P. Thompson, who was 40 on the final roll. That makes the identification probable rather than proven. It is not said whether J. P. Thompson sat in the House or the Senate, or which county sent him.

It is a small bill, but it places Joseph in the council when the Nation's land had already been divided: the year before, he had gone to Atoka to select the family's allotments. The acts of the 1902 and 1903 sessions contain no bill proposed by a Thompson, so the dates of his House term, his years as county judge and his time in the Senate are not known.

EXTRA.name: Goodland, Kiamitia County
EXTRA.rel: Place story: Eunice Pisachubbe's post office and her county's court ground
EXTRA.place: Goodland, Kiamitia County, Choctaw Nation (now Choctaw County, Oklahoma)
EXTRA.title: Goodland court ground: Kiamitia County's seat in the Pisachubbes' years, 1889–1902
EXTRA.hook: Eunice Pisachubbe's post office in 1899 was Goodland. For thirteen years Goodland was also where Kiamitia County held court, until the council moved it three miles south to the new railroad town of Hugo in December 1902.
body: Goodland began as a Presbyterian mission station. George Ainslie, a missionary who had served there, wrote about it in a letter printed in 1939. He put it about twelve miles southwest of Goodwater and eighteen miles from Doaksville, and said its church was "a colony from Goodwater." When he first saw it in 1852 it was "a pretty and pleasant station" of a mission house and a church that also served as the school, "surrounded by forest with no prairie near." In the same letter he notes that Goodland had only a day school.

The railroad changed its place in the county. On 28 October 1889 the General Council passed two acts for Kiamichi County, as the laws spell it. One moved the Clear Springs election precinct to "Good Land station" and set the first election there for the first Wednesday in August 1890. The other removed the county court ground from Clear Springs to "Good Land station on the St. Louis & San Francisco railway," with court to sit on the first Monday of every month beginning in January 1890. The county judge was to sell the old courthouse at Clear Springs and set the money aside for a new one at Good Land.

That is the Goodland of the family's records. On 10 May 1899 Eunice Pisachubbe, 49, her sons William H. and Robert, and her ward Edward were enrolled for Kiamitia County, post office "Goodland, I.T." The Secretary of the Interior approved their enrollment on 12 December 1902.

A week later the court ground left. In an extra session in December 1902 the council moved the Goodland election precinct to Hugo, "about three miles south of the present site," with the first vote there in August 1903 (approved 18 December). An act approved 19 December removed the county court ground "from its present site, at Goodland" to Hugo, told the county judge to choose a house in the town, and set the first term for the first Monday in February 1903. Another act, approved the same day, let the judge sell "the building formerly used as a court house at Goodland" and buy a building in Hugo "at the junction of the Arkansas & Choctaw Railroad and the St. Louis & San Francisco Railroad." All three were proposed by Jeff Fulton.

Hugo became the family's town. William Harrison Pisachubbe's funeral in 1937 was held near the Long Creek school house, Robert and Lizzie lived at Speer and then with Simon and Frances at Jeter, and Simon and Frances are buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, . Where on the Goodland road Eunice's own house stood is not known.

EXTRA.name: Edward Tims, Company G, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles
EXTRA.rel: Possibly Judge Edward Ward Tims, 3rd great-granduncle (identification is a lead)
EXTRA.place: Confederate Indian Territory
EXTRA.title: A corporal named Edward Tims, 1862
EXTRA.hook: An Edward Tims was third corporal in a Choctaw company in 1862, with no age or home given, so whether he was Betsy's uncle Edward is an open question.
body: Whether any relative served in the Civil War is open. A small Confederate file survives for "Tims, Edward" of Company G, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles, "also known as Cavalry." It gives his rank as corporal and holds a single card.

The card copies one line of a pay roll. "Edward Tims," "3d Corpl," of Capt. Coleman E. Nelson's Company, 1st Regiment Choctaw Mounted Rifles, appears on a roll of enlisted men for commutation of clothing "for the last six months of the year ending November 23, 1862." The sum is twenty-five dollars. The roll date is written "Aug 13, 1862," which falls before the end of the period it covers; that is not explained. A printed note says Nelson's company was also known as Company G.

Nelson's own file sets the regiment's scene. As captain of Company G of the 1st Choctaw Regiment he signed a petition dated at Fort McCulloch in June 1862, from officers of the Indian regiments in Confederate service, asking that their colonel, Sampson Folsom, be made a brigadier general in the Provisional Army. On the clothing roll his name appears only as the signature to the certificate.

The obvious candidate is Edward Ward Tims of Towson County. In 1899 he gave his age as 58, so he would have been about twenty in 1862, and he is the only Edward Tims among the Choctaw by blood. But the war record names no county, father or age, nothing ties Nelson's company to Towson County, and nothing in his own life mentions service. So it stays a possibility.

Confederate pension applications turn up no help: the only Tims is Mary Amanda, widow of Francis Marion Tims of a Texas regiment, and there is none from Edward or from his wife Willie Jane, who died four months before him in 1922.
