EXTRA.name: Benjamin F. Hulsey, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)
EXTRA.rel: Probably B. F. Hulsey of the 1880 census, the provisional father of 2nd great-grandfather George Washington Hulsey (identity not proven)
EXTRA.place: Cedar Glades, Montgomery County, and Little Rock, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Born in Fannin County: Benjamin F. Hulsey signs on at Cedar Glades, 1864
EXTRA.hook: His own enlistment paper, signed with his mark, names the north Georgia county where he was born.
body: When Benjamin F. Hulsey, private, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, joined the Union army, he made two papers. On his volunteer enlistment, sworn at Cedar Glades, Arkansas, on 14 January 1864 before Lt. J. B. Spiva of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, he stated that he was "born in Fannin Co in the State of Georgia," aged eighteen, a farmer, and volunteered for three years. On the declaration of recruit he signed "Benjamin F Hulsey, his mark." The form for a parent's consent in the case of a minor was left blank.

The papers describe him as having black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion. They do not agree on his height: the enlistment gives five feet nine inches, while the descriptive roll and the company descriptive book both give five feet three. He was mustered into service at Little Rock on 17 February 1864. The detachment roll assigns him to Company L, but every company muster roll carries him in Company D. He brought his own mount: the rolls credit him with pay "for use and risk of horse and equipments" from enlistment to 20 June 1864.

He was present on every muster roll from enlistment through April 1865. In November 1864 he was on daily duty "at work on stables," and in February and March 1865 he was on detached service in the quartermaster's department as a teamster. He was mustered out with the company at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, still recorded as eighteen. The regiment had been ordered disbanded on 2 June 1864, "the War Dept not sanctioning the raising of a one year Regt"; his rolls nonetheless run on to June 1865.

Fannin County was created in 1854 from parts of Gilmer and Union counties. A boy of eighteen in January 1864 was born about 1845 or 1846, before the county existed, so the name he gave is most likely the county his birthplace lay in by the time he enlisted. In 1850 a Benjamin, three, was in the Union County household of the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey, and in 1880 the B. F. Hulsey of Center Township, Montgomery County, gave his age as 32 and his birthplace as Georgia. The three ages differ by a year or two. The Fannin County birthplace fits the Union County household and is the first time Benjamin himself names where he was born, but it names no parent.

He was not the only family name on that day's list. On the same 14 January 1864, at Cedar Glades and before the same Lieutenant Spiva, Gillam Graves, 45, born in Randolph County, North Carolina, signed his own enlistment into the same company. Gilliam Graves was the grandfather of Sarah Rebecca Graves, who in 1901 married George Washington Hulsey.

EXTRA.name: Gilliam Graves, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)
EXTRA.rel: 4th great-grandfather (father of Jesse Graves; identification probable)
EXTRA.place: Cedar Glades, Montgomery County, and Little Rock, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: A horse lost near Harrold and two months' pay: Gilliam Graves's service record
EXTRA.hook: On the day Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades was shot, the enemy took Gilliam Graves's horse in a fight in his own county.
body: Gillam Graves, private, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, swore his volunteer enlistment at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864 before Lt. J. B. Spiva. It says he was born in Randolph County, North Carolina, was 45 years old and a farmer, with black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion, five feet ten inches tall. He was mustered into the service at Little Rock on 17 February 1864. The company descriptive book repeats Randolph, N.C., as his birthplace. The family genealogy gave that birthplace too, but the enlistment is his own statement. His name also appears as Gillman Graves.

Like most of the company he rode his own horse, and the rolls pay him for its use from enlistment. A notation of 1869 explains a gap in that pay: "Horse and equipments captured by the enemy while engaged in action near Harrold Montgomery Co. Ark. March 1st, 1864," so that he was "not entitled to pay for use of horse from March 1st, 1864 to April 10th, 1864." The first of March 1864 is the day the Union men of Montgomery County said Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades was shot down, and the day the army lists a skirmish at Cedar Glade . Harrold is spelled as written; the place has not been identified.

The rest can be told. The return for September 1864 has him absent without leave, and in October he "Deserted Oct. 12/64 at Little Rock," with $18 stopped for arms and accoutrements. He returned on 25 December 1864, "in arrest" on one roll and "restored to duty without loss of pay" on the next. He was then tried by a general court-martial for absence without leave and sentenced to forfeit two months' pay and allowances, under orders of 28 December 1864. He was present on the rolls for early 1865 and was mustered out at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, last paid to 30 June 1864.

He did not serve alone. Benjamin F. Hulsey enlisted the same day before the same officer, and Alson Graves, eighteen, who is probably the Alison Graves of the orphaned household Gilliam had in his guardianship, was in Company D as well.

EXTRA.name: Alson (Allison) Graves
EXTRA.rel: Ward of 4th great-grandfather Gilliam Graves (relationship not established)
EXTRA.place: Montgomery County and Little Rock, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Alson Graves, the ward who enlisted at eighteen
EXTRA.hook: One of the orphans in Gilliam Graves's guardianship turns up beside him in the same Union company.
body: In January 1854, and again in April 1861, Gilliam Graves was named guardian of the minor children of Samuel and Sarah Graves of Montgomery County, Arkansas. In 1860 they were a household of their own: William (Riley), 22, Alley, 17, Ursa, 15, Alison, 14, and Madison, 11, all born in North Carolina.

The story carries forward in a Union record filed as "Graves, Allison," the name being given as Alson Graves. Alson Graves, eighteen and a farmer, volunteered at Little Rock on 21 November 1863 for three years, enlisted by William Brown, recruiting officer of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, before Capt. Geo. H. Hand. He signed by his mark. He was six feet tall. He first appears on a detachment muster-in roll of Lieut. Vance's company, 3rd Arkansas Cavalry, dated at Benton, Arkansas, on 6 December 1863, whose card notes that the organization afterward became part of the 4th. He was mustered into Company L of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Little Rock on 21 April 1864, and from then on the company rolls carry him in Company D.

The papers disagree about where he was born and what he looked like. The enlistment and the detachment roll say New Hanover County, North Carolina, with black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion. The company descriptive book says Randolph County, North Carolina, with grey eyes, dark hair and a fair complexion. Randolph County is where the Graves genealogy places the 1837 marriage of Samuel Graves and Sarah Cole.

He was present on every roll from enlistment to April 1865. His first roll notes "No horse," and later rolls pay him for the use of a horse. He was mustered out with the company at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, his age still given as eighteen. His guardian Gilliam Graves served in the same company, which he had joined at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864.

The name, the age (fourteen in 1860, eighteen in late 1863), the North Carolina birth and his service in his guardian's company all fit the Alison of the 1860 household and the 1861 guardianship, and nothing seen contradicts them. How Samuel and Sarah's children were related to Gilliam remains unknown.

EXTRA.name: William Elam Fletcher Stevenson
EXTRA.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Fort Donelson; Camp Douglas, Illinois
EXTRA.title: W. E. F. Stevenson of the Third Tennessee: Fort Donelson, Camp Douglas and back
EXTRA.hook: Abner Stevenson's eldest son went to war at nineteen with a Giles County company and spent the summer of 1862 in a prison camp in Chicago.
body: William Elam Fletcher Stevenson was the eldest son of Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson, born on 9 April 1842. His initials, W. E. F., are unusual enough to follow: W. E. F. Stevenson, private in the 3rd (Clack's) Tennessee Infantry, enlisted on 17 May 1861 at Nashville, mustered by Inspector Scudder for twelve months. One record describes the regiment as first organized at Lynnville, Tennessee, on 16 May 1861.

The Third Tennessee was organized at Lynnville, "this county," on 16 May 1861, and that five of its ten companies came from Giles County. Among them was Company K under Capt. F. C. Barber, which at the reorganization in September 1862 became Company A. Stevenson was carried first in Company K and then in Company A, exactly as that company was renumbered.

The regiment went to Fort Donelson in February 1862. W. E. F. Stevenson was captured there on 16 February and appears on a roll of prisoners of war at Camp Douglas, Illinois, of 1 August 1862. A roll dated at Camp Douglas on 7 September 1862 lists him among the prisoners sent to Vicksburg to be exchanged; its endorsement records that 824 prisoners were received on board the steamer Jno. H. Done near Vicksburg on 23 September 1862. The regiment was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi, three days later.

He was present on every muster roll from August 1862 through February 1864, once noted as absent from Chickasaw Bayou on detached duty, and by early 1864 his term was entered as "war." He drew clothing on 30 April 1864, signing "E F Stevenson," and again on 7 June 1864, when the receipt has only a mark. He was admitted to the 1st Mississippi C.S.A. Hospital at Jackson, Mississippi, on 28 October 1864 with intermittent fever, and returned to duty on 22 November. The record stops there. The regiment was merged into the 4th Consolidated Tennessee Infantry about 9 April 1865 and paroled at Greensboro, North Carolina, on 1 May 1865, but no parole is recorded for him.
His younger brother Frank, the family's 2nd great-grandfather, was born in Giles County in November 1861, six months after William enlisted. So, as his nephews did, one of Abner's own sons served.

EXTRA.name: Robert Hulsey, Company B, 8th Battalion Arkansas Infantry (Confederate)
EXTRA.rel: Possible brother of B. F. Hulsey (lead)
EXTRA.place: Arkansas; Meridian and Marion, Mississippi
EXTRA.title: A Georgia-born Robert Hulsey loses an eye: a Confederate discharge, December 1862
EXTRA.hook: Two years before Benjamin F. Hulsey rode for the Union, a Robert Hulsey of the right age was sent home from a Confederate hospital half blind.
body: Robert Hulsey, private, Company B, 8th Battalion Arkansas Infantry, left a short record, chiefly his certificate of discharge. The certificate, written at the General Hospital "Okolona" at Meridian, Mississippi, on 15 December 1862, says he was enlisted by Capt. Imboden on 5 March 1862 to serve three years, at a place in Arkansas that reads like "Cordova." It gives his birthplace as Habersham County, Georgia, his age as 30 and his height as five feet six inches, with a dark complexion, blue eyes and dark hair, a farmer.

The examining board of three surgeons found him unable to serve "because of chronic ophthalmia & loss of one eye and serious injury of the other," and recommended his discharge under General Order No. 72. He was honorably discharged at Marion, Mississippi, on 21 December 1862.

Why this Robert matters is his age and birthplace. Thirty in 1862 places his birth about 1831 or 1832. The Robert in Salathiel Hulsey's Union County, Georgia, household was 17 in November 1850, and the Georgia-born Robert Hulsey of Hempstead County, Arkansas, was 27 in 1860; both point to about 1833.

Nothing names his parents, his wife or his home county in Arkansas. He may be Salathiel's son Robert and the Hempstead County farmer, and so a possible older brother of the Benjamin F. Hulsey who joined the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry in 1864, but none of those links is proven.

EXTRA.name: Grady Moffitt's brothers and sisters
EXTRA.rel: Great-granduncles and great-grandaunts (Grady's brothers and sisters)
EXTRA.place: Randolph and Stone counties, Ark.; Choctaw Co., Okla.; Texas
EXTRA.title: Henry and Hannah's other children: a section hand, a plainsman and three sisters
EXTRA.hook: Grady was the youngest. His brother Tom farmed next door to him in Oklahoma, and his brother Jesse went all the way to the Texas plains.
body: Henry and Hannah Moffitt started their family in Randolph County, Arkansas. In 1880 at Janes Creek Township they had Josephine, 3, and Jesse, 1. Hannah later said she had borne seven children and that six were living, so one died young and left no record. By 1900 the family was in Franklin Township, Stone County, with Jesse; a daughter “Gimsa,” born in August 1883; Bertha, born in March 1886; Tom; and the youngest, Woodford Grady. Josephine, who would have been about 23, was no longer at home.

Thomas Berry “Tom” Moffitt, born at St. James in Stone County on 17 February 1889, was the first of the children known to be born in Stone County. After his father died in 1901 he stayed with his widowed mother, and in 1910 he was working as a railroad section hand. By 1920 he had followed, or led, his brother across the Red River and was farming next door to Grady in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma. His wife Vesta died at Holdenville, Oklahoma, in October 1930, aged 38. Tom ended up at Paris, Texas, where he died on 21 March 1953; his grave marker is carved for service in both world wars.

Jesse Gee Moffitt (1879–1957) went the farthest, out onto the Texas plains. He is buried at Tahoka in Lynn County, and family notes place his death at Amarillo. Of the sisters, less is known. A Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888–1930) is buried at Herpel Cemetery near her mother and may be the Bertha of 1900, but that is not proved.

EXTRA.name: The Hulsey brothers and sisters
EXTRA.place: Garland and Montgomery counties, Arkansas; Sulphur Township and Wright City, McCurtain County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: Ten children of a preacher, from Hot Springs to Wright City
EXTRA.hook: Oscar was the fourth of ten. Here is what the records say about the other nine, and where they go quiet.
body: George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves married on 22 December 1901 and had ten children over twenty-one years. The first three were boys: William Roy in 1904, John Wesley in 1906 and Noah in 1908. In April 1910 the young family was in Mountain Township, Garland County, Arkansas, with “William R.,” “John W.” and Noah at home. Their father farmed, and the family remembers him as a preacher. Oscar arrived that October at Hot Springs.

Then the family started moving. Fred came in 1913 and Ruby Ellen in 1915, the first daughter after five sons. Grady was born in 1918, the year his father, whose home was at Story in Montgomery County, registered for the draft while working on the Camp Pike construction job near Little Rock. By 1920 the household had crossed into Oklahoma and was tenant-farming in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, with six children at home. Louis Daniel was born at Bethel that May. Grace Irene followed in 1923, when her mother was about 39, and George Paul, the last, in 1925, when his father was nearly fifty. In 1930 they were a renting household of ten near Wright City, deep in the sawmill country.

Their father died on 5 August 1935 and was buried at Breashears Cemetery near Story. The eldest, William Roy, was about 31; the youngest, George Paul, was nine or ten. Their mother later went west and died at Bandon, Oregon, in 1972. When Oscar died in 1982, four brothers and two sisters were still living. Ruby, who married a Stipe, and Grace, who married a Dunagan, are the only daughters in the family list, so they were evidently those two sisters. Three of the ten had died by then, Louis Daniel among them.

After 1935 most of the siblings are hard to follow. A John Hulsey (1929), a Noah Hulsey (1930) and a Roy Hulsey (1931) married in McCurtain County, and a Roy Hulsey, 34, married in Montgomery County, Arkansas, in 1938. Any of them may be Oscar’s brothers, but nothing names their parents.

EXTRA.name: John C. Satterfield's brothers and sister
EXTRA.rel: 2nd great-granduncles and grandaunt (siblings of John C. Satterfield)
EXTRA.place: Butler and Allen counties, Ky.; Dakota County, Minn.; Clay Co., Ark.
EXTRA.title: Kentucky, Minnesota and back: John C.'s brothers and sister
EXTRA.hook: Their father took the family to Minnesota and brought it home again, and one brother married his brother's wife's cousin.
body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography names six children of his first marriage, to Malissa Gibson: “Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C.” It also says that “in 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky.” Malissa died in 1877, soon after the move back, and James remarried in 1878.

Sidney Rufus, born 2 September 1865 and the third son named in the sketch, stayed in Kentucky and kept the family close. He married Eliza “Ancie” Johnson, a daughter of James P. Johnson and Martha J. Clark. Martha was the older sister of Melvina (Clark) Johnson, the mother of Samantha, who married Sidney's brother John C. in 1892. So two Satterfield brothers married first cousins from the same Clark-Johnson family. Sidney died at Richardsville, Warren County, on 19 November 1949, and Ancie in 1951; both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson.

James Doiser was born in February 1867 in Allen County, the year the family left for Minnesota. He married in 1889, had five children, and went south to Arkansas; he died at Hickoria, Clay County, on 10 July 1929 and is buried at Redenbo Cemetery. The only child known to have been born in Minnesota was a daughter, A. M., on 23 July 1870. She married Calvin H. Coots in 1891 and died on 25 May 1892, only 21. Her Minnesota birth bears out the family's Minnesota years.

EXTRA.name: Artie Pearl's brothers and sister
EXTRA.rel: Great-grandmother Artie Pearl's brothers and sister
EXTRA.place: Butler County, Ky.; Hagansport, Tex.; Soper, Grant and Hugo, Okla.
EXTRA.title: Pearl's brothers and sister: two soldiers, a Riddle wedding and a death at seventeen
EXTRA.hook: John C. and Samantha Satterfield's children followed them from Kentucky to Texas to the Oklahoma side of the Red River, and most came home to be buried near their mother.
body: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield was the oldest surviving child. His World War I and World War II draft cards both give his birth as 28 December 1895 at Morgantown, Butler County, Kentucky; his headstone at Soper Cemetery says 9 January 1896, so the stone is probably the mistake. The stone is marked “TEXAS PVT. U.S. ARMY World War I,” which fits the family's move to Franklin County, Texas, about 1907. In 1925 he married Jewel Dale Weems, and they settled in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, near his mother. He died at Soper on 24 March 1952, aged 56, and lies in plot E4, the same plot as Samantha.

James Bethel was born on 12 May 1901 in Butler County and was about six when the family went to Texas. He married Alice Elizabeth Riddle, and they had seven children between 1922 and 1940; one, Charlie, died in 1940 at about ten. James died at Paris, Texas, on 7 December 1964 and was buried at Soper, near his mother.

Stella B., “little Stella” in the Hagansport household of April 1910, was born on 6 October 1907, one of the two children born after the move to Texas. She married Clifford Calvin Riddle. Whether her husband and her brother James's wife Alice were brother and sister is not known. Stella died on 25 January 1925, only 17, and was buried at Chillicothe Cemetery in Hardeman County, Texas, far from the rest of the family. No cause of death is given.

The two youngest were boys. Ira L. was born in 1905 in Kentucky, was five at Hagansport in 1910, served in World War II (his stone reads “AMRY WWII”), died in 1977 and is buried in plot B2 at Grant Cemetery, where Pearl and Charles Oscar Smith also lie. Jewel Thompson Satterfield, the last child, was born at Talco, Titus County, Texas, on 3 May 1912. He married Marie Nabors in 1929, when he was 17, had five children, and died at Hugo on 13 January 1995. He is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery in Hugo.

EXTRA.name: Mary Tinsley Shackleford's brothers and sisters
EXTRA.rel: Great-granduncles and great-grandaunts (siblings of Mary Tinsley Shackleford Moffitt)
EXTRA.place: Etowah Co., Ala.; Delta Co., Tex.; Apache and Lawton, Okla.; California
EXTRA.title: From Gadsden to Apache and California: Mamie's brothers and sisters
EXTRA.hook: John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford raised a big family that scattered from Alabama to the Pacific, and two obituaries twenty years apart count them off.
body: In June 1900 at Gilbert, Etowah County, John Shackleford, 37, and his wife Elizabeth, 28, married ten years, had five children, all living: “Balous,” 8; Myrtle, 6; May, 5, who was Mary Tinsley; Robert, 3; and Eddie, 8 months. More were born after the family moved to Texas, among them Hazel, born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County.

Balis Anthony, the eldest, was born on 5 February 1892 in Alabama and went west. He married Bertha Mae Fox, and he died in Los Angeles County on 9 January 1982, nearly ninety, and is buried at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes. Robert Yates, born at Gadsden on 25 October 1897, also ended up in California. When he died at Oroville in June 1961, aged 63, he was called a World War I veteran (his stone carries a World War II marker) and named his survivors: brothers “Bayles of Los Angeles and Ed and John of Oklahoma,” and six sisters, among them “Mamie Moffett” of Oklahoma.

Hazel stayed closest to the Red River. She married John Wesley King, who died in 1968, and she died at Paris, Texas, on 22 December 1980. Her parents were named as John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton and listed her surviving sisters, Mrs. Joe Haskell, Mrs. Beula Hutchings and Mrs. Helen Josey, all of Apache, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Eular Tillman of Lawton, and her brothers Balis of California and John S. and Edward of Apache. Three of her six pallbearers were Moffitts. Two of them, Donald and Odis, were very likely Mamie's sons and so Hazel's nephews, though no relationships are given.

Apache in Caddo County was where much of the family landed: Lizzie moved there from Dawson County, Texas, in 1933 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery. Two of the 1900 children, Myrtle and Eddie, do not appear in either obituary; they may have died young or be known by other names. Josephine, Eulah and Beulah are known only by their married names, so their birth years and places are still open.

EXTRA.name: Oscar Franklin Hulsey & Katie Cornelia (Stevenson) Hulsey
EXTRA.place: District court, Idabel, McCurtain County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: Twenty-six divorces in one day, January 1946
EXTRA.hook: Katie's divorce from Oscar went through on the day McCurtain County set a record for them.
body: After the war, the McCurtain County courthouse at Idabel was busy undoing marriages. On Saturday, 12 January 1946, the Idabel paper reported on its front page that a county record had been broken that Wednesday: District Judge George R. Childers had granted 26 divorces in a single day, one more than the previous record of 25, according to the court clerk, Buel Grinage.

The paper printed every one of them, the first name of the spouse who filed followed by the other's full name: Addie from C. L. Mahon, Lorene from Jesse Ramage, Floyd from Mary Dimmitt, and so on down a column of twenty-six names. Near the bottom, between Rosa Bell from Lonnie Lewis and John from Dorothy Keiss, is “Katie from Oscar Hulsey.”

It was the second time the marriage had ended on paper. An Arkansas divorce had already been entered in Montgomery County in September 1941, and Oscar had remarried five weeks later. Katie's Oklahoma suit had run as a notice by publication from late November to mid-December 1945, addressed “To: Oscar Hulsey.” The January list closes the file. The same front page, a column over, carried the homecoming notices of local men just out of the Army and Navy, which may explain why the judge had so much to do.
kv: 26 divorces in one day, breaking the record of 25 (court clerk Buel Grinage)
McCurtain Co. district court no. 12,652, notice by publication Nov–Dec 1945
EXTRA.note: The article names the parties only as “Katie from Oscar Hulsey,” but the 1945 notice in the same county court names Katie Hulsey as plaintiff and Oscar Hulsey as defendant, so the identification is firm. The day the record was set is the Wednesday before the 12 January issue. The link between the postwar homecomings on the same page and the number of divorces is the paper's juxtaposition, not a stated cause.

EXTRA.name: John Winfred Moffitt
EXTRA.title: Wildcat whisky: three and a half pints in Hugo, 1957
EXTRA.hook: The sheriff counted it out to the half-pint. And yes, he drank it.
body: On the morning of Thursday, 30 May 1957, The Hugo Daily News reported that Johnny Moffitt, 31, of Hugo had pleaded guilty to a disorderly-house charge before Justice of the Peace Bert Bush. He had been arrested the night before by Sheriff Ed Thornton and Constable Lonnie Wright, who said they found one quart and three half-pints of “wildcat whisky” at his home.

“Wildcat” was the old word for liquor made without a license, and it has never sounded like anything you would want to drink. He drank it anyway. The sheriff, to his credit, counted precisely: one quart plus three half-pints comes to three and a half pints, so nobody could later argue about the arithmetic. That makes the half-pints sound less like a stockpile and more like a supply.

The law was the point. Oklahoma had been officially dry since statehood in 1907 and did not repeal statewide prohibition until 1959, so in May 1957 a cupboard with the wrong bottles in it was a matter for the sheriff and the justice of the peace. Four years later a much more serious whisky case followed. This one stayed small.

EXTRA.note: Identification as the family’s John Winfred Moffitt is probable, not proved. The notice gives the name “Johnny Moffitt,” an age (31) that fits his 25 October 1925 birth, and the town of Hugo. It names no wife, parent or street address, so another Johnny Moffitt of the same age in Hugo cannot be ruled out.

EXTRA.name: William Thompson Jr.
EXTRA.place: Hugo, Choctaw County, Oklahoma
EXTRA.title: Deer tags and a five-year pin: Junior in the Hugo papers, 1961–62
EXTRA.hook: One November he lined up with the rest of Hugo for a deer tag. The next spring he got a pin from the glove factory.
body: Deer season in Oklahoma opened on a Wednesday in late November 1961, and Hugo took it seriously. On Tuesday, 21 November, The Hugo Daily News ran “Local Sportsmen Purchase Deer Tags” across the top of its front page. Tags were on sale at D. C. Patterson Hardware, Leard Hardware and Askew Service Station, and one seller, Mrs. Tom Baskin, had sold all 25 of hers by Monday. Many hunters had already moved into the woods to set up camp. The paper then printed the name and town of everyone who had bought a tag, a list that ran down several columns, from a 12-year-old to a 78-year-old. Partway down the second column is “William Thompson Jr., Hugo.”

Four months later, on 2 April 1962, a front-page photograph showed a crowd of employees of the Wells Lamont glove factory in Hugo receiving five-year service pins, standing with the assistant manager, Robert Bowen. The caption lists them by name, and among them is “Junior Thompson.” A five-year pin in April 1962 would mean he had been on the factory's payroll since about 1957, the year after his marriage license with Mary Ellen Hulsey was announced.
Neither item says much, but together they fill in an ordinary working life that the censuses skip: a young husband in Hugo with a factory job and a deer tag.

EXTRA.note: The 1962 Wells Lamont photograph is proven: the family recognizes Junior in it. The 1961 deer-tag listing gives no age or address and is probably him. The 1957 start date is inferred from the five-year pin.

EXTRA.name: Noah Smith
EXTRA.place: Greenup County, Ky.; Titus and Franklin counties, Texas
EXTRA.title: Noah Smith: Kentucky farmer, Franklin County justice of the peace, Confederate pensioner
EXTRA.hook: John B. Smith's father farmed around Mount Pleasant and Hagansport, with his son beside him through 1880.
body: In the summer of 1870 Noah Smith, 40, born in Kentucky, farmed near Mount Pleasant in Titus County, Texas, with land worth $1,200 and $200 in personal property. In the house were Mary, 16; John B., 11; and a girl, Annie L. No relationships were given in 1870, but ten years later they were.

In 1875 the southern part of Titus County became Franklin County, and in June 1880 Noah Smith, 51, was in its Precinct 2, listed as a farmer and a justice of the peace. His wife was Mary E., 25. The household was spelled out this time: John B. Smith, 20, son; Anna L., 11, and Eliza A., 8, daughters; Mary B., 5; George R., 2; and a baby boy a month old. Noah gave his father's birthplace as Maryland and his mother's as Virginia. Twenty years later John B. Smith, the 2nd great-grandfather of this family, was farming his own land in the same Precinct 2 of Franklin County.

On 5 July 1899, at about seventy, Noah applied to the State of Texas for a Confederate veteran's pension from Franklin County. In 1900 he was still on his own farm in Justice Precinct 2, now a widower, with two young daughters, Flora, 17, and Oma, 15. He died on 28 January 1906 and is buried at Smith Cemetery in Franklin County; his memorial gives his birth as 6 June 1831 in Greenup County, Kentucky.

Who John B.'s mother was is still open. Noah's wife in 1880, Mary E., was only 25, and a later death record for their daughter Flora names her mother as Mary Keith. Born about 1855, Mary Keith cannot be the mother of a son born in the late 1850s. John B.'s mother was evidently an earlier wife, and no record names her.

EXTRA.note: The 1880 census names John B. Smith as Noah's son. Identifying that John B. with the family's John B. Smith is probable: same name, same Franklin County precinct in 1880 and 1900, and a sister Annie L. carried from the 1870 household to the 1880 one. But his age does not agree: 11 in 1870 and 20 in 1880 point to a birth about 1859–60, while the family tree and the 1900 census use July 1856. Noah's own age also drifts (40 in 1870, 51 in 1880, 71 in 1900; Find a Grave says 1831), and his parents' birthplaces are Maryland and Virginia in 1880 but Kentucky in 1900. The pension file itself has not been read, so his regiment is not yet known. Ancestry family trees pair Noah with Mary P. Keith as John's parents; the records point instead to Mary Keith as a later wife.

EXTRA.name: Catherine and Hannah Moffitt
EXTRA.rel: 4th great-grandaunts (William Moffitt's daughters, sisters of Robert)
EXTRA.title: Two Moffitt sisters, two Cox grooms
EXTRA.hook: William Moffitt's daughters Catherine and Hannah married Nathan and Jacob Cox, probably brothers, at Holly Spring and Cane Creek in 1789 and 1791.
body: On 16 April 1789, at Holly Spring Meeting on the waters of Deep River, Nathan Cox, twenty-six, took as his wife Catherine Moffitt, who had turned twenty-four eleven days earlier, the daughter of William and Mary Moffitt. Two years and eight months later, on 22 December 1791, Jacob Cox, about twenty-four, married her sister Hannah at Cane Creek Meeting. The two grooms are listed together in the Cox family under Harmon and Jane Cox, so they were probably brothers, from a family that had been on Deep River so long the neighborhood was called the Cox Settlement.

Nathan and Catherine raised a family there: Jane (born 23 August 1790), Mahlon (2 March 1792), Jonathan (27 January 1795), William (22 November 1797), Mary (15 April 1800), Nathan (2 February 1809), Margaret (25 March 1812), and others between. One account prints a death for Catherine on 9 March 1792, a week after Mahlon's birth, and that cannot stand: children kept arriving through 1812, and when Catherine's mother, Mary Moffitt, made her will in 1820 she still left "Catharine Cox" the dresser and cupboard. Nathan died on 10 October 1842. A misprint of 1842 for 1792 would make the dates fit, but nothing shows it.

Hannah and Jacob had at least three children: Harmon, Mary, and a daughter Hannah (1798 to 21 January 1844), who married Charles Cox on 23 March 1820. The family's printed birth date for Hannah Moffitt, 22 December 1771, is the day and month of her wedding twenty years later and looks like a wedding date copied into the birth field; her birth itself is not recorded. Between them the two Moffitt sisters carried the family into the Cox households of Randolph County, where Moffitts and Coxes were marrying each other for three generations.
EXTRA.src: Cox family outline ("Cox Family in America" and North Carolina Quaker records), pp. 20-22 and the Harmon Cox section, Internet Archive coxfamilyoutline00buff (https://archive.org/details/coxfamilyoutline00buff), read 4 Nov 2026; will of Mary Moffitt, Randolph Co., N.C. (23 Sep 1820)

The 1792 death date for Catherine is the outline's; 1842 is a guess from the children and the 1820 will. Hannah's printed birth, 22 December 1771, equals her wedding date and is unsupported.

EXTRA.name: Charles Moffitt and Mary Cox
EXTRA.rel: Probable brother of William Moffitt (5th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.title: Which Hugh? Charles Moffitt, Mary Cox and fourteen cousins
EXTRA.hook: The 1928 Moffitt family book gives William's probable brother Charles a Cox wife and fourteen children, which raises a puzzle about two men named Hugh.
body: The family tradition counts Charles Moffitt among the brothers who came from Donegal to Philadelphia and on to Randolph County, North Carolina. His wife, in the 1928 Moffitt genealogy, was Mary Cox, and together they had nine sons and five daughters: Hugh, Margaret, Charles, Robert (born 1778), Solomon, John, Samuel, Catharine, Ruth, Isaac, Jonathan, Mary, Silas (1794) and Rebecca (1797). Even the family knew little about Mary: the tradition was that her people had come from Holland and that she had been born on shipboard on the way over. Those children were first cousins of our Robert Moffitt, and the Robert born in 1778 shares his birth year, which makes the two men easy to confuse.

The next generation can be followed in Quaker records. Hugh Moffitt, son of Charles and Mary (Cox) Moffitt, married Hannah Cox on 15 March 1798. Elizabeth Cox, born 6 July 1784, married a Charles Moffitt at Cane Creek on 14 March 1805. Margery Cox, born in 1794, married Jeremiah Moffitt, "bro. of Charles," at Whitewater, Indiana, in February 1824. And Silas, the youngest son, married Hannah Wilkinson, a granddaughter of William Moffitt, in Randolph County on 4 May 1820; the two of them took their children to Hamilton County, Indiana, and are the people the 1928 book was written for.

The puzzle is Hugh. The 1928 book says William married Mary Davis and Hugh married Hannah Davis, both daughters of Charles Davis, which makes Hugh William's brother, and the family has long said he built the mill on Richland Creek that gave the community of Moffitt its name. The Cox outline, though, has a Hugh who is Charles's son marrying Hannah Cox in 1798. They can be two men, an uncle and a nephew, both Hugh Moffitt, which would also explain why "Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt" witnessed William's will in 1796. No one knows which Hugh signed.
EXTRA.src: Frank Moffitt, Moffitt Genealogy: A Genealogical Record of Silas Moffitt and Hannah Wilkinson Moffitt (1928), pp. 3-4, Internet Archive moffittgenealogy00moff (https://archive.org/details/moffittgenealogy00moff); Cox family outline, Internet Archive coxfamilyoutline00buff (https://archive.org/details/coxfamilyoutline00buff), both read 4 Nov 2026; will of William Moffitt (1796)

EXTRA.name: Holly Spring Meeting
EXTRA.rel: Quaker meeting where William Moffitt's daughter married
EXTRA.title: Holly Spring and the Cox Settlement
EXTRA.hook: The Quaker meeting on Deep River where William Moffitt's daughter married was so full of Coxes that it was first called the Cox Settlement.
body: Friends living on the waters of Deep River asked Cane Creek Meeting in the second month of 1758 for leave to hold a meeting every First-day, and the request was granted. The old stone graveyard on Cox land holds some two hundred pioneers, the first of them, tradition says, two Indians, and a Cane Creek minute of 1765 mentions a Meeting of Indulgence on Mill Creek in Cox's settlement. The name Holly Spring first appears in the minutes of the eighth month of 1769, when Christopher Hussey and Joseph Comer were appointed overseers. In 1787 Richard Caswell deeded fifty acres to Benjamin Cox for the use of the Quakers at a place named for the holly trees over a nearby spring. The first meetinghouse was of logs; a frame house went up about 1830 and a new one in 1890.

The oldest certificate of membership was brought down from Pennsylvania by William Cox in 1752 and had to wait at Cane Creek until Holly Spring was established. The community was first known as the Cox Settlement because of the abundance of Cox families, and the other early names were Moffitt, Barker, Hadley, Comer, Hinshaw, Kemp, Davis and Allen. William Moffitt's daughter Catherine married Nathan Cox there in 1789. A Preparative Meeting was set up in 1790, and an independent Monthly Meeting in 1818 with Robert Moffitt as clerk; the history does not say which Robert, and one candidate is the Robert born in 1778 to Charles Moffitt and Mary Cox, who would have grown up in this very settlement.

The meeting policed its members closely: committees labored with Friends who had slipped in dress and conduct, and disowned those who would not change. By 1832 the great western migration had set in, and Holly Spring never again was the stronghold it had been. The Civil War hurt it worse, since men unwilling to bear arms were severely punished and Friends in the North sent help. That is the world Nathan Moffitt left in the 1840s.
EXTRA.src: Southern Quarterly Meeting of Friends, Historical Sketches of Southern Quarterly Meeting and Its Constituent Monthly Meetings (North Carolina Yearly Meeting, 1966), pp. 15-17, Internet Archive southernquarterl00nort (https://archive.org/details/southernquarterl00nort), read 4 Nov 2026; Cox family outline (Holly Springs marriage, 16 Apr 1789)

EXTRA.name: Silver City, Montgomery County
EXTRA.rel: Place where B. F. Hulsey (probable 3rd great-grandfather) was working in 1880
EXTRA.place: Center Township and Silver City, Montgomery County, Arkansas
EXTRA.title: Silver City, 1880: the boom B. F. Hulsey walked into
EXTRA.hook: The summer B. F. Hulsey gave his work as miner, a crossroads on Gap Creek held more than a thousand people hunting silver, and within two years it was nearly empty.

imgs.cap: Joseph “Diamond Jo” Reynolds, the riverboat owner and railroad builder who held the Minnesota mine at Silver City. A portrait of a mine owner, not of the family.
imgs.credit: University of Chicago Biographical Sketches, vol. 1 (1922), p. 224, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain

body: For a few years around 1880 the crossroads called Silver City, in the eastern end of Montgomery County, was the most crowded place in the Ouachita hills. Men had been picking at lead and silver near Gap Creek since before 1840, but it took the news of the mid-1870s to bring the crowd. Miners pushed out of the Colorado and California camps drifted in, the crossroads got its name in 1876, and after 1878 they came faster. By 1880 Silver City was said to hold more than a thousand people, with hundreds of claims and prospects scattered within a few miles of it.

Some of those claims belonged to men with far deeper pockets than a Georgia-born miner. Joseph “Diamond Jo” Reynolds, the riverboat magnate who built the Hot Springs Railroad, owned the Minnesota mine. A Joplin smelter owner, Elliott R. Moffet, who had been Joplin’s first mayor, worked the Walnut. About three dozen mines actually shipped ore and made the newspapers. The rest were holes in a hillside and a hope.

In June 1880 B. F. Hulsey, 32, was a miner in Center Township, whose center sits about six-tenths of a mile from Silver. His wife Sarah G., 30, born in Arkansas, was keeping house, and with them were Margaret, six, George W., four, and Charles F., five months old. Two other men on the same page also called themselves miners. Whether Hulsey held a claim of his own, dug for wages or hauled ore is not known, and nothing names a mine. But a man who wrote “miner” in that township that summer was working in the boom, at the busiest moment it ever had.

It did not last. By the end of 1882 every mine had closed. A gold rush at Bear City, in Garland County, gave Silver City a brief second wind in 1888, until the Bear hills turned out to be barren and the rush was blamed on crooked assayers. Silver City settled back to the size it had been before the boom and stayed that way into the 1900s.

George was not yet seven when the mines closed. A Benjamin F. Hulsey of about the right age turns up in Garland County, with a marriage license in 1893 and households there in 1900 and 1910, which is the county where the next boom had been, but no record ties that man to this household, and the boom itself ties nothing. All the 1880 page can honestly say is that the family’s earliest known home in the Ouachitas sat next to a silver camp, in the one season when the camp was full.

EXTRA.name: Benajah Nordyke
EXTRA.rel: Brother of Aden Nordyke (probable 6th great-grandfather); son of Abraham and Mary (Rogers) Nordyke
EXTRA.place: Wilkes County, Georgia, 1779–1782; Lincoln County, Kentucky, 1852
EXTRA.title: Benajah Nordyke and Captain Dunn’s company
EXTRA.hook: A Quaker boy in the Georgia backcountry went off with the rebels, and seventy years later, at 87, he asked for a pension because he thought a man ought to work while he could.

imgs.cap: Kettle Creek battlefield, Wilkes County, Georgia, where Benajah Nordyke said he fought in February 1779 (photographed 2010). Photo: Chris Crookston, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
imgs.credit: Chris Crookston, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

body: Abraham and Mary Nordyke took their Burlington County Quaker household south in the 1770s, and the family’s own history says they spent eight years in Georgia. It remembers two things from those years: little Micajah, four, hiding all night in the woods when an Indian invasion was feared, and Aden, the oldest, being shot in the arm in an Indian attack. It says nothing at all about the war. The war was there anyway.

The Quaker settlement of Wrightsborough in Wilkes County, founded in 1768 by Joseph Maddock, was no place to sit out a rebellion. Its leaders leaned toward the Crown, and its young men leaned the other way. Twenty members of the meeting were dealt with for military activity during the Revolution and fifteen were disowned. One of them, Josiah Dunn, had been put out of the meeting in 1775 and went on to lead rebel partisans, recruiting young men from among the Wrightsborough Friends he had left.

Benajah Nordyke was apparently one of those boys. In November 1852, at 87, he stood before a magistrate in Rockcastle County, Kentucky, and swore that he had been a volunteer soldier in Wilkes County, Georgia, from 1779 to 1782, about eighteen months in all. He named Captain Dunn among his officers, and Colonel Few’s regiment; he had been at Kettle Creek, and at the siege of Augusta in 1781, when the British commander Colonel Brown was shut up in the town, and he had served as drum major. Captain Josiah Dunn, he said, was killed at Kettle Creek. Eighty-seven in 1852 makes him about fourteen in 1779.

He had waited a long time to ask. He said he had never applied because he thought every man ought to work for his living while he could, and that freedom had been pay enough; now he was old, and had begun to lose his memory, and could find no living comrade to vouch for him. A minister who had known him fifty years, and two others, signed for his good name. The file number suggests the claim was not allowed.

That he was Abraham’s son is probable, not proven. The Quaker habit of recording the hour of birth gave the family history “Benajah at 9:00 P.M.” between Aden (1762) and Micajah (1771), the name is rare, the age fits that gap, and his soldiering was done in Georgia in the years the Nordykes were there. The pension file does not name his parents. If he is the boy, then the Nordykes who are remembered for the long walk to Ohio had a fighting son among them first.

quotes.t: Freedom was sufficient pay for him while he could work
quotes.c: Benajah Nordyke, declaration, Rockcastle Co., Ky., 15 Nov 1852 (pension file R7691, as transcribed by Will Graves)

EXTRA.note: Evidence: probable. Identity rests on the name, the age gap in the family’s birth-hour list, and the Georgia years of Abraham’s household, not on a document that names Benajah’s father. The family history places the Nordykes in Georgia for eight years before 1788 without naming a meeting; Wrightsborough is the likely Quaker settlement, not a stated one. The file’s Kettle Creek may be the 14 Feb 1779 battle or a later fight on the creek: the pension transcriber and Robert S. Davis, Jr. disagree about Dunn’s death, and neither is verified here. R-numbered pension files are typically rejected or unaccepted claims. Verify the original images (see paid queue).

EXTRA.name: Stephen Henry Nordyke
EXTRA.rel: The Nordyke family legend about Henry Nordyke (proposed 8th great-grandfather)
EXTRA.place: Holland (legend); Burlington County, New Jersey (records)
EXTRA.title: Stephen Henry Nordyke and the Czar’s mill
EXTRA.hook: A family story sends the first Nordyke to Holland to teach Peter the Great to grind grain. The New Jersey papers find a young man named Henry in debt and in love in 1731.

imgs.cap: Peter the Great, painted by Godfrey Kneller in 1698, the year after the Dutch visit of the family legend. Royal Collection, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
imgs.credit: Royal Collection (RCIN 405645), Wikimedia Commons, public domain

body: The Nordykes tell a good one. When Marmon Motor Car Company’s history was printed in an Indianapolis trade paper in 1927, it opened with the family: the Nordykes, it said, were descended from Stephen Henry Nordyke, who in 1697 taught Peter the Great the art of grinding grist when the Czar traveled to Holland to learn Western ways. His three sons, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, then went to Pennsylvania. The family’s 1960 genealogy has a fuller version, printed earlier in an 1895 Indiana biographical encyclopedia: Peter fell in love with a Dutch girl, a morganatic marriage followed, and the son was Stephen Henry, who took the girl’s name. Nordyke, it adds, would be “north dike.”

It is exactly the sort of story a family of mill builders would keep. The Nordyke and Marmon works in Indianapolis made flour-mill machinery before it made the Wasp that won the first Indianapolis 500, and the first Nordyke at the Czar’s mill gave the whole business a pedigree.

The papers are plainer. Peter was in the Dutch Republic from mid-August 1697 to January 1698, and a man who could teach a monarch his trade that autumn was no boy; he would have been far past fifty when Rebecca Perkins married a Henry Nordike at Willingboro, New Jersey, in 1731/2. The New Jersey wills have a Henry Nordike in Burlington County owing and being owed in his father-in-law’s estate, and signing as a witness to Rebecca’s brother’s will, which is a young householder’s paper trail, not a courtier’s. The family trees that call him Stephen Henry took the first name from the legend; none of the New Jersey papers has it.

What the legend does carry correctly are the sons’ names. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are the names the family trees give to Henry and Rebecca’s sons, and Abraham’s birth about 1736 and his 1761 marriage to Mary Rogers are what make him our ancestor. The sons did not start in Holland. The family appears to have kept the right children and put them in a more romantic doorway.

Where Henry came from is not known. There were Dutch families with similar names around the Raritan, in Piscataway, whose Van Nortwick name could easily shorten, and a Burlington County widow’s will of 1766 leaves five shillings to “Hannah Nordike,” so the name was in use there. That is a guess, not a link.

quotes.t: taught Peter the Great the art of grinding grist
quotes.c: Automotive Daily News, 13 April 1927, history of the Marmon Motor Car Company

EXTRA.name: Lizzie and Molsey Pisachubbi: two applications at the Indian Office, 1914-1915
EXTRA.rel: Lizzie: 2nd great-grandmother; Molsey: 3rd great-grandmother (identification of the 1914 entry is probable)
EXTRA.title: A full-blood woman's land and the long road to Washington, 1914–1915
EXTRA.hook: Two Austin women from Choctaw County each asked Washington to lift the restrictions on their allotments: Molsey in July 1914, Lizzie in July 1915. Both were answered within days of reaching the capital, but each waited months for the paperwork to get there.
body: A full-blood Choctaw's allotment was not hers to sell. Congress had settled that in 1908: land of Indians with less than half Choctaw blood came free of restrictions, land of those with half to three-quarters blood lost its restriction except for the homestead, and everyone else, full-bloods above all, stayed under the Secretary of the Interior's eye until he chose to lift it, wholly or in part. The Assistant Commissioner of Indian Affairs told a House committee in 1916 that about 26,800 of the 101,500 citizens of the Five Civilized Tribes were full-bloods, and that some 33,000 people were still restricted. For a woman like Lizzie Pisachubbee, the way out of those restrictions began with a written application and ended at a desk in Washington.

Lizzie was a full-blood, enrolled at Fowlerville at seven in 1899 as the daughter of Legion and Molsey Austin, and by 1915 she was about 23, married to Robert Pisachubbe, and living on a farm near Speer. On 17 July 1915 her application was made out. It went first to the Superintendent for the Five Civilized Tribes at Muskogee, who sat on it for eleven weeks before forwarding it on 2 October. It reached the Indian Office on 5 October, was acted on on 8 October, and went back to the superintendent on 9 October: four days in Washington after eleven weeks at Muskogee. The printed list of cases does not say whether the answer was yes or no, and nothing else turned up says what it was.

The same list has the older woman's case a year earlier. "Molsey Pisachubbi, née Austin" applied on 22 July 1914; the superintendent forwarded the papers on 14 January 1915, the Indian Office received them on 18 January and decided on 23 January, and they went back on 25 January. The name is probably Lizzie's mother, who had been Molsey Austin in 1899 and appears with the Pisachubbi name in this one line. The "née Austin" is a puzzle, since Austin was her husband Legion's name and not her own; the clerk may simply have written what he found on the card. She died in 1924. If she did marry a Pisachubbi after Legion's death, the papers have not yet turned up.

What did a lifted restriction mean for a household like this one? It meant that the land could be sold, mortgaged or lost for taxes, and the same Assistant Commissioner told the committee that an estimated nine out of ten Choctaws, Chickasaws, Creeks, Cherokees and Seminoles freed by Congress were by then landless. Some families wanted the freedom, to settle debts, to buy equipment, or to leave a farm too poor to live on. The land that these women owned stayed in the family in the end. In 1920 Lizzie and Robert were farming their own place in Jeter Township, and when Robert's mother Eunice died in 1927 her 159 acres still needed a county judge's approval before they could be sold.

quotes.t: It is estimated that 90 per cent of the enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes who had their restrictions removed by legislation are to-day without any lands whatever.
quotes.c: Assistant Commissioner of Indian Affairs, testimony, House Committee on Indian Affairs hearings on H.R. 108 (1916), p. 27

EXTRA.name: The Doaksville Trading Company and the move to Fort Towson
EXTRA.rel: Place where the Tims and Thompson families traded and got their mail
EXTRA.title: The year Doaksville's store moved to the railroad, 1903
EXTRA.hook: When the railroad came through in 1903, the first store of the new town of Fort Towson was stocked by the Doaksville Trading Company, and the older village that the Tims family had known for seventy years began to empty.
body: For the Tims and Thompson families, Doaksville was where you bought what you could not raise. Joel Thompson remembered that his people did "all of our trading" there, and the same crossroads had been V. B. Tims's stand in the 1830s and 1840s, in front of the old rock jail. The name outlived the stand by a long time. It was still the family's post office on their enrollment papers of 1899.

In 1903 a railroad was being built through that part of the Choctaw Nation, and a new town was laid out beside the line, not far from the ruins of the old fort that gave Fort Towson its name. A history of Oklahoma printed in 1916 says the new town "was established in 1903," and that the first store in it was built and stocked by the Doaksville Trading Company, which had grown into a substantial business at Doaksville. Other merchants followed from the older place, "the result being that within a comparatively short time Doaksville became little more than a memory." The post office followed the stores: on 12 June 1903 the Doaksville office took back the name Fort Towson, and the Thompsons, who had been writing Doaksville on their papers for years, found themselves at Fort Towson on a pencil note of 1905 and, after August 1904, at Corinne over the mountain.

The man who bought the old company's stock was William Ward Wilson, called Billy, a cattleman who had herded on the very ground where the new town went up, with his brother. By 1915 the Wilsons and a partner controlled the First National Bank of Fort Towson, and Billy Wilson, not yet sixty in 1916, could remember deer in herds of forty or fifty within a few hundred yards of the abandoned army post. That is how recent the old frontier was. Joseph Thompson's boyhood, Betsy Tims's school days and the old trader's grandchildren had all come out of it, and by 1916 a banker could talk about them as the people who had known the country when it was wild.

Judge Edward Tims, the old trader's son, had been Doaksville's postmaster from 1887, and the log house that may have been his father's stand was still known as the family's in 1940, when a newspaper suggested making it a museum. Doaksville itself dwindled to a cemetery on a hill.

quotes.t: The Town of Fort Towson is new and vital. It was established in 1903, at the time when a line of railroad was in process of construction through this section.
quotes.c: Thoburn, Standard History of Oklahoma (1916), vol. 5, p. 1814, sketch of William W. Wilson
